  String? description,
  GroupUpdate? canMentionGroup,
  // … other group-valued settings …
}) {
  // …
}
```

and the example caller above would look like:

```dart
    onSave: (GroupValue initialValue, GroupValue newValue) {
      try {
        await updateUserGroup(store.connection, {
          userGroupId: widget.userGroupId,
          canMentionGroup: GroupUpdate(old: initialValue, new: newValue),

                                The ID of the video call provider.
```

Can a `realm op: update` event exist with, e.g., a `property: 'realm_available_video_chat_providers'` and a `value` that's an object like the one described there (IOW not a `string | boolean | integer`)?

## Shared OpenAPI descriptions

*2021-11-18 to 2021-11-23 · 29 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/Shared.20OpenAPI.20descriptions/with/1283750)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-18 18:08 UTC

This thread could go in #**documentation**, but I think this aspect of the API documentation is something worth a discussion that gets attention from users of the documentation.

One of the things that is unhappy about our OpenAPI file is that there is a great deal of duplication of the descriptions of parameters.  E.g. for settings, we have essentially the same set of settings available for /api/update-settings as on /api/update-realm-user-settings-defaults, since the latter is the endpoint for adjusting the defaults of the former for new users.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-18 18:09 UTC

#20246 is a project that would deduplicate those descriptions in the OpenAPI source file; if we could integrate it in a happy way, that'd be pretty great: the diffstat suggests it net removes 500 lines of duplicated content in our 15K line OpenAPI definitions file.  (And if we could figure out good techniques of this form, we could repeat that sort of process several times).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-18 18:13 UTC

The problem is that the OpenAPI format doesn't have a clean way to support sharing 90% of the description for an object, while having some parts only display in one or the other place.  So, for example, the /api/update-settings has as its description of the `twenty_four_hour_time parameter:

```
Whether time should be displayed in 24-hour notation.

Changes: Before Zulip 5.0 (feature level 80), this setting was managed by the PATCH /settings/display endpoint.
```

That **Changes** line is correct for this endpoint, but not for /api/update-realm-user-settings-defaults, which was only introduced in feature level 96.  And it's kinda harmful for it to be there, because actually the /settings/display endpoint never had anything to do with the /api/update-realm-user-settings-defaults setting, which is about the defaults for new user accounts, not about your account.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-18 18:13 UTC

So while I'd really like to integrate this sort of deduplication, it's unacceptable to remove those Changes entries and also enough fields have Changes entries that it's annoying for them be duplicated in multiple places.

(E.g. our `User` objects all have a complex set of different changes entries because we did a project 1-2 years ago of making them all the same, but we still need to document when those changes happened at different times for each endpoint)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-18 18:15 UTC

For that specific instance, @Lauryn Menard has a reasonable workaround, which is to have a list of which settings were managed by that old endpoint detailed in a single **Changes** entry at the top of the /api/update-settings description, rather than detailing it in the description of each field.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-18 18:15 UTC

But I don't like that as a general approach for every change -- it's clearly useful to be able to only read the description of the field itself to see its history, and not have to scroll to the top of the page and check a second place.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-18 18:20 UTC

I think there's a couple reasonable paths forward here:
* We could abandon hopes of deduplicating these content, or go with a single-field based deduplication strategy that might allow one to to at least not have duplicates for both of the fields.  The current arrangement results in a lot of annoying searching for duplicates to update (often with different indentation) when improving the text of descriptions, which makes improvements feel more costly than it should, but it's an option.
* We could try to just push through with the strategy taken in #20246.
* We could try to find some sort of OpenAPI-supported mechanism for e.g. appending something to the description of a field -- we've tried asking upstream but haven't gotten a response yet.
* We could define in our Markdown extension for rendering the API documentation a syntax for noting something that only applies to a single endpoint.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-18 18:26 UTC

Exploring the Markdown extension approach, I'm imagining that we could a syntax with the goals of
* Feeling convenient for developers to read and program with while working on the API docs.
* Being human-intelligible if you see it in output from a third-party OpenAPI tool.
* Being nicely rendered in our official documentation.

To throw out a direction that we could play with, one could imagine putting this in your description for a field:

```
**Changes(/api/update-settings): Before Zulip 5.0 (feature level 80), this setting was managed by the PATCH /settings/display endpoint.**
```

And that would produce a sentence that only appears on the /api/update-settings endpoint's description, perhaps with some nice linkification (we could play with whether we put 5.0/80 in the data so that we can link to that part of the API changelog automatically, which has been a thing I've wanted to do but never felt was worth editing every reference to feature levels in the docs for).  And I think if you saw that bold string in some third-party OpenAPI tool, you'd probably be able to figure out this is saying the change only applies to that endpoint.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-18 18:29 UTC

Problems with that specific syntax:
* It's somewhat parser-friendly as long as we don't use bold in the descriptions, which is currently a pattern but feels somewhat risky.
* It seems like it might feel pretty messy in situations where we want to have a multi-paragraph changes entry or otherwise have a block.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-18 18:30 UTC

That said, the problem with using an HTML tag like a `<div class="api-change-entry" data-endpoint="update-settings">` for this is that the metadata for which endpoint it applies to would likely be invisible when processed by a non-Zulip OpenAPI tool that renders Markdown.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-18 18:32 UTC

(I guess another note about an ideal syntax/design is that we may want to be able to note details that aren't changes for an individual endpoint's copy of some detail, e.g. advice about how to use an X that's only relevant for this endpoint)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-18 18:32 UTC

Thoughts?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-18 18:55 UTC

These field descriptions also get copied into struct field doc-comments in the generated bindings and used in editor typeahead. This is another reason to make an effort to use them as intended: they’re for describing a data model, not for annotating the documentation for specific operations you might perform on the data.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-18 19:29 UTC

Sure.  Certainly the openapi-generator model would like us to have a shared type for objects that are the same since that will help it generate reasonably named classes for return types (etc.).  

I think that argues for an approach like the one that I describe with the Markdown extension: Having shared objects containing text that might be overly verbose (Mentioning the change history for all the endpoints using that object when it is different) that we can potentially do fancier things with in our official web documentation.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-18 19:31 UTC

To some extent we'll get to delete a lot of these variations over time -- part of the background here is that last year we did a purge of places where the API disagreed about the shape of the same object, and perhaps eventually we'll feel it's OK to delete change history older than 2 years or whatever.  But in the meantime, I think this class of approach is a way to move forward and unify the descriptions without making the documentation wrong or confusing.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-18 19:41 UTC

I thought I was arguing *against* making up a nonstandard Markdown extension…

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-18 19:46 UTC

You're arguing against having something nonstandard that isn't human-readable.  As an example, suppose we added a linkifier that translates `Zulip 5.0 (feature level 15)` into a link to the relevant part of the API changelog with the same label -- there's no cost to folks using openapi-generator, and it results our documentation being a nicer experience -- from that standpoint, it's the same thing as linkifying a URL that might appear in the documentation.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-18 19:47 UTC

(And it's not like we could readily use a link with a relative URL and have that accomplish anything for your local editor)

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-20 03:16 UTC

I'd love to have these descriptions deduplicated, for the reasons Tim describes.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-20 03:19 UTC

I think the strategy of adding a Markdown extension could work. We'd need to be mindful to have it come out as something readable when interpreted as plain Markdown, so that it works properly in other contexts as Anders pointed out.

It'd also be subject to this kind of problem:
> * It's somewhat parser-friendly as long as we don't use bold in the descriptions, which is currently a pattern but feels somewhat risky. * It seems like it might feel pretty messy in situations where we want to have a multi-paragraph changes entry or otherwise have a block.
and I think some amount of that is fundamental to this strategy.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-20 03:21 UTC

Here's an alternate strategy that I think could also work:
* Have the OpenAPI YAML file no longer be our source file for these docs, but instead be generated from some other form that we maintain as the source.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-20 03:22 UTC

Then the descriptions that actually make it to OpenAPI can be perfectly standard Markdown (or whatever variation OpenAPI expects, if it does), and we'd arrange for them to be different between the different copies as appropriate.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-20 03:28 UTC

That leaves open a wide design space for what that source form would look like. Probably it'd look something like:
* a YAML file that's a lot like the `openapi.yaml` we'll generate;
* a little script that parses the YAML, manipulates the result some, and then serializes YAML back out.

Some of the manipulations we want to make could even be hardcoded in the script, if we find that convenient.

One version could be that we make up a new key that goes alongside a description, and describes a change. Then the script looks for that key, interprets it by modifying the description as appropriate, and leaves that key out of the generated result.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-20 03:30 UTC

In fact now that I've thought through to that, I think something like this:
> One version could be that we make up a new key that goes alongside a description, and describes a change. Then the script looks for that key, interprets it by modifying the description as appropriate, and leaves that key out of the generated result.

probably ends up having much of the same advantages as a Markdown extension, but cleaner.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-22 04:44 UTC

Yeah, I think I proposed a `zulip.yaml.source` model where we do some preprocessing as a potential solution to other problems (I think maybe the use of relative /help/ links) and don't recall getting feedback on that model.  

Though Markdown as a language isn't designed to support automated Markdown => Markdown rewriting in a clean fashion; so if we went that route we might need to have the generated `openapi.yaml` file have HTML-format descriptions.  So we could do macros with this, but it might not actually be a good solution for the /help/ links problem.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-22 04:44 UTC

So I'm not convinced that for this particular problem, a `zulip.yaml.source` model would be a good solution

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-22 18:37 UTC

Relative /help/ links seem like a different problem.

For the problem of shared descriptions: it's true that Markdown isn't designed to cleanly support automated rewriting. But it's also not designed to support clean syntax extensions. The kind of rewriting we'd need to do to implement "Changes" sections is pretty small, and I think is better suited to come out cleanly than a syntax extension to mark those sections in a single Markdown source.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-22 18:42 UTC

That's in addition to the advantage that it'd mean that when you're looking at the description in some other environment, like an IDE when you're working with a generated binding, a "Changes" section that doesn't actually apply to the thing you're looking at would simply not be present.

Whereas with a solution like `**Changes(/api/update-settings): …**`, the best case would be that the reader eventually figures out that the `(/api/update-settings)` or whatever means the paragraph only applies to that endpoint, and is able to work out whether that means the thing they're looking at or something else. Better than simply having the paragraph there with no such indication, but it's going to be confusing.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-23 00:07 UTC

I guess another direction would be for the syntax to be something that's more like a block:
```
~~~ only(/api/update-settings)

~~~
```

though the problem is that doing something Markdown-like for the block will make it invisible in a thing that renders Markdown, and a block definition that isn't Markdown-block-like feels weirder to parse.  I kinda like that more than the `Changes` inline syntax described above, though.


## never expiring invitations.

*2021-12-02 to 2021-12-03 · 13 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/never.20expiring.20invitations.2E/with/1290114)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2021-12-02 19:14 UTC

#20410 adds support for creating invitations that never expire. The database level value of `expiry_date` field is `None`.

But we need to decide what we should use for API-level value of a variable like `invite_expires_in_days`. As of now we use `-1` as the API level value similar to what we do for message retention setting. Other option is that we can use a string like `never`. Thoughts?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-02 19:17 UTC

I think we have generally been using strings like "never" for this sort of thing.  The downside with using a number like `-1`, especially for a thing like this which is structurally a number of days, is that naive code will likely end up doing math with `-1` that doesn't make any sense.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-02 19:17 UTC

So it's better to use something with a type that's conceptually a `Union[str, int]` to help protect folks working with the API from that sort of error.

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-02 19:51 UTC

I agree with those comments.

The other reasonable value to use here would be `null`. That aligns with the name: there is no number of days in which the invite expires.

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-02 19:51 UTC

(And that's the direct translation of Python `None` when you serialize it to JSON.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-02 20:09 UTC

We generally use `null` when sending things from `server=client`.  We have been avoiding that for `client=>server` API endpoints, because our request-processing framework uses `null` for "no value sent".

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-02 20:10 UTC

Which makes for nice Python code for checking which parameters the user asked to change, but doesn't provide a natural way to encode "The client sent an explicit `null` value".

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-02 20:11 UTC

We could potentially change that by just having some special value for that purpose, which could even be a parameter-specific value like "never" or a special ClientSentNull class or whatever -- it's a problem where the messy code it would create would be entirely in the server codebase, not the API or clients.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-02 20:12 UTC

I think ultimately that would lead to a cleaner system.  I would be OK with trying to prototype that for this parameter and see if we like how that looks; and then if we like that, convert the ~3 existing organization/stream settings using the integer-or-string system to use the `null` model.

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-02 20:14 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> Which makes for nice Python code for checking which parameters the user asked to change, but doesn't provide a natural way to encode "The client sent an explicit `null` value".

Hmm, I see.

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-02 20:15 UTC

Cool, that sounds like a good plan.

**Sahil Batra** · 2021-12-03 14:32 UTC

To be more clear, for this particular case of invites, clients always send `invite_expires_in_days` values, it is never the case of "no value sent from clients". But instead there are functions in the server code like `filter_to_valid_prereg_users`, `do_send_confirmation_email`, `create_confirmation_link`where there can be cases when no value is sent for the variable storing number of days after which the invite will expire.

We can use `None` as value for the never expiring invites and then use a class like `NoValueSent` as value when no value is sent for the particular argument as Tim suggested. Will prototype this.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-03 22:17 UTC

Yeah, the context where `None` is ambiguous is more in our settings endpoints, like `message_retention_days`.

*2021-12-05 to 2022-01-27 · 29 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/realm.20user.20default.20settings.20object/with/1291980)*

## email address visibility

*2021-12-11 to 2023-02-07 · 91 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/email.20address.20visibility/with/1296131)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-11 01:33 UTC

I just posted an updated proposed technical design for how `email_address_visibility` will work following our migration to having it be a personal setting: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/20102#issuecomment-991401555

The intent is to replace the current fairly confusing API model:
* User objects always contain a `.email` field, which is `EMAIL_ADDRESS_VISIBILITY_EVERYONE` equals / `.delivery_email`, and otherwise is a fake value of the form `user{user_id}@domain`.
* User objects contain a `.delivery_email` field for organization administrators only if `EMAIL_ADDRESS_VISIBILITY_ADMINS`.

The biggest problem with this model is that a client cannot readily determine whether the `email` field it has is correct, other than by checking its own role, which won't be correct once individual users can configure their email address visibility.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-11 01:37 UTC

The part that I think is clear is that we should change the model for `delivery_email` to be as follows:
* User objects contain a `delivery_email` field always.  Its value is a real email address if the current user has permission to see the target user's email address; otherwise it is `null`. Additionally, events are sent whenever things change (role changes, `email_address_visibility` setting changes, or email address changes), setting `delivery_email` to either `null` or the email address as appropriate.

I think with that model, a correct/modern client should never look at the `.email` field; it should just always look at `.delivery_email`.  (Since it's internal code only uses IDs to reference users).  And it can display the email address or a *(Email not available)* type string (or nothing) as appropriate based solely on `.delivery_email`.  I imagine we'd work towards deleting the `.email` field and then eventually renaming `.delivery_email` to `.email`, if we can.  We might even be able to be clever and do a single client-side migration, to basically have the client assume a `.email` field is a renamed `.delivery_email` field at feature level >=N+1, where N is the feature level for the migration for the new `delivery_email` semantics, so that we don't need to make any further client changes to do the final rename of the `email` field down the line.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-11 01:39 UTC

The big question is what to do with the `email` field on user objects. It seems possible that existing clients like the mobile apps may rely on that value being a real email address in organizations with the current `EMAIL_ADDRESS_VISIBILITY_EVERYONE` setting. So I think the simplest model would be to preserve its high-level semantics, which with the new `delivery_email`  semantics would become:
* `user.email = user.delivery_email` when `user.deliver_email !== null`, otherwise a fake email address.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-11 01:41 UTC

I believe that design would allow legacy/existing clients that don't know anything about `delivery_email` to continue working as-is, with no real downside.  And I think that's preferable to e.g. making `user.email` always a fake email address for such clients.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-11 01:42 UTC

So the event you'd get when you lost access to a user's email address would be one that sets `delivery_email=null, email={fake_email}` (or maybe it'd be two events?  Haven't thought about that detail yet).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-11 01:43 UTC

@*mobile* @Neil Pilgrim (neiljp) for attention on this thread;  @Sahil Batra and I are hoping to finish this API change before I go on vacation in about a week.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-11 01:45 UTC

Specifically the design describes here differs from the implementation in #20102 in that the PR attempts to have `delivery_email` not appear at all, rather than being `null`, when email address data isn't available to the user; I think that is probably a legacy decision that we don't want to stick with.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-09 19:09 UTC

I skimmed the mobile codebase and web codebase and there's basically 3 parameters that define the behavior of the presence system. Here's a proposal with some specific ideas for names:
* `server_presence_ping_interval_seconds`. The heartbeat frequency, called `ACTIVE_PING_INTERVAL_MS` on web: 50 seconds on web, 60s on mobile (source: `src/presence/PresenceHeartbeat.js`). This is how often clients do the API request that reports their own presence state, returning the presence state of other users in the realm.
* `server_presence_offline_threshhold_seconds`. The time that a "last active/connected" timestamp can be stale before the client marks the user as offline. Logically, should always be somewhat greater than twice the  MAX(client values for `ACTIVE_PING_INTERVAL_MS`), since data being displayed can be up to 2 pings stale plus any network latency, assuming no errors. Probably we'll want to move that to 3 to account for the possibility of one of the requests failing with a transient error.
* `server_presence_idle_timeout_seconds`. Currently hardcoded in the web app as `DEFAULT_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS = 5 minutes`. This is how long after the last time the user focused the Zulip window (in the web app) the browser should assume that the user is offline. I'm not sure this one is coherent for the mobile apps given the different interaction model, so possibly this should just live as a hardcoded value in the web app if we're not sure.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-06-08 19:14 UTC

> Hmm, what confuses me on this one - if there is enough traffic to get the presence queue backlogged, doesn't that also imply that doing immediate presence writes while processing requests would go pretty badly?

The queue processor for presence is a single-threaded queue worker, so making it run immediately would eliminate the possibility of it backlogging as long as the server isn't overloaded in total. 

The reason we originally did that design back in ~2013 was that we were really concerned with limiting the ability of presence write load to take down the server's availability for functionality that's more important like fetching messages. I'm pretty sure an important part of the motivation for that queue is that we used to have a presence cache, which we'd update every time we got a presence request for a given realm, and we didn't want to be doing several of those in parallel for a high traffic realm, as that'd generate cubic total work. We removed the cache a few years ago and just directly query the database; the queries should be really cheap on an index, especially with the new data model.

I think in any case the years of experience we have with the presence system since when we removed the cache and hardly ever seeing it backlog for a reason that isn't "general RabbitMQ outage" certainly suggest the failure modes we were worried about at the time aren't actually realistic.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-12-30 20:48 UTC

I definitely agree the client should just store data in a map from user IDs.

The reason we would potentially want the API to send data slightly older than the date of the last presence request is races. In particular, a presence request from a client that says "User X is active as of time T" might be fully processed as of time `T + t`, and so a different client that does a simultaneous fetch that queries the database at time `T + t/2` would potentially never 

So I think we need an (ideally entirely internal to the server implementation) bit of logic send data on all other clients with a timestamp newer than `data_since_time - max_race_duration`, where `max_race_duration` is some internal detail of the server implementation that represents the maximum possible delay between a presence request being received and being fully processed.

We can reason about how to calculate that delay more precisely later, but it seems likely that just hardcoding 5 minutes would be overkill for the issue (at least if we get rid of the `user_presence` queue) and have little actual performance cost -- the set of users active in the last 5 minutes is likely to be pretty similar in size to those active in the last minute.

**Greg Price** · 2024-01-02 19:47 UTC

Hmm, I see.

This feels like a problem that we should be able to solve exactly, without worrying about whether a particular length of time is a reliable upper bound on races and without duplicating work. The key is to have the timestamp, or cursor index, that the polling request starts from be something that's present internally in the sequence of records being returned, rather than an external wall-clock time.

For example, the main events queue solves this problem by having the cursor be an event sequence number.

**Greg Price** · 2024-01-02 19:47 UTC

Here, I think one solution would be for the client to ask about presence data newer than the latest presence item it received last time, instead of newer than the timestamp of its last request. That should mean that the data it gets back on successive requests has no gaps and no overlaps.

This does mean that when things are quiet (when no other users are present in the realm), it'll keep making the same request, asking about updates since a time T that's increasingly far in the past. But that T will nevertheless be the very latest record for that realm — or I guess the next-to-latest, after this user themself — so with the appropriate index it should be just as quick for the server to answer.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-03 20:38 UTC

I guess concretely, one option is we could change the current `UserPresence` model in the server, which presently has `last_connected_time`, `last_active_time` fields, to get a new `last_update_time`, which would be an auto-now field that is written to by the Postgres database when it actually stores an update to that user's presence.

And then the protocol for asking for presence data would involve the server storing the current time as `data_since_time`, and then querying the database.

But I think that proposal would involve using an integer auto-incrementing sequence number (or almost certainly better, one sequence number per realm?), and using that instead of a timestamp to avoid having to do inexact comparisons.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-03 20:40 UTC

So structurally, we'd have something like a simple `PresenceSequence` table mapping realms to a `max_update_id` integer, and each presence entry would have a `last_update_id` field, and each write to the presence table would be a transaction that does, ideally in a single SQL query rather than doing it in multiple round-trips in Python:
* Increment `max_update_id` for the realm in `PresenceSequence`.
* Write the update to `UserPresence` including the new `last_*` values and `last_update_id = max_update_id`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-03 20:42 UTC

And then the read queries would just return every record where the `realm, last_update_id` pair is greater than the previous `last_update_id` that the client received in the previous request.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-03 20:45 UTC

I am not sure about the naming of the fields, but I think that protocol would feel pretty clean. I expect that a 64-bit signed integer per realm would be sufficient to not have to think about wraparound ever? So we can use a `PositiveBigIntegerField` (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.0/ref/models/fields/#positivebigintegerfield)

I like doing per-realm since that makes all sorts of sharding considerations simple.

I'd suggest a format for the updated event that looks like this:

- `event_type`: "presence"
- `user_id`: {user_id}
- `active_timestamp`: {integer}
- `idle_timestamp`: {integer}

i.e., basically exactly matching the `POST /presence` modern presence API format, except without the map layering.

@Kunal Sharma are you up for picking up this migration? Basically the goal would be to change the `presence` event type, if and only if the client registered for events with `presence_last_update_id` in its register event, to request the modern protocol.

**Greg Price** · 2025-07-17 22:26 UTC

@Chris Bobbe [schrieb](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/presence.20rewrite/near/2223790):
> Cool. So zulip-flutter would […] expect servers at or above a certain feature level to interpret that as asking for the new event format, and so expect the new format. We’d add a TODO to remove the FL condition after the FL ages out of our server support window.

I'd adjust this logic a bit: instead of having a condition on the feature level, we'd look for the new format, and if it's not present then look for the old format. (And either way, we'd produce an object internally that aligns with the new format.) Then the TODO would be for deleting the fallback to the old format.

That's generally how I prefer to write compatibility fallback conditions where possible, which includes almost all the times we're interpreting a response from the server. (On the other hand, explicit FL conditions are often needed when deciding what request to send to the server.) It has the advantage that it's more intrinsically robust: one fewer detail to need to get right.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-12-22 20:43 UTC

And wow, the JavaScript story for encoding UTF-8 as base64 is atrocious. It involves intentionally round-tripping through mojibake: `btoa(String.fromCharCode(...new TextEncoder().encode(s)))`.

**Chris Bobbe** · 2021-12-22 20:49 UTC

Oh, I see we have the following in a [util file](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-mobile/blob/main/src/utils/encoding.js) that we use elsewhere, but could probably use here too?

```js
/**
 * Encode a string as the base64 representation of its UTF-8 bytes.
 *
 * This lets us pass an arbitrary string through a channel (like the
 * `postMessage` on RN's WebViews on Android) that tries to do something
 * like percent-decode it, or (like an HTML attribute) that forbids certain
 * characters.
 *
 * See also `base64Utf8Decode` for the inverse.
 */
export const base64Utf8Encode = (text: string): string =>
  // References on reliably encoding strings to Base64:
  // https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WindowOrWorkerGlobalScope/btoa#Unicode_strings
  // https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WindowBase64/Base64_encoding_and_decoding
  //
  // In short:
  //  * base64 encoders want bytes, not really Unicode strings, so they
  //    insist their input consist of the characters U+0000 to U+00FF;
  //  * `encodeURIComponent` together with `unescape` is a way of getting
  //    that, effectively producing the UTF-8 encoding of the input.
  //
  // We use `base64.encode` because `btoa` is unavailable in the JS
  // environment provided by RN on iOS.
  base64.encode(unescape(encodeURIComponent(text)));

/**
 * The inverse of `base64Utf8Encode`, above.
 */
export const base64Utf8Decode = (str: string): string =>
  decodeURIComponent(escape(base64.decode(str)));
```

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-12-22 20:50 UTC

Yeah, that’s equivalent.

**Chris Bobbe** · 2021-12-22 21:47 UTC

#M5178

**Chris Bobbe** · 2021-12-22 21:50 UTC

**Chris Bobbe** · 2021-12-22 21:55 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-23 00:30 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> And wow, the JavaScript story for encoding UTF-8 as base64 is atrocious.

Yup.

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-23 00:38 UTC

(replying to Chris Bobbe)
> Oh, wait. If zulip-mobile encodes using our `base64Utf8Encode` (quoted above), then doesn't that obligate the server to decode with something like our `base64Utf8Decode`, quoted above? It's probably not doing that already, I would guess?

Yeah, changing from `base64.encode` to `base64Utf8Encode` will avoid an error within the client as it tries to encode, but it's only effective if the server interprets it in the corresponding way.

It might be already. That's probably actually the most natural thing you get when implementing in Python.

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-23 00:40 UTC

Oho, in fact it looks like the definition of HTTP basic auth basically already specifies that `base64Utf8Encode` is exactly what we should be doing:
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7617#section-2.1

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-23 00:41 UTC

(modulo the part where the implementation details of `base64Utf8Encode` go ridiculously through URL percent-encoding)

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-23 00:45 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)
> Oho, in fact it looks like the definition of HTTP basic auth basically already specifies that `base64Utf8Encode` is exactly what we should be doing: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7617#section-2.1

Mmm, it's not quite as clean as that. But:

> To receive authorization, the client
>   1.  obtains the user-id and password from the user,
>   2.  constructs the user-pass by concatenating the user-id, a single colon (":") character, and the password,
>   3.  encodes the user-pass into an octet sequence (see below for a discussion of character encoding schemes),
>   4.  and obtains the basic-credentials by encoding this octet sequence using Base64 […]

And then:

> The original definition of this authentication scheme failed to specify the character encoding scheme used to convert the user-pass into an octet sequence. In practice, most implementations chose either a locale-specific encoding such as ISO-8859-1 ([ISO-8859-1]), or UTF-8 ([RFC3629]). For backwards …

And then there's a way for the server to tell the client what encoding scheme it'd like to see... and the only allowed value for the server to say there is "UTF-8". So the spec certainly *wants* you to use UTF-8, and for compatibility reasons just stops short of trying to mandate it.

**Chris Bobbe** · 2021-12-23 02:44 UTC

So the remaining question is whether the server decodes the base64 as UTF-8, as it's (kinda) supposed to? The Python code doesn't have to be aware of our `encodeURIComponent`/`unescape` implementation detail?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-12-23 03:11 UTC

## still_url

*2021-12-30 to 2021-12-30 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/still_url/with/1302573)*

**Steve Howell** · 2021-12-30 03:18 UTC

@Greg Price We added a field called `still_url` for realm emojis to feature level 97.  It's the URL of the "still" version of an animated emoji.  I don't believe mobile uses it yet.  In upcoming feature level 113 we intend to always include the field, but make it null when the emoji is not animated.  The idea here is that we want to know that the backend actually tried to populate the field, as opposed to skipping it due to oversight.  I don't believe this should negatively impact mobile.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-12-30 03:22 UTC

The way that the webapp handles this is that we only attempt to display the URL if a truthy value is provided.  If the field is omitted, set to null, or set to undefined, we ignore it.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-12-30 03:58 UTC

https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/20643#discussion_r776556554 is also relevant

**Steve Howell** · 2021-12-30 04:01 UTC

I checked to make sure that `still_url` is not on mobile's main branch, but it's plausible there's some dev branch this would impact.

~~~
$ git log | head -3
commit e71d55d024ffae57145431282d8b53413306efbf
Author: Greg Price <greg@zulipchat.com>
Date:   Tue Dec 21 20:27:51 2021 -0800
(zulip-py3-venv) ~/zulip-mobile (master)
$ git grep still_url
(zulip-py3-venv) ~/zulip-mobile (master)

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-30 04:44 UTC

Thanks for asking! Yeah, we don't currently look at that field and I'm not aware of any work in progress that would. So changing its semantics is all good as far as mobile is concerned.

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-30 04:50 UTC

(From @Anders Kaseorg on that GitHub thread:)
> It is true, however, that non-required items weaken Mypy’s checking: Mypy won’t protect you from implicitly assuming the item is present when it might not be. So the API change still has potential value.

Hmm, that's a shame. Flow doesn't have that hole -- if you have something like `x: { still_url?: string, ... }`, with `?` to say the property is optional, then it knows that `x.still_url` has type `string | void`, not simply `string`. I don't know offhand the situation in TypeScript but my wild guess would be that it also doesn't have that hole.

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-30 04:58 UTC

I guess the corresponding spec is basically [this](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0589/#supported-and-unsupported-operations) in PEP 589:
> Type checkers may allow reading an item using `d['x']` even if the key `'x'` is not required, instead of requiring the use of `d.get('x')` or an explicit `'x' in d` check. The rationale is that tracking the existence of keys is difficult to implement in full generality, and that disallowing this could require many changes to existing code.

Sounds like basically they weren't confident that their analysis of how the types get refined through control flow was good enough to make that not a big pain.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-12-30 05:10 UTC

TypeScript also gives `string | undefined`. This is easier for JavaScript, where a missing item is retrieved as `undefined` rather than throwing an error.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-12-30 05:12 UTC

For Python, Mypy would have to remember that you previously did a `"still_url" in x` check and reason about how far this fact can be propagated. Which is of a similar nature to some of the reasoning it occasionally does already, but would still probably be a pain to implement.

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-30 17:46 UTC

Yeah, that reasoning is what I was referring to by "their analysis of how the types get refined through control flow". It's true, that gets harder to work with than when there's just a value you can give a different type to, like `string | void` vs. `string`.

**Greg Price** · 2022-01-12 19:35 UTC

Then the most substantive item is:

What is true is that for many errors the `code` is a generic one, `code: "BAD_REQUEST"`.

**Greg Price** · 2022-01-12 19:38 UTC

> Where present, clients should check `code`, rather than `msg`, when looking for specific error conditions, since the `msg` strings are internationalized (e.g. the server will send the error message translated into French if the user has a French locale).

This should be stronger: clients should always check `code`. Checking `msg` will essentially always be buggy code, because those strings are translated. If a client needs information that isn't present except in `msg`, then the solution is to file an issue or start a thread in this stream, in order to get a specific `code` and/or relevant additional fields for relevant data.

**Greg Price** · 2022-01-12 19:46 UTC

* Another feature of Zulip API error responses which this page should mention is that in addition to `code`, some errors will contain other fields as well with further details.

                        }
                    }
```

We can have an `if` block that rejects the `muted_topics` event and doesn't let it get placed in the event queue if `user_topics` is also present in `event_types` requested by the client. Thoughts?

```python
    def accepts_event(self, event: Mapping[str, Any]) -> bool:
        if self.event_types is not None and event["type"] not in self.event_types:
            return False
        if event["type"] == "message":
            return self.narrow_filter(event)
        if event["type"] == "typing" and "stream_id" in event:
            # Typing notifications for stream messages are only
            # delivered if the stream_typing_notifications
            # client_capability is enabled, for backwards compatibility.
            return self.stream_typing_notifications
        if self.user_settings_object and event["type"] in [
            "update_display_settings",
            "update_global_notifications",
        ]:
            # 'update_display_settings' and 'update_global_notifications'
            # events are sent only if user_settings_object is False,
            # otherwise only 'user_settings' event is sent.
            return False
        return True
```

**Greg Price** · 2022-02-09 21:32 UTC

I think it would be simpler to not have an `op` field. The `visibility_policy` field already expresses the same information, so long as we make `'default'` be one of the values we send for it.

The way I'd think about the semantics is:
* These records are unique for a given (user, stream, topic_name) triple. For a given client connection / a given stream of events, that means they're unique for a given (stream, topic) pair.
* So the model here is a map from a topic -- identified by the pair (stream, topic_name) -- to some data about this user's relationship to that topic. Currently that data is just an enum `visibility_policy`, plus a bit of metadata which is the `last_updated` timestamp.
* When there's a change, we simply send the client the new record.

Because we simply send the complete new record for the given topic, we don't need additional metadata like an `op` field to say what kind of change it was. If the client cares, it can always compare the new record to the existing old record it had.

**Greg Price** · 2022-02-09 21:34 UTC

This also makes it extend nicely to a possible future where there's some other bit of data on these records, beyond the `visibility_policy` enum and the `last_updated` metadata. There won't be a need to make up additional types of events, with their own set of fields and different `op` values to tell them apart -- the new field will just be in these records each time we send them.

**Greg Price** · 2022-02-09 21:47 UTC

One background fact about this feature's data model which is part of why that design works well: conceptually, there is a `visibility_policy` for every user with respect to every topic.

We don't represent those explicitly -- that would be an enormous, quadratic amount of space, plus we'd be constantly creating one of these records per user every time someone made a new topic. So there is a "zero" value of `visibility_policy`, a value that it has when there isn't any explicit record saying what it is. That's described here in the `UserTopic` class:
```py
    # Implicitly, if a UserTopic does not exist, the (user, topic)
    # pair should have normal behavior for that (user, stream) pair.
```

So when one of these rows is created in the database, conceptually it's not really creating a "new" thing, the way that creating a new user or stream does. In the conceptual model of this feature, it's just updating something that was already there, with a value of `'default'`, to instead have a value of `'muted'` -- no different from updating a value that was `'unmuted'` (in a future where we have that feature) to instead be `'muted'`.

**Greg Price** · 2022-02-09 21:49 UTC

And because of this part:

> We don't represent those explicitly -- that would be an enormous, quadratic amount of space, plus we'd be constantly creating one of these records per user every time someone made a new topic.

there will also have to be a similar "zero" value, in this sense:

> So there is a "zero" value of `visibility_policy`, a value that it has when there isn't any explicit record saying what it is.

for any future other bit of data we might add to these user_topic records. So the design with no `op` will continue to work well then.

) -> List[Tuple[str, str, float]]:
    query = UserTopic.objects.filter(user_profile=user_profile, visibility_policy=UserTopic.MUTED)
    # Exclude muted topics that are part of deactivated streams unless
    # explicitly requested.
    if not include_deactivated:
        query = query.filter(stream__deactivated=False)
    rows = query.values(
        "stream__name",
        "topic_name",
        "last_updated",
    )
    return [
        (row["stream__name"], row["topic_name"], datetime_to_timestamp(row["last_updated"]))
        for row in rows
    ]

```

To my understanding, we need a `get_user_topics` function to be used for the initial data fetch, which would return an array of objects with `stream_id`, `topic_name`, `visibility_policy`, and `last_updated` keys. 
In the current scenario, where we only have two possible states for `visibility_policy` (`muted` and `default`), this array will have the same information as returned by `get_topic_mutes`, so there'll be two data structures representing similar data.  But as we'll expand the possible visibility policies, it will represent various kinds of user-topic relationships.  Thoughts?

Also, If this seems right, what would be an appropriate place to add the helper `get_user_topics`?

Looks like that's in a small file zerver/lib/topic_mutes.py.

Tim may have other thoughts for you, but my inclination would be:
* Have the new function next to the existing one, because they are basically two views of the same data.
* Before adding it, rename the file to something like user_topics.py.

In the future as we add features like following a topic, or unmuting it when the stream is muted, the other functions in that file (like `add_topic_mute`) are likely to grow more complex too, or gain their own twins. No need to do that eagerly, but giving the file a more general name will make a natural home for those changes to happen.

To implement this behavior while sending initial state data to clients, here is the code that I have added to `fetch_initial_state_data`.

```python

if want("muted_topics"):
    if event_types is None or not want("user_topic"):
         state["muted_topics"] = [] if user_profile is None else get_topic_mutes(user_profile)
  
if want("user_topic"):
    state["user_topics"] = [] if user_profile is None else get_user_topics(user_profile)

```

In case, when a client requests for both `user_topic` and `muted_topics`, we send only `user_topic` events. In that case, both `want("user_topic")` and `want("muted_topics")` evaluate to true. So, to decide whether to send the `muted_topics` state, we have to check whether it has been requested alongside all the `page_params` or just `user_topic`. So, we check `if event_types==None`. If that's true, we send `muted_topics`. If that's false, we send `muted_topics`, if the user doesn't `want("user_topic")`.

I'd love to hear some feedback on this and whether there can be a better approach, like doing something with the `want` function.

It's certainly a problem with a model where we send a Topic object for every topic that has existed historically to clients in order to display a stream. There are certainly streams with 1000+ topics out there, and organizations with 10K+ in their history. In theory the API could just send data on all 10K topics to clients, but that's the kind of scaling property we really try to avoid because they create scaling bottlenecks.

The data storage issue is one of several reasons why we designed resolved topics with having a checkmark at the start of the name rather than doing something like this (the other big reason is that it means it display nicely in input boxes).

## GET /messages/{message_id}

*2022-03-01 to 2022-03-11 · 19 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/GET.20.2Fmessages.2F.7Bmessage_id.7D/with/1336731)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-01 01:41 UTC

OK, I have an API design question that's somewhat timely. In #20553, we want a way to fetch a single message's full details via the API that feels more natural than a `GET /messages` query with very specific parameters.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-01 01:42 UTC

We have an existing endpoint, `GET /messages/{message_id}` that currently returns the raw markdown for a message, used for viewing raw content of messages and message editing, whenever the client doesn't have that data present already (E.g. it will if you sent the message yourself using that client).

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-01 01:42 UTC

The current proposal is to add an `include_full_message` parameter, which if specified would result in returning the whole message.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-01 01:43 UTC

But it seems like it'd make for a much cleaner API if we instead made this URL return that format by default, with perhaps a `raw_content_only`  parameter if we want the old behavior.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-01 01:43 UTC

I don't think there's even really a significant performance cost to just returning the whole message unconditionally, actually, since we're just fetching a single message.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-01 01:44 UTC

And certainly from a "client application author" standpoint, I'd really expect that URL to just give you the message with that ID.

**Alex Dehnert** · 2022-03-01 01:55 UTC

"Return the whole message" definitely strikes me as better for an endpoint like that, if there's not a backwards compat issue.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-01 02:10 UTC

There shouldn't be a backwards-compatibility issue, in that the old thing wants a `raw_content` field, so worst case we also send that field unnecessarily.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-03-01 11:00 UTC

My vote is to unconditionally return both raw content and rendered content for the single-message endpoint.  (It's still plausible that we will eventually want a bulk-fetch-messages API that works off of message ids, but I believe we recently deprecated that idea.)

**Steve Howell** · 2022-03-01 11:01 UTC

Hopefully none of our clients or third-party apps calls this in a loop.  If that's the case, then we certainly don't need to over-optimize this.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2022-03-02 01:59 UTC

Ok, I will make the change then.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-05 01:32 UTC

This is now tracked in #20576, which I've handed off to @Lauryn Menard for the last few steps of cleanup.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-05 01:33 UTC

I made one other change to the API not detailed above, which is to support the `apply_markdown` parameter from `GET /messages`, and officially deprecate the `raw_content` field in favor of calling this endpoint with `apply_markdown=false` and then accessing the `content` field from the message object returned.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-05 01:34 UTC

It'll be like a year before we can actually delete `raw_content` since we need to wait for mobile/terminal clients to migrate and then versions without the change to age into being EOL, but this at least gives us a path to this endpoint having the interface it most naturally should have :).

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-03-05 01:36 UTC

From a security perspective, I don’t like the idea of having a single type-confused field that may or may not be HTML.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-05 01:40 UTC

It's possible we should change the API of `GET /messages`, but I think this minor endpoint should use the same API.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-05 01:41 UTC

I do agree that we probably want to have separate field names and have the parameter control which fields you get, but that's probably an independent design discussion.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-05 01:42 UTC

(Sending both has performance considerations since you end up sending two copies of the message content, so we want it to be possible to not have that happen for `GET /messages` at least)

**Lauryn Menard** · 2022-03-11 17:29 UTC

I've got #21391 up with the API updates (replaces #20576).


## GET /messages/{msg_id} anchor=first_after_date

*2022-03-08 to 2022-03-31 · 24 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/GET.20.2Fmessages.2F.7Bmsg_id.7D.20anchor.3Dfirst_after_date/with/1340540)*

**Dinesh Ch** · 2022-03-08 07:35 UTC

We use `PATCH {{ api_url }}/v1/messages/{msg_id}` to edit message's content, topic and also stream. We also use the same endpoint to change the topic (and/or stream) of a whole thread or a bunch of messages with the help of the `propagate_mode` param which has options `change_one`, `change_later`, `change_all`.

In #20502, we want to make it possible to move messages by recency. For that, we can extend `propagate_mode` to `change_last_24_hours` and `change_last_week`. But there isn't much use of `msg_id` for these cases except for getting old stream, topic values.

Should we consider adding a new endpoint for the latter 3 options of `propagate_mode`? I feel like it'd be cleaner to have an endpoint like `/messages/move` which takes in the old and new stream, topic values. And maybe just use this for other cases of moving messages with an anchor message by accepting a `msg_id` param while using `/messages/{msg_id}` just for changing the content (but we may have backwards compatibility concerns?).

#20501, where we want to allow moving private messages to topics is also something we need to be conscious of while thinking of this.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-08 18:11 UTC

If we're going that route, I think we want a `propagate_mode=change_recent` with a separate parameter for the window of messages; that way, the API can remain relatively clean.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-08 18:12 UTC

@Dinesh Ch Interesting question. One thing that's a bit messy about that direction is the security angle -- we generally want to limit what messages you can move to those you can access, and it's convenient to just start with an `access_message_by_id` call rather than fetching messages and then doing a `has_message_access` check.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-08 18:13 UTC

An alternative implementation approach would be to extend `GET /messages` to support "Get me the oldest message this stream/topic that I can access within the last <date range>".

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-08 18:15 UTC

Which I think would be roughly a `GET /messages` call with:
* The appropriate narrow
* num_before=0
* num_after=0
* Instead of the `anchor` parameter, a `date_anchor` parameter that's potentially just a time (i.e. the client would do the computation).

And then it could just call the existing edit endpoint with the `change_later` style and the message ID obtained above.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-08 18:16 UTC

The thing I like about that approach is that the `date_anchor` parameter support for `GET /messages` could be useful when fetching messages and I think would be relatively simple to implement, since it could parallel the existing `anchor="first_unread"` approach.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-08 18:17 UTC

I suppose actually we might want to encode it as `anchor="first_after_date"` with a separate `target_date` parameter, or something.

**Dinesh Ch** · 2022-03-10 13:53 UTC

I really like the alternative approach, Thanks!  Will start by extending `GET /messages` to support `anchor="first_after_date"`. To be clear, we need `target_date` to support date+time, right?

Do we have any endpoint that accepts a date parameter that I can look at? I'm currently uncertain about what's the standard way of sending and processing dates in GET requests.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-10 21:03 UTC

@Dinesh Ch yeah, `target_date` should be an encoding of a `datetime`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-10 21:04 UTC

We have this, which is just for dates (I think for the custom profile field format):
```
def check_date(var_name: str, val: object) -> str:                                                       
    if not isinstance(val, str):                                                                         
        raise ValidationError(_("{var_name} is not a string").format(var_name=var_name))                 
    try:                                                                                                 
        if datetime.strptime(val, "%Y-%m-%d").strftime("%Y-%m-%d") != val:                               
            raise ValidationError(_("{var_name} is not a date").format(var_name=var_name))               
    except ValueError:                                                                                   
        raise ValidationError(_("{var_name} is not a date").format(var_name=var_name))                   
    return val                                                                                           
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-10 21:06 UTC

It appears the one place we parse a date is in our undocumented API for "Send later", which uses this function for parsing:
`from dateutil.parser import parse as dateparser`

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-10 21:07 UTC

I don't particularly have time to think through whether that's a format we should be excited about for in the API here, but it's probably a fine choice for prototyping.  

(I'd appreciate others doing a bit of such investigation).

**Dinesh Ch** · 2022-03-11 17:20 UTC

Okay, I haven't spent much time on the format of the date but was considering ISOstring. Not sure how all this plays out with different timezones.

I've spent most of today writing https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/21394/commits/4b3a03239c823099c0e35a37012c180f2ced3f06 to add appropriate code to fetch first unread. Am I going in the right direction?

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-11 19:41 UTC

@Dinesh Ch yeah, that looks like the right direction.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-11 19:41 UTC

Generally if one's going to send a time value that doesn't come with a timezone, one should do it in UTC.

**Dinesh Ch** · 2022-03-15 05:47 UTC

About sending the datetime, after looking at [this StackOverflow discussion](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/9581692/recommended-date-format-for-rest-get-api), I think we can do one of these:
* Send ISO string(`2022-03-15T05:22:35.645Z` or `20220315T052235.645Z` w/o any `:`). This would include timezone information which helps ensure clients don't make any errors in terms of sending it in UTC. This means simply sending `.toISOString` for js based clients.
* epoch time (`1331162374`): This wouldn't include any timezone info.
* A custom format we enforce. I think it'll be a hassle for clients.

I'll continue with PR assuming an ISO string to be sent since that seems like a better option. Let me know if not something we want to do.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-15 20:14 UTC

I think an ISO string is a very reasonable choice of format here, since that should be easy to parse in Python, and we already use with slight variations in our `<time` syntax. `<time:2022-03-15T13:13:51-07:00> `

## schema type: date-time

*2022-03-22 to 2022-03-22 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/schema.20type.3A.20date-time/with/1349633)*

**Dinesh Ch** · 2022-03-22 05:08 UTC

#21394 extends `GET /messages/{msg_id}` to retrieve first message after a particular date+time which is sent through the param `target_date` in ISO 8601 format.

In the view function, I've set the type of `target_date` to `Optional[datetime]` and used a converter function(`to_datetime`) I [added](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/21394/commits/9e801832077be837b5c4818558280104a19d7ed3#diff-b7124e7ad233b10ecdf27d15fbea07348c33f273d592980351b9119158294be2R540).

In `zulip.yaml`, I've specified the type as a `string`. `target_date` is fundamentally a string and we seem to only have types: `string`, `integer`, `boolean`, `object`, `NoneType`.

Now, `zerver.tests.test_openapi.OpenAPIArgumentsTest.test_openapi_arguments` which asserts that the mypy types match with the ones in `zulip.yaml` fails with OpenAPI type considered as `str` while the one in function considered as `datetime.datetime`.

Is the right fix here to add a `datetime` type to [`test_openapi.VARMAP`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/zerver/tests/test_openapi.py#L36-L42)?

`schema` also supports a [`format`](https://swagger.io/specification/#data-type-format) value which has a `date-time`. Should we tweak code to consider `format` while inferring the types in [`test_openapi.schema_type`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/zerver/tests/test_openapi.py#L45-L53)? I kinda feel like this would be cleaner than mentioning a new type in zulip.yaml `schema`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-22 05:15 UTC

I think `date-time` is probably the correct `format` after chasing OpenAPI's docs that it should be an ISO 8601 datetime.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-22 05:16 UTC

So I think that makes sense and extending `VARMAP` makes sense to me as well, but I'm not totally sure.

**Dinesh Ch** · 2022-03-22 06:05 UTC

I think we should try to restrict `type` to primitives mentioned in https://swagger.io/specification/#data-type-format and rely on `format` from an API documentation perspective(though we don't mention the `format` in our [docs](https://zulip.com/api/)).  OpenAPI validator would require us to mention this in `content["application/json"]["schema"]` if we are going with setting `type=date-time` which I think makes it look complex.

So, I'll go ahead with this change to fix the test
```diff
+++ zerver/tests/test_openapi.py
@@ -1,6 +1,7 @@
 import inspect
 import os
 from collections import abc
+from datetime import datetime
 from typing import Any, Callable, Dict, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple, Union
 from unittest.mock import MagicMock, patch
 
@@ -49,6 +50,8 @@ def schema_type(schema: Dict[str, Any]) -> Union[type, Tuple[type, object]]:
         return schema_type(schema["oneOf"][0])
     elif schema["type"] == "array":
         return (list, schema_type(schema["items"]))
+    elif schema["type"] == "string" and schema.get("format", '') == "date-time":
+        return datetime
     else:
         return VARMAP[schema["type"]]
```

**Dinesh Ch** · 2022-03-22 06:05 UTC

Does it make sense?

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-22 17:49 UTC

Yeah, that seems like a reasonable extension to me.

**Dinesh Ch** · 2022-03-22 18:24 UTC

Okay, I've updated #21394 to pass all tests. Please review when you get time.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-08-12 19:21 UTC

So just an update as I think I'll be merging the main  read receipts PR (#18935) today; the only thing that's really changed in the API is that we've added a realm level setting to disable read receipts for an organization, `realm_enable_read_receipts`, that the server will enforce, but where clients probably want to hide the option if unavailable.

There's a very large block comment about the design decisions behind this that I'll post below, since it may answer things that come up. I think the actual conclusions like "No sender" are covered in the API documentation; but certainly if you find yourself referring to this to block comment to discover any details, we should fix that in the API documentation, since this comment is more intended to be the "why" for the model we've selected, with far more detail than implementations should need.

``` python
# This query implements a few decisions:                           
# * Most importantly, this is where we enforce the                 
#   send_read_receipts privacy setting.                            
#                                                                  
# * The message sender is never included, since presumably they    
#   read the message before sending it, and showing the sender as  
#   having read their own message is likely to be confusing.       
#                                                                  
# * Deactivated users are excluded. While in theory someone        
#   could be interested in the information, not including them     
#   is a cleaner policy, and usually read receipts are only of     
#   interest shortly after a message was sent.                     
#                                                                  
# * We do not filter on the historical flag. This means that a user
#   who stars a public stream message that they did not originally 
#   receive will appear in read receipts for that message.         
#                                                                  
# * Marking a message as unread causes it to appear as not read    
#   via read receipts, as well. This is consistent with the fact   
#   that users can view a message without leaving it marked as     
#   read in other ways (desktop/email/push notifications).         
#                                                                  
# * Bots are included. Most bots never mark any messages as read,  
#   but one could imagine having them to do so via the API to      
#   communicate useful information. For example, the `read` flag   
#   could be used by a bot to track which messages have been       
#   bridged to another chat system or otherwise processed          
#   successfully by the bot, and users might find it useful to be  
#   able to inspect that in the UI. If this behavior is not        
#   desired for a bot, it can be disabled using the                
#   send_read_receipts privacy setting.                            
#                                                                  
# Note that we do not attempt to present how many users received a 
# message but have NOT marked the message as read. There are       
# tricky corner cases involved in doing so, such as the            
# `historical` flag for public stream messages; but the most       
# important one is how to handle users who read a message and then 
# later unsubscribed from a stream.                                
```

I have a few questions around the practical details of potentially changing the wire format for transmitting emoji in message bodies from primarily colon-strings (with unicode support, albeit bugged due to incomplete data) to primarily unicode:
* To what extent would we have control over how emoji are displayed inside the text input in the compose box? It'd probably be a bad experience if you pick an emoji in the emoji picker that displayed the Google emoji set you've picked, but then your Mac renders a different image in your compose box because your browser has the Apple emoji font setup. 
* Are we OK with custom emoji having a very different representation in the compose box from unicode emoji? Or do we have a plan for how custom emoji would be displayed directly as the glyph inside the compose box?
* Would we want to desupport colon strings for unicode emoji, or just have the emoji picker and/or typeahead never generate them? There's probably a backwards-compatibility period we'd need to support colon strings for regardless to avoid breaking integrations.

  But it looks like the web client actually doesn't use `order` when showing a user's profile. Instead, it goes through the `custom_profile_fields` array and just takes the fields in the order they're found in that array. Effectively, it's assuming that the `custom_profile_fields` array will always be sorted by `order`.

  That seems like a pretty reasonable invariant for the server to provide. Can we make that a part of the API?

**Greg Price** · 2022-05-21 00:08 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2022-05-21 00:13 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2022-05-21 00:15 UTC

  > An array of dictionaries where each dictionary contains details of a single new custom profile field for the Zulip organization.

  In other words, it's an array of *new* fields; so the new overall set of fields would be the existing ones plus these new ones. (And no provision for removing existing fields.)

  But in fact, it appears that the actual behavior is that the event's `fields` array is the new complete list of custom profile fields for the realm -- so it's all the existing ones that still exist, plus any new ones.

  Specifically, the web client assumes that's the case: when it gets one of these events, it just sets `page_params.custom_profile_fields = event.fields;`.

  That actual API seems pretty sensible, so I think this one is just a docs bug.

  A pretty reasonable API here would be: it's `value: string | null`, where a string is the new value and null means that the field was deleted. Is that the actual behavior? If so, let's write that down; if there's some further wrinkle, I'll be curious to discuss it.

  And then as I said after that, a further point there is that it's not really a dictionary/object, but instead a string which is the JSON encoding of such a thing. That's a docs bug that it's not clear about that -- and also I think it'd be an API design improvement to make it the actual object instead.

Current API:

```json
"{\"0\":{\"text\":\"emacs\",\"order\":\"1\"},\"1\":{\"text\":\"vim\",\"order\":\"2\"},…}"
```

Improvement 1: double-encoded JSON as string is dumb.

```json
{"0": {"text": "emacs", "order": "1"}, "1": {"text": "vim", "order": "2"}, …}
```

Improvement 2: dictionary with `order` is dumb, use a list.

```json
[{"id": 0, "text": "emacs"}, {"id": 1, "text": "vim"}, …]
```

Improvement 3 (potentially more debatable): `id` is dumb, just store the strings.

```json
["emacs", "vim", …]
```

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-02 03:32 UTC

It's unfortunate that the types here vary so widely, and in such a nonlocal way. The `value` can be either:
* Some user-entered text, to display literally;
* A key indexing into a realm-wide map of options;
* An ISO 8601 date;
* A URL;
* A user-entered string meant to get spliced into a URL (for an external account); or
* A JSON-encoded list of numbers, which are user IDs.

These are all basically fine choices for their respective types of fields, with the exception that it'd be better not to double-JSON-encode the list of user IDs.

But to know which one it is, you have to go look up the "id" for this field -- the key it was found at in the user's `profile_data` -- off in a different data structure far away. That makes it basically impossible to write down the type of this `profile_data` object in a reasonable way.

**Greg Price** · 2022-05-26 19:48 UTC

Given that the API presents it as three boolean properties on the stream (that just have some disallowed combinations), I think the right tactical fix is that the server should accept requests that only provide whatever subset of those properties the client wants to set -- the same way that endpoint behaves for the other properties.

So in the code, which looks like this:
```py
    if description is not None:
        # … validate description …
        do_change_stream_description(stream, description, acting_user=user_profile)
    if new_name is not None:
        # … validate new_name …
        do_rename_stream(stream, new_name, user_profile)
```

when it gets to the three privacy/permission booleans, it should say:
```py
    if is_private is not None or history_public_to_subscribers is not None or is_web_public is not None:
        do_change_stream_permission(
            stream,
            invite_only=is_private,
            history_public_to_subscribers=history_public_to_subscribers,
            is_web_public=is_web_public,
            acting_user=user_profile,
        )
```

instead of the current version, which is exactly the same but with the `if` condition only mentioning two of the three properties that the body would go and set.

The way I'd want to think of it is that when a stream is public (including web-public), `history_public_to_subscribers` is always true. After all, the stream's history is indeed public to subscribers, as well as to everyone else.

So if you send `history_public_to_subscribers: true`, that would not be an error, because it's just setting the field redundantly to the value it already has.

But if you send `history_public_to_subscribers: false` (when `invite_only` is false, or when the request also has `invite_only: false`), that would be an error, because you're trying to set it to an invalid value.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-26 18:56 UTC

For some background, the idea with external accounts was that we'd have a few specific third-party services where we'd provided the metadata, but you could also provide your own.

```
# Default external account fields are by default available                                               
# to realm admins, where realm admin only need to select                                                 
# the default field and other values(i.e. name, url) will be                                             
# fetch from this dictionary.                                                                            
# text: Field text for admins - custom profile field in org settings view                                
# name: Field label or name - user profile in user settings view                                         
# hint: Field hint for realm users                                                                       
# url_pattern: Field URL linkifier                                                                       
DEFAULT_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNTS = {                                                                            
    "twitter": {                                                                                         
        "text": "Twitter",                                                                               
        "url_pattern": "https://twitter.com/%(username)s",                                               
        "name": "Twitter",                                                                               
        "hint": "Enter your Twitter username",                                                           
    },                                                                                                   
    "github": {                                                                                          
        "text": "GitHub",                                                                                
        "url_pattern": "https://github.com/%(username)s",                                                
        "name": "GitHub",                                                                                
        "hint": "Enter your GitHub username",                                                            
    },                                                                                                   
}                                                                                                        
```

```
{"subtype": "twitter"}

{"subtype": "custom", "url_pattern": "https://linkedin.com/%(username)s"}
```

So it looks like the current behavior is:
* There's a `subtype` property.
* If `subtype` is `twitter` or `github`, the client is expected to know what the URL pattern should be.
* Otherwise it's `custom`, and there's a `url_pattern` property which has the URL pattern.
  * The URL pattern is an old-Python-style format string. Specifically, `%(username)s` is the placeholder. The user's `value` for the field should be substituted there.

        field_url_pattern = field.field_data.url_pattern;
    } else {
        field_url_pattern = page_params.realm_default_external_accounts[field_subtype].url_pattern;
    }
    return field_url_pattern.replace("%(username)s", field.value);
}
```

And indeed, over on https://zulip.com/api/register-queue there is documentation of `realm_default_external_accounts`. It looks like that's just a mirror of the `DEFAULT_EXTERNAL_ACCOUNTS` that @Tim Abbott quoted above.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-06-01 22:50 UTC

Yeah

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-01 22:53 UTC

The `realm_default_external_accounts` doc could also use some fixes:
* The descriptions of `name` and `text` are vacuous. The info in the comment you quoted above would be better.

  Though also, maybe we should change the API to just have one of those. I'm not sure there's a good use case for having them different -- seems just confusing.

* The description of `url_pattern` is inaccurate and also incomplete:

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-16 06:01 UTC

I think it is possible to fix these bugs in a purely backward-compatible way if we make one tweak that kind of *looks* like an API change, but that existing clients shouldn't actually notice:
* When making up an ID for a new value choice, choose a random number from a wide range.

  In particular, `Math.floor(Math.random() * (2 ** 54))` is the most one can get while using JS number values, and is enough that it's extremely unlikely it will ever pick the same ID for two choices in the same custom profile field, even if Zulip becomes ubiquitous and this feature is wildly popular.

Then when reordering or deleting values, let the remaining values keep the IDs they already had, even though they no longer correspond to their order. This may require the settings UI code to better track which value is which, by attaching their IDs to them.

Alright! So to summarize:

* The register response will have two new properties `unicode_emoji_hash: string` and `emoji_data_url`. 
  * If the properties aren't present, then emoji on mobile should work as they did before we updated supported emoji.
  * If they are present, then mobile makes a request to the url
* `unicode_emoji_hash` is a lower-case hex of SHA-256 of the json object sorted by keys with all whitespace removed
* `emoji_data_hash = { name_to_code: { $name1: $code1, $name2: $code2, ... }}` where names include both canonical names and aliases

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-21 20:26 UTC

For getting that optimization where it's shared across Zulip Cloud: there's a settings variable in the server that says what the server's overall base URL is. In a single-realm server (including a typical self-hosted server), that'll be the same as the realm URL. On Zulip Cloud, I believe it'll be `https://zulip.com/` while the realms are at base URLs like `https://foo.zulipchat.com/`.

So then just put the same path on the server's overall base URL instead of the realm base URL, and it'll be shared across the different realms on a server.
