**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-08-04 23:11 UTC

The current internal format has

* `names`: flat array of emoji names and aliases
* `name_to_codepoint`: map from emoji names and aliases to codepoints
* `codepoint_to_name`: map from codepoints to primary emoji names
* `emoji_catalog`: map from category names to arrays of codepoints
* `emoticon_conversions`: map from `:)`, `:(`, etc. to emoji colon-strings

The current PR subsumes the first two. My proposal subsumes the first three. The last two would be fine to add separately later, since there’s not really anything to be gained by combining them.

## custom profile fields in small profile

*2022-06-09 to 2025-01-27 · 98 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/custom.20profile.20fields.20in.20small.20profile/with/1390650)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-06-09 00:50 UTC

So we need to settle an API naming detail for #21588, which adds support for requesting that some custom profile fields appear in the small popover. The current specification is that you're allowed to do this for up to 2 custom profile fields. 

Example profile fields that one might want this for are Pronouns and external accounts like one's Github username, but we'll of course want to make it easy to do something more general.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-06-09 00:52 UTC

The main question is what to call the setting in the API; the pull request has  `display_in_profile_popover`, which is reasonably clear, but I'm not sure how it would be interpreted in mobile (which may not have "popovers").

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-06-09 00:52 UTC

So one proposal would be `include_in_small_profile`, which maybe frames a bit more semantically what we have in mind: If your UI includes a "small profile" widget that only contains some custom profile fields, then this is one you should include in that UI.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-06-09 00:53 UTC

@Yogesh Sirsat, you'll want to follow the discussion.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-06-09 00:56 UTC

Most of the API design for this is mostly straightforward:
* This field will just be another field on custom profile field objects.
* The server will be responsible for enforcing that a realm doesn't have more than 2 of these (or whatever the rule evolves to be). I don't think many clients will want to build administrative UI for changing realm settings, but if they do, I can imagine we may want to make that 2 not hardcoded so clients can have the UI no longer offer to let you add more once 2 are enabled, as the web UI does. But I think we can kinda punt on that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-06-09 01:00 UTC

There's one detail that touches on `realm_default_external_accounts`, which is that this PR includes support for displaying an `fa-github` icon next to your GitHub username (or similar) if you have an external account of the `github` subtype. The PR doesn't propose an API design for how we'd do that in general -- it just displays an icon if there's an font-awesome icon matching the `name` of the subtype.

We probably don't want that precise design as part of the API specification, since it's fragile. One option is we let the webapp hardcode something here and not worry about it, but I think it'd probably be better to extend the `realm_default_external_accounts` in some way. How would we want to do that extension? I can imagine a world where we add an `icon_url` field, though to make that nice we'd need to figure out URL to specify for where to serve the icons.

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-09 04:44 UTC

Yeah, I think something semantic like "small profile" is a much better direction than "popover", which is specific to the web app's current UI.

Perhaps "short profile" (so e.g. `include_in_short_profile`)? Or "profile summary"? For me at least, "small profile" somehow doesn't naturally suggest that it's talking about a distinct piece of UI -- I want to read it as instead saying that the data making up the user's profile is small, or something. But "small profile" would be fine in the end too, thanks to docs.

**Greg Price** · 2022-06-09 04:46 UTC

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-07-12 19:58 UTC

`dataclasses_json` in Python seems fine with it too, with a bit more bureaucracy.

```python3
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

from dataclasses_json import DataClassJsonMixin, config
from operator import not_

def exclude_false() -> bool:
    return field(default=False, metadata=config(exclude=not_))

@dataclass
class MyRecord(DataClassJsonMixin):
    some_flag: bool = exclude_false()

my_record_schema = MyRecord.schema()

print(MyRecord(some_flag=False).to_dict())
# {}

print(MyRecord(some_flag=True).to_dict())
# {"some_flag": true}

print(my_record_schema.load({}))
# MyRecord(some_flag=False)

print(my_record_schema.load({"some_flag": True}))
# MyRecord(some_flag=True)

print(my_record_schema.load({"some_flag": 5}))
# marshmallow.exceptions.ValidationError: {'some_flag': ['Not a valid boolean.']}
```

## default value for a setting based on user groups

*2022-06-23 to 2023-02-05 · 38 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/default.20value.20for.20a.20setting.20based.20on.20user.20groups/with/1395603)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-06-23 16:52 UTC

As discussed in #**design>New permissions model** , I am working on adding new setting for who can unsubscribe others from the stream. We will use a foreign key to `UserGroup` for the setting. We need to set a default value for the setting, which will for most of the settings be the administrators system user group. 

We can pass a default argument as something like 
```python
can_remove_subscribers_group: Optional[UserGroup] = models.ForeignKey(UserGroup, default=get_admin_system_group, on_delete=models.SET_DEFAULT)
```
but we need realm also to get the correct user group and we cannot do that using the `default` option.

One approach is that we can modify `save` method, to set the group to admins group if it is null. But in such case, the code will be called even if we update some other properties for the object. 

Or when checking for whether a user is allowed to remove others, if `can_remove_subscribers_group` is null, we check whether the user is part of the admin group or not. Basically the value for this setting in database will be null only and we will consider it to be equivalent to admins group.

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-06-27 17:57 UTC

A follow up of the above question about how we would need to think about cases when user groups are deleted. If we modify the `save()` method to set the group to admins group (or any other default group depending) upon the setting, I am not sure what we would do when deleting a user group. Using [`SET()` for `on_delete`](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.0/ref/models/fields/#django.db.models.SET) will pose the same problem as we would need `realm` to get the correct user group.

And if instead keep the `can_remove_subscribers_group` setting as null by default and consider it to be equivalent to admins group, then not all settings by default would allow admins to do that task, some may also allow moderators, so in case when setting is null we would need to check whether user is admin while for some other setting we would need to check whether user is moderator or above role. This would mean we would need to write separate conditions for different settings.

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-06-28 02:49 UTC

@Tim Abbott thoughts?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-06-28 03:10 UTC

Why does it need to have a (model-level) default?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-06-28 03:13 UTC

The usual pattern would be a migration with three operations: first create it as nullable with default `None`, then fill it in so no rows are `None`, then alter it to be non-nullable without a default.

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-06-28 03:16 UTC

Ok. In that case too how we would handle the case when the user group is deleted?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-06-28 03:17 UTC

Either the code or the user is required to change the permission before deleting the group.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-06-28 23:26 UTC

Yeah, ideally we'd have on `on_delete` configuration to reject deleting the group if it's used in this sort of foreign key, I think?

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-06-28 23:27 UTC

I think probably definitionally, it might be better for `None` in the database to mean "Nobody has permission to do this thing"; and then we'd have code during realm creation (and the migration for adding the field) that would initialize the field with whatever we think its default value should be.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-06-28 23:29 UTC

I’d rather not have a `None` at all. You can create an empty group if you want that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-06-28 23:37 UTC

Well, I think a "Nobody" system group would be necessary to translate some of our settings, and I'm not sure we've created one; so that's a thing we should look at if we're going with that approach.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-06-28 23:38 UTC

But I think it'll still be possible (even if an invariant violation) for one of these fields to be `None` during realm creation, since one can't create a `UserGroup` without first creating the realm that contains it, and some of these settings will be on the Realm object. Probably we can prevent that state from happening in actuality using transactions, but it's a thing that deserves some thought.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-06-28 23:39 UTC

(In part because there are likely to eventually be dozens of such settings on the `Realm` object)

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-06-30 17:38 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> Yeah, ideally we'd have on `on_delete` configuration to reject deleting the group if it's used in this sort of foreign key, I think?
Yes, we can do this. 

We have not created "Nobody" system group yet. And yes, there would be no groups before creating the realm, so the realm settings would be `None` I think initially. This will not be a problem for stream settings though. Not sure how we can actually prevent this, will think a bit more on this.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-09 00:25 UTC

So coming back to this, because a decision here is the remaining blocker for merging our first group-based setting in #22589.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-09 00:27 UTC

As noted above, we will surely want "Nobody" to be an option you can select for who has permission to do something for some settings. We also need it for backwards-compatibility, since we have a half-dozen existing settings that have "Nobody" as an option.

**Notification Bot** · 2022-09-09 00:32 UTC

This topic was moved here from #**backend>default value for a setting based on user groups** by @Tim Abbott.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-09 00:33 UTC

So I think the main question is whether we think the "Nobody" option for a permissions setting (the group of users who can remove another user from a stream is our test case) is best represented in the API by adding an empty system group similar in structure to the system groups for roles, or whether it would be better to represent that as `null` in the API. I can't tell whether that would be cleaner; we need that to be a valid possibility in the types when creating `Realm`/`Stream`/etc. objects. 

This is largely an API design question; so moving the conversation there.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-09 00:34 UTC

I think it's likely that the "nobody" system group might provide an opportunity for simpler client code -- since "nobody" wouldn't be a special case.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-09-09 00:36 UTC

> (the group of users who can remove another user from a stream is our test case)

Can’t any administrator do that, at present?

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-09 00:40 UTC

Correct, the intent is to make it possible to make a wider group have that permission.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-09-09 00:41 UTC

Oh, I thought you were suggesting this is a use case for an automatic Nobody group. We don’t need to do anything special to let users create a manual Nobody group.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-09 00:42 UTC

The other API design question is naming, since that's a pattern. We currently have `can_remove_subscribers_group`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-09 00:45 UTC

The `None` encoding issue came up here: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/22589#discussion_r930520604

Basically, the order in which way we implement the data import/export logic with these `group` settings hanging off of both `Realm` and `Stream` currently means we need to temporarily set `None` values for this field partway through the import process, and then fill them in with a non-`None` field later. (Same issue applies in realm creation). So maybe it's not required, but it'd be very helpful to have clarity on whether `None` is expected to be an impossible value or not.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-09 00:47 UTC

A related design question on whether we want to let you create an empty user group or make an existing user group empty. I **think** that came up in the last few days elsewhere. I think the answer is yes, since there's lots of situations even in the middle of messing with a set of groups where it might be helpful, and it's needed to encode "Nobody" if we're not doing the `None` thing. 

But this would be different from streams, which currently don't allow having no subscribers. (I'm not sure that's the ideal policy, but we also don't need to change it now).

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-09-09 00:49 UTC

Leaving `None` impossible will simplify permission checks, as well as the kind of checks we’ll want to prevent you from irreversibly locking everyone out of your organization or whatever.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-09 00:50 UTC

Anyway I guess my design proposal is that:
* We stick with `can_remove_subscribers_group` as the naming convention for the Django model; of course that'd be `can_remove_subscribers_group_id` in API contexts where we're sending just the ID.
* `can_remove_subscribers_group` and similar settings are typed as `Optional[UserGroup]` in the data model, but are only allowed to be `None` when creating a new stream or during data import, and the invariant should be maintained that for the purpose of product code, this field is never `None`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-09 00:51 UTC

Thoughts? Also @Sahil Batra FYI since we've moved the thread.

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-09-09 13:20 UTC

Sounds good.

But we do not need the settings to be `None` while creating streams, since groups have already been created and we can set the default value according to the setting. But for realm settings we would need to set them `None` as groups are created after creating realm as discussed before.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-09 19:36 UTC

@Sahil Batra yeah, I understand -- my thinking is just that we're going to be adding a lot of realm settings. I think you're right that we can leave the stream settings not nullable, since they don't have the same ordering constraint.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-09 19:36 UTC

(We just need to create the `UserGroup` objects before streams in the import tool)

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-09-14 16:38 UTC

Updated the PR #22589 to fix the import code.

Also, do we also want a `Nobody` group by default now based on the above discussion?

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-14 23:02 UTC

@Sahil Batra yeah, let's make a `Nobody` group as a follow-up.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-14 23:15 UTC

I've merged #22589. For context for others, this means we are now internally representing this new setting for who has permission to do this using a system user group, which corresponds to the administrator role. So there's no change in user visible behavior as of yet, but we now have done a complete test of the internal plumbing for having a setting that is represented as a user group.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-14 23:19 UTC

I think that means our upcoming next steps are:
* Prototype an initial "user group picker" UI for this new setting.
* File issues with the mobile/terminal projects on the new user groups system, if we haven't already, so that they can start maintaining the data structures and functions they'll need to change a permissions setting that was previously represented using roles to checking groups. Ideally we'd make a plan for getting the plumbing in place such that it's a quick mobile app project to handle migrating the check for an existing permissions setting being migrated to being controlled via groups rather than roles. (We likely will be able to change various settings to work based on user groups before then by only allowing system groups to be selected).
* Adding the `Nobody` group.
* Probably some other things I haven't thought of for the moment; @Sahil Batra should feel free to add more items here :)

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-09-16 18:09 UTC

Sounds good. I do not have any other things to mention at the moment. But will add if I can think of any.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-05 20:58 UTC

Just an update that I'm merging #23992 today, which largely implements the UI corresponding to the `can_remove_subscribers_group` API detailed above, but also adjusted the API to allow setting that field when creating or editing a stream. (Previously, it had a fixed value of the "administrators" group and thus had no effect whatsoever).

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-05 21:00 UTC

I believe that the mobile/terminal clients don't support adjusting the stream subscriptions of other users yet, and thus this isn't an API change of any real importance from a migration standpoint. **Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-07 19:31 UTC

I chatted with Alya a bit about this in person. In short:
* We don't have concrete abuse use cases but it's also not clear we have real non-abuse use cases beyond fixing our labels being bad.
* The whole point of these "default" type fields is for clients to use alternative UI for displaying them that might not even have a visible name or hint field (The `name` might be visible in a tooltip, but eventually the field might just appear in your settings UI as a "Link with GitHub" button, and it might only appear in your profile as `{account_provider_icon} {username}`).
* For these reasons, it's probably not worth much effort to allow changing these fields in the API design.
* It would require significant effort to do so, because we'd have to document for clients some complex algorithm where you merge the default data with the specific field's data client side, or something messy like it.

1. Do a pass on the names/hints for the existing default fields (GitHub/Twitter) to values we feel good about folks not wanting to change. 
1. Add API support for changing one of these default external fields to a custom external field (initialized with the appropriate default values if not specified in the API request). The reverse operation would not be possible.
1. **Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-17 19:30 UTC

That code is still wrong, because you're calling `str()` to evaluate it at the wrong time.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-17 19:31 UTC

I think you need to write a `get_default_external_accounts` function that does the stringification of the `name` field, and have `zerver/lib/events.py` call it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-17 19:32 UTC

@Yogesh Sirsat do you understand why that code has the same bug? We only know the language of the user at the time that we're processing a request from that user, so any code that runs at Python process startup time, like defining a global variable or a class, will just use English as the language for everyone. And the point of the lazy translation objects it that they'll only be evaluated (and thus the language used to translate them) at the time you call `str` on them.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-17 19:33 UTC

So it doesn't help at all to just call `str` on a lazy object during Python process startup -- you've just made it non-lazy.

## mark-as-unread request

*2022-09-06 to 2022-11-19 · 227 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/mark-as-unread.20request/with/1431139)*

**Greg Price** · 2022-09-06 23:46 UTC

So, we had a long and successful discussion at #**api design>mark-as-unread (update_message_flags)** about how the API looks when the server tells the client that some messages have been marked as unread.

I think we haven't had a discussion (AFAICT) of how the client asks the server to mark some messages unread.

The way the feature currently works from a user perspective is: point at a message, and that message and subsequent ones in the conversation (or the narrow?) get marked as unread.

The API endpoint I see for marking messages unread is https://zulip.com/api/update-message-flags . Is that the one the current implementation in web is using?

**Greg Price** · 2022-09-06 23:46 UTC

That endpoint takes a list of message IDs; it doesn't know anything about conversations or narrows.

**Greg Price** · 2022-09-06 23:48 UTC

What does the current web implementation do if the conversation is a long one, and there are lots of messages after the one selected -- more messages than the client currently has locally? Does it only mark unread the messages it knows about, or does it go loop through fetching more in order to mark them unread?

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-07 00:04 UTC

Yes, the web app is currently using the existing API endpoint that accepts a set of messages.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-07 00:05 UTC

Good question. It looks like it's currently doing this:

```
export function mark_as_unread_from_here(message_id) {                                
    const message_ids = message_lists.current.ids_greater_or_equal_than(message_id);  
                                                                                      
    console.info("marking as unread:", message_ids); // eslint-disable-line no-console
                                                                                      
    message_lists.current.prevent_reading();                                          
    message_flags.mark_as_unread(message_ids);                                        
}                                                                                     
```

That algorithm only considers messages present on the client.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-07 00:06 UTC

So yeah, that's a bug. In the web app, it may be hard to actually trigger, but certainly going to be an issue on mobile.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-07 00:07 UTC

Obviously there is an option to do an API request to fetch messages for the purpose, but that feels silly.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-07 00:08 UTC

One possible algorithm option would be to try to replace the set of endpoints defined here: https://zulip.com/api/mark-all-as-read with a new endpoint for "Bulk update message flags given a `GET /messages` style queryset / narrow definition and an `anchor`".

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-07 00:19 UTC

There could be some tricky perf issues around cases where you're trying to change 10K+ messages, but I assume that's not a thing that will happen often.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-07 00:20 UTC

I'd also like the response to have -- and I think we discussed this too -- some information equivalent to the `found_newest` (and for symmetry `found_oldest`) property in the /api/get-messages request. That way the client knows when it's done and can stop.

**Greg Price** · 2022-11-14 22:27 UTC

The basic thrust of that conversation, as compared with the discussion in this thread above, was a concern that the behavior of /api/mark-all-as-read is undesirable in that it asks the server to do an unbounded amount of work.

In particular, in the context of marking as *un*read, we may be asking the server to create UserMessage rows that didn't previously exist (if the request covers messages to streams the user wasn't subscribed to when they were sent, but is now). And doing so with the behavior of /api/mark-all-as-read would mean an unbounded number of those.

So we want to have the server cap the number of messages it'll act on in one such request. That requires the client to handle batching and drive the loop, which requires it to get back in the response the information it needs to do so.

**Greg Price** · 2022-11-14 22:29 UTC

We also discussed the `messages` property in the existing /api/update-message-flags responses.

It turns out this property is useless, in that its actual behavior is to just echo back the `messages` array that was in the request. And we'd like to stop returning it, because it's voluminous if there are lots of messages involved.

But existing clients, in particular mobile, do use that response property when marking messages as read, in the expectation that it does what it says and lists the messages that were actually acted on. So we have to maintain compatibility.

**Greg Price** · 2022-11-14 22:35 UTC

What I believe we settled on was:
* We'll keep sending the property for existing types of requests. We'll mark it as deprecated, and plan to remove it in the future when clients have adapted.
* We'll introduce a request parameter to say to leave it out. New clients can send that.
* We'll also leave it out when the request includes parameters that aren't currently accepted -- like `anchor` or `narrow`.

In other words, /api/update-message-flags will gain a kind of "strict mode", of much the same flavor as e.g. JavaScript's strict mode:
* The effect of strict mode is that some deprecated behaviors that only exist for compatibility (here, sending `messages`) are removed.
* One can enter strict mode by explicitly opting in.
* One can also enter strict mode by using a feature (here, sending `anchor` or `narrow` etc.) that didn't exist before strict mode was introduced.

**Greg Price** · 2022-11-16 06:47 UTC

The API calls these messages "affected", in the names `affected_count` etc. in the response. But in the normal English meaning, those messages (or UserMessage records) were not affected at all.

I think that name is OK — partly because it's common to refer to "affected rows" in the context of a database query, and there too it includes rows that matched the conditions but where a field was set to the value it already had. But if we do use that name, we should be explicit in the API docs what's happening.

**Greg Price** · 2022-11-16 06:52 UTC

Alternatively, perhaps we can come up with a set of names that avoids suggesting that misleading meaning.

Among databases, the term "affected rows" isn't universal for this concept. [PostgreSQL calls it](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/plpgsql-statements.html#PLPGSQL-STATEMENTS-DIAGNOSTICS) `ROW_COUNT`. [MS SQL Server has](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/odbc/reference/develop-app/determining-the-number-of-affected-rows?view=sql-server-ver16) "affected rows" in the prose of the docs, but `SQLRowCount` in the actual API. So we could follow that, just with s/row/message/, and say `message_count`, `first_message_id`, `last_message_id`.

**Greg Price** · 2022-11-16 06:57 UTC

Alternatively alternatively, we could change the actual behavior so that it filters the query to just the messages that don't already have the flag the way the request wants it.

But that will be an unindexed query, in general and particularly in the case of marking a wide swath of messages as unread. (As some of you know well but for others in the thread: we have an index to find your *unread* messages efficiently; but in order to keep that index nice and small, we use PostgreSQL's handy partial-index feature so that that index only covers unread messages, not read messages. So there's no index to specifically find *read* messages, the ones ripe to be marked as unread.) So I think it's probably best to skip doing that, in order to meet the goal of bounding how much work a single one of these requests can ask the server to do.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-11-16 21:46 UTC

OK @Anders Kaseorg and I had a call to talk through these considerations, and we're going with a plan where the API endpoint will pay attention to which messages already had the requested flags in the inner `do_update_message_flags` code path, which means:
* We will be able to report a count of messages that actually had their flags change (so messages that were "already read" won't be reported in this count). Any events sent by the code path will be for things that actually changed, fixing the bug where we'd potentially send events that didn't correspond to actual state changes.
* Clients that wish to show progress even if the first several batches may find no messages to change can choose to report the number of messages that were processed or the total messages that were actually changed at their discretion. I'm not yet certain what will prove the best UI for these progress indicators, but their options won't be artificially constrained by the server here.
* We're still doing the `message_fetch` style query on the exact requested narrow -- this preserves the "bounded runtime for a batch" goals of the original design. 
* The start-of-range and end-of-range ID will be for "messages matching the narrow" -- not messages that were actually modified. So we'll be using some version of `first_processed_message_id` as their variable names, not `first_affected_id`.
* Clients specifically doing a "mark all messages as read" operation can include `is:unread` in their query to optimize it. This isn't an option for "mark messages as unread from here" for correctness reasons cited in Greg's upcoming message, and wouldn't help performance anyway due to a lack of an index.

diff --git a/static/js/unread_ops.js b/static/js/unread_ops.js
index 6e3c238706..2396aeb583 100644
--- a/static/js/unread_ops.js
+++ b/static/js/unread_ops.js
@@ -23,7 +23,11 @@ let loading_indicator_displayed = false;

-        anchor: "first_unread",
+        // We use an anchor of "oldest", not "first_unread", because
+        // "first_unread" will be the oldest non-muted unread message,

+        anchor: "oldest",

## ‘to’ parameter encoding

*2022-09-13 to 2022-09-15 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/.E2.80.98to.E2.80.99.20parameter.20encoding/with/1434518)*

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-09-13 07:17 UTC

Our `POST /messages` handler (`zerver.views.message_send.send_message_backend`, `zerver.actions.message_send.extract_stream_indicator`, `zerver.actions.message_send.extract_private_recipients`) currently accepts the `to` parameter in a number of different forms:

* Stream name as a plain string: `api design`
* Stream name as a JSON-encoded string: `"api design"`
* Stream name as a JSON-encoded one-element array: `["api design"]`
* Stream ID as a JSON-encoded integer: `378`
* Stream ID as a JSON-encoded one-element array: `[378]`
* PM recipient emails as a comma-separated plain string: `alice@host,bob@host`
* PM recipient emails as a JSON-encoded comma-separated string: `"alice@host,bob@host"`
* PM recipient emails as a JSON-encoded array: `["alice@host", "bob@host"]`
* PM recipient IDs as a JSON-encoded array: `[1357, 2468]`.

Some of these, especially the JSON-encoded comma-separated string, are dumb but probably harmless. But the plain string forms could cause real problems. They’ll be misinterpreted if you try to use them to message a stream whose name collides with a valid JSON representation, such as `true`, `false`, `null`, or `2022`. They also can’t be specified in OpenAPI. I opened #22934 to avoid them in the test suite.

Do we want to go further and deprecate the plain string forms, complain about them in the server logs, and eventually remove them?

**Greg Price** · 2022-09-13 09:35 UTC

I would love to see the forms that are fundamentally buggy get removed.

**Greg Price** · 2022-09-13 09:41 UTC

We have the following hilarious code for constructing that parameter in mobile:
```js
      const to =
        item.type === 'private'
            // TODO(server-2.0): switch to numeric user IDs (#3764), not emails.
          ? recipientsOfPrivateMessage(item).map(r => r.email).join(',')
            // TODO(server-2.0): switch to numeric stream IDs (#3918), not names.
            // HACK: the server attempts to interpret this argument as JSON, then
            //   CSV, then a literal. To avoid misparsing, always use JSON.
          : JSON.stringify([streamNameOfStreamMessage(item)]);
```

I.e. we send a stream name as a JSON-encoded one-element array, or PM recipient emails as a comma-separated plain string. The reason for the JSON-encoded stream name is precisely to avoid those problems.

(The thing we need to do before switching to numeric stream IDs and user IDs is #M5102, giving a proper error message if the user tries to connect to a server so old that those won't work.)

**Greg Price** · 2022-09-13 09:42 UTC

I guess for PMs we should switch to a JSON-encoded array of emails, even before #M5102 and a JSON-encoded array of numeric IDs? How old is the server's acceptance of that form?

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-13 19:04 UTC

I think we made the decision a few years ago to not document the older forms that were not an array, with a view towards being able to remove them entirely. So hopefully there are at least not new clients being written using them.

https://zulip.com/api/send-message#parameter-to

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-13 19:07 UTC

https://zulip.com/api/changelog#changes-in-zulip-20 suggests that we added support for passing arrays of IDs in Zulip 2.0, which is older than our support cutoff (and also predates API feature levels). So I think the mobile apps can safely just use that feature without blocking on #M5102.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-09-13 19:23 UTC

The one-element array forms are silly too. Not every JSON value needs to be a container.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2022-09-13 20:00 UTC

That's quite flexible input! For ZT we're using the python lib so I assume it does automatic conversion to what's appropriate. We're migrating to ids for compose, and define these params as per our typeddict, even though the lib doesn't enforce that in mypy. While the API docs mention specific behavior, would it help to also have typeddicts or similar to pin that down for future users who use our libs?

**Greg Price** · 2022-09-14 10:46 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> https://zulip.com/api/changelog#changes-in-zulip-20 suggests that we added support for passing arrays of IDs in Zulip 2.0, which is older than our support cutoff (and also predates API feature levels). So I think the mobile apps can safely just use that feature without blocking on #M5102.

No, the point of #M5102 is that when someone does connect to an old server, we don't want to just silently give them a Zulip experience that doesn't actually work. (E.g., where messages never successfully get sent.)

That's because if we do, they're not going to blame it on their server admin not having upgraded. By definition, they will have no idea that that's even what happened -- #M5102 is what would give them that information. They're going to blame it on the Zulip app being broken.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-15 17:27 UTC

OK, makes sense. I had sorta been assuming that the number of pre-2.0 servers in the wild was dwindling enough that it might not be a material issue in practice ... but the work is important anyway, and we're not in a huge rush on this, so blocking on that is probably fine.

## event data and api response for message edit settings

*2022-09-22 to 2022-09-28 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/event.20data.20and.20api.20response.20for.20message.20edit.20settings/with/1439319)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-09-22 14:29 UTC

Currently, when we change any of the `allow_message_editing`, `message_content_edit_limit_seconds` and `edit_topic_policy` setting, the [event data](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/53015471f35b7e0994608755ddce5d54a87a72d0/zerver/actions/realm_settings.py#L157) and [api response](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/53015471f35b7e0994608755ddce5d54a87a72d0/zerver/views/realm.py#L274) contains all three setting values irrespective of whether they have actually changed.

Previously having `allow_message_editing` and `message_content_edit_limit_seconds` both made sense since both the settings were coupled with each other and were represented by a single element in webapp UI, but now both are independent settings as per [this commit](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/21837/commits/2242b96402b467e807ce1d83f1b3b5efff88ac15). One more question - whether we would like to send a single event if multiple settings are changed or do we want to send separate events for separate settings? The change expected is primarily that a correct client should offer allowing you to move messages even if `allow_message_editing` is False, if the other policy settings allow it.

## URI Template API

*2022-10-04 to 2023-04-19 · 56 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/URI.20Template.20API/with/1444496)*

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-10-04 17:34 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> Instead the ad-hoc format we use for linkifier expansions (loosely based on Python printf-style format strings with broken escaping), I found the standard we probably should be using: [RFC 6570 URI Templates](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6570.html). It has a couple of Python implementations: [p …
We are planning to add support to the standard URI Template format.
The question of how we should treat the old APIs ([add](https://chat.zulip.org/api/add-linkifier) or [update](https://chat.zulip.org/api/update-linkifier)) arises.
There are two possible solutions:
- Keep the url_format_string parameter, note that change in the documentation, and update the validation method so that only a valid URI Template will be accepted. We can transit from the old format to the new one immediately with only internal changes. The problem with this is that the old URL format string might also be valid as a URI Template, while misleading as the variables, in this case, will not be recognized.
- Add a `uri_template` parameter, and deprecate `url_format_string`. This will allow both types of formats to coexist for a longer period of time, and two code paths will be maintained at the same time.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-10-04 17:50 UTC

Now I'm thinking of another approach: either `url_format_string` and `uri_template` parameters are allowed. Whenever `url_format_string` is received, we convert that to a URI Template and always store that instead.  This allows backward compatible transition while we can fully remove the old format internally.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-04 18:34 UTC

I am not aware of any non web app clients that will add new linkifiers; if there are, they're likely not going to be hard to update. So I think it's reasonable to just desupport the old API. If it's easy to convert to `url_format_string` to a `uri_template`, I suppose that's fine, but probably `url_template` or `uri_template` will prove to be a better long-term parameter name in the API, so I'd prefer to switch to a new field name.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-10-04 19:05 UTC

We also need to decide between `url_template` and `uri_template`. `uri_template` is more about the underlying implementation for linkifier expansion, while `url_template` is more accurate in terms of how the linkifiers behave. I'm feeling that `url_template` is actually more appropriate here.

*2022-10-04 to 2022-11-07 · 43 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/new.20pronouns.20field.20type/with/1444560)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-04 18:53 UTC

So in #23135, we're adding a new custom profile field type for the first time in several years; structurally, it works exactly like the basic "short text" field type in the API, but has different typeahead behavior. 

I'm wondering to what extent existing mobile/terminal clients will work correctly on seeing a custom profile field type ID that they don't know about. My current thinking is that we should specify in the API documentation for custom profile fields what clients should do with an unknown field type (ignore it is probably fine) so that clients fail in a safe way if we add new field types in the future. 

@Greg Price @Neil Pilgrim (neiljp) FYI since this is a somewhat timely design question for including this feature in 6.0.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-04 18:55 UTC

There are other ways we can manage this particular API change if we have clients in the wild that would crash on seeing an unknown field type to still integrate the feature (we can make it subtype of "short text" field, since displaying it as a short text field should just work).

Current mobile clients will silently ignore a custom profile field that has a type they don't recognize.

(Silently to the user -- it will log a warning to Sentry.)

**Greg Price** · 2022-10-06 23:54 UTC

If we're adding this for 6.0, though, we should really try to also have actual support for it in mobile.

Having a new type of custom profile field wasn't in the plans we'd discussed before, and there isn't an issue for it in mobile (or if there is, it doesn't have the "server release goal" label.) What we had had in the plan was the feature to highlight some custom profile fields in the UI, with pronouns as the main motivating use case.

**Greg Price** · 2022-10-06 23:58 UTC

So I guess let's have that part of the API-design discussion.

It sounds like for a client that (like mobile) doesn't support editing custom profile fields, only displaying their values, this will be a new value for `type` and will otherwise behave exactly like the existing "Short text" type.

And the current implementation in #23135 makes that new `type` value be 8, the next unallocated value.

**Greg Price** · 2022-11-02 20:41 UTC

@Sahil Batra asked a pair of questions on #23309 which I replied to there, and on second thought it seems best to have them here. So, copying them now.

Sahil asked:
> * I have not added it to `client_capabilities` dict and we instead calculate it in the server code itself from `User-Agent` value.
> * Not sure how we want to document these changes and do we want to bump the `API_FEATURE_LEVEL` for this.

**Greg Price** · 2022-11-02 20:42 UTC

I replied:

> Yeah, good questions.
> 
> Adding a client capability would be the more formal way to do this. The advantage would be that arbitrary other clients, beyond just web and mobile, would get the benefit of this compatibility logic.
> 
> The cost is that it'd be one more item that modern clients have to pass in their `client_capabilities` lists forever. (Until some future where we start sunsetting those, but that itself would be a slow, multistage process.) Anyone writing a new client would have to remember to pass it, or else get this subtly quirky behavior where this one type of custom profile field, namely pronouns, doesn't show up properly.
> 
> And back on the benefits side, custom profile fields are a rather long-tail feature, which it's unlikely any client other than web, mobile, and terminal is much concerned with. (And I don't know the state of terminal's interaction with them.) So the practical cost of limiting the compatibility logic to those known clients is very low.
> 
> For those reasons, the strategy we've chosen for this particular compatibility shim is this hackier approach of just looking at the User-Agent.

**Greg Price** · 2022-11-02 20:42 UTC

and:

> Re the feature level… I'm inclined to just not document this compatibility behavior, in keeping with the fact that it's kind of a hack.
> 
> Or to perhaps put the reasoning better: from the perspective of someone consuming the API docs, writing an API client, there's nothing really actionable to do about this compatibility hack -- so there's no benefit to having it in the docs.
> 
> That's because in a client, the thing to do is to handle the Pronouns type as well as the other types described in the docs. You can't elicit the compatibility hack except by pretending in your User-Agent to be an outdated version of the Zulip mobile app… and it's really much easier to just handle Pronouns and give them the same treatment as Short Text, like the current mobile app does.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-08-09 02:05 UTC

It's worth explaining that the *reason* we do that rewriting is that we want the preview (video length, thumbnail image) to go through `go-camo` if it's an external resource, so we don't leak the user's IP.  Browsers do this by makign a `Range:` request, which Camo honors, so it's only moving a small amount of data around.

But we *don't* want to serve the whole multi-GB external resource through Camo, so we rewrite the URL to be the un-Camo'd URL upon click, and then show them the controls.  If we show the controls earlier, then the user can scrub around and pull down the data through Camo, which we'd like to avoid.

## Introducing 206 "Partial Success" response

*2022-10-24 to 2023-09-19 · 32 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/Introducing.20206.20.22Partial.20Success.22.20response/with/1454648)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2022-10-24 19:43 UTC

In #23128 we're introducing a new response type (not used in our API before) for the `/mark_all_as_read` endpoint - `206` meaning "partial success". 

Basically, the endpoint can time out while processing the request if there's too many messages to be marked as read - but it will successfully make partial progress in the meantime. So the idea is to return a response that means "partial work was done, but you need to repeat the request". 

As Tim suggested in the PR
> I think we should also discuss this explicitly in #api design; can you post a summary of the API change and get feedback on it there? I think there's a few details about the sample response (like what value we use for result -- we possibly want that to be a special "partial_success" string, rather than "success" or "error"?) that probably deserve the extra visibility.

The current response looks like this, with code `206`:
`{"result": "error", "msg": "", "code": "PARTIAL_SUCCESS"}`.

We're using `JsonableError` which implies `"result": "error"` but we could extend the class to support custom `result` strings if appropriate

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-10-24 20:47 UTC

I'm absolutely responsible for suggesting it be a `JsonableError` -- but seeing the`"result": "error"` which that causes now makes me rethink.  We can either extend JsonableError to support things that aren't errors, which seems like an odd naming choice then, or reuse the `code` logic in some other, new, class?

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-24 20:56 UTC

I think we can figure out how to make it ergonomic in the codebase; let's figure out what we want the API to be.

Looking more closely at the context: it seems to me that HTTP 206 is not appropriate here at all. 206 is for [partial content](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#status.206) specifically in response to [range requests](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#range.requests), and it’s specified with various hard requirements that do not apply to our situation, e.g. “A client MUST inspect a 206 response's Content-Type and Content-Range field(s) to determine what parts are enclosed and whether additional requests are needed”.

**Greg Price** · 2023-08-24 18:05 UTC

It looks like I missed previously that there was a proposal here to add a new `result` value, the `partially_completed` to go alongside `success` and `error`.

This is a major change, because it's a departure from what is otherwise a global property that's consistent across our whole API: the response always has a `result` property, and its value is either `success` for a 2xx response or `error` for a 4xx or 5xx response.

We document that invariant in prose here:
https://chat.zulip.org/api/rest-error-handling
and I'm not aware of any other places that we break it.

**Greg Price** · 2023-08-24 18:15 UTC

Breaking that invariant has a significant cost in that it makes the whole API more complex. Any client-side code that tries to express what a Zulip API response looks like has to add this complication, even though only two endpoints are meant to actually use it.

Alternatively, if a generic abstraction like that is written in a way that doesn't include that complication, then those two endpoints need to forgo that abstraction and be exceptions that do something else. Which also means either duplicating code from that abstraction, or giving the abstraction itself a more complicated nesting of sub-abstractions.

(This arose in the context of someone auto-generating Rust bindings, and working on tweaking both our definitions and the third-party tool consuming them to make the output more usable:
https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/412-api-documentation/topic/api.20definitions/near/1630485 )

**Greg Price** · 2023-08-24 18:18 UTC

I don't think the added option for `result` gives us something here that's worth that cost.

**Greg Price** · 2023-08-24 18:18 UTC

If we're sending a HTTP status code of 200, we should set the `result` property to `success`, like we do everywhere else in the API. For expressing further nuance about how far the success went, we can send additional properties, just as many other endpoints do on success.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-08-24 22:12 UTC

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-08-24 22:22 UTC

The server isn’t just deciding out of the blue that it can only perform part of the task the client was expecting. The API contract here is that the client expects the server to mark some slice of messages as read and report how far it got. The server is successfully upholding that contract. Hence, `{"result": "success", "complete": false}`.

## unreads in unsubscribed streams

*2022-10-28 to 2025-01-07 · 47 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/unreads.20in.20unsubscribed.20streams/with/1456527)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-28 19:14 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> I ran in another code path that would pop up that notice yesterday, that noted down as a thing to debug but hadn't had a chance to report. Specifically: * If you unsubscribe from a stream where you had had unread messages, in theory that should mark those messages as read via a background queue work …

As detailed above in the second bullet (the rest of the context is helpful), we have a quirk in the `unread_msgs` data structure in its handling of unread messages in unsubscribed streams. Specifically:

* The `unread_msgs` data structure included in `/register` does not include any unread messages in streams you are no longer subscribed to. This is consistent with the fact that we mark as read all unread messages in streams you're no longer subscribed to.
* The `message_details` data structure included in `update_message_flags` events will, if you did a "mark as unread" operation in a view that includes streams you are not subscribed to (For example, a stream narrow for a public stream, or the `streams:public` view), include the message IDs of all the messages you asked to mark as read, the `message_details` data structure currently does NOT include data for messages inside unsubscribed streams.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-28 19:14 UTC

Clearly, there's a bug here, but I'm not entirely sure where we want to make a change to fix it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-28 19:27 UTC

Structurally, there's a few properties that we want to be true, but can't all be.
* We currently have an invariant "No messages can be unread in unsubscribed streams". It is not a strong invariant -- as noted in the above discussion, the server does some processing in a queue worker; but in a way mostly invisible to clients (since the `unread_msgs` data structure from `/register` excludes messages in streams where the user is not subscribed, thus hiding that background worker detail from clients). However, this is leaky; the `GET /messages` API does not do similarly hiding of that detail.
* We also have the property one would really hope to be true that messages present in an `update_message_flags` event all appear in the `message_details` object in that event that's designed to indicate what stream/topic/etc. those messages are in, so clients can update their `unread_msgs` data structures efficiently.
* From a UI perspective, it's potentially nice if you can mark any message as unread if you can see the message.
* It'd be nice if all unread messages that clients are aware of can be found via the left sidebar; note that an unread message in a stream you're not subscribed to is hard to get to, since it won't appear in the sidebar. Though this isn't strictly required; one can have a client know about this situation and just have them be invisible in total counts (total unread mentions, for example).

@Anders Kaseorg @Alya Abbott @Greg Price FYI since this is probably relevant for all of you.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-28 19:29 UTC

There's a few options for what we can do here:

* One option is to restore the invariant that "No messages can be unread in unsubscribed streams", and thus modify the behavior of API endpoints that can mark messages as unread to ignore messages in streams you're not currently subscribed to, rather than marking all matching messages messages as unread (with the `historical` flag) if you have access to them. Clients would need to either not offer "Mark as unread" in views like `streams:public` or somehow convey to the user that we're ignoring some messages they might think of as matching what they did, or something.
* Another option is to let you mark any message you can access as unread. This probably involves including them in the `unread_msgs` data structure, and making sure all of clients handle this situation reasonably. (Unreads in a stream you're not subscribed to might not be included in any of the totals on the sidebar, but should probably display with the green "this message is unread" bars when viewing them in the UI). This is nice in some ways but also may feel weird for users who resubscribe to such a stream and just have the 10 messages that matched a search they did one time as unreads there.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-28 19:29 UTC

I don't think I've thought of other options that don't have soundness issues.

**Alya Abbott** · 2022-10-28 19:49 UTC

Thanks for laying out those details! I think we should go with a variant of option 1. Marking messages as unread in streams you are not subscribed to won't help you find them later anyway, so I don't think it's a particularly useful action to enable. (And as @Tim Abbott points out, it might be confusing if you later subscribe to the stream and unexpectedly have a smattering of unreads in it.)

So specifically, I would propose:

1. Drop the "Mark as unread" option from the three-dot menu for messages in streams you're not subscribed to.
2. "Modify the behavior of API endpoints that can mark messages as unread to ignore messages in streams you're not currently subscribed to," which will just be relevant in interleaved views.
3. As a follow-up (not a release blocker), show a notification banner whenever some messages were ignored by "Mark as unread". Something like:
- Because you are not subscribed to `#foo`, messages in this stream were not marked as unread.
- Because you are not subscribed to `#foo`, `#bar`, `#baz`, messages in these streams were not marked as unread.

## reserved feature levels

*2022-11-17 to 2026-06-01 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/reserved.20feature.20levels/with/1466779)*

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-11-17 19:46 UTC

For the 3.0, 4.0, and 5.0 releases, we bumped the API feature level with no changes, and reserved 2–4 extra feature levels for potential use by stable bugfix releases. I’m not sure why we do either of these things. If we were ever to make use of these reserved feature levels, it would violate feature level monotonicity. The right way to signal a backported API change would be with feature *flags*.

Some previous discussion: #**backend>feature levels**.

**Greg Price** · 2022-11-17 23:02 UTC

In the 3.x series, there were a couple of these that we actually used:
https://zulip.com/api/changelog#changes-in-zulip-31

I've forgotten what the story was there. Did those changes also appear in main, at the same feature levels -- so, before any other feature-level bump that we made in main?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-11-17 23:06 UTC

We had not yet branched 3.x from main at that time.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-11-17 23:08 UTC

Yeah, I think that's correct for those.

The use case for being able to insert a feature level is if we have a change of the form "The mobile app really needs X feature of the API to do Y" that we really want to backport, and it's something we can readily add, then we'd get to write in the mobile app something like this for whether the server has that feature.

`if feature_level >= 203 || 155 < feature_level < 157`

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-11-17 23:09 UTC

We can of course do that with a capabilities object of some sort, but right now we only have `client_capabilities` and a server feature level; so we'd need to implement some new `server_capabilities` mechanism (or do some less organized thing, like checking for a certain new key existing or checking the reported server version or something) instead.

**Greg Price** · 2022-11-17 23:16 UTC

Yeah, I guess in that previous discussion, my thoughts on breaking monotonicity of feature levels were (stitching together a few messages):

(replying to Greg Price)
> For the gap: if we did then put something in that gap, it would break the monotonicity assumption, that the only interesting question to ask about a feature level to tell if the server has a given feature is, is it at least some threshold. I.e. it'd mean the story is that "feature levels 26-30 and 3 …

**Greg Price** · 2022-11-17 23:16 UTC

i.e. it'd be inelegant but probably actually fine to end up writing code like the example Tim just gave

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-11-17 23:18 UTC

I think my current leaning is we should reserve a couple feature levels for now just so we can start merging commits into `main` without thinking too hard, but that we should probably design a `server_capabilities` object inside `server_settings` that can reply this hacky option, and add that as a normal API change, so that we don't have as reason to do this next time.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-11-17 23:19 UTC

I think the cost of eating a couple IDs is low and I don't want to rush into a design for that sort of API feature.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-11-17 23:20 UTC

Okay.

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-06 22:13 UTC

This came up again [on #31525](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/31525#issuecomment-2334688287).

Since the previous discussion above, it looks like we've used the reserved feature levels once, at feature level 157 in Zulip 6.2:
https://zulip.com/api/changelog#changes-in-zulip-62

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-06 22:14 UTC

I think my view is the same as described above: if a client ends up needing to check for a feature that's expressed this way, it'll be inelegant but will work fine.

**Greg Price** · 2023-08-23 20:14 UTC

I think in order to do that, what we potentially want in the server implementation is for it to make the request directly from the Django web-server process (like we do when the client wants to register a new device), rather than from a queue worker (like we ordinarily do for a notification about a message).

That will make it quite straightforward to send a success/failure result back to the client, whereas it seems like it'd be complicated to do so if the request to the bouncer is done asynchronously by a queue worker.

**Greg Price** · 2023-08-23 20:16 UTC

That would come at a certain cost in the realism of the test, though. We could have the queue worker do it and still get the result back to the client — it'd just require more work. **Tim Abbott** · 2023-08-23 21:03 UTC

Yeah. We don't want to do that for notifications in general, because cutting the queue would mean we'd have to work harder to avoid "The Zulip push bouncer is down for 5 minutes caused self-hosted Zulip servers to lose notifications during that period". 

But the "send test notification" sendpoint does not those constraints and I agree it should immediately attempt to send a notification.

@Chris Bobbe Do you have any thoughts on whether it should be the bouncer endpoint or the remote server that defines the core of the payload (`event`, `alert.title` for APNs etc.)?

My thinking has been that the remote server should just send `get_base_payload` to the bouncer (because the bouncer doesn't have that info) and the bouncer fills out the `event` and others  before sending the notification to the device. The justification being, that if it's on the bouncer, we are free to modify the format of that notification as we wish - while if it's on the remote server, then it depends on when they'll upgrade to the new code and we can end up with differing formats across versions etc.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2023-09-05 21:10 UTC

@Greg Price It's like this:

```python
def get_base_payload(user_profile: UserProfile) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Common fields for all notification payloads."""
    data: Dict[str, Any] = {}

    # These will let the app support logging into multiple realms and servers.
    data["server"] = settings.EXTERNAL_HOST
    data["realm_id"] = user_profile.realm.id
    data["realm_uri"] = user_profile.realm.uri
    data["user_id"] = user_profile.id

    return data
```

so aside of the `user_id` which the remote server should send as an arg anyway, it's all information that's not known to the bouncer otherwise (`data["server"]` should match `RemoteZulipServer.hostname` I think, but might not even be always correct if the server changed its domain after registering)

**Greg Price** · 2023-10-25 00:17 UTC

(replying to Mateusz Mandera)
> @Greg Price Can you confirm whether this extra key won't cause issues for the mobile app?

Yeah, in general the mobile app ignores extra fields in notification payloads (just as it also does for JSON objects all over the main API).

In this case, the app will already ignore these particular payloads, because the `event` field (which is oddly named, but can be read like "event type" ­— it's our "type" field for the notification payloads) is set to a new value that isn't the `message` or `remove` that the existing code expects.

That will cause parsing the payload to fail, and cause the handler to [log a warning and then drop](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-mobile/blob/0f3cbae1be0983cafc6f9571c6825b21ee164da9/android/app/src/main/java/com/zulipmobile/notifications/NotificationUiManager.kt#L93-L97) that particular notification message.

**Greg Price** · 2023-10-25 00:37 UTC

Zooming out a bit to a process level: our normal rule is that an API change isn't considered ready to merge in the server until there's at least one implementation of the client side, ideally two.

That would probably have been a helpful rule to follow here too. It's actually fairly straightforward to test client-side notification changes on Android:
https://github.com/zulip/zulip-mobile/blob/main/docs/howto/push-notifications.md#testing-client-side-changes-on-android
as well as server-side changes for both Android and iOS:
https://github.com/zulip/zulip-mobile/blob/main/docs/howto/push-notifications.md#testing-server-side-changes-ios-or-android

It's a bit more complicated when bouncer changes are involved, but still doable — the approach is to deploy the changes to the staging environment of Zulip Cloud, and then point either chat.zulip.org or a dev server at the staging bouncer.

Separately, there's a wart in this API that I missed when I reviewed it last month but would be good to fix:

The type given for these notification payloads (in the field which for historical reasons is called "event") is "test-by-device-token". That name doesn't make a ton of sense — from the client's perspective receiving the notification, it's really just a test notification and any details of how the test was triggered aren't fundamental. It's also inaccurate, because these can be triggered for all a user's devices without specifying a token.

A good value for "event" would be simply "test". That'd parallel how we have "message" for a new message, and "remove" for removing a notification.

          description: |
            The name of the custom emoji to delete.
            The emoji name can only contain letters, numbers, dashes, and spaces.
            Upper and lower case letters are treated the same, and underscores (\_)

            handles emoji).

Instead of spelling out the rules on what a Zulip emoji name can look like, I think it'd be better to have this endpoint not care what the name looks like — the only thing that matters is whether it is indeed currently the name of a custom emoji in the organization.

## JWT auth API change docs

*2023-02-03 to 2023-02-05 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/JWT.20auth.20API.20change.20docs/with/1502311)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-03 23:29 UTC

So the IETF folks are interested in seeing #24199 backported to the 6.x series. It includes a couple API changes of the form that we would usually document via an API feature level bump, though the specific changes are adding a new endpoint and changing an endpoint that was previously completely undocumented (for JWT authentication) and now is documented with a more sane interface than the original one had. It is in `main` as feature level 160, with feature level 159 being an unrelated significant migration that we definitely don't want to backport.

Fortunately, we have a practice of reserving a couple API feature levels for backported changes. I propose using API feature level 157 for "6.2 with this change backported". Thoughts?

**Greg Price** · 2023-02-04 01:12 UTC

Seems OK to me.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-02-04 01:28 UTC

This means that api level 158 and 159 will *not* support it, though, which is very weird.  ISTR @Anders Kaseorg bringing this up earlier.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-02-04 02:21 UTC

Yeah, this is where we would ideally use a feature flag, and the client-side feature detection would be “feature level ≥ 160 or feature flag `jwt_fetch_api_key` is present”.

(Although this particular feature is not one where feature detection is useful. Either you have a JWT token that you already expect the server to support, or you don’t have a token and there’s no reason to care.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-05 02:32 UTC

It's a bit weird, but a client that cares about this feature can write `api_feature_level == 157 or api_feature_level >= 160`, and that seems pretty easy to document. But I don't think anyone is going to write that code, for the reason Anders mentioned.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-02-05 06:28 UTC

Even in your weird world, that condition wouldn’t be right. The right one would be `157 <= api_feature_level < 159 or api_feature_level >= 160`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-02-05 06:29 UTC

## partially move messages as per time limit setting

*2023-02-10 to 2026-04-29 · 77 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/partially.20move.20messages.20as.20per.20time.20limit.20setting/with/1506823)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-02-10 18:01 UTC

We recently added two new settings to configure time limit for moving messages within the stream and between streams.

As discussed in #**design>time restrictions on topic editing**, we decided to change  the current behavior to not move messages that were sent before the allowed limit. I started work on this in #23906 considering we would have one setting for both moving messages within stream and between streams, so the PR is still not up-to-date, but the overall approach will remain same. Just wanted to start a discussion here about how the API will work as Tim mentioned [here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/23906#discussion_r1101990430).

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-02-10 18:08 UTC

We first decided to use a parameter like `check_time_limit_constraints` (which now TIm suggested to be something like `partial_move_if_limited`) which if passed as True will check whether the user can move all the messages as requested and raise an error.

If the parameter is passed as `False`, we would not check and move only the messages that the user is allowed to move. (The thread linked in above message has more discussion about how this API would be used by web-app). 

We also need to decide what should be the default value of the new parameter.

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-02-10 18:10 UTC

Other solution that Tim suggested in the PR is to not add an extra parameter and just raise error if user tries to move messages that they are not allowed to and include the first message ID that they can move in the error message. And then the client sends another request with that particular message ID as anchor and `propagate_mode` set to `change_later`.

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-02-10 18:16 UTC

Would appreciate feedback and suggestions.

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-03-03 02:35 UTC

(1)  API will accept a boolean parameter like `partial_move_if_limited`. If this parameter is set as `False`, the API will return an error if some of the messages that are requested to move are old and cannot be moved due to time limit. If the parameter is set to `True`, the old messages will be ignored and the allowed messages will move to the new topic or stream as requested. 

The client behavior in such case would be the client will first send `partial_move_if_limited=False` and a modal will be opened if API returns error showing information abount count of messages that are allowed to move. Clicking on `Confirm` in the modal will send `partial_move_if_limited=True`.

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-03-03 02:37 UTC

(2) There will be no extra parameter sent to API. If all of the messages are not allowed to move, the API will return error along with the first message ID that is allowed to move. The client will then be expected to send that new message ID as `anchor` to the API.

The client behavior would be to show the modal in case API returns error and then clicking on `Confirm` should sent the request with the messaeg ID received with the error response.

If we want to present the modal again, then I think it would be better to use (2). In (1), we pass `partial_move_if_limited=True` which just ignores the part of raising error and will silently move only the allowed message.

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-04-03 07:46 UTC

We currently pass 3 parameters in the error response -
- `first_message_allowed_to_move` - ID of the first message which is allowed to move as per time limit. This is sent so that we can send a new request with this ID as the anchor and `change_later` proagate mode using the modal in webapp.
- `total_messages_in_topic `- Number of messages the user tried to move to show in the modal content. For streams without access to history, this only contains the messages that user is allowed to see.
- `messages_allowed_to_move` - Number of messages the user is allowed to move to show in the modal content.

The current behavior for returning the  `MOVE_MESSAGES_TIME_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` error code with other data like count of messages and the ID of first message that the user can move, is when the target message, i.e. the message with which the user made the request, has not passed the time limit. We explain the current beahvior currently in the error response here https://zulip.com/api/update-message#response.

I was thinking we should return the `MOVE_MESSAGES_TIME_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` even when the target message has passed the time limit but user can still move some messages in the topic since the user's request was eventually to move the whole topic. Any thoughts if we should do this?

## realm string_id

*2023-02-16 to 2023-02-22 · 25 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/realm.20string_id/with/1508900)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-02-16 19:20 UTC

I don't think we're exposing the realm's `string_id` via `page_params` or any other means right now.  We expose `realm_uri` but you can't just take the leftmost part of the domain name, since that'll be wrong for sites with only one realm, and it'll also be wrong for `chat.fhir.org`.

Any objections to adding a `realm_string_id`?  My goal is to use it in client-side error reporting, in part to provide the same tags as the server side does, but also just in general for error segmentation.

**Greg Price** · 2023-02-16 21:34 UTC

That sounds reasonable but I'd want us to expand a bit on what it's supposed to mean, and perhaps adjust the name in light of that.

**Greg Price** · 2023-02-16 21:34 UTC

What is the `string_id` for a realm like `chat.fhir.org`?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-02-16 21:53 UTC

For those who don't know, chat.fhir.org is hosted on Zulip Cloud but CNAME'd, with some additional configuration on the zulip Cloud side to support the additional hostname.  So one can access it either via https://fhir.zulipchat.com/ or https://chat.fhir.org/, and its `realm.string_id` is `fhir` on both.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-02-16 21:53 UTC

`string_id` is unique for all realms on a server.  However, due to things like CNAME'ing, it may not be evident what is actually the "same" server.

**Greg Price** · 2023-02-16 22:10 UTC

(replying to Alex Vandiver)
> For those who don't know, chat.fhir.org is hosted on Zulip Cloud but CNAME'd, with some additional configuration on the zulip Cloud side to support the additional hostname. So one can access it either via https://fhir.zulipchat.com/ or https://chat.fhir.org/, and its `realm.string_id` is `fhir` on b …

(Further, the `realm_uri` is also the same value on both:
```
$ curl -sS https://fhir.zulipchat.com/api/v1/server_settings | jq .realm_uri -r
https://chat.fhir.org
$ curl -sS https://chat.fhir.org/api/v1/server_settings | jq .realm_uri -r
https://chat.fhir.org
```
)

**Greg Price** · 2023-02-16 22:16 UTC

I'm thinking about what kinds of uses a client could have for this value. I think it has to always be something specific to dealing with a particular server, because these identifiers really have meaning only in the context of the particular server's internal operation.

And it's not needed for anything where the client talks *to* the server, because then it just talks to the server, and the HTTP `Host` header tells the server what realm it's talking about.

So it's talking to some other service, but in a way that's specific to that Zulip server. Like your current use case of reporting errors to the server's admins, via some separate error-reporting service that the Zulip server admins have set up.

**Greg Price** · 2023-02-16 22:17 UTC

How are you thinking you'll tell the client what error-reporting service it should be talking to? I wonder if this can be usefully thought of as part of the configuration of that.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-02-16 22:32 UTC

We're using Sentry, where the configuration for that uses a "DSN":
https://docs.sentry.io/platforms/javascript/configuration/options/

But that's set per-*server*, not per-*realm*, so it makes sense to build into the webpack'd Javascript.  The realm needs to be obtained from the realm.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-02-16 22:33 UTC

The rest of the "configuration" is things like pulling the user-id out of `page_params`, or the user's role.  Hence why it feels like it makes sense to look for the realm identification from there as well.

**Greg Price** · 2023-02-16 22:44 UTC

OK, so the information of "use Sentry, and in particular talk to sentry.io using this DSN" would be built right into the webpack'd JavaScript.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-02-16 22:47 UTC

It's that or put it in `page_params` as well, as part of the server configuration.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-02-16 22:48 UTC

Though the DSN is specific to Javascript reporting -- i.e. we don't want to imply that mobile clients should use the same DSN for error reporting, since generally Sentry segements into different projects (and thus DSNs) by codebase.

**Greg Price** · 2023-02-16 22:49 UTC

I'm kind of tempted to say that in that case, the best way to handle this piece of information would be to put it into `page_params`, but not into the Zulip server API. That is, there's some code that the particular server is choosing to inject into this particular client (the web client), and so the `page_params` that it sends to the web client is colluding with that by including some data that code needs.

**Greg Price** · 2023-02-16 22:49 UTC

IIRC I think we have a handful of such things already.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-20 16:24 UTC

Yeah I agree that probably belongs in the page params, probably with a name that indicates it's purpose (Sentry DSN?), even if it happens to match the string_id, which is intended to be an internal to the server implementation detail.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-02-21 16:23 UTC

I'm not sure what your "(Sentry DSN?)" parenthetical is implying -- if you're suggesting that as a name for the `string_id` in `page_params`, the Sentry DSN is different value (`https://bbb@bbb.ingest.sentry.io/1234`) we also need to send.  We can either send the DSN in `page_params` or build it into the compiled webpack.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-21 18:13 UTC

For the web app, taking the server's instructions for where to send Sentry reports makes sense because the code is itself coming from the server.

But for the mobile app, the code whose issues are being reported to Sentry is the same regardless of the server. So I wouldn't want to switch to taking those instructions from the server; we currently bake them into the app, and that makes sense to continue.

The first change, which I think is relatively straightforward, is to make the search backend support the new names (and treat the old ones as aliases).  Concretely in the server implementation, this probably involves taking the somewhat magic/overly clever logic where we determine a function to call to filter on a given search keyword using `method_name = "by_" + operator.replace("-", "_")` and just changing it to a dictionary mapping operator names to functions with `by_` in their name, or something sensible like that, having both the old and new names work, and documenting the API change.

The second change, which is where things are likely to get messy, is changing logic where we __generate__ a narrow URL to . The reason this is messy as an API change is that clients like the mobile apps parse narrow URLs containing tokens like `/pm-with/`, and we don't want to break those clients' ability to handle links.

**Greg Price** · 2023-03-02 01:50 UTC

While we did put attention into making this work when designing our URL structure, I don't think it's very common to send around a link to a group PM conversation.
