## duplicate request to update UserTopic row

*2023-03-07 to 2023-03-15 · 21 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/duplicate.20request.20to.20update.20UserTopic.20row/with/1519868)*

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2023-03-07 16:11 UTC

The discussion is regarding: [(comment)](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/24236#issuecomment-1457423519)
**Should we do nothing or raise Error, if there is a duplicate request to update `UserTopic` row?**
---
**Little Background**
 * **What if the topic already has the target visibility policy**

1. Initially, we had two checks for duplicates: [(comment)](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/21535#issuecomment-1416697323)
```
# Topic muting
    if topic_is_muted(user_profile, stream.id, topic_name):
        raise JsonableError(_("Topic already muted"))

    try:
        do_mute_topic(user_profile, stream, topic_name, date_muted)
    except IntegrityError:
        raise JsonableError(_("Topic already muted")
```
2. [bd80e484](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/24354/commits/bd80e4847c5e826454824cb6644c76978d8a426c#diff-b29cc2e41beb0253c91f84321a36c2ba0d581746db762216ec626ae6ac8ffb08L38) removes the first check, which is actually not needed.

3. Finally, in #24236.
We decide to raise JsonableError from [`set_user_topic_visibility_policy_in_database`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/24236/commits/1943accb30149826fa736d291832124add8b4f1a#diff-97e4a396cdf669d3e133f04bc7fe98e0057cc6eece60ef2aa80ea3fd40a9eb3bR149).

Reason: Earlier (before UserTopic.UNMUTE) we had to just Create or db raised Integrity Error.

Now, we have to manually `create/update/Integrity-Error` depending on the situation.
So, instead of manually raising Integrity Error, we directly raise JsonableError.

---
Discussion needed:
As [mentioned](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/24236#issuecomment-1457423519) by @Tim Abbott 

* The other big semantic thing that probably deserves discussion in "api design" is what we want the long-term semantics to be around "What if the topic already has the target visibility policy"
> Often it's a cleaner API to just do nothing than return an error, since, for example, a repeated request due to some client-side retry race would just have both calls 200, rather than the first 200 and then the second fail (and thus generate a user-facing error when in fact the right thing happened).

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2023-03-07 16:14 UTC

@Tim Abbott 's statement makes sense.

I'm curious about the possible cases in this scenario, where raising Error is beneficial?  -- if any?

**Greg Price** · 2023-03-07 18:11 UTC

Yeah, if the client asks to set the visibility policy to some value and it's already that value, that should just be an easy success, not an error.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-03-07 20:58 UTC

Given the agreement here, @Prakhar Pratyush perhaps you can do a PR that's a documented API change for this little tweak in semantics -- I think it'll let us simplify things significantly, since in particular that error handling logic is one of the main differences between the "mute" and "unmute" branches.

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2023-03-13 10:43 UTC

Re 1., why do we need to disallow setting a visibility policy for a topic with no messages? Is it to handle cases where a bad API user tries to flood up the `UserTopic` table with random topic names?

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2023-03-13 12:30 UTC

>  Is it to handle cases where a bad API user tries to flood up the UserTopic table with random topic names?

Yes, that is one of the reasons.

Also,
Logically, topic names in `UserTopic` table should be a subset of the topics created during message-send (first message).


> why do we need to disallow setting a visibility policy for a topic with no messages?

When all the messages in a Topic are deleted, the topic itself is deleted. (To be precise: deleted by those having permission to do so, not the (deleted) text). 

So, I think there's no point in having topics with some visibility_policy, if they actually don't even exist.

**Greg Price** · 2023-03-13 21:01 UTC

(replying to Prakhar Pratyush)
> 2. As we are planning to not raise an error on a duplicate request to change visibility_policy. Similarly, we shouldn't [raise any error](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/zerver/lib/user_topics.py#L133) when there is a request (visibility_policy=INHERIT) to delete the UserTopic row and the U …

Agreed, this should work on the same principle.

**Greg Price** · 2023-03-13 21:07 UTC

(replying to Prakhar Pratyush)
> Logically, topic names in `UserTopic` table should be a subset of the topics created during message-send (first message).

This is an invariant we won't maintain in general, because messages can be moved or deleted.

For a bad API user, there are better solutions like rate limits. And if someone's determined to create a lot of rows, I don't think restricting to topics that have an existing message will have much effect.

From the other direction, there can be legitimate use cases for pre-emptively unmuting a topic before anyone's sent messages to it. For example, perhaps you have some code that goes and sets up some webhook integration, and then immediately unmutes for you the topic that it's going to send to. The integration may not have sent any messages there yet, but you nevertheless know exactly where it will send them, so the request makes perfect sense.

**Greg Price** · 2023-03-13 21:08 UTC

So in short there should be no requirement that the topic already have messages in it when creating a UserTopic record.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2023-03-17 18:57 UTC

Documentation-wise, that seems to cover it :+1:

I've just opened #T1329 to wrap the parameter-passing for ZT, which will default to no notifications on moves within a topic. That's an easy enough default behavior to change, but without that PR we're just relying on the server defaults, so this normalizes that.

Personally I find it odd to update an entire topic and end up with a trailing notification, particularly if I misspell a couple of times and end up with multiple notifications - but that's a client-side decision. I understand the need to move forward to an improved API, eg. prompt integrations/bots to have good defaults, but the unexpected change in behavior with no parameters is not great, minimal as this is. I can imagine situations where the topic might be updated repeatedly by bots to show the current status (akin to (un)resolving), and this could generate lots of spurious notifications.

**Greg Price** · 2023-03-20 18:43 UTC

(replying to Neil Pilgrim (neiljp))
> I can imagine situations where the topic might be updated repeatedly by bots to show the current status (akin to (un)resolving), and this could generate lots of spurious notifications.

Yeah. Thinking about the question of what the defaults *should* be: I think a good angle on this in general is that the defaults should be what we would want a simple hacky bot to end up doing, and/or the behavior that someone writing a simple ad-hoc bot (on the scale of a little shell script invoking `curl`) would most likely want.

By contrast it doesn't much matter whether the default at the API level resembles the behavior we'd want to be the default inside the UI of a full-blown client like Zulip's web or mobile or terminal clients. Those clients are going to explicitly choose the behavior that's appropriate for them.

And in this instance, as you say, I think that angle points to the right API-level default being to not send notifications. (Even though the right user-facing default, in a UI where the user is moving messages, may be different.)

**Joseph Ho** · 2023-04-01 02:46 UTC

In #24309, we are introducing a new user setting that is currently called `do_not_mark_messages_as_read`, which we can use to determine whether or not we should automatically mark messages as read when a user scrolls through their feed.

One issue that Tim pointed out is that the web and mobile apps may want the same or different configurations. Another issue that was pointed out is that the name sounds like we'll never mark messages as read. This is confusing and we should determine a better naming for this field. (replying to Joseph Ho)
> We should decide whether or not we want the same configurations on both apps and if this field should controll the behaviour on both apps.

This is an example of a setting where it's quite likely someone will want different behavior on mobile vs. web, because of the different physical contexts: if you use mobile to quickly check on some things, but then want to usually use your desktop's nice big screen and real keyboard (with the web/desktop app) to take care of things that call for action from you, then it makes sense to have mobile leave things unread until you explicitly mark them read.

## user ID in fetch-api-key

*2023-04-04 to 2023-04-04 · 13 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/user.20ID.20in.20fetch-api-key/with/1540592)*

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-04 00:08 UTC

I'd like the /api/fetch-api-key endpoint to gain one more property in the response: namely the user's user ID.

Currently it tells you the user's API key (that's the main purpose of the endpoint) and also their email (which is often the same thing that the client already passed as the "username", but can be different in the case of LDAP.)

In general we've been migrating over the years for the API to be in terms of the stable numeric user IDs, rather than email addresses. For that reason, it's useful for the client to know the user ID associated with an account, even when it doesn't remember much else.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-04 00:08 UTC

In particular, I'd like the mobile client (and in particular the Flutter-based mobile client, where I'm working on this area right now) to know the user ID by the time it first records the account in its accounts table, at the conclusion of the login flow. That way, that can be a required column of the table, and not something that we have to leave nullable and have to keep handling the potential absence of.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-04 00:09 UTC

So the cleanest way to do that would be to have the user ID returned in the /api/fetch-api-key response, alongside the API key and the email.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-04 00:10 UTC

Pending that (and for existing server versions that don't have it), the workaround I plan to apply is to add a fetch to /api/get-own-user and just pluck out the user ID from that. That adds a round trip, which isn't a catastrophe but would be nicer to avoid.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-04 00:22 UTC

This seems easy and a good idea.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-04 00:28 UTC

Cool. I'll file an issue.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-04 00:30 UTC

Thanks!

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-04 00:31 UTC

#24980

In the latter case, editable by admins might be the best policy?

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-04 05:52 UTC

The API currently allows administrators to edit other users' custom profile fields, yes; and it's accessible in the settings UI as well.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-04 23:56 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-05 02:31 UTC

## hotspots / onboarding steps

*2023-04-11 to 2023-12-04 · 46 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/hotspots.20.2F.20onboarding.20steps/with/1545341)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-11 16:48 UTC

In #25040, @Lalit has done some initial work towards making our existing Hotspots API / data model something that can be used a bit more flexibly for onboarding state. I wanted to start a thread about what we wanted that part of the system to look like long term.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-11 16:48 UTC

One thought is that we might want to rename them to something more generic like `OnboardingSteps` -- so that the name doesn't encode a specific visual display display design for them.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-11 16:49 UTC

And it's possible that while thinking about that, we want to think about naming patterns and the like that might support this being used for other clients.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-11 16:51 UTC

Structurally, what the existing API is is a system where we have defined in the server a set of objects describing named onboarding steps -- things like "Saw the introduction to topics" widget, with a simple table to store which have been done:
```
class UserHotspot(models.Model):                            
    user = models.ForeignKey(UserProfile, on_delete=CASCADE)
    hotspot = models.CharField(max_length=30)               
    timestamp = models.DateTimeField(default=timezone_now)  
                                                            
    class Meta:                                             
        unique_together = ("user", "hotspot")               
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-11 16:51 UTC

And then there's a set of definitions of what hotspot objects exist:
```
INTRO_HOTSPOTS: List[Hotspot] = [                                           
    Hotspot(                                                                
        name="intro_streams",                                               
        title=gettext_lazy("Catch up on a stream"),                         
        description=gettext_lazy(                                           
            "Messages sent to a stream are seen by everyone subscribed "    
            "to that stream. Try clicking on one of the stream links below."
        ),                                                                  
    ), 
    ...
}                                                                     
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-11 16:52 UTC

And the server sends to the client the set of declared hotspots that do not appear in the `UserHotspot` table (items there represent things that have been completed).

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-11 16:53 UTC

I don't want to overfocus on the existing API -- fundamentally it's just a place the web application currently uses to store onboarding state -- but it's worth pointing out it has a couple problems, including that the implementation is split between the web app and the server codebase in a pretty tightly linked fashion.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-11 16:54 UTC

The frontend then has the other half of the implementation in a `HOTSPOT_LOCATIONS` object, that has describes the DOM elements and configuration for how to display the content in a popover:

``` js
    [                              
        "intro_topics",            
        {                          
            element: ".topic-name",
            offset_x: 0.8,         
            offset_y: 0.39,        
        },                         
    ],                             
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-11 16:55 UTC

I think conceptually, one thing we should do is just move the strings from the server blob to the client-side blob; I'm pretty sure that's some ancient legacy (this system was written like 9 years ago and we've mostly avoided touching it since).

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-11 16:56 UTC

But I'd like to think a bit more broadly about what the right structure is for this.

**Lalit** · 2023-04-11 16:57 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> One thought is that we might want to rename them to something more generic like `OnboardingSteps` -- so that the name doesn't encode a specific visual display display design for them.
Yeah, I also think we should settle on a more generic name.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-11 16:57 UTC

I do think we need a system to support the server keeping track of what onboarding steps the user have completed, so that we're not stuck showing all the tutorial/onboarding content every time you open the mobile apps on a new device, for example.

**Lalit** · 2023-04-11 16:58 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> The frontend then has the other half of the implementation in a `HOTSPOT_LOCATIONS` object, that has describes the DOM elements and configuration for how to display the content in a popover: ``` js [ "intro_topics", { element: ".topic-name", offset_x: 0.8, offset_y: 0.39, }, ], ```

Also, to note that it might not always be the case that we would want to show some onboarding steps in a popover.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-11 16:59 UTC

Right, I think logically the data model is what this thing is -- a place for clients to store certain keys (like `intro_topics` in this case) and have the server keep track of which it has stored, and report that to the client.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-11 17:03 UTC

There's some tension around the design of this sort of thing. In an ideal world, the server wouldn't need to have any registry or what values are valid, so that clients like mobile can use this feature without having to coordinate with the server version. But it's also nice in other settings to have some server-side validation. I think the former consideration is probably more important?

There's also a question of whether we want this to be more generic than just "onboarding steps"; there might be other things that are very similar that we might want to support, like "has the user seen this notice about new Zulip features", though one can certainly imagine a feature like that working via Zulip messages rather than this system.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-11 17:07 UTC

But I think what I'm coming towards as an API design concept is:
* Clients can store values in a `ClientSteps` table, which is basically a set of strings.
* The server API just sends the set of `ClientSteps` objects that have been stored there, with clients responsible for comparing with which ones have already been "done" and the like.
* Clients are encouraged to use a name like `web_intro_topics` prefixed by the client type, to avoid conflicts. Or maybe we have a separate field for the client type, but I feel like it might be useful for the mobile clients to have the information as to whether `web_intro_topics` has been shown or not.
* Do we need some plan for how to limit rogue clients from filling up their `ClientSteps` table with garbage? Possibly not beyond our usual rate limiting, but I suppose we could not let you have more than 100 of these.

**Lalit** · 2023-04-11 17:09 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> There's also a question of whether we want this to be more generic than just "onboarding steps"; there might be other things that are very similar that we might want to support, like "has the user seen this notice about new Zulip features", though one can certainly imagine a feature like that workin …

I think making this system generic might be a good idea because there can be a lot of "has the user seen this thing before" states which we need to manage for a user?

**Lalit** · 2023-04-11 17:14 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> * Do we need some plan for how to limit rogue clients from filling up their `ClientSteps` table with garbage? Possibly not beyond our usual rate limiting, but I suppose we could not let you have more than 100 of these.
We could maybe do a server-side validation to check for valid `ClientSteps` strings?

**Lalit** · 2023-04-11 17:15 UTC

But I guess that will again mean tight coupling between clients and server.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-11 23:45 UTC

Right, I think any server-side validation might be fine for webapp usage, but certainly wouldn't make sense for mobile/terminal usage. So I think it's maybe a question of whether other clients would find this sort of thing being part of the API in a sane way more useful; or whether we should just do what is expedient for the web app codebase.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-11 23:45 UTC

#25040 is probably a useful step forward towards making the web app codebase support a saner API here regardless, but it'd be nice to figure out a bit more about where we're going directionally.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-11 23:54 UTC

I think if we implement a feature like this at some point in the mobile app, I'd be happy to have it backed by just local storage on the device.

That makes it easier to think about the possible states the state can be in. It also fits naturally with sharing the onboarding state across different accounts the user might log into, which is the way I think we'd want it to work from a product perspective.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-12 16:52 UTC

**Lalit** · 2023-04-12 17:43 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)

    if (delivery_type == "send_later" or delivery_type == "remind") and defer_until is not None:

    if scheduled_message_id is not None:

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-12 19:38 UTC

So for a bit of background, the API in `main` for `POST /messages` has for multiple years had the 4 parameters related to scheduling a message present, including `delivery_type` and `defer_until`; basically legacy from when we thought we could do these features without all the extra work to let you edit/manage them, and had a working version that we decided not to integrate because of those concerns. (There's support for both "remind me of this message" and "send later" in that existing API). It's all marked as `documentation_pending` because we hadn't decided on that API.

We should feel free to change any of those details about how to send a scheduled message, since no API clients have UI using that old existing support, but I figure it's worth providing that context for why @Aman (amanagr) started this thread just talking about the API to view, edit, and deleted scheduled messages; the "schedule a message in the first place part" already existed when he started working on it.

``` python
@has_request_variables                                                                        
def send_message_backend(                                                                     
    request: HttpRequest,                                                                     
    user_profile: UserProfile,                                                                
    message_type_name: str = REQ("type"),                                                     
    req_to: Optional[str] = REQ("to", default=None),                                          
    topic_name: Optional[str] = REQ_topic(),                                                  
    message_content: str = REQ("content"),                                                    
    local_id: Optional[str] = REQ(default=None),                                              
    queue_id: Optional[str] = REQ(default=None),                                              
    delivery_type: str = REQ("delivery_type", default="send_now", documentation_pending=True),
    defer_until: Optional[str] = REQ("deliver_at", default=None, documentation_pending=True), 
    tz_guess: Optional[str] = REQ("tz_guess", default=None, documentation_pending=True),      
    time: Optional[float] = REQ(default=None, converter=to_float, documentation_pending=True),
) -> HttpResponse:                                                                            
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-12 19:40 UTC

I think one of the major questions in my mind is whether we're better off doing the sending/editing via a `POST /scheduled_messages` endpoint; it'd share maybe 2/3 of the parameters of `send_message_backend`, and not much of the actual implementation; right now there's a bit of parsing logic that's shared, but mostly they just call different functions.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-12 19:45 UTC

I think the answer is probably yes; one possible plan for that would be to merge #23670 using the existing API for scheduling a message in parallel with, and make it a 7.0 release goal to split creating/editing scheduled messages to its own API endpoint with better names for all the existing parameters. 

#23670 is already very complex with ~1200 lines of changes, and I kind don't want to entangle it further with adding another complicated migration to it; and I think it'd be perfectly reasonable for clients that support "send later" to just not offer it for versions before 7.0 final; it'll likely be just a couple weeks' worth of Git history where it exists in the UI but has this older API. (I think that'll probably be a better use of our time than documenting the old `POST /messages` API?).

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-12 19:52 UTC

So I think the big questions for #23670 in my mind are:
* Do we like the API for `DELETE /scheduled_messages/{id}` for cancelling a "Send later".
* Do we like the API for `GET /scheduled_messages` for removing these.
* Do we want to split out a separate endpoint for `POST /scheduled_messages` rather than having it be a flag on the main "send a message" endpoint? If we don't, then we might want to spend a lot more time discussing the exact details of how this should interact with the rest of the endpoint.

For that third question, I'm not sure what the answer is. While I think we want a very parallel API in terms of how we encode things like message content and where you're sending to, it seems to me like most of the actual implementation on both client and server sides will be in different `if` statement branches regardless, because how we manage things like local echo and thus whether we need a `local_id` parameter and how that might work will certainly be different between normal messages and scheduled messages (the latter currently has none; one can imagine a future feature where we display messages you have scheduled at the bottom of conversation views).

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-12 19:57 UTC

The other question we should have in the back of our minds is how "remind me of this message" should work from an API perspective. Right now, the server-side implementation of that feature involves basically the same data structures as "send later" -- a stored message object to be sent in the future by Notification Bot, so I think it probably does make sense to share implementation with it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-12 19:59 UTC

But possibly it deserves its own API endpoint anyway. The only thing the API should really need to request one is a `(message_id, time specification)`, and it might want to grow additional features that may or may not be unique to it, like "Is the reminder a PM or a message to the conversation itself", "Cancel the reminder if someone sends a message to the conversation", etc.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-28 19:15 UTC

Looking at #25318, a couple of small notes that don't fit in the existing more-specific topics:

* The draft operation ID for create/edit is "create-or-update-scheduled-messages". That should be in the singular — it operates on a single scheduled message at a time.

  The operation ID is salient because it's what turns into the method/function name in any generated binding from the OpenAPI description. We don't yet auto-generate such bindings, because last we tried, our use of OpenAPI was quirky enough that it didn't produce good results. But I'd like us to in the future, and recently I've made a practice of using the operation IDs for our hand-written bindings. The operation ID is also what appears in the docs URL.

  Unlike event types, I think we have been pretty consistent about keeping operation IDs singular when their meaning is singular.

* An operation ID of "create-or-update-scheduled-messages" is pretty long, even without the trailing "s". It'd mean a method name like `createOrUpdateScheduledMessage`, or `create_or_update_scheduled_message`.

  I'd prefer to pick one verb there, even if the meaning is a bit of a fudge.

* But also: do we want a single endpoint combining these actions? I think the more typical thing would be to have one endpoint to create, and another to update.

  In particular, in this draft the `type` and `to` and `content` and timestamp are all required, even when you're just updating. That seems unergonomic. If I'm updating, I'd prefer to be able to only specify the parts that are relevant — e.g., only edit the timestamp and not have to recite the whole content again, or only edit the content and not have to recite the list of recipients again. In fact if I have to recite all those again, I'd become concerned about races and bugs.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-28 19:16 UTC

* In create/edit, the `to` accepts users by ID or email, but streams only by ID. If we're accepting users by email (which can be convenient for some integrations), I think all the same reasons point to accepting streams by name; so it'd be good to accept streams by name too.

* On edit, we may get an explicit timestamp from the client, or the client may leave the timestamp untouched. If we get an explicit timestamp, validate it the same way as on create — if in the past, reject.

  But if the client isn't specifying the timestamp, and the timestamp is already in the past, then I think it'd make sense to interpret the client's intent as "please send this fixed message ASAP", and proceed accordingly. Which, reading between the lines above, I think may mean updating the timestamp in the database so that it's now (instead of in the past).

I'd kinda expect a client that was offering UI for editing these to want to make you pick a time in the future for your previously scheduled message while you're working on it before submitting the request to the server, since if you wanted to just send it now, you could have used the "unschedule and bring to compose box" option instead.

**Greg Price** · 2023-11-04 02:49 UTC

I'm happy for the field to have gone away — as we discussed above, the API is better this way, and there wasn't any compatibility issue because we weren't using it. (Plus from [commit bd2545b0d](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/commit/bd2545b0d#diff-7d09c06f7ab16ed46eeff8eb6e1a342f75fc9f3c780c6f10643303145316581eL5789-L5795) which removed it, it looks like it was clearly labeled as unstable before it was removed.)

But I guess this serves as an occasion to mention that even when there's no compatibility issue when something's removed, it's valuable to us as consumers of the API docs to have an explicit tombstone for it: an explicit record that it had been there in the past, and stopped being there at a certain point.

**Greg Price** · 2023-11-04 02:57 UTC

That's because we have existing code — our API bindings most of all, but potentially also code that invokes those bindings — that reflects an understanding of what the API was up to some point in the past. And whenever we consult the API docs, if there's a discrepancy between the docs and our code, we'll want to understand what that means in order to work out what to do with it:
* Did something change in the API?
* If so, what precisely was the change? (This affects what further implications there might be for other code of ours that should be updated for the change.)
* And when precisely did the change happen? (This affects any compatibility conditionals we might need; and it lets us know when we can simplify away any complications, like making types non-nullable instead of nullable, even if the code itself had no need to condition on the feature level.)
* Alternatively, was there something we'd just had incorrect all along? (In which case there again might be further implications for other code we should change.)

In order to work that out, it's valuable to be able to see from the API docs that yes, what's in our code does faithfully reflect what the API was at a certain point in the past; and then from that starting point, such-and-such has changed, which we can then reflect in our bindings.

So that's why "**Changes**" notes and API changelog entries are valuable for us even when we never actually used the old feature, and (as in this case) will never want to use the old feature even on servers that had it. So long as the old state of things was visible in the API docs, we may have it reflected in our API bindings, and that makes it something where we want to understand the history of changes.

If we need only a small subset of the data that can be given a simple description, then we may be able to describe the API in the normal way, as an explicit set of properties with explicit structure and meaning.     "state": {
      "description": "State of the issue; either 'open' or 'closed'",
      "type": "string",
      "examples": [
        "open"
      ]
    },
    "state_reason": {
      "description": "The reason for the current state",
      "type": [
        "string",
        "null"
      ],
      "enum": [
        "completed",
        "reopened",
        "not_planned",
        null
      ],
      "examples": [
        "not_planned"
      ]
    },
```

In particular GitHub shows a `closed`/`completed` issue with a purple circled-checkmark icon, but a `closed`/`not_planned` issue with a gray circled-slash.

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-12 20:41 UTC

In the case where the upstream (like GitHub) is down, or where the upstream is refusing to answer because the Zulip server has hit its rate limit, I think the key thing is probably actually — returning to a previous idea in this thread — to set an appropriate HTTP status code. :smile: 

Specifically, in those cases, the client has made a perfectly good request, where there's nothing the client should have done differently; the only thing wrong is on the server side. (Possibly not really the *Zulip* server's fault specifically, and GitHub's instead; but even then, from the client's perspective, that's just another backend layer that the Zulip server is relying on, and that detail is the server's business.) The HTTP status code should therefore be in the 5xx range, not the 4xx range that we usually use.

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-12 20:45 UTC

Perhaps 503, "Service Unavailable":
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#status.503
or 504, "Gateway Timeout".

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-12 20:46 UTC

Then we can combine that with still giving a well-formed Zulip API error blob, with a Zulip API error code, as in /api/rest-error-handling .

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-12 20:46 UTC

Perhaps a new code with a name like `EXTERNAL_SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE`?

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-12 20:50 UTC

I think affecting an availability metric is appropriate — a backend service the server is relying on is down or is refusing to respond, and that's causing an outage of a user-visible feature.

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-12 20:50 UTC

One thing the operator can do is adjust the cache lifetime of the data gotten from GitHub. That's a trade-off between freshness and availability, which the operator can make.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-05-12 20:53 UTC

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-04-17 17:53 UTC

A question that occurs to me is why we have `realm_uri` at all. The client already knows what URL it connected to. Maybe this was intended as some kind of redirect mechanism? But HTTP already has redirects, so barring some kind of historical HTTP client API limitation on mobile preventing the use of HTTP redirects that I imagine would be fixed by now, we should just use those.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-04-17 18:01 UTC

Or maybe it was used as a check that the server is really Zulip, but now `zulip_version` is much better for that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-17 21:37 UTC

Hmm, good question. I don't think it was intended as a redirect mechanism.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-17 21:49 UTC

We do rely on it as a way of getting a canonical name for the realm. I think that purpose could be served by an HTTP redirect, but we'd need to build that.

In particular, when we get a mobile push notification, that isn't in direct response to any HTTP request we made, so we don't inherently know what realm it was from. We rely on the `realm_uri` field in the notification payload to tell us that. For that to work properly, when we're logging into a realm we need the server to tell us what it uses as the realm's canonical URL, because that's the one the server will use when it sends a notification.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-17 21:51 UTC

In many cases that canonicalization is something the client could do offline from just looking at the URL, but not all. In particular:
```
$ curl -s https://fhir.zulipchat.com/api/v1/server_settings | jq .realm_uri -r
https://chat.fhir.org
```

So if a user types `fhir.zulipchat.com` into the URL field to log into Zulip, we're going to get push-notification payloads that say `"realm_uri": "https://chat.fhir.org"`. Looking at the `realm_uri` in the /api/get-server-settings response is what we rely on in order to understand those.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-04-17 21:56 UTC

Yeah, that’s what I had in mind when saying “redirect mechanism”. Good point about push notifications. I imagine `push_account_id` in the encrypted push notifications proposal will replace that.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-17 21:58 UTC

Yeah, that seems right.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-04-17 21:58 UTC

I’m not sure if it makes a difference, but when mobile gets the canonical URL, does it send future API requests to that URL, or is it only used for matching?

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-17 21:58 UTC

It sends future requests to that URL.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-17 21:59 UTC

That's partly motivated by an old issue where a small number of routes had a different tolerance than the rest of them for URLs like `https://chat.example///////api/v1/name_of_route`.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-17 22:05 UTC

Spent a couple of minutes just now trying to find that one in the tracker and no success, but I believe the routes with the different behavior were those that accept the API key in the URL query, like for uploaded files.

So the symptom was something like, if you logged in using a URL with an excess slash or two at the end, we'd propagate the excess slash to the URLs we used and then everything would work except images.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-17 22:06 UTC

Ah, no, here it is: #M3567

It was /api/get-events .

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-04-17 22:09 UTC

Yeah, that makes sense as a likely bug on the Django–Tornado boundary, and at least something we don’t test.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-17 22:12 UTC

## max values for stream _seconds parameters

*2023-04-21 to 2023-04-24 · 21 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/max.20values.20for.20stream.20_seconds.20parameters/with/1552688)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-04-21 15:40 UTC

We saw a request 500 in Zulip Cloud because someone tried to set `move_messages_within_stream_limit_seconds` to `59999999940`, aka 1,902 years.  This errored out because the number is bigger than fits in the database column, which is an `integer`, and thus only supports up to `2147483647` (~68 years).

In the UI, this has options for:
 - Any time
 - 2 minutes
 - 10 minutes
 - 1 hour
 - 1 day
 - 1 week
 - Custom (enter number of minutes)

Should we:
 - Convert "custom" values over some length (5 years?) into "Any time"
 - Refuse "custom" values over some length (5 years?)

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-04-21 15:42 UTC

The longest anyone in Zulip Cloud actually has it set to is 7 days.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-04-21 15:43 UTC

The same set of options is provided for edit and delete timeframes, and it's probably easuest to apply the same limit to all of them.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-04-21 15:50 UTC

OK, the max currently attested in Zulip Cloud for both `message_content_edit_limit_seconds` and `message_content_delete_limit_seconds` is currently `600000000` seconds, which is about 19 years.  We can of course potentially push those into "forever" with a migration.

It seems like the *intent* for most things over 1 year is effectively "forever."

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-21 16:18 UTC

(replying to Alex Vandiver)
> We saw a request 500 in Zulip Cloud because someone tried to set `move_messages_within_stream_limit_seconds` to `59999999940`, aka 1,902 years.

Fun. I guess that fits with the UI being in terms of minutes — presumably they entered "999999999" into that form.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-21 16:18 UTC

I think clamping giant values to something like 60 years would make sense.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-21 16:19 UTC

i.e., the longest duration we can conveniently represent that's also a round number in time-reckoning terms

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-21 16:22 UTC

Alternatively, reading your suggestion with better reading comprehension this time:

(replying to Alex Vandiver)
> Should we: - Convert "custom" values over some length (5 years?) into "Any time"

I think this would be a fine choice, but I'd go for a longer period, like that longest available round number of "60 years".

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-04-21 18:26 UTC

I mean, that's not even a round number because "a year" is a not a defined number of seconds or minutes, and the only UI we present for this is in minutes.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-04-21 18:28 UTC

If someone is manually entering in 7 or more digits into that box, I don't think they are actually thinking about how big the number actually means.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-21 20:42 UTC

Hmm. I guess I think I favor clamping all values over 60 years years to "Any time" as how we manage it. 

I don't like the idea of clamping to values <5 years, since at some point you have to think about whether someone might want that policy.

There are Zulip organizations with >10 years of history, and I can imagine there being some time-based setting that someone, and it'll be kinda nice if we can just apply this sort of clamping to them all (including, say, the message retention policy durations) without having to spend any attention thinking about product questions around whether someone might want that duration as their configuration.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-04-21 20:49 UTC

How many of those 60 years are leap years?  Are there any leap-seconds?

60 years in seconds just isn't well-defined or round.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-21 22:53 UTC

(replying to Alex Vandiver)
> How many of those 60 years are leap years?

The Julian answer — 15 of them.

That means that starting in the year 2100, the "60 years" will actually refer to the past 60 years and one day, until the year 2160 when it goes back to meaning the past 60 years exactly. I think that's OK.

> Are there any leap-seconds?

No. Our timekeeping is in Unix timestamps, and there are never leap-seconds in Unix timestamps.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-21 22:55 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> There are Zulip organizations with >10 years of history, and I can imagine there being some time-based setting that someone, and it'll be kinda nice if we can just apply this sort of clamping to them all (including, say, the message retention policy durations) without having to spend any attention t …

Yeah. That's why I'd like whatever we do to have a limit of at least like 10 years before it starts clamping times, or rounding them to infinity, or otherwise mushing them together.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-21 22:56 UTC

I'm thinking of the "round number" here not in terms of what appears in a box that's showing a number of minutes (or seconds), but in terms of the documentation.

If we go with rounding to infinity, then the limit value never gets shown in the UI as a number — it'd get shown as "Any time" or equivalent.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-04-24 13:29 UTC

Hm, OK.  Thinking of the roundness of the number as a documentation property makes more sense.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-04-24 13:31 UTC

In that case, 50 years seems a bit "rounder" than 60, and I don't think there's any actual use cases that would care about the difference, but I can also see wanting to provide closer to the full dynamic range, even if we don't expect that it's practically useful.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-04-24 13:33 UTC

We also just hit a different bug, with message retention having been set to 9999999 days, which is 27397 years, which overflows Datetime objects (the max year in a Datetime is 9999).  Because this box is in days, not seconds, we overflow the Datetime before we overflow the integer.  I want to cap that to the same time range as the other ones for consistency, despite that not being the top of the imposed limit.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-24 18:13 UTC

(replying to Alex Vandiver)
> In that case, 50 years seems a bit "rounder" than 60, and I don't think there's any actual use cases that would care about the difference, but I can also see wanting to provide closer to the full dynamic range, even if we don't expect that it's practically useful.

Yeah. Because it's not a multiple of 4, it also means there's less of a glib answer for what to do about leap years (though the difference of one day doesn't really make a practical difference anyway.)

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-24 18:14 UTC

Capping message retention to the same limit as other things sounds good to me.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-24 21:54 UTC

Yeah, that plan sounds good to me.

## scheduled messages: send_time parameter

*2023-04-26 to 2023-04-28 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/scheduled.20messages.3A.20send_time.20parameter/with/1556114)*

**Lauryn Menard** · 2023-04-26 14:16 UTC

So, the existing implementation for creating scheduled messages has two parameters for determining when the message will be sent:

- `defer_until: Optional[str] = REQ("deliver_at", default=None, documentation_pending=True)`
- `tz_guess: Optional[str] = REQ("tz_guess", default=None, documentation_pending=True)`

**Lauryn Menard** · 2023-04-26 14:16 UTC

`defer_until` / `deliver_at` is the date and time at which the message will be sent. And `tz_guess` is the current timezone of the user, and if not specified, the user's default timezone will be used.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2023-04-26 14:16 UTC

From [@Tim Abbott's  comment](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/25240/files/d67c7ee48a8bd8301fd13bdb5a781d0c6bf81437#r1175789152) on the work in progress for adding the new create/edit scheduled message endpoint:
> We discussed the ideal semantics in "api design", but I think we should replace these two parameters with a single `send_time` parameter that is required to be UTC, or something like that, and have the client be responsible for sending a precise time?
> 
> (I think we needed this mainly for a slash command style interface to ask for something to happen in a few hours, which I'm not sure really makes sense to support at all once we have this first-class feature; "reminders" might be different on that front as a `/remind` slash command seems convenient, but we plan to have a different API anyway).

**Lauryn Menard** · 2023-04-26 14:16 UTC

So I wanted to check-in here that the proposed `send_time` parameter sounds good to folks and the format to use for that parameter.

I'll note the current implementation has the scheduled message dictionaries with a `deliver_at` property that's a Unix timestamp (seconds only) representing when the scheduled message will be sent by the server.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-26 17:23 UTC

Yeah, I agree it's better for the client to just say directly what actual time it wants (in UTC).

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-26 17:28 UTC

And it should be in a nice machine-oriented format. Unix timestamp is good because that's what we use elsewhere in the API, like for `timestamp` in /api/get-messages.

The name `send_time` seems fine.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-26 17:30 UTC

The name should match what's in the scheduled-message objects in the events, though.

Both `deliver_at` and `send_time` seem fine to me ­— just should be consistent.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-26 21:14 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)
> Yeah, I agree it's better for the client to just say directly what actual time it wants (in UTC).

Yeah, the background is that the original prototype could only be accessed via a slash command, like you'd write `/schedule <time>` as the first line of your message (just to be able to play with and think about it without any UI existing yet), and that's probably related to why we had the two parameter model originally (only the first would be in the thing the user typed; the other would be added by the web app).

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-26 21:21 UTC

I guess we use `date_sent` as the value in a `Message` object for when a message was sent in the database, but `timestamp` is the value in the API for those, and that's probably what we want to be consistent with.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-26 21:30 UTC

One option would be `scheduled_timestamp`? The problem with that is that it sounds like it's the time you scheduled the message, not the time it's going to be sent.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-26 21:30 UTC

`scheduled_delivery_timestamp` would be very clear, but a bit long.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-26 21:38 UTC

`timestamp_to_send`?

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-26 21:38 UTC

`send_at_timestamp`?

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-26 22:39 UTC

I think I prefer the long option over either those.

**Greg Price** · 2023-04-26 23:26 UTC

WFM.

Okay, #25318 is up with the update to `scheduled_delivery_timestamp`, which is the UNIX timestamp in UTC seconds.

*2023-04-26 to 2023-04-28 · 21 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/schedule.20messages.3A.20event.20formats/with/1556133)*

        "type": "scheduled_messages",
        "op": "add",
        "scheduled_messages": [

        ],
    }

Editing a scheduled message - op: update;
```python
    event = {
        "type": "scheduled_messages",
        "op": "update",
        "scheduled_message": scheduled_message_object.to_dict(),
    }
```

**Lauryn Menard** · 2023-04-26 14:53 UTC

Deleting a scheduled message - op: delete:
```python
    event = {
        "type": "scheduled_messages",
        "op": "remove",
        "scheduled_message_id": scheduled_message_id,
    }
```

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-11 21:00 UTC

(replying to Purushottam Tiwari)
> For a non-admin user /api/update-user-group-members would not allow user to to add oneself. As that user does not have edit permissions for the target group.

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-11 21:01 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-11 21:03 UTC

In other words: that is the endpoint for adding or removing members of a user group.

So the permissions constraints it'll enforce will be: you can only use it when you have permission to add or remove those members from that group.

Currently the model for who has that permission is relatively simple, and in the future it'll be more complex. Whatever that model is, though, that's what the endpoint uses.

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-11 21:10 UTC

This is similar to how /api/get-messages is the endpoint for getting messages, and the permission constraints it enforces are that you can only get the messages you have permission to get.

There's a number of different cases involved in those permissions. You can see a given message if
* you have a UserMessage record for it (e.g. because it was a DM to you, or it was to a stream you were subscribed to at the time);
* or it's to a public stream, or shared-history private stream, you're subscribed to now;
* or it's to a public stream and you're an org member;
* or it's to a web-public stream;
* and there may well be further wrinkles I'm forgetting.

But all of them use the same endpoint. We don't have separate endpoints for "get messages I have UserMessage records for" or "get messages to a shared-history stream I'm subscribed to" or "get messages to a public stream, and I'm an org member" etc.

Which is good because that'd be a mess.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-11 22:55 UTC

That plan sounds good to me.

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-16 22:22 UTC

The whole thing, edited slightly, is:
```js
export function messageMoved(event: UpdateMessageEvent): null | MessageMove {
  // The API uses "new" for the stream IDs and "orig" for the topics.
  // Put them both in a consistent naming convention.
  const orig_stream_id = event.stream_id;
  if (orig_stream_id == null) {
    // Not stream messages, or else a pure content edit (no stream/topic change.)
    return null;
  }
  const new_stream_id = event.new_stream_id ?? orig_stream_id;
  const orig_topic = event.orig_subject;
  const new_topic = event.subject ?? orig_topic;

  if (new_topic === orig_topic && new_stream_id === orig_stream_id) {
    return null;
  }
  return { orig_stream_id, new_stream_id, orig_topic, new_topic };
}
```

- When considering only the date, the search results can be displayed based on the user's timezone, showing the first message of the searched date in their local time zone.

The UTC information can be displayed in the link to indicate that the datetime is in UTC. **Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-25 00:00 UTC

I think the API design question, which I'd appreciated feedback on, is how the server is supposed to know what timezone to use for the user. One option is to use the user's configured display setting timezone, which is available to the server in `user_profile.timezone`. 

The downside of that approach is that we don't actually use that value when displaying timestamps in the apps - we use the values we get from the user's OS/browser, which are more likely to be correct for users travelling to a different timezone. I don't like the idea of searching for `2023-05-01` returning results that appear to the user as a few hours off because your configured display timezone is different from your current timezone.

So this presents the question in my mind whether this API needs to include a `timezone` parameter, which might be optional (defaulting to the server value), but that browsers would send to avoid that kind of mismatch.

Thoughts?

- We should strive for **consistency** in displaying timestamps throughout the application. If the app generally displays timestamps based on the user's OS/browser timezone, it may be preferable to continue using that approach for search results as well.
- We can provide users with the ability to specify their timezone explicitly during the search can be valuable. This empowers users to **control** how the search results are interpreted, especially when sharing links with others in different timezones.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-25 23:48 UTC

*2023-05-17 to 2023-05-20 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/add.20mentioned_me_directly.20parameter/with/1571307)*

**Notification Bot** · 2023-05-19 00:57 UTC

This topic was moved here from #**backend>add mentioned_me_directly parameter** by @Tim Abbott.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-19 00:58 UTC

So the background for this is that we're trying to treat personal @-mentions differently in the left sidebar from wildcard mentions, basically because in muted topics we ignore wildcard mentions but not personal ones in other contexts, and the goal is to make the left sidebar consistent with that logic.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-19 00:59 UTC

The problem is that the `unread_msgs` data structure just has the `mentions` array of unread mention message IDs (as well at metadata); and similarly the event sent when doing "mark as unread" for live-updating that data structure that also can't distinguish whether we're talking about a personal mention or a wildcard mention.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-19 01:02 UTC

I'm not sure what a good solution might be from an API perspective. One option would be, given that mentions are kinda rare, to just extend those data structures with more details about each mention. 

Another idea would be to just have the client query the server for the full copies of the rare messages where this question is of interest (mentions in muted topics) and try to backfill it that way; for that goal, one thing that might be of use is a `GET /messages` variant where you send a set of message IDs and it returns those if you can access them, and basically defer this problem to a v2 of the `unread_msgs` structure, which could fix a few other quirks we've identified over the years.

I mostly mention that second option because we've had weird API gaps where that sort of API endpoint could solve our problem without too much server load cost, and thus buy us time to think through a nicer unified API to solve the problem.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-19 01:03 UTC

(I think for #25588 we'll just have the client make its best guess if it doesn't have the data to know; I think the cases where it'll be wrong will be somewhat rare, at least as long as, 5 minutes after a Zulip window loads, we have full history of unread messages cached locally anyway)

**Greg Price** · 2023-05-19 01:04 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> I think for #25588 we'll just have the client make its best guess if it doesn't have the data to know

This means we don't need to try to rush an API change for this for the upcoming release, right?

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-19 01:25 UTC

Yes, I don't think that's a realistic plan and the consequences of guessing wrong are pretty minor.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-20 00:17 UTC

Here's the comment I merged along with #25588:
``` js

// have no way to correctly compute whether the mentions            
// are personal mentions or wildcard mentions, because              
// message_info doesn't contain that information... so we

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-03 04:14 UTC

To prepare the bouncer for the migration, we would probably want to have it support both:
- the pre-migration `str | None` format `extra_data` generated from an `orjson.dumps` call or omitted;
- the post-migration `dict`-style `extra_data` directly converted from `JSONField`'s through `model_to_dict`.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-03 04:17 UTC

My current proposal is changing the validator to `check_union((check_none_or(check_string), check_dict()))`, and converting the `dict` into a `str` so that we can populate `extra_data` for `RemoteRealmAuditLog`. This makes the API forward-compatible.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-03 04:19 UTC

Once the analytics bouncer starts its migration to support `JSONField` for `RemoteRealmAuditLog`, we begin to convert `extra_data` into `dict` using `orjson.loads` for requests from from pre-migration remote servers.

#25877 implements the first half of the proposal assuming no migration for the bouncer.

    def by_id(

**Greg Price** · 2023-06-28 19:47 UTC

One thing that came up as we looked at this further for zulip-flutter (#F189 / [26b693a2f](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-flutter/commit/26b693a2ff66d2ae3eb8b24fcc81844bd3e41b9c)) is that it seems like this "near" operator may not really make sense in the first place for the narrows that /api/get-messages accepts. So it may be better to deprecate and eventually remove it, rather than revise it.

**Greg Price** · 2023-06-28 19:47 UTC

In particular, the "near" operator doesn't appear to actually do anything. The implementation is, in main:
```py
    def by_near(self, query: Select, operand: str, maybe_negate: ConditionTransform) -> Select:
        return query
```

and in #26020 it grows a broader argument type and an error check, but still returns `query` unmodified. So either way, it looks like adding a "near" operator to a narrow has no effect at all on what the endpoint will return, except by potentially causing an error.

**Greg Price** · 2023-06-28 19:55 UTC

This makes sense because it's not clear what semantics a "near" operator *should* have that would be useful. The point would be for it to correspond to a `/near/$id` component in the URL fragment… but the semantics of one of those is covered already by the `anchor` parameter.

And in any case those semantics don't really fit into the model of what a "narrow" is about. Conceptually, a narrow refers to some set of filters on the entire message history; if you fetch stream #**general**'s latest 100 messages, and then you fetch the next 100 messages before that, those are two queries to different parts of history in the same narrow, not two different narrows. That's why those fetches would typically have the exact same `narrow` parameter to /api/get-messages, and differ only in `anchor` and its associates `num_before`/`num_after`.

Those latter three parameters control what point within the narrow's history we're asking for. That's the same job as a `/near/$id` component does in the URL fragment, and it's conceptually quite orthogonal to the question of what narrow we're asking about.

**Greg Price** · 2023-06-28 20:00 UTC

I suspect that the reason the server accepts (and then largely ignores) a "near" operator in the narrow is basically as a workaround for a client bug in the web app.

Specifically, the URL fragment is mostly about expressing a narrow (when you're looking at a message list at all), and so the web client is naturally going to take the fragment and translate it into the narrow to fetch messages from. For the most part, this translation is one-to-one where each component-pair `/foo/bar` turns into a narrow-filter with operator "foo" and operand like "bar".

So given that background, it'd be a pretty understandable bug for the client to see `/near/12345` and translate that into an operator "near" and operand "12345".

But it is nevertheless a bug, because the meaning of that `/near/12435` really isn't about the narrow — it's about the anchor. And the client must already be interpreting it to figure out what anchor to use, too.

**Greg Price** · 2023-06-28 20:12 UTC

Instead, when the client sees `/near/12345` in parsing a URL fragment, it should leave that out of the narrow that it sends to /api/get-messages .

This is already what zulip-flutter effectively does ([26b693a2f](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-flutter/commit/26b693a2ff66d2ae3eb8b24fcc81844bd3e41b9c)) when going in the reverse direction: when constructing a link, the function takes `Narrow narrow` as one parameter and `int? nearMessageId` as another. We'll do the same when we add parsing of Zulip-internal links in the future.

**Greg Price** · 2023-06-28 20:18 UTC

In the web client, the "near" information is currently expressed in the same `Filter` data structure that holds the details of the narrow, and separating it from that might require a significant refactoring job. But I think there is nevertheless a clean way to fix it so it doesn't send "near" to /api/get-messages :

* There's already a method on `Filter` whose job is to say how to represent the narrow in an /api/get-messages request: it's called `public_operators`.
* So, first, give that method a more expressive name, perhaps `narrow_for_server_api`.
* Then add to that method a bit of logic to filter out `near` operators.

**Greg Price** · 2023-06-28 20:20 UTC

(The same method is used for /api/check-messages-match-narrow , which seems equally appropriate.)

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-27 23:09 UTC

The implementation scenario is purely hypothetical. We might want to have a placeholder when the list is empty. If we allow nullable event types, there is still no type-checking guarantee that the list will be non-empty when it is not `null`. **Greg Price** · 2023-06-28 03:44 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2023-06-28 03:44 UTC

I think the event-types system only really makes sense if there's not just one event type, but at least two of them. So even if we represent "doesn't support event types" with an empty list, there will still be values that fit the type but are invalid: any one-element list is an invalid value.

The list of event types also must have all its values distinct. So there's another class of values that fit the type but are invalid: any list with some elements equal to each other, like `["foo", "bar", "foo"]`.

**Greg Price** · 2023-06-28 03:46 UTC

In general, it's normal for there to be some invariants that can't be expressed in the type system. So although when possible it's nice to write the types so that they rule out invalid values, that criterion isn't as important as some other criteria.

**Greg Price** · 2023-06-28 03:47 UTC

In particular, when there are different values that are really qualitatively different in what they mean, it's best if those are represented by different branches in the type, rather than just by special values like `[]` or `""` or 0 or -1 that happen to fit inside the same type as the rest of the values.

When the meaning is like "there is no data on this" or "this question is not applicable here", then `null` is a good candidate for how to represent that.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-28 03:56 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)
> when there are different values that are really qualitatively different in what they mean, it's best if those are represented by different branches in the type

I'm down with this intuition! Thanks for the clarification.

**Satyam Bansal** · 2023-06-28 20:26 UTC

So we will use `null` when the `ALL_EVENT_TYPES` is not defined -- which also leaves room for some product flexibility and we might use `[]` or something in the else in the future when the `ALL_EVENT_TYPES` exists but maybe isn't just valid.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-07-04 05:33 UTC

@Satyam Bansal yeah that sounds right to me.

Yeah, there are two problems with the `property`/`value` format seen in realm/update events:

* As discussed above, it doesn't have a clean way to handle updating several properties at the same time.

  For some kinds of updates, there are several properties that are related to each other and need to be updated simultaneously in order to avoid going through a state that's incoherent or means something incorrect.

* It's also a pain to write down a meaningful type for such an event.

  Here's how we write [types for stream/update events](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-mobile/blob/c979530d6804db33310ed7d14a4ac62017432944/src/api/eventTypes.js#L175-L193) in zulip-mobile, which use the same `property`/`value` format. So I would prefer to not add any more places where we use the `property`/`value` format, and instead use the dictionary format for anything new.

## end-to-end encryption protocols

*2023-07-14 to 2025-04-18 · 27 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/end-to-end.20encryption.20protocols/with/1610048)*

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-14 19:20 UTC

On a tentatively introduced setting `PUSH_NOTIFICATION_ENCRYPTION` in #15229, @Greg Price  [said](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/15229/commits/00ed21e9fb4a15ed1d3c403fb511235f7837bb47#r486167278):
> We should back up and discuss these different settings -- at the server level, at the device-record level, and in the request the client makes. There should be some idea of what they each mean -- and how they interact -- and that idea should be written down somewhere. Then we can discuss that idea a …
Before we actually work on the implementation in #26262, I want to discuss if and how we should allow disabling push notification encryption at the server level, and lay out the specifics of our encryption protocols.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-14 21:56 UTC

I think a separate setting for enabling/disabling end-to-end encryption might not be necessary. We should always enforce security by default when encryption is available. Here we assume that the client and the local server are trusted; Kandra Labs' mobile push notification bouncer and APNs/GCM bouncers are untrusted third parties.

## When the server supports end-to-end encryption:
- We should have an API feature level dedicated to end-to-end push notifications encryption support. At this feature level, extend the device registration endpoints to take an additional `prefer_push_notification_encryption` parameter; when set to `true`, failure to create a device token with an encryption key should result in an HTTP 5xx response.
- No actions should be needed to enable registering devices with end-to-end encrypted push notifications.
- In the future, we can deprecate device registration without push notification encryption, making end-to-end encryption required.

## When the client supports end-to-end encryption
- The client is responsible to look up server settings to check if both end-to-end encryption (by feature level) and push notification are available.
   - If the server supports encryption, the client should:
      1. send a request to register (or remove and register) a device token with `prefer_push_notification_encryption` set to `true`.
      2. expect that all the following notifications will be encrypted. Potentially we can have pushed mobile notifications before with unencrypted data. It is up to the client to decide what to do with these notifications.
   - If the server does not support encryption, the client should:
      1. send a request to register a device token with `push_notification_encryption_preferred` set to `false` when there isn't a device token.

## When the client does not support end-to-end-encryption
- The old device token without an encryption key will be used. If there isn't one, the device will still register without setting `prefer_push_notification_encryption` to `true`.

## Server invariants
- Notifications for devices that have `notification_encryption_key` set should always be encrypted.
- At feature levels that have end-to-end encryption support, client requests for device registration with `push_notification_encryption_preferred=True` should always succeed with the encryption key set (all-or-nothing) unless there is an internal server error.

Ideally, in this implementation, our notification bouncer for remote servers shouldn't care about if encryption is enabled. However, It will need a separate API change to accept multiple (device token, payload) pairs in a single request.

## how specific should our error codes be?

*2023-07-20 to 2023-07-20 · 31 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/how.20specific.20should.20our.20error.20codes.20be.3F/with/1613309)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-07-20 19:45 UTC

We have the following error codes currently:
```python3
class ErrorCode(Enum):
    BAD_REQUEST = auto()  # Generic name, from the name of HTTP 400.
    REQUEST_VARIABLE_MISSING = auto()
    REQUEST_VARIABLE_INVALID = auto()
    INVALID_JSON = auto()
    BAD_IMAGE = auto()
    REALM_UPLOAD_QUOTA = auto()
    BAD_NARROW = auto()
    CANNOT_DEACTIVATE_LAST_USER = auto()
    MISSING_HTTP_EVENT_HEADER = auto()
    STREAM_DOES_NOT_EXIST = auto()
    UNAUTHORIZED_PRINCIPAL = auto()
    UNSUPPORTED_WEBHOOK_EVENT_TYPE = auto()
    ANOMALOUS_WEBHOOK_PAYLOAD = auto()
    BAD_EVENT_QUEUE_ID = auto()
    CSRF_FAILED = auto()
    INVITATION_FAILED = auto()
    INVALID_ZULIP_SERVER = auto()
    INVALID_MARKDOWN_INCLUDE_STATEMENT = auto()
    REQUEST_CONFUSING_VAR = auto()
    INVALID_API_KEY = auto()
    INVALID_ZOOM_TOKEN = auto()
    UNAUTHENTICATED_USER = auto()
    NONEXISTENT_SUBDOMAIN = auto()
    RATE_LIMIT_HIT = auto()
    USER_DEACTIVATED = auto()
    REALM_DEACTIVATED = auto()
    REMOTE_SERVER_DEACTIVATED = auto()
    PASSWORD_AUTH_DISABLED = auto()
    PASSWORD_RESET_REQUIRED = auto()
    AUTHENTICATION_FAILED = auto()
    UNAUTHORIZED = auto()
    REQUEST_TIMEOUT = auto()
    MOVE_MESSAGES_TIME_LIMIT_EXCEEDED = auto()
    REACTION_ALREADY_EXISTS = auto()
    REACTION_DOES_NOT_EXIST = auto()
```

Some of these are pretty specific (e.g. `INVALID_ZOOM_TOKEN`) and some are, at least on their surface, pretty generic (e.g. `UNAUTHORIZED`).  However, `UNAUTHORIZED` currently specifically means "your request did not provide authentication information" (which seems not-quite-right for "unathorized," but it's too late to change that now).  Should we be reusing `UNAUTHORIZED` for other cases where access is not authorized (e.g. [creating a stream where one exists with that name already](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/26287#discussion_r1267351658)), or should we make a new specific code for that case?

My gut says to continue to lean into specific error codes that are pretty much only returned by one endpoint, but that could certainly quickly balloon into too many disorganized codes.

**Greg Price** · 2023-07-20 21:53 UTC

My general view is that we should default to using the totally generic BAD_REQUEST, using that for the great majority of new error conditions, and we should pick a code more specific than that only when we foresee a concrete use case for a client to actually care.

For the great majority of possible errors, the only information a client is likely to usefully take from it is:
* There was an error.
* It's an error with the request, so don't waste time retrying.
* Here's an error message to show to the user.

The second point is conveyed by being a 4xx response, rather than 5xx.

For the third point, our error responses already include a user-facing message string, separate from the error code. That error string is nicely translated to the user's language. I think we generally do a pretty good job of choosing a reasonable string to put there, suitable for the client to show to the user in an error dialog or the like, and we should naturally continue to do that.

**Greg Price** · 2023-07-20 21:59 UTC

The reasons I think a presumption in favor of the generic BAD_REQUEST is the right policy are basically:
* For the great majority of possible errors, there's no benefit to the client from being more specific, as described above.

* When we do pick something more specific, that's an additional piece of API surface area that calls for making a thoughtful choice.

  If we foresee a concrete use case for the information, then we have a basis for thinking about that API choice, and also that's the situation where we're likely to give adequate review attention to the choice. But if we just pick something because we have a policy (whether implicit or explicit) of generally doing so, then there's a high probability of picking something that's not a great API choice. Your example where `UNAUTHORIZED` currently is used with a meaning that doesn't really fit its name is an example of the sort of result that a not-well-thought-through API choice can look like.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-07-20 22:09 UTC

Those are all arguments in favor of "don't make a new error code unless we have a compelling API reason to do so."  I agree with those, generally.

The question I was asking was more -- given that we have an API reason to have something other than `BAD_REQUEST` (namely, [wanting to show a better UI for duplicate stream names](https://github.com/alexmv/zulip/blob/575f51ed08fd41ac5c18e9050cb8e01c1eddb8e4/web/src/stream_create.js#L284)), should we be trying to have *generic* error codes, like `DUPLICATE_OBJECT_NAME`, or *specific* error codes, like `STREAM_CREATE_FAILED_DUE_TO_STREAM_NAME_ALREADY_IN_USE`.  These are both over-exaggerated examples in both directions, but hopefully you get the point.

**Greg Price** · 2023-07-20 22:09 UTC

Plus:
* If in the future we find there's a real client-side use case for more information about a given error, then we can always add more information then — and if the status quo is that we're using BAD_REQUEST, then there is basically no compatibility cost to that, because that is a pretty near guarantee that no existing clients are depending on the current details.

  This part would not be true if we had a much wilder and woollier client ecosystem. So for many APIs that aren't Zulip's, and perhaps for Zulip's API in the future, a different policy would be more appropriate — choosing more-specific error codes from the beginning, which would have to come with putting more systematic effort than we ever have to date into selecting what codes to use where.

  But it is absolutely true that when we're using BAD_REQUEST, no client can be depending on the details without being quite buggy, because the only information to look at is then the message string — which is translated, and which we may revise at any time. And with the client ecosystem we have:
  * Mobile never inspects the details of a message string.
  * I believe zulip-terminal never does either.
  * There aren't a ton of other clients out there — basically the rest of the ecosystem AFAIK consists of bots people have written for a variety of needs. A small bot is unlikely in the first place to want to attempt to inspect the details of an error. And in any event we're generally comfortable with making API changes that don't affect mobile, don't affect terminal, and won't affect any client that's correctly using the API.

**Greg Price** · 2023-07-20 22:10 UTC

(replying to Alex Vandiver)
> Those are all arguments in favor of "don't make a new error code unless we have a compelling API reason to do so." I agree with those, generally.

Cool. And I'd state it a bit more generally: unless we have a compelling API reason, don't make a new error code, *nor* reuse an existing error code other than the completely generic BAD_REQUEST.
