*2024-03-09 to 2024-11-05 · 18 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/follow.20topics.20with.20message.20containing.20alert.20words/with/1755341)*

**Rohan Gudimetla** · 2024-03-09 19:18 UTC

In  #28777/ #29254/ #**design>notifications for alert words**  it was asked to implement a feature with each alert word having a checkbox, upon checked, when message sent to a particular topic contains an alert word configured by the user, then that topic is automatically followed.

So, to implement this, I added a new field -- `follow_topic_containing_alert_word` to `models/alert_words`, indicating whether to follow topics containing alert words or not. 

I have updated the POST of `users/me/alert_words` -- [`add_alert_words`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/29ca4ba6620f16598e1171be7495356f56b84328/zerver/views/alert_words.py#L24)  to accept alert words to be added as `List[Union[str, Tuple[str, bool]]]`. **Rohan Gudimetla** · 2024-03-09 19:24 UTC

So regarding the events sent, they are of the form `Union[List[str], List[Tuple[str, bool]]]`. So if the follow topic policy is False for all the alert words, then only the list of alert words is returned, whereas if it is set True for at least one alert word, then list  of tuples of alert words and the follow topics policy pair is returned.

This is done to make sure that if this is merged, then the terminal/mobile apps could still use the same api, since they would make a POST of list of alert words, and receive a list of  alert words for events (the `follow_topic_containing_alert_word` is set by False by default for the alert words then).

## Groups events for deactivated users

*2024-04-04 to 2025-09-19 · 70 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/Groups.20events.20for.20deactivated.20users/with/1774518)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-04-04 00:47 UTC

So in #29498, we are changing the structure for how deactivated users are handled in the groups APIs. Previously, the IDs of users who had been included in lists of group members in the API, and clients would be responsible for filtering them from the group management UI. I don't totally remember the motivation, to be honest, but I suspect it is to avoid confusion related to deactivated users cluttering those views.

The new model is that the server should not return the IDs of deactivated users in a group (And there will be a prompt when reactivating a user whether to restore their group memberships). 

The question is how that should interact with the events system -- if user X is a member of 5 groups, and gets reactivated, I think the server definitely needs to send the "user X is now in this group" event to clients, since the clients didn't have the data to know the user had been a member of those groups. 

Should it do the opposite when a user is deactivated? In theory, the client has the information to live-update its data structures given just the "deactivate" event. If so, is it important in what order the "remove user group group" and "deactivate user" events are sent?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-04-12 00:38 UTC

That's an interesting complication! I guess there's a few valid answers:
- We do nothing about that problem -- effectively deciding we're OK with guest users' view of group membership having potentially inaccurate live-update data here. - We go back to the idea of sending events to all their groups, which I don't love in part because it's potentially a big loop.

## support streams

*2024-04-08 to 2024-05-10 · 21 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/support.20streams/with/1776631)*

**sanchit sharma** · 2024-04-08 06:05 UTC

In #19434 / #29520 / #**general>Support team feature?** / #**general>Private Topic IDEA** , we are planning to implement the functionality to make topics private within a support stream. This means that users with restricted permissions will only be able to create and reply to topics that the user created within the support stream, without seeing topics created by other users. Non-restricted users, on the other hand, will have normal access, able to view and reply to all topics.

To implement these changes, I propose adding new fields to the `models/stream`. Firstly, I suggest adding a field called `is_support_stream`, to identify support streams. Streams with `is_support_stream=true` will be treated as special cases, affecting the handling of `UserMessage` row insertion and stream history access for restricted users.

Additionally, I suggest adding a field named `stream_topic_view_policy`, which will differentiate between restricted and unrestricted users. This field will tell us which users have normal access to the stream (i.e who is not a restricted user). This field can use the same values as `stream_post_policy`, with `stream_topic_view_policy=1` indicating access for everyone, as indicated by `STREAM_POST_POLICY_EVERYONE = 1`. By default, streams other than support streams will have `stream_topic_view_policy=1`.

Technically we don't need `is_support_stream` field and can handle all the special cases with support stream by checking if `stream_topic_view_policy` is not `1`. But adding `is_support_stream` will make things much simpler and cleaner.

Expansion of `PERMISSION_POLICIES` within `models/stream` is also necessary to include support streams. I propose adding two policies: `support_public` and `support_private`, with `is_support_stream=true`. The only difference between these two policies will be the `invite_only` parameter, set to `false` for `support_public` and `true` for `support_private`. All the other policies will have `is_support_stream=false`.

During the creation of support streams in the client, we will ensure that users cannot select `stream_topic_view_policy=1`, as this would just create a regular `public` or `private` stream.

Creating additional fields like `STREAM_TOPIC_VIEW_POLICY_EVERYONE = 1` specifically for `stream_topic_view_policy` may not be necessary. Using the same structure as `stream_post_policy` should enough.

My inclination would be to not add a boolean `is_support_stream` if the information it carries is redundant with another field `stream_topic_view_policy`.

For one thing, having both raises the question of what to do if they disagree. That applies to clients; and if the two fields live separately in the database, then it applies to code within the server as well.

If they find it convenient, both the server and any clients can add accessor properties that just wrap the underlying field. Like this (untested):
```py
    @property
    def is_support_stream(self) -> bool:
        return self.stream_topic_view_policy != STREAM_POST_POLICY_EVERYONE
```

Unlike having separate fields in the API and/or the database, that avoids any risk of disagreement.

Names like `STREAM_POST_POLICY_EVERYONE` don't actually appear in the API as it stands. So this question is a matter of code organization within the server implementation and doesn't affect the API.

For what does appear in the API, see e.g. under `stream_post_policy` at /api/get-stream-by-id :

> * `stream_post_policy`: integer [Policy](https://zulip.com/api/roles-and-permissions#permission-levels) for which users can post messages to the stream. * 1 = Any user can post. * 2 = Only administrators can post. * 3 = Only [full members](https://zulip.com/api/roles-and-permissions#determining-if-a …

If the values for `stream_topic_view_policy` correspond in a uniform way to those for `stream_post_policy`, then that's potentially somewhat convenient for clients and I'd be happy to see that happen. If that doesn't quite work out, though, then that's fine too.

**sanchit sharma** · 2024-04-26 14:34 UTC

**sanchit sharma** · 2024-04-26 14:42 UTC

> What are the semantics of `stream_topic_view_policy`? For example, suppose the value of that field is "only moderators", and the user is not a moderator. What are the effects of having the field set to that value?


That means the user is restricted in terms of having access to topics created by someone else. The value of `stream_topic_view_policy` defines non-restricted users. It should work similarly to how we check if user can post in stream based on `stream_post_policy` as defined in the function below.

```python
def check_stream_access_based_on_stream_post_policy(sender: UserProfile, stream: Stream) -> None:
    if sender.is_realm_admin or is_cross_realm_bot_email(sender.delivery_email):
        pass
    elif stream.stream_post_policy == Stream.STREAM_POST_POLICY_ADMINS:
        raise JsonableError(_("Only organization administrators can send to this stream."))
    elif (
        stream.stream_post_policy == Stream.STREAM_POST_POLICY_MODERATORS
        and not sender.is_moderator
    ):
        raise JsonableError(
            _("Only organization administrators and moderators can send to this stream.")
        )
    elif stream.stream_post_policy != Stream.STREAM_POST_POLICY_EVERYONE and sender.is_guest:
        raise JsonableError(_("Guests cannot send to this stream."))
    elif (
        stream.stream_post_policy == Stream.STREAM_POST_POLICY_RESTRICT_NEW_MEMBERS
        and sender.is_provisional_member
    ):
        raise JsonableError(_("New members cannot send to this stream."))

```

OK. So it sounds like the semantics will be something like: you can see a message if either
* you're in the `stream_topic_view_policy` group,
* or you created the topic the message is in.

Is that right?

And what about sending messages? I'm guessing the idea will be something like: you can send a message
* to a new topic that isn't already present,
* or to a topic you can see messages in based on the rule above (so either because you created it or because `stream_topic_view_policy` gives you permission).

*2024-04-20 to 2024-04-24 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/Migrating.20alert.20words.20to.20watched.20phrases/with/1784780)*

**Rohan Gudimetla** · 2024-04-20 21:31 UTC

I was working on #28779, involving migrating alert words to watched phrases. So while migrating, so as to make the api backward compatible, I added a new endpoint - `users/me/watched_phrases`, and some methods corresponding to requests made to it.

I am stuck at how should the events be sent in such case so as to ensure the backward compatibility is maintained -- should i be sending both the possibilities of events (the new /watched_phrases api and the existing /alert_words api) each time so that each of the clients would be handling their corresponding events (web would handle the events of new api and terminal/mobile apps the old api events)?

**Rohan Gudimetla** · 2024-04-24 22:05 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> I think the backwards-compatibility plan for this is that we just also send the `alert_words` data structure in its preexisting format.
Yes, the current implementation would also send the `alert_words` type event along with `watched_phrases` type. Web client is migrated to use `watched_phrases` type, while  others can still utilise the `alert_words` type sent, in case you are referring to that.

```py
    event = dict(type="watched_phrases", watched_phrases=[w.dict() for w in phrases])
    send_event(user_profile.realm, event, [user_profile.id])
    event = dict(type="alert_words", alert_words=[phrase.watched_phrase for phrase in phrases])
    send_event(user_profile.realm, event, [user_profile.id])

*2024-04-22 to 2024-04-30 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/deleting.20email.20invitations/with/1785307)*

**Lauryn Menard** · 2024-04-22 11:44 UTC

IIUC this endpoint is only about "email invitations", and "reusable invitation links" aka "multiuse" invites are a separate kind of thing from those. So "used" should mean it can't be used again, and there's no meaning to revoking it.

**Greg Price** · 2024-04-25 23:15 UTC

I'm not sure it's helpful to give it a distinct error code in the API, though.

The value of a distinct error code is that it lets clients reliably pick out a specific class of failure, so that they can trigger specific logic to respond to it. But "the request included both parameter A and parameter B, and those are incompatible" is a programming error — it's a bug in the client. So there's no sensible logic the client can have that's specific to that error; if the client developers anticipated that error, then the sensible thing to do would have been to make a correct request in the first place.

## subscribing invited user to default streams

*2024-04-26 to 2024-05-09 · 17 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/subscribing.20invited.20user.20to.20default.20streams/with/1788362)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2024-04-26 06:52 UTC

Currently, when inviting a user and configuring the invite to subscribe the users to default streams of the organization, the user is subscribed to the streams that were default at the time when invite was sent and not the default streams when user accepted the invitation.

Note that we now have an "Subscribe to default streams" checbox in the webapp invite UI apart from the list of streams, so the user might assume that the new user would be susbcribed to just the default streams.

So, to instead subscribe the new user to streams that were set as default at the time of user accepting the invitaion, #25739 adds `subscribe_to_default_streams` parameter to the `POST /invites` and `POST /invites/multiuse` endpoints. With this change, the new user is either subscribed to the exact streams passed with `stream_ids` parameter or the default streams if `subscribe_to_default_streams` parameter is set to `True`.

**Sahil Batra** · 2024-04-26 06:52 UTC

Had to discuss two things here -
- Any feedback on the parameter name (and subsequently the field name in `PreregistrationUser` and `MultiuseInvite` models? @Tim Abbott suggests we can name it something like `subscribe_to_exactly_default_streams`.
- The API currently allows the user to either have the `stream_ids` be a non-empty list or pass `subscribe_to_default_streams` as `True`, but not both at the same time. Is this fine? And is it worth to [mention this](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/25739#discussion_r1580273259) in the API docs every time like in the description of both the fields for both the email and multiuse invite endpoints.

**Greg Price** · 2024-04-26 17:22 UTC

Having the two parameters be mutually exclusive seems fine.

If they are mutually exclusive, then I think the name `subscribe_to_default_streams` is clear already and doesn't need to add the word "exactly". There aren't any other streams in sight that the user might potentially get subscribed to. (Fine for its documentation to have a few words making that explicit, though.)

**Greg Price** · 2024-04-26 17:24 UTC

Alternatively, I think it'd be pretty reasonable to accept both parameters, and then have the semantics be that they combine with each other. So if you pass both `subscribe_to_default_streams` and a `stream_ids` list, then the new user will get subscribed to both the default streams and any other streams that appear in the list.

To me that suggests another reason to leave "exactly" out of the parameter's name: even if we don't permit the combination now, it's a reasonable extension we might do in the future, and then it'd be awkward if the parameter had a more-specific name that conflicted with that.

**Greg Price** · 2024-04-26 17:26 UTC

(replying to Sahil Batra)
> And is it worth to [mention this](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/25739#discussion_r1580273259) in the API docs every time like in the description of both the fields for both the email and multiuse invite endpoints.

Definitely sounds to me like something that should be mentioned in the docs; seems like an important part of the semantics for clients to know.

But I'm not sure what "every time" means — are there a lot of places these same two parameters appear, so that it feels repetitive? In that case it's possible there'd be a way to deduplicate that information.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-04-26 21:24 UTC

Ooh, yeah, I like the idea of having what you get include the `streams` list if nonempty when `subscribe_to_default_streams` is passed -- I think that's a very reasonable type of invitation like to create ("default streams plus these 3 for your team", so supporting that in the API at least makes sense, and we can follow-up on how to expose that in the UI as we further rework the invitation modal.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-04-26 21:26 UTC

So I think we can keep this name as-is, and I'm fine with either:
- Tweaking it to do a union of the streams list and the default streams when both parameters are provided.
- Merging the PR as written (requiring that the streams list be empty), and considering the tweak noted above to be a fairly low priority follow-up.

At @Sahil Batra's discretion.

**Sahil Batra** · 2024-04-29 14:42 UTC

Updated te PR to do a union of streams list and default streams if both parameters are set.

**Sahil Batra** · 2024-04-29 14:44 UTC

Also [posted](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/25739#issuecomment-2082933043) a couple of questions. Also posting them here, just in case to get more visibilty -
* Do we still need a migration for existing `PreregistrationUser` objects to set `subscribe_to_default_streams` as `False` where the streams list is non empty? I think we can considering the invitation was originally sent assuming the new user will be subscribed to the streams passed in the list and not the default streams as well.
* Currently not allowed in the UI, but users who are not allowed to subscribe others can set the `subscribe_to_default_streams` parameter as `False`. Is this fine?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-03 23:50 UTC

For the first question, yes, we should have a database migration such that invitations created before this PR behave identically after the PR. I don't think it's much of a choice -- we never want to have the user making the security decision have set a given configuration of what streams to enable, but then have the app do something different just because we changed some defaults intended to apply to new invitations.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-03 23:52 UTC

(replying to Sahil Batra)
> * Currently not allowed in the UI, but users who are not allowed to subscribe others can set the `subscribe_to_default_streams` parameter as `False`. Is this fine?

This is a bit of a security model question. But basically the impact is that a user who has permission to invite others to the organization but not add users to any streams in the organization would have the ability to create an invitation link such that users who join via that link arrive with 0 stream subscriptions. 

I think this is an unlikely configuration but probably in that configuration, it's probably fine that they're able to do that? And it might be best to not try to have a check here because eventually the permission as to which streams you can add users to will be more distributed between configuration for different individual streams.

**Sahil Batra** · 2024-05-09 03:37 UTC

## Synchronized UI renames?

*2024-05-01 to 2024-05-01 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/Synchronized.20UI.20renames.3F/with/1790997)*

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2024-05-01 05:43 UTC

While these aren't API-compatibility issues as such, with the recent changes to `Combined Feed` and `Channels`, are there specific feature levels which correspond to these changes?

My original thought in #**zulip-terminal>Combined feed renaming** was anything after 8.x could update these names, based on a hypothetical v9.0 feature set.

Terminal didn't make the change to direct messages server-dependent, so we could just switch right now in a similar way, but running against an older server would have different UI terms in different clients.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-05-01 17:01 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-01 17:01 UTC

Yeah, #F634 is for updating it in the Flutter app

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-01 17:04 UTC

Our thinking on the "Combined feed" change (though I forget where we discussed this — might have been in the mobile team meeting?) was that that was a small and localized enough change that it wasn't worth trying to synchronize it based on the user's server version — better instead to have each user see the new string as soon as they upgrade their respective clients.

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-01 17:05 UTC

A runner-up would be direct messages, which until recently we called "private messages". But even that one I don't think we synchronized like this, and it was fine.


## HTML pattern for truly inline images

*2024-05-06 to 2026-02-18 · 161 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/HTML.20pattern.20for.20truly.20inline.20images/with/1794378)*

**Nehal Sharma** · 2024-05-06 20:07 UTC

Here's an example of a paragraph with 2 image links, that is followed by the images' previews in another paragraph of their own. This is the existing image preview feature:

**HTML code:**
```html
<p>
    this para has 2 image links
    <a href="/user_uploads/2/62/WzVnIOIidA024zO0JVkqzAw1/zebra.gif" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"
        title="Download zebra.gif">this</a>
    and
    <a href="/user_uploads/2/95/JX5TEW8tUCXLOdOju8jbf3Z4/Screenshot-2023-12-10-at-17-54-04-Untitled-design.png"
        target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"
        title="Download Screenshot-2023-12-10-at-17-54-04-Untitled-design.png">this</a>. Both previews are in the
    next para:
</p>
<div class="message_inline_image">
    <a href="/user_uploads/2/62/WzVnIOIidA024zO0JVkqzAw1/zebra.gif" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"
        aria-label="this"><img src="/user_uploads/2/62/WzVnIOIidA024zO0JVkqzAw1/zebra.gif" /></a>
</div>
<div class="message_inline_image">
    <a href="/user_uploads/2/95/JX5TEW8tUCXLOdOju8jbf3Z4/Screenshot-2023-12-10-at-17-54-04-Untitled-design.png"
        target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" aria-label="this"><img
            src="/user_uploads/2/95/JX5TEW8tUCXLOdOju8jbf3Z4/Screenshot-2023-12-10-at-17-54-04-Untitled-design.png" /></a>
</div>
```

**Result:**
[image.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/74/4L_jixEt3HK4pehJ8asXSKe3/image.png)

***

Now, this is an example of the proposed truly inline images using the standard markdown `![alt](url)` (being discussed at #**issues>image names when multiple images are attached**, PR is #29300):

**HTML code:**
```html
<p>This para has 2 <em>inline</em> images, <span class="message_inline_image true_inline"><a
            href="/user_uploads/2/30/2NPPskJ2jV5cPtH-0ltAEhKx/spotify-indie-and-chill-poster.png" target="_blank"
            rel="noopener noreferrer" aria-label="spotify-indie-and-chill-poster.png"><img
                alt="spotify-indie-and-chill-poster.png"
                src="/user_uploads/2/30/2NPPskJ2jV5cPtH-0ltAEhKx/spotify-indie-and-chill-poster.png"></a></span> and
    <span class="message_inline_image true_inline"><a
            href="/user_uploads/2/95/QGLlVLodpHju_S4NKn6pFuE8/markdown-todo.png" target="_blank"
            rel="noopener noreferrer" aria-label="markdown-todo.png"><img alt="markdown-todo.png"
                src="/user_uploads/2/95/QGLlVLodpHju_S4NKn6pFuE8/markdown-todo.png"></a></span>. Both will show in
    place.
</p>
```

**Result:**
[image.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/ca/PlKKPpf-nL_dEi6tbLtp0ECW/image.png)

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-07 00:07 UTC

So in terms of the markup, these are the differences of note:
- Most significant is that the `message_inline_image` outer element is a `span` rather than a `div`. This is probably what breaks existing clients' handling of the styling. To be honest, the way these image previews work feels more like a `div` use case, in that the only inline arrangements you can do with Zulip's image syntax looks ugly, so I'm not entirely sure I feel OK about this direction.
- It has this `true_inline` class added to it. What is its meaning? I feel like that class might be an unnecessary detail.

**Nehal Sharma** · 2024-05-07 00:11 UTC

`.true_inline` ensures no bottom margin (which other image previews have) to align the image with the text, if any, inline with it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-07 00:13 UTC

I think the `true_inline` detail seems like a thing that should be client-side processing in `rendered_markdown.ts` for the web app, if we need a class for it at all -- seems like we could also just have CSS on `span.message_inline_image` directly.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-07 00:15 UTC

I'm still not entirely convinced that we want to render images as inline elements rather than doing some version of hoisting them to sit after the current inline element within its first containing block element, which is kinda what we do with image previews today.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-05-07 01:04 UTC

There are plenty of valid use cases for inline images, and the whole point of this exercise is to remove pointless divergence from the Markdown specification and unpredictable heuristics. When a user wants an image on its own line, they’ll write it on its own line.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-07 01:10 UTC

I think it's not that simple, in the sense that we're resizing the image with a surrounding 150x100 container, and the cases where someone wants an image inline are probably going to be those where they want the image to appear at its original (small) size where it might look good in the middle of a sentence... or where they want some styling applied to the image.

I have yet to see any specific scenario where in Zulip, one actually wants a 150x100 image in the middle of an inline element, and every scenario we've seen in discussion just looks buggy, which is why I feel not entirely settled on this approach making sense.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-07 01:11 UTC

Now, maybe there's a theory that Zulip should be using a different size than 150x100 for a `span.message_inline_image` that is designed for inline use, but in that case, we probably want to avoid the ones on a line by themselves using `span.message_inline_image`, so that that they use `div.message_inline_image`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-07 01:12 UTC

I think that might actually be the crux of the problem here -- that we probably do want different styling for the inline/span use case from the block element use case.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-07 01:13 UTC

And so of course it's going to look bad if we take styling designed for the block setting and apply it to the span/inline setting.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-05-07 01:14 UTC

Firstly, it doesn’t need to be the middle of a sentence. It could be a list item or a table cell or a link, or just multiple images next to each other.

Secondly, the question is not whether users want images in the middle of a sentence. The question is whether we want to diverge from the Markdown specification in order to prevent them from doing that, which is a very different question that requires a much stronger justification than “but I think it’s ugly”.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-07 01:16 UTC

In which case our approach should be:
- Create `span.message_inline_image` styling for all clients as an API change.
- Consider a markdown post-processor transformation with a flavor something like "If there's a block that only contains `span.message_inline_image` elements in a block context, transform them into `div.message_inline_image` elements". Don't have time to think through a more concrete proposal as I'm about to go AFK.

But that would entail just a post-processor on top of Markdown a la our existing image previews feature, while achieving the product goal that you get block images if you, say, put one or more images on a line by itself.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-07 01:19 UTC

IDK, maybe that doesn't make sense for your poll example case, though -- it's a bit unclear whether you'd want a 150x100 image or an inline size 24x16 (or whatever fits) image in your poll, and we could guess which is better UI, but there'd be no clean way to specify which of those you're asking for.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-05-07 01:20 UTC

One could imagine more use cases for inline images if we displayed small images at their native size, so as to give that choice to the user. (I know this involves work to avoid layout-shifting regressions during loading and scrolling.)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-05-07 01:30 UTC

- We don't get blocked on compatibility issues involving mobile support.
- Actually having one of our 150x100 image elements in the middle of a paragraph is basically always ugly, and we likely need to do a substantial design discussion/change process to figure out how to address that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-05 18:26 UTC

The simplest option for how to do that implementation-wise would be to just have the same post-processor that does preview of image links also do "previews" of inline image elements, with the exact same logic for lifting them to sit after the current paragraph; the only thing that would be different is that this processor would actually delete the `img` tag from the HTML tree at its original location; whereas the current "link" processor leaves the `a` element in place while adding a preview.

The result is that clients wouldn't need any changes to support this feature, beyond perhaps some small local-echo logic tweak.

I think we may need a separate conversation about how to handle `camo` images, since we don't have sizing metadata for those. An option is replacing `camo` with thumbnail …

When we were spec'ing out thumbnailing, we also came up with a spec for thumbnailing third-party images, involving accessing them via `/thumbnail?` URLs.  Looking at what I wrote up previously, there's the issue that, as it's written, we replace `![Alt text](https://example.com/image.png)` with a spinner, and a background worker fetches the URL, performs thumbnailing, and caches the result.  However, this means that the spinner cannot know how much space to preserve -- as you note, the only way to get that sizing data is to block writing the HTML until we can complete an HTTP request, which can take arbitrary time.

- The `![title](url)` syntax is what the CommonWork standard does, so it's easier to use third-party code for interacting with Markdown doing that, than if we do something different. (Though it is of course possible to do post-processing in the backend instead of the frontend when desired).
- The Flutter mobile clients will likely find the revised syntax easier to work with, since they are translating the Zulip markup into their own components, and a single HTML element with all the data attached to it is simpler to work with there.
- Wrapping an image in a link to the original image is potentially helpful in `zulip-archive`, since otherwise you'd only have ready access to the thumbnail's URL. If we decide this is a problem, we can make `zulip-archive` do similar wrapping pretty easily.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2025-05-26 20:41 UTC

The backend should not auto-wrap inline images in an `<a>` tag, because that would prevent the user from wrapping the image in a link of their own. (`<a>` inside `<a>` is [invalid HTML](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-a-element:concept-element-content-model), and in practice browsers interpret it such that the inner link wins.)

**Greg Price** · 2026-01-09 01:43 UTC

And I agree that in general we want to avoid creating landmines in clients that make it harder to freely change things on the server.

The tension there is that by definition, accepting a form that the server doesn't currently produce means *making assumptions* about what that form would mean if the server does someday start producing it. If those assumptions are violated, then a client that accepts that form would end up showing misleading information to the user, or otherwise going astray.

**Greg Price** · 2026-01-09 01:43 UTC

As a result, accepting a more general form can only make sense in the context of some sort of convention that we intend to be constrained by on the server in making future API changes.

Put another way, it still relies on a forward-looking promise in the API. It's just that that forward-looking promise may be some general principle that applies to a broad swath of the API, rather than something we specify on a particular endpoint or feature.

**Greg Price** · 2026-01-09 01:49 UTC

We've generally been successful in avoiding annoying compatibility constraints in most of the API. The most important of the general principles that's enabled that is that in all the JSON-encoded responses the server makes, if the client sees a JSON property name it wasn't expecting, it just ignores that property.

That client behavior is enabled by our practice, when making API changes on the server, that if we're giving an object some new meaning, we never express that solely by adding some hitherto-unknown property. Either the new thing appears in a different place so that existing clients don't see it, or else it only shows up when the client passes some capability flag or the like.

For example, when we started including archived channels in the lists of channels in /api/register-queue, we didn't just start including them while slapping an `"is_archived": true` flag on them, because if we did that then existing clients would have innocently treated those as additional non-archived channels (and therefore wrongly shown them in the list-of-channels screen, etc.). That's something we needed to do because we have this practice of the client ignoring properties it didn't expect.

**Greg Price** · 2026-01-09 01:52 UTC

When it comes to adding new features to the message HTML, we haven't really worked out yet the contours of this sort of general convention for how the API will evolve. That's basically for two reasons:
* It's a much smaller API surface area than all the JSON combined is, so we make a lot fewer such changes in a given year.
* Until the advent of the Flutter app, clients largely weren't looking all that closely at it. The legacy mobile app handed the HTML off to a webview with minimal processing, so mostly just interacted through a short list of CSS style rules.

So in short we've just had very little experience yet as a project with managing API changes of this kind.

**Greg Price** · 2026-01-09 01:58 UTC

As long as we're in this phase where we haven't yet established those general conventions for this area, I think it'll therefore be good for us to be fairly explicit in the API docs about the difference between facts about the server's current behavior on the one hand, and facts we intend as part of the client-facing spec on the other.

In this instance that would mean being clear that we're not saying the `src` attribute will necessarily be a thumbnail URL. (And if it's some other URL, then is it clear what the client should do with that?)

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-01-09 03:05 UTC

When we get to thumbnailing remote images, we're pretty clearly going to have to either delay message rendering (and thus sending) until we make a network request to get some metadata about the remote image, *or* we have to accept that the initial layout will have to be done without any information about the aspect ratio of the image (or even if it *is* an image!).  With uploaded files, we take the time to look at image headers during upload, so we've opted to effectively do the delayed-message-sending route -- but our latency hit to do that is very small, compared to having to wait on the whims of some other server.

So yes, I think we should assume we'll have to come up with a layout plan for rendering images when we don't know their sizes.

## Disallow editing option - select field data

*2024-05-07 to 2024-05-16 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/Disallow.20editing.20option.20-.20select.20field.20data/with/1794895)*

**Shubham Padia** · 2024-05-07 15:32 UTC

From [comment](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/29880#issuecomment-2092362778). 

In Custom profile fields, we allow editing the options of a select field. This can lead to unintended changes to the field user has selected whenever an org admin will edit the option. The current proposal is not to allow to edit an option once it has been saved. The option can only be deleted, ultimately unsetting whatever option users have chosen in their profile.

In PATCH `realm/profile_fields/<int:field_id>`, whenever the field type is `SELECT` and the `text` attribute of any existing option is being edited we can raise a `ValidationError` with the message: `The value of an existing option cannot be changed.` This will be a breaking change. 

Would appreciate some feedback on this proposed change :man_bowing:

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-07 18:01 UTC

Hmm, is this endpoint documented? Looks like it's not — some related endpoints are, like /api/reorder-custom-profile-fields , but not this.

```
        "/realm/profile_fields/{field_id}",
```

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-07 18:02 UTC

What's the current interface of this endpoint? That would help in understanding exactly what's proposed to change.

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-07 18:03 UTC

In any case, from a compatibility perspective, mobile doesn't interact with this endpoint at all. I'd guess that terminal doesn't either, but not sure — @Neil Pilgrim (neiljp) would be best able to say.

In that case this would be something that we can change freely without worrying about compatibility with existing clients.

**Shubham Padia** · 2024-05-07 18:19 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)
> What's the current interface of this endpoint? That would help in understanding exactly what's proposed to change.

The endpoint accepts `field_data` amongst other fields to update [CustomProfileField](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/df693c5cb0aa105b359c8cde7d466d068f432d20/zerver/models/custom_profile_fields.py#L59). If `field_type` is `SELECT`, we accept `field_data` with the following type: 

```
{
  [key: string]: {
    order: string;
    text: string;
  };
}
```

The proposed change will not modify the interface. Instead, it will give the aforementioned error if someone tries to edit the `text` part for an existing key.

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-07 18:29 UTC

Cool, seems reasonable.

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-07 18:30 UTC

(FWIW I would call that a change to the interface — the types aren't changing, but the "interface" includes also all the other information a client needs to know in order to invoke it correctly.)

## renaming to "channel" across API

*2024-05-09 to 2024-05-09 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/renaming.20to.20.22channel.22.20across.20API/with/1796686)*

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-09 20:22 UTC

Hmm, good question. I think the answer basically depends on how we want to handle the stream/channel rename in the API in general.

I'm not sure what the best plan is that. There are a lot of distinct names in the API that mention the word "stream", so it's a big undertaking.

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-09 20:29 UTC

Possibly the right strategy is something like:
* For now, everything is "stream", with a few exceptions (made where the API peeks through to the user) like wildcard mentions and narrow URLs.
* At some point, we make a systematic sweep so that *all* the names that were "stream" now accept "channel".
* When that's done, we do a rapid second pass to make "channel" names the canonical ones, and "stream" deprecated.
* Clients update. This will take a while.
* A few major releases in the future, we make a sweep and stop supporting the "stream" versions, with probably a handful of exceptions.
  * Or just cut the "stream" versions from the documentation? Possibly do that relatively soon, and drop actual support a while later. In between, the docs can mention in one central place that "stream" name variants are supported too, but it doesn't clutter everything.

That story is too simple because it only really covers names for the server to *accept*, not for it to send. For names it sends, I guess we do something like a client capability to say "I can handle 'channel' names for everything".

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-09 20:31 UTC

Anyway, if we go with a strategy that has that general shape, then it's probably cleanest if the few new stream/channel-related names we add between now and executing that rename all stick with "stream". That way everything's alike across the API (except those handful of spots like wildcard mentions and narrow URLs), both now and at each major intermediate phase.

So I think the best thing here would be to not have the server (at /api/get-messages ) start accepting a `with` operator, even as a no-op. **Greg Price** · 2024-05-16 21:36 UTC

@Tim Abbott and I discussed this feature in the office, and we agree it'd actually be good to have the server implement the redirecting behavior as part of /api/get-messages .

This means there'd be an operator with a name like `with`, taking a message ID as operand. Its meaning would be:
* If the message exists and is visible to the user, then replace any "conversation" filters — channel/stream, topic, DM conversation — with filters corresponding to the conversation the message is in.
* Otherwise, ignore the `with`.

The second case is important because e.g. the individual message may have been deleted, and then we still want the link to fall back to showing you the rest of the conversation around it. (This is the behavior `/near/` links already have, just implemented on the client side.)

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-16 21:37 UTC

Then clients can use that operator when visiting links with either `/with/` or `/near/`. That partly replaces the existing client-side implementation of this behavior for `/near/`.

(Clients will still want to look and see if the message is one that they *already* know about, from their local cache. When they do, they may be able to avoid a new server request entirely.)

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-16 21:41 UTC

The reason it's good to have that redirecting behavior implemented on the server is that it can reduce two round-trips to the server to just one. When the client doesn't already know where the message is, what it does today is:
* Ask the server about that one message.
* Use the answer to make an /api/get-messages request.

With a `with` operator, it can instead go straight to the /api/get-messages request.

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-16 21:47 UTC

There's a second place where this "topic permalinks" feature #21505 will appear in the API:

We want these links to be what you get when you write a #-mention of a topic, like #**api design>topic permalinks**. That's a key part of this feature.

After discussing it in the office, @Tim Abbott and I think the way we want to do that is on the server side. That is, the Markdown for a topic mention will be the same as today, like `#**api design>topic permalinks**`. The server will turn that into one of the new topic permalinks. That means it needs to find what is the latest message in the given topic which the sender has access to, so it can put that message ID in the link.

This is a bit complicated because the Markdown processor itself can't make database queries. But there's an existing pattern for handling this, which is used for uploaded files. A first pass scans the message source for anything that could be an example of the syntax; then the necessary database fetches are made for all those; then that data is passed along when the message source is handed to the Markdown processor for real.

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-16 21:53 UTC

The alternative would be to have the client do that lookup, using its own data about the messages in the topic.

But that would mean including the answer in the Markdown somehow. The syntax would then look something like `#**api design>topic permalinks|1801566**`, or some other variation — it'd be less pretty to look at. We already do something similar for @-mentions, when they'd otherwise be ambiguous because of duplicate names… but that's uncommon, and this would be in every topic mention. Making the syntax uglier like this would hardly be the end of the world, but it'd be nice to avoid.

The other issue with having the client do it is that it would sometimes introduce a lag. Whenever the client didn't already know what the latest message ID in the given topic was, it'd have to go make a request to find out. To deal with that, we'd probably need to insert some sort of placeholder, make the request, and then when the request completes go update the placeholder. (Just like we do today for uploading files.) Doable, but makes things more complicated.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-14 00:21 UTC

For defining a crisp semantics that gives that behavior as well as the other behaviors we want, we could say:
* The point of a `with` operator is to get a particular conversation — the conversation that had a specified message.
* If the `with` operand is valid (it's the ID of some message you can see), then that's that: we replace any conversation-specifying operators with just the ones specifying that message's conversation.
* Then if it's invalid, we fall back to the conversation specified by those other operators… but only if they're enough to specify a single conversation. That is, only if there's both a `channel`/`stream` and a `topic` operator, or there's a `dm` operator.
  * The rationale for giving effect to those operators at all, when there was a `with` operator but its operand was invalid, is that they're expected to correspond to where the intended conversation once was. So even if the individual message has been deleted (or moved to a private moderation stream or something), it's worth a try to see if the rest of the conversation can still be found there.
* But if the `with` operand is invalid, and there aren't other operators that identify a single specific conversation, then we're out of options for giving the user the conversation they were looking for. So we tell them that, by showing an error.

## migrating stream creation setting to groups

*2024-05-17 to 2024-06-10 · 48 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/migrating.20stream.20creation.20setting.20to.20groups/with/1802021)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2024-05-17 06:52 UTC

We are planning to start migrating existing role based settings to use groups by starting with converting one of the stream creation settings. There are three settings currently - `create_public_stream_policy`, `create_private_stream_policy` and `create_web_public_stream_policy` and we can start with any one of them.

I wanted to discuss about backwards compatibility of this change with respect to mobile and terminal apps. The change will be - the setting parameter in `PATCH /realm` will now accept the new [`{old: ..., new: ...}` format](https://chat.zulip.org/api/group-setting-values#updating-group-setting-values) and the settings values returned in the `/register` response can either be an [integer or `{direct_subgroups: [], direct_members: []}` object](https://chat.zulip.org/api/group-setting-values#group-setting-values).

Currently both the values, i.e. the parameter to change the setting and the setting value in `/register` response, are integers.

I don't think we allow changing realm settings from clients other than webapp so that should be fine, but not sure hwo the setting values in `/register` response are read by the client. The webapp UI will only show role-based groups options as of now, so the value in `/register` response should be integer in most cases.

@Greg Price @Neil Pilgrim (neiljp) FYI.

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-17 23:34 UTC

The thing is that when the same integer has a different meaning in any two of these permissions settings at all, it means we can't make that guarantee for both of them.

For example, looking now just at the handful of these that we interpret in zulip-mobile: the three policy enums discussed in this thread are all consistent with each other, but `email_address_visibility_policy` disagrees. Concretely:
* 1 means "all members" in the former, but "everyone" in the latter
* 2 means "admins and owners" in the former, but "all members" in the latter
* 3 means "all full members" in the former, but "admins and owners" in the latter
* 4 means "moderators, admins, and owners" in the former, but "nobody" in the latter

So if we make `role:moderators` be group ID 4 to allow these stream-creation policies to pun as group IDs, then `email_address_visibility_policy` cannot be punned as group IDs. Same thing in reverse if we make `role:nobody` be group ID 4.

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-17 23:34 UTC

So potentially we could do that for some policies, but at most some subset that are all consistent with each other in the meanings they've given to the values.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-20 22:48 UTC

So there are a few anomalies, but from a quick audit, I believe it's the case that:
- We do have something called `Realm.COMMON_POLICY_TYPES` in the server, which uses a shared enumeration mapping for every realm-level setting except for `realm.wildcard_mention_policy`.
- `UserProfile.email_address_visibility` and the related field on the realm-defaults for user settings use a different mapping.
- `Stream.stream_post_policy` also uses its own enum mapping.

So I think we can write a single common function for doing mapping from a system group to the legacy enum for all but the 3 specific enum settings flagged above, and use that for all of these settings.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-20 22:52 UTC

I think there's basically two good plans for backwards-compatibility when migrating such a setting to groups:
- We keep sending `create_public_stream_policy` type settings to clients, but the value is always whatever corresponded to `EVERYONE` in the previous system. So legacy clients would basically assume you're able to do these things, and thus present UI to everyone. If the user in fact doesn't have permission, they'll get a server error when they try to do the thing. This might be appropriate for something like `realm.wildcard_mention_policy`, where it's really not a big deal to have the server reject your request instead of the client.
- We keep sending `create_public_stream_policy` type setting to clients with variable values: Basically if the current setting for it is a role-based system group, compute the corresponding enum in the old system and send that value. As noted above, we'd just need to write a single function doing this mapping that can be reused for ~15 settings that use the common/standard legacy enum values. And if the value is anything other than a singleton system group, we fall back on the approach suggested above: Report to legacy clients that "EVERYONE" can do it and let legacy clients get an error from the server if they allow someone who doesn't actually permission to attempt an operation.

Since the UI doesn't offer non-system-groups yet, we'd have some time for clients to transition before that last `EVERYONE` fallback would be live code.

And the handful of `_length` items are pretty cheap to just send with both names.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-28 23:34 UTC

So I think it does make material progress towards being able to actually complete the migration if we take the opportunities of these groups-related transitions to standardize on `_channel_` type names for these permissions settings. 

In my mind, it's a pain to rename fields in the database, and a moderate pain to have different names in the API vs the database, so we save a lot of future work by creating these new permission settings have `channel`-based names.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-28 23:38 UTC

So this would be proposing a migration workflow that looks something like this:
- Now, we start migrate all the easy things as convenient, such as when we're introducing a new setting field as part of some other refactor of the API.
- We do a push to rename everything that doesn't have API compatibility considerations for clients, which would largely be all of the settings UI things that aren't interacted with by clients.
- We audit the remaining items, and figure out a plan for how we'll move forward with them.
- Once the list is small enough, we define a client capability that lets us cut over some or all of the remaining items.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-05-29 15:08 UTC

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-05-29 15:08 UTC

Oh, and I think this would interact with this logic:
```python3
class DetectProxyMisconfiguration(MiddlewareMixin):
    def process_view(
        self,
        request: HttpRequest,
        view_func: Callable[Concatenate[HttpRequest, ParamT], HttpResponseBase],
        args: List[object],
        kwargs: Dict[str, Any],
    ) -> None:
        proxy_state_header = request.headers.get("X-Proxy-Misconfiguration", "")
        # Our nginx configuration sets this header if:
        #  - there is an X-Forwarded-For set but no proxies configured in Zulip
        #  - proxies are configured but the request did not come from them
        #  - proxies are configured and the request came through them,
        #    but there was no X-Forwarded-Proto header
        #
        # Note that the first two may be false-positives.  We only
        # display the error if the request also came in over HTTP (and
        # a trusted proxy didn't say they get it over HTTPS), which
        # should be impossible because Zulip only supports external
        # https:// URLs in production.  nginx configuration ensures
        # that request.is_secure() is only true if our nginx is
        # serving the request over HTTPS, or it came from a trusted
        # proxy which reports that it is doing so.  This will result
        # in false negatives if Zulip's nginx is serving responses
        # over HTTPS to a proxy whose IP is not configured, or
        # misconfigured, but we cannot distinguish this from a random
        # client which is providing proxy headers to a correctly
        # configured Zulip.
        #
        # There are a couple complications to the above logic --
        # first, we do expect that requests not through the proxy may
        # happen from localhost over HTTP (e.g. the email gateway).
        # Second, we also expect that the proxy itself may make
        # healthcheck requests, which will not have an
        # X-Forwarded-Proto or X-Forwarded-For.  We handle the latter
        # case in the nginx config (as it involves CIDRs and proxy
        # ranges) and the former case here.
        if (
            proxy_state_header != ""
            and not request.is_secure()
            and request.META["REMOTE_ADDR"] not in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
        ):
            raise ProxyMisconfigurationError(proxy_state_header)
```

Solveably, I think, but it gets more complicated.

## API feature levels rebasing idea

*2024-05-31 to 2025-12-09 · 48 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/API.20feature.20levels.20rebasing.20idea/with/1811578)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-31 22:59 UTC

I've been thinking a little bit about how to improve the merge-conflict experience around API feature levels, and here's an idea:
- When working on an API change, we give it a codename; these can be randomly generated as something like `users-porcupine`, that references something about the endpoints involved but mostly is just intended to be unique.
- The API documentation source gets written as `Changes: New in {feature-level users-porcupine}` -- syntax TBD, but the idea is that this would be something that can be replaced with the final feature level either at the time the thing is merged, or even just replaced dynamically when displaying it.
- There's a registry mapping between feature level numbers and those codenames, and it's only that registry that needs to be updated when merging something.

What I don't like about it is that the indirection is a bit less readable when looking at the source; we'd probably end up having a `zulip.yaml.in` file that gets processed into a finished `zulip.yaml` with those variables substituted, which may be an architecture we probably want for other reasons anyway to let us do Markdown extensions in our documentation while having third-party tools able to inspect the resulting OpenAPI spec file happily.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-31 22:59 UTC

The problem statement here being that it's kinda annoying that whenever we merge an API change, we need to renumber all the other ones that have open PRs, and those rebases are nontrivial: You have to go through and update the API docs in 4 places to update the feature level numbers.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-06-03 04:01 UTC

I could see that working well but not sure about the cost of implementing and maintaining it.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-06-03 04:08 UTC

Another strategy that comes mind is using CI to bump the API version and replace it in code placeholders like `BUMPED_API_VERSION`  based on if commit message incluses `NEW_API_FEATURE` as scope of commit title.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-02-13 00:50 UTC

So I think rebasing pain is pretty significant at this point. I have a refined version of this idea that seems pretty solid. It has two parts. When you start working on an API change, you:
- Run a script that generates a new empty file of the form `api_docs/unmerged.d/ZF-ABCD12`, using a unique 6-character random hexadecimal ID.
- You put your changes destined for `api_docs/changelog.md` in that file.
- In `zulip.yaml`, you reference `Zulip 10.0 (feature level ZF-ABCD12).`
- Your PR now rebases happily on top of all other API change PRs.

When we merge a PR, there's a tool that generates an automated commit that squashes all `api_docs/unmerged.d/` files and puts the result at the top of `api_docs/changelog.md`, bumps `version.py` with a new feature level number, and does a find/replace of `ZF-ABCD12` into `361`, or whatever the assigned feature level is. 

That tool could live in a GitHub Action, generating an automated commit, or a script I run when merging.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-02-13 00:51 UTC

Probably for v1, we would have that second part be a script, and then we can try to figure out how to turn it into a GitHub Action once we've tested it locally enough. @Kunal Sharma would you be interested in prototyping this?

**Greg Price** · 2025-02-13 00:58 UTC

Sounds like a good plan. (I think you and I and @Anders Kaseorg discussed it in the office last week.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-02-13 01:02 UTC

Yes, and the key insight was from @Anders Kaseorg, forgot to mention that after getting excited on seeing we'd already discussed the previous simpler version I'd come up with, and so I didn't need to write as much background to propose it.

I think the only thing that is new compared with the office brainstorming is the `unmerged.d/` name.

**Greg Price** · 2025-02-13 01:05 UTC

One subtlety that I think didn't come up in that discussion, but which I noticed reading this now, is what order the script should assign feature-level numbers in if there are several `unmerged.d/` files. (In typical operation that shouldn't happen, but it'll likely sometimes happen when running the script gets forgotten on a given PR and then it's catching up after the next PR. Also if one PR introduces several files.)

It's not terrible if it ends up with an arbitrary order. But I think it wouldn't be too hard to get a sensible consistent order: if there's more than one such file, the script looks at each one in `git log`, and orders by the commit where each was first introduced, in commit-log order.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-02-13 01:05 UTC

In terms of benefits of this approach compared to the previous version, they include:
- It eliminates the need for a macro, which avoids moving our Markdown away from something that third-party code can work with. (The other big existing issue for tools like `openapi-generator` is all our URLs in API documentation links are relative, e.g. `/help/foo`).
- The random hex codes are closer in length to an integer feature level, resulting in less line-wrapping ugliness.

**Greg Price** · 2025-02-13 01:06 UTC

Oh and one minor suggestion: I'd go for lowercase hex rather than uppercase. Bit easier to type, and it also seems more conventional these days (for everything but Unicode code points).

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-02-13 01:06 UTC

I think it's probably correct to just squash everything into a single new feature level at each merge point. At least if it's a GitHub action that runs just after merging, what it means for there to be two directories at once is that they were merged ~simultaneously.

**Greg Price** · 2025-02-13 01:07 UTC

Sure, that'd be reasonable too.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-02-13 01:08 UTC

This would be kinda convenient actually, if you're making a PR that stacks together several API changes in sequence. You can just make each discrete API change in the PR its own file, and if we merge a prefix with just some of those changes, the set that were included get put into a new feature level, but the unmerged ones stay as they were.

## presence rewrite > how much data to fetch at initialization

*2024-06-01 to 2024-06-03 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/presence.20rewrite.20.3E.20how.20much.20data.20to.20fetch.20at.20initialization/with/1811907)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2024-06-01 20:35 UTC

The webapp will be sending `last_update_id=-1` to the server at initialization, to request all presence data.
However, until now we've been  only returning presence data from the last two weeks, and excluding older data.

So we have two choices here for the new API, when the client sends `last_update_id=-1`:
- Fetch all presence data, regardless of how old it is.
- Keep the old behavior, and return all presence data **from the last two weeks**.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2024-06-01 20:35 UTC

The "only last two weeks" restriction was probably particularly important till now, because we were
fetching all data on every presence fetch request. With this `last_update_id` API implementation,
a full fetch will only happen at webapp  initialization, so it might be more plausible to include all data,
without restriction?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-03 18:51 UTC

I think we definitely want to get rid of the 2-week restriction; I expect we'll want to do some load testing to figure out what threshold we want. Even "1 year" would be significantly cheaper than "forever" for big organizations like chat.zulip.org.

Just to explain the cost, we send 2 timestamps per user to the client, and those will compress only moderately well, since there's a lot of entropy in there. (One can imagine doing some smoothing of timestamps older than 2 weeks ago to round to the nearest hour for better compression as a future optimization).

So on chat.zulip.org, the full data set would add ~60k pairs-of-medium-entropy-integers-spelled-with-strings to the `/register` data set. It might be that this is not actually a big deal, because the `subscribers` data set is already huge in comparison, but that is a thing we need to fix, so probably best to not add a new big data set.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-03 18:58 UTC

One theory would be that `/` doesn't give you the full data set under any circumstances, but you can always send a separate request with `-1` as your cutoff? But I think maybe from an API standpoint, perhaps the right model for this merge point is "the server may give you only the most recently active users' data", which could be limited by time, number of rows, or whatever other algorithm.

The thing that's ugly about that is then the client doesn't know what cutoff it has, which is important for displaying the "more than 2 weeks ago" that we currently display in the UI for users where we don't have any data available to the client.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-03 18:59 UTC

Ultimately, we might want to clean that sort of quirk out of the UI in various ways, potentially including using browser local storage to cache the presence data set on most clients.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-03 19:01 UTC

My leaning is to start with the same 2-weeks rule that we had pre-changes for the initial transition, and then we can experiment dynamically in chat.zulip.org and Cloud to find a cutoff that we like, and then circle back to encoding that in the API as a follow-up documented API change.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2024-06-03 20:18 UTC

I kind of like keeping the 2-weeks rule at the start as well, to keep us from adding this concern as a potential confounder in evaluating the performance impacts of this API transition.


## presence rewrite > response last_update_id when no new data

*2024-06-01 to 2024-06-03 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/presence.20rewrite.20.3E.20response.20last_update_id.20when.20no.20new.20data/with/1811909)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2024-06-01 20:38 UTC

When the server returns some presence data to the client, it also includes the `presence_last_update_id`
parameter in its response, which is just the Max of `last_update_id`s of UserPresence at the time of
doing the fetch. However, there's the question of what value to return when there's no new presence
data to return.

The currently implemented approach is to just return the `last_update_id` the client sent in the request.
So if the client has `last_update_id=100` and sends that to the server, when there's no presence updates,
the server just sends `last_update_id=100` back - there's no state change after all.
There's the hypothetical extreme edge case - which may even be impossible, where there's no presence
data **at all**. Then the "no new data" response occurs even in the following two special cases: 

(1) Webapp initialization: the implemented behavior of the webapp at initialization is to send `last_update_id=-1`. 
  The description in the previous paragraph dictates that the server should return `last_update_id=-1` in this case.
  This is probably quite reasonable?

(2) Old `slim_presence` client: As discussed [here](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/378-api-design/topic/presence.20rewrite/near/1792207),
  we include `last_update_id` in the response whenever the client specifies `slim_presence=true`. An older
  client will make requests with `slim_presence=true` and no `last_update_id`.
  What `last_update_id` should the server return in this scenario, when there's no presence data? We could return `-1`,
  or we could just not include the parameter at all. Currently the PR implements
  returning `None` in this case. Not sure what's best; but this kind of client doesn't even look at
  these values, so this probably doesn't matter much?

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2024-06-01 20:41 UTC

I guess (2) can quite plausibly happen if an organization had no activity in more than two weeks. Because in the old API, we only return data that's more recent than last two weeks, so there'd be nothing to return here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-03 18:38 UTC

It is probably possible to have no presence data -- if you're the only user and you've set the privacy setting to not send presence data, for example.

I think in those cases, having the client send a `-1` in its next request (to ask for "all the presence data" seems correct.

I like the idea of `last_update_id` always being an integer, type-wise, so I think my preference for case 2 would be to return `-1` -- basically replace a `None` response with a `-1`.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2024-06-03 20:15 UTC

Yeah that plan makes sense to me.


## presence rewrite > add last_update_to /register?

*2024-06-01 to 2024-06-03 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/presence.20rewrite.20.3E.20add.20last_update_to.20.2Fregister.3F/with/1811911)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2024-06-01 20:42 UTC

The webapp doesn't use `/register`, so `last_update_id` has not been added to the endpoint,
but do we want to add it so that the mobile app and other potential clients can implement this?

In particular, as pointed out in https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/29999/#discussion_r1593244047
this could enable a useful mechanic where the mobile app caches presence data and just asks for new data only
upon restarts.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-03 16:29 UTC

I think we could reasonably add that as a `/register` parameter -- probably needs a name like `presence_last_update_id`. 

The idea would be that the mobile apps could just have a persistent cache of their understanding of presence data for the account/server, and just send the `presence_last_update_id` appropriate.

The other approach would be for the mobile apps to not include `presence` in `fetch_event_types`, just in the `event_types` request, and do an independent `presence` API request to fetch the data. That is pretty likely be what we do in the implementation today... But I think it probably is reasonable for the server to have the capability in its `/register` API in case a client wants to use `/register` to get initial presence data.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-03 16:29 UTC

The main downside of such a cache system is that it's not completely robust in the event that a `UserProfile` gets completely deleted from the user database while the mobile client is offline -- the client will have no way to delete that record from its database. Seems harmless, since such a user ID would, in the protocol, not be expected to have its presence data ever displayed.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-03 16:31 UTC

But I think it'd have considerable upside for network costs for the mobile clients, and a pretty simple algorithm.

## deactivate user - error only owner

*2024-06-17 to 2024-06-25 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/deactivate.20user.20-.20error.20only.20owner/with/1828661)*

**Lauryn Menard** · 2024-06-17 18:20 UTC

(replying to Lauryn Menard)
> * Updating [/api/deactivate-user](https://chat.zulip.org/api/deactivate-user) error documentation for `code: "CANNOT_DEACTIVATE_LAST_USER"` comes with `is_last_owner: boolean`

So, it looks like the documentation for /api/deactivate-user and /api/deactivate-own-user are correct, and each endpoint returns a different error response for the case where the request is trying to deactivate the only user with the "owner" role in the organization.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2024-06-17 18:20 UTC

```python
@typed_endpoint
def deactivate_user_backend(
    request: HttpRequest,
    user_profile: UserProfile,
    *,
    user_id: PathOnly[int],
    deactivation_notification_comment: Optional[
        Annotated[str, StringConstraints(max_length=2000)]
    ] = None,
) -> HttpResponse:
    target = access_user_by_id(user_profile, user_id, for_admin=True)
    if target.is_realm_owner and not user_profile.is_realm_owner:
        raise OrganizationOwnerRequiredError
    if check_last_owner(target):
        raise JsonableError(_("Cannot deactivate the only organization owner"))
    if deactivation_notification_comment is not None:
        deactivation_notification_comment = deactivation_notification_comment.strip()
    return _deactivate_user_profile_backend(
        request,
        user_profile,
        target,
        deactivation_notification_comment=deactivation_notification_comment,
    )


def deactivate_user_own_backend(request: HttpRequest, user_profile: UserProfile) -> HttpResponse:
    if UserProfile.objects.filter(realm=user_profile.realm, is_active=True).count() == 1:
        raise CannotDeactivateLastUserError(is_last_owner=False)
    if user_profile.is_realm_owner and check_last_owner(user_profile):
        raise CannotDeactivateLastUserError(is_last_owner=True)

    do_deactivate_user(user_profile, acting_user=user_profile)
    return json_success(request)
```

**Lauryn Menard** · 2024-06-17 18:21 UTC

I'm not sure if that was an intentional or unintentional choice, so I thought I'd check-in here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-18 22:06 UTC

I doubt that's intentional, we can standardize the nicer error code from the "self" case, I expect.

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-25 04:08 UTC

SGTM. Mobile doesn't use these endpoints, so no compatibility concern from that side.

Thanks @Lauryn Menard for spotting this!


## client capability for can_create_streams and related fields

*2024-06-21 to 2024-06-24 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/client.20capability.20for.20can_create_streams.20and.20related.20fields/with/1833441)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2024-06-21 14:49 UTC

We currently pass fields like `can_create_streams`, `can_create_public_streams`, `can_create_private_streams` and `can_create_web_public_streams` as a boolean value for whether the user has permission to create streams in `register` response. As we have migrated these settings to groups-based framework, an extra query is needed to compute these fields.

Webapp does not use these fields and instead directly use the setting value to determine whether the user has permission or not.  So, we are planning to add a client capability to decide when to include these fields in response or not so that we can atleast save queries for webapp and probably other clients who do not need these fields.

I wanted to discuss about what we should name the client capability field. We have a field named `user_avatar_url_field_optional` for deciding whether to pass avatar url to clients, and the urls are passed to clients if the field is `False`.  We can probably name it something similar, but here we would have a single client capability controlling multiple fields. One that I could think of is `can_create_streams_fields_optional`, but we could use something better.

**Sahil Batra** · 2024-06-21 14:51 UTC

Also, there are a couple of similar fields which are not for stream creation permission like `can_subscribe_other_users`, `can_invite_others_to_realm`. These settings would also be migrated to groups framework in future, so we can also send these based on client capability and if we want a single client capability for all these fields, then we might need to think of some other name like `user_permission_boolean_fields_optional`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-21 20:03 UTC

Thinking about this a bit, I wonder if we can just use a single query in the server to compute all of these fields. Specifically, if we did a single query to answer "What is the set of groups, recursively, that the current user is a member of", then that data structure would answer the question for which of these permissions the current user has; just check if the group ID for that setting is in that user's list of groups.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-21 20:03 UTC

We'd need to pay a query in races settings in `apply_events` to recalculate those, which is kinda annoying, but I think it'd eliminate most of the impact on `register` of this question, and allow us to skip doing an API change around this detail.

**Sahil Batra** · 2024-06-22 04:04 UTC

Yeah, we can do that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-24 22:18 UTC

This was done in #30554. I think we can probably defer making an API change here; it seems efficient enough and I feel these `can_` permissions variables are might be helpful for writing simpler API clients.

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-29 00:12 UTC

Just to recapitulate the process a bit, since content HTML changes are something we have less practice with than API changes of the kind that appear in our OpenAPI spec:

Whatever we do, before merging we should:
(a) Make sure existing clients don't crash, or otherwise behave substantially broken, with the change.

(b) Write down very concretely what the new API is. Normally we do this in the docs at /api/rest, as part of the server PR; but for HTML changes, since we don't currently have such docs for them at all, we can settle for a mention in /api/changelog and the details just going in this channel.

(c) Ideally, implement the client side of the new API, in order to validate end-to-end that it works well from a client perspective.

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-29 00:13 UTC

We fairly often skip (c), and since the timeline is getting tight for 9.0 this may be one of the times we skip it. (It tends to add to the timeline because it serializes developing a server implementation, then developing the client against that, and only then being ready to merge on the server.)

But that will then put an extra premium on being thorough in (b).

## detecting inactive streams

*2024-06-25 to 2024-12-04 · 46 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/detecting.20inactive.20streams/with/1837791)*

As detailed in [this conversation](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/6-frontend/topic/fetching.20message.20history/near/1836600), we have a feature to [demote inactive channels](https://zulip.com/help/manage-inactive-channels) in the left sidebar, basically sorting to the bottom channels where we have no recent message history.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-25 17:02 UTC

It probably makes sense to just have the server be responsible for computing that answer, along these lines:

(replying to Aman (amanagr))
> > I think we should discuss the right approach for it; I'm not sure where in the API an answer should live. This could just be a part of the stream data that we send to the clients. What do you think about running a cron job once per day which updates `is_recently_active` flag on stream based on if …

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-25 17:04 UTC

Architecturally, I think that's probably the right overall design; it should be a relatively easily scaled query on the server to compute which streams have at least one message after some date threshold, and then it can be cached and sent out to clients requesting stream data.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-25 17:05 UTC

(And then the exact definition of which streams are active can be held in the server logic that can be changed one if we decide we want a different date cutoff or whatever).

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-06-25 17:27 UTC
