**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-06-25 17:51 UTC

Yeah, that is a thing this desing doesn't perform well for but in most cases, the first fetch will have the messages sent since the last cron job update and we can use it to update the active / inactive status locally before the streams get rendered in the left sidebar. So, this might not be a real life problem.

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-25 17:53 UTC

It's not a problem for web, for that reason, but it is certainly a complication in the semantics of the API

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-25 17:54 UTC

If we want mobile to support this feature of demoting inactive channels — and I think we should, it'd be good for making Zulip feel like a coherent experience between different platforms — then it'd be good if we can have those updates reflected already in what the server sends

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-25 17:55 UTC

One way to do that would be to have the transition inactive → active happen when a message is sent, and only the reverse happens in a cron job

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-25 17:58 UTC

Another would be for the database to record the last message ID, or the latest message timestamp, on each channel, and keep that updated on sending a message. Then "is recently active" is just a comparison on that.

To avoid creating a lot of contention, that field might be like "*approximate* latest message timestamp", and on send it only gets updated if the existing value is more than like a day old or a week old.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-06-25 18:00 UTC

I want to avoid storing last message id / time on stream because it will add to making moving messages between streams even slower.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-06-25 18:00 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)
> One way to do that would be to have the transition inactive → active happen when a message is sent, and only the reverse happens in a cron job

That sounds like a great idea to me.

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-25 18:03 UTC

On moving messages, any update to whether the stream is active (or when it was last active) will be O(1), while the updates to the messages themselves are O(n) in the number of messages, so I think it shouldn't make a significant difference there.

But also, for purposes of "is this stream active", I think it's OK if a stream counts as active because it had some recent messages in it but they got moved elsewhere. So we could skip that update on the old stream entirely.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-25 18:04 UTC

(replying to Aman (amanagr))
> I want to avoid storing last message id / time on stream because it will add to making moving messages between streams even slower.

I think we need it for a "recent conversations" API anyway, so I support adding that.

**Greg Price** · 2024-06-25 18:04 UTC

(and therefore also skip any query to find the latest remaining message)

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-25 18:04 UTC

Also, if the messages being moved don't include the latest message in the channel, we can detect that without doing any database queries in the message-move code path.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-25 18:07 UTC

The main risk I see in adding a `last_message_id` field at the stream level to the database (even if not the API) is that we do want to make the API support a "recent conversations" view for mobile, and that will likely entail making a whole set of Topic/UserTopic tables to cache information about what topics exist (and are accessible to the current user, where that's limited due to protected history stream permissions) and their range of messages.

And it's very possible that once we do that work, we'll find we don't need or want this data structure at all, since we can use the tables/indexes that the above requires us to build.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-06-25 18:11 UTC

It sounds like we should decide on what we need for the recent conversations API support before working on this?

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-06-26 14:08 UTC

Why 180 days? Since that is amount of days web tries to backfill once the app is loaded. See `target_days_of_history: 180` in `message_fetch.js`.

This approach seems like will have us not think about message access permissions, moving messages and has low chance of us feeling  in the future that keeping the stream data updated in not worth the cost since it is cheap to keep `is_recently_active` updated.

Also, it has no impact on initial load time which we will have if we track last message in stream model to compute if the stream is active. 

I don't think we will need to track last message in stream to support recent view or anything else. Even `stream_topic_history.get_max_message_id` is only used in tests right now.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-27 23:03 UTC

Yeah, that's probably a fine answer. We can then do future work that computes `is_recently_active` a different way, but having it exposed to the API as a high-level concept seems nice for clients to be able to work with it..

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-07-02 13:37 UTC

Do we want to send events for change in `is_recently_active` or do we want clients to handle that locally?

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-07-02 13:38 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-09 18:57 UTC

We may very slightly want clients to be able to handle `is_recently_active` events, just because moving the only recent conversation out of a channel could in theory toggle it to `false`, though we may not bother implementing that interaction in the server for now?

But I think mostly we probably do want clients to just update it when they see a message, to avoid having to think about races. (E.g. when you send a message and it's locally echoed, you may want the channel to immediately appear as recently active, and you may not particularly want the channel to relocate again if the message fails to send).

So I'm not sure what the right policy is.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-09 23:31 UTC

Yeah, on a new message I think it's best for the client to just apply the update as one more thing that `message` events imply. The `message` event already carries all the relevant information.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-09 23:34 UTC

If the server does mark a stream as inactive when messages get moved out of it (or deleted), then that'd probably be good for the server to send an event for. The client doesn't necessarily have the needed information for that, because it may not know the time (or even the message ID) of the next-latest message.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-09 23:36 UTC

And then once we're sending events for that, probably cleanest to send events also when the cron job marks a stream as inactive. That way clients don't have to set up their own cron-job equivalents — those are often among the trickier parts of a client's data model to write.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-09 23:37 UTC

(Also that way there's no subtle glitch where the server and a client might slightly disagree about which streams are inactive, because the client has already noticed it's been 180 days and the server's cron job is still hours away from running. That's a very small polish issue, though.)

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-07-10 06:18 UTC

Okay, it sounds like it would be easier to get a version of this integrated without the events complexity. So, I will update the PR without using events so that it makes it to 9.0.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-10 08:02 UTC

That's OK as long as we're fine with clients, including the web app, never marking a channel as inactive after seeing it as active.

If clients are to deal with marking inactive on their own, that will be more complex than if the server takes care of sending an event for it. (For the two different reasons I mentioned above.) But clients marking a channel as active when a new message comes in is easy and fine.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-10 08:03 UTC

Oh I guess another potentially tricky thing for clients to handle is when messages get moved into a previously-inactive channel.

It's easy for the client to update something like a latest message ID of the channel, because it has the message IDs of the moved messages. But it may not have their timestamps. So the client can't reliably update a latest message *time* for the channel, and therefore can't reliably tell if the channel should be marked as active.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-10 08:05 UTC

So if we were to try to do without events for this, I think we'd basically inevitably have a bug where a channel remains inactive (as far as clients with an already-live event queue see it) when messages get moved into it.

## deleting messages when not subscribed

*2024-07-01 to 2026-01-30 · 56 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/deleting.20messages.20when.20not.20subscribed/with/1842975)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-01 19:42 UTC

In #30440, we are looking to solve the fact that if an organization administrator views a stream they're not subscribed to and deletes a message there, they don't get the "message deleted" event (since they're not a subscriber) and thus will not see their action having succeeded.

The proposed fix is to send an event

Any concerns with this API change? Should we do a feature level bump and documentation for it? At the very least, we do need to update the text that says "Sent to all users who received the message" (https://zulip.com/api/get-events#delete_message):

> Event sent when a message has been deleted. Sent to all users who received the message. This event is also sent when the user loses access to a message, such as when it is [moved to a channel][message-move-channel] that the user does not [have permission to access][channel-access].

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-01 19:50 UTC

We could specify "As well as the currently acting user". Oh, but reading the implementation, it looks like at some point we changed the logic to send the event for a deleted stream message to "current subscribers who are not long-term idle", regardless of whether they received the original event. Which is still potentially a subset of users who have access to the message; for example, deleting a message in a public stream with 5 subscribers on chat.zulip.org will send the event to only those 5 users, not the 30k users who can access public streams.

So maybe we want something to the effect of "Sent to all active users who currently are subscribed to the messages' recipient. May also be sent to additional users who had access to it, such as an administrator deleting messages in a stream that they are not subscribed to.".

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-01 20:40 UTC

I guess part of my thinking is that I don't think it's valuable to over-specify the circumstances in which clients will get this event. The main detail to clarify is "you might not be currently subscribed to the stream containing this message", but beyond knowing that, a client likely doesn't care about the details of why the server is sending this event from the standpoint of correctly implementing the handler for it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-01 20:41 UTC

So I think it's an API change we need to analyze and document because a client might have previously been making an assumption about only receiving deleted-message notices for streams where it is currently subscribed.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-09 20:14 UTC

Feedback on this would be appreciated.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-09 23:11 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-09 23:11 UTC

Ideally we'd find a clean way to say "all the users that should get the event get the event", except with enough concreteness on "should" that it's reassuring instead of tautological, and then when we discover wrinkles like this it's just a matter of fixing a bug.

## thumbnailing URLs

*2024-07-02 to 2024-07-16 · 39 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/thumbnailing.20URLs/with/1843871)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-07-02 17:19 UTC

Splitting this off from #**api design>thumbnail placeholder** -- cc @Greg Price.

For an image accessible via `/user_uploads/.../filename.png` (note the on-disk and S3 storage have differing number of subdirectory elements in `...` -- 3 and 2, respectively), the server provides thumbnails at a URL of `/user_uploads/thumbnail/.../filename.png/150x100.webp`, where `150` is the max width of the thumbnail, and `100` is the max height, and `webp` is the format.  This image is a *static* thumbnail; if the image is animated, animated thumbnails may also be available by appending `-anim` after the resolution -- e.g. `/user_uploads/thumbnail/.../filename.png/150x100-anim.webp`.

In the rendered HTML, thumbnailed images appear as non-thumbnailed images currently do, except with a `src` URL beginning with `/user_uploads/thumbnail/`.  By default, if a source image was an animated image, the image URL provided will be to an animated thumbnail.  A `data-animated="true"` attribute is also provided on such images.

Currently, the implementation also provides a `data-src-fullsize="/user_uploads/.../filename.png"` attribute pointing to the non-thumbnailed original.  This was for ease of quick implementation, since this allows use of the existing mostly-removed previous `THUMBNAILING=True` client codepath, which provided such an attribute.  The plan is to remove that attribute, since clients can derive that URL from the thumbnailed URL.


To make this concrete, currently the content of:
```
[Screenshot-2024-06-25-at-12.52.42PM.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/d6/Xu0_JW9EThE1PO0aGdzwE3BR/Screenshot-2024-06-25-at-12.52.42PM.png)
```
..is currently rendered as:
```html
<p><a href="/user_uploads/2/d6/Xu0_JW9EThE1PO0aGdzwE3BR/Screenshot-2024-06-25-at-12.52.42PM.png" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" title="Download Screenshot-2024-06-25-at-12.52.42PM.png">Screenshot-2024-06-25-at-12.52.42PM.png</a></p>
<div class="message_inline_image"><a href="/user_uploads/2/d6/Xu0_JW9EThE1PO0aGdzwE3BR/Screenshot-2024-06-25-at-12.52.42PM.png" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" aria-label="Screenshot-2024-06-25-at-12.52.42PM.png"><img src="/user_uploads/2/d6/Xu0_JW9EThE1PO0aGdzwE3BR/Screenshot-2024-06-25-at-12.52.42PM.png"></a></div>
```

With the thumbnailing changes, this message would be initially rendered as:
```html
<p><a href="/user_uploads/2/d6/Xu0_JW9EThE1PO0aGdzwE3BR/Screenshot-2024-06-25-at-12.52.42PM.png" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" title="Download Screenshot-2024-06-25-at-12.52.42PM.png">Screenshot-2024-06-25-at-12.52.42PM.png</a></p>

```

...which, after thumbnailing completed, would have a silent-edit event to replace it with:
```html

```

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-07-02 17:29 UTC

As part of client registration, the server provides a list of (size, format, animated) elements which describe the formats that it will generate for any image.  Clients can use this list to swap out whatever default thumbnail the server is offering (e.g. `150x100.webp`) for one which is better-suited to its display.

We can either choose to offer this list as a list of thumbnail filenames -- e.g:
```json:
["150x100.web", "150x100.avif"]
```
...or as a richer JSON structure, which doesn't require the client to assume it knows how to parse those:
```json
[
  {
    "name": "150x100.webp",
    "max_width": 150,
    "max_height": 100,
    "format": "webp",
    "animated": false
  }, 
  // ...
]
```

I assume that the richer format is probably preferred, and thus what we should spec.

Note that historical messages may contain `img src="/user_uploads/thumbnail/...` references which are *not in the current list of thumbnail formats*, since they may have been removed at some point.  Those URLs will continue to work, since we generate on upload, but clients cannot assume that for any `src` that they see, the current server information will contain a description of that format.

Conversely, clients *may* request a format which is currently supported but which was not generated when an old image was uploaded.  The server will generate the thumbnailed image for that format on-demand.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-07-02 17:35 UTC

A somewhat tangential-question is if you have a sense, @Greg Price, of what sizes/formats mobile may want.  Currently the implementation is generating:
```python
THUMBNAIL_OUTPUT_FORMATS = [
    ThumbnailFormat("webp", 150, 100, animated=True),
    ThumbnailFormat("webp", 150, 100, animated=False),
    ThumbnailFormat("avif", 150, 100, animated=False),
    ThumbnailFormat("jpg", 150, 100, animated=False),
    ThumbnailFormat("avif", 600, 400, animated=False),
    ThumbnailFormat("webp", 600, 400, animated=False),
]
```

...but the web client is only going to use the 150x100 size -- the 600x400 was just to test multiple scales, and thus will probably be removed before this is merged.  But even if mobile doesn't yet support this protocol, shipping 9.0 which also generates the right size/format for what mobile will want will make the experience better for those mobile clients.

Yeah, good question.

It looks like zulip-mobile currently shows a max height of 160 logical pixels and max width of basically the screen width, scaling up if the image is small:
```css
.message_inline_image img /* , … */ {
  width: 100%;
  height: 160px;
  object-fit: contain;
}
```

So we could think of that as a 240x160 box, which is a bit bigger than the one on web.

Crucially, though, the unit called "px" there is a [*logical* pixel](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-mobile/blob/e352f563ecf2fa9b09b688d5a65b6bc89b0358bc/docs/background/layout.md). So 160 logical pixels is 320 or 480 physical pixels by default on a modern iPhone, and on a modern Android device it takes various values ranging from around there to somewhat more. (It's 540 physical pixels by default on my Pixel 8.)

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-03 02:16 UTC

… OK, I'm not immediately finding data that's directly on point, but here's some based on the physical density of pixels. Nominally 160 logical pixels is supposed to be 1 inch (good old 25.4mm), so a device with 540 pixels per inch corresponds nominally to the same logical-to-physical ratio as the Pixel 8.

And it looks like there are [some Sony Xperia devices](https://www.gsmarena.com/results.php3?nDisplayDensityMin=600) that claim more than 600ppi. A few years ago they even had some a hair over 800 ppi, but it seems they've stopped making those; [the latest](https://www.gsmarena.com/sony_xperia_1_v-12263.php) is 643ppi.

All devices from other vendors are under 580ppi, according to that database.

So I'd be pretty comfortable with sticking to a 3.5x scale factor, so 840x560 for the size of the thumbnail.

**Greg Price** · 2024-08-15 05:13 UTC

We use the time zone not only for the time right now, but for times in the past and future: in particular for "global times" in messages.

So if you see a message about a meeting next week, and Zulip tells you it means 10am in your time zone but it actually means 9am in your time zone (and 10am in some neighboring time zone that is the one Zulip was set to), then I think the problem this issue is meant to solve won't have really been solved.

**Greg Price** · 2024-08-15 05:14 UTC

Looking back [at the MDN page](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/DateTimeFormat/resolvedOptions#timezone) that @Anders Kaseorg linked to in the original issue #16957, though, it says this:
> All browsers canonicalize time zone names, but in different directions. For example, `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { timeZone: "Europe/Kiev" }).resolvedOptions().timeZone` and `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { timeZone: "Europe/Kyiv" }).resolvedOptions().timeZone` will return the same string in the same browser, but maybe different strings in different browsers.

So that suggests we should be able to just ask the browser to canonicalize, and compare those.

**Greg Price** · 2024-08-15 05:15 UTC

(And the only thing we have to take care with is that the two things we compare are *both* the results of canonicalizing in the current browser — whatever the server gives us, we ask the browser for its canonical name for that.)

**Kislay Udbhav Verma** · 2024-08-15 05:17 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)
> So that suggests we should be able to just ask the browser to canonicalize, and compare those

Indeed, that's what I ended up doing.

```js
function is_browser_timezone_same_as(timezone: string): boolean {
    if (timezone === "") {
        return false;
    }
    const date1 = Date.parse(
        new Date().toLocaleString("en-US", {timeZone: timerender.display_time_zone}),
    );
    const date2 = Date.parse(new Date().toLocaleString("en-US", {timeZone: timezone}));
    return date1 === date2;
}
```

The `timeZone` passed will first be canonicalized by the browser.
We're then checking whether the current instant has the same representation in the browser time zone and the one set in user settings.

**Greg Price** · 2024-08-15 05:21 UTC

(PDT and PST aren't really "time zones" in the sense that's become standard for computers. Rather, `America/Los_Angeles` is the time zone we colloquially call "PT" or "US Pacific Time", and it refers to the whole schedule for alternating between PST and PDT through the years.

One way to get a realistic example of the kind of situation you mentioned is to take `America/Los_Angeles` aka PT (alternating -0800 and -0700) and `America/Phoenix` aka MST (-0700 all year). Or the latter and `America/Denver` aka MT (alternating -0700 and -0600).)

**Greg Price** · 2024-08-15 18:02 UTC

DST definitely makes things complicated.

I think it's a useful system for countries away from the equator to use, where the days are a lot longer in summer than in winter. When the sun rises in June several hours earlier than it does in December, it's natural to want to get up earlier in June than in December, in order to enjoy the daylight. DST is a way of solving the coordination problem to let everyone do that, in a society where everyone's schedules intersect with lots of others' — their coworkers, their kids' schools, the places they do business, and so on. ## thumbnailing transition for 9.0

*2024-07-12 to 2024-07-16 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/thumbnailing.20transition.20for.209.2E0/with/1886620)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-12 19:21 UTC

So here's a proposal for how the uploads thumbnailing transition could work in 9.0:
- We ship the API designed in #**api design>thumbnail placeholder** and #**api design>thumbnailing URLs**.
- We use a high-resolution thumbnail, something like 840x560, as the default image size in the `img src=`  element, used for clients unaware of thumbnailing. This should mean a minimal regression in the visual user experience.
- Presumably a thumbnailing-unaware client's lightbox/download button will download the thumbnail, not the originally uploaded image. This might be OK as a thing to document; use cases for full-size original images on mobile devices are limited, and there's an effective workaround of using the web app (on your phone or otherwise) to get the image.
- Mobile RN is updated to support downloading the original image. I posted #**mobile-team>react native image viewer** to investigate whether it's possible that this happens to work already, or can be made to do so in simple ways. But potentially we should be thinking about a design with a separate "Download original" button that gets you the full-quality image, rather than making the only options for downloading the image do that; some uses cases.
- When mobile adds full thumbnailing support in the Flutter app, it'll be rewriting the `<img>` tags itself anyway, and can just select whichever options it wants from the menu supported by the server for the different use cases.
- Then perhaps for the 10.0 release cycle, we can look at downsizing the default `img src=` quality, which would at that point mainly be used by `zulip-archive` among official clients, to something lower resolution if appropriate.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-12 19:23 UTC

I think with that transition plan, we'd be able to take advantage of thumbnailing in the web app fully in 9.0, have minor regressions at worst for mobile at 9.0 launch (I think probably on balance, most users would take being unable to download the original-quality image on their phone over having images consume tons of bandwidth on slow networks), and not require further server changes except those motivated by bugs/errors for mobile to take full advantage of thumbnailing with 9.x servers as the mobile development roadmap permits.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-12 19:27 UTC

Just adding a backlink to #**release management>9.0 thumbnailing plan** in case we end up using that other topic as well.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-12 22:50 UTC

So I think with this plan the one thing we'd need to do in the legacy mobile app is to handle the placeholders.

… That and to test it end-to-end. Things *should* work, apart from placeholders, but it'd be good to avoid surprises.

*2024-07-18 to 2024-07-18 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/rendering_only.20update_message.20events/with/1894060)*

https://zulip.com/api/get-events#update_message says:
> `stream_name`: string Only present if the message was edited and originally sent to a channel.

Our `rendering_only` updates [do not send this key](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/e1f3c54a1d1b1f047a23033d4376301991a19b0c/zerver/actions/message_edit.py#L373-L379) (or `stream_id`, which is also documented the same way):
```python
def do_update_embedded_data(
    user_profile: UserProfile,
    message: Message,
    content: str | None,
    rendering_result: MessageRenderingResult,
) -> None:
    timestamp = timezone_now()
    event: dict[str, Any] = {
        "type": "update_message",
        "user_id": None,
        "edit_timestamp": datetime_to_timestamp(timestamp),
        "message_id": message.id,
        "rendering_only": True,
    }
    changed_messages = [message]
    rendered_content: str | None = None

    ums = UserMessage.objects.filter(message=message.id)

    if content is not None:
        update_user_message_flags(rendering_result, ums)
        rendered_content = rendering_result.rendered_content
        message.rendered_content = rendered_content
        message.rendered_content_version = markdown_version
        event["content"] = content
        event["rendered_content"] = rendered_content

    message.save(update_fields=["content", "rendered_content"])

    event["message_ids"] = update_message_cache(changed_messages)
```

Is this a documentation bug, or an implementation bug?

is probably actually meant to be a way of documenting this behavior.

For one, it doesn't make a lot of sense if you read it in the most obvious way — the event is always about the message being edited, right? Or else *moved*, but clearly these fields are present in that case because that's where they're most relevant.

And then here's from the top of the event's doc (emphasis added):
> Event sent when a message's content, topic and/or channel has been **edited or when** a message's content has a rendering update, such as for an inline URL preview.

## thumbnailing dimensions

*2024-07-22 to 2024-09-06 · 41 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/thumbnailing.20dimensions/with/1898379)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-22 00:34 UTC

So there's one aspect of the current thumbnailing design that isn't great: There's a lag before you see anything when you click on an image in the message feed, while it fetches the original image from the server. 

What we should do instead is display the (potentially somewhat blurry) thumbnail instead, while fetching the original-quality image from the server, and swap it into place once we receive the high-quality version. The problem with doing this is that because the lightbox opens images at a scaling level based on the original image's dimensions, we need the original image's dimensions, not those of the thumbnail, to do this weel.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-22 00:37 UTC

In practical terms, this means we need the thumbnailing processing pipeline to encode the original image's dimensions into the Markdown, so that is available to lightbox rendering code. We will want be able to make use of that information for other purposes, like potentially using previews shaped like images for those with unusual aspect ratios (see #25168 for example context, though the issue was written about embeds, not Zulip uploads).

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-22 00:43 UTC

So the question is how we want to encode the information? My proposal would be something like `data-original-dimensions="1200x900"`. Some notes:
- I think we want `original` in the name to be clear that we're talking about the original image's dimensions.
- While parsing an `{width}x{height}` specification is a bit of client-side complexity, that's an encoding format we're already using implicitly in the data (E.g.,`300x200.webp`) passed to clients in the `thumbnail_formats` part of the `/register` response), because that's part of how `libvips` works. So even though clients don't need to parse that, it feels nice to not make somethin else up.
- It feels a bit nicer to just have a single `data` attribute for dimensions rather than splitting it between a `data-original-width` and `data-original-height`, since I think most clients are going to want to use those two values together. And it's probably a bit cleaner to do `const original_dimensions = parse_dimensions($elt.attr("data-original-dimensions"))` to get your TypeScript object with `.width` and `.height` attributes, than needing to grab two different things.
- The other direction we could consider is a more general `data-original-metadata` JSON object that might contain `width/height` keys but could potentially be extended with other properties if desired. I don't envision any obvious other properties that we'd want to add, though, and we can always use some other`data` attribute for such things in the future.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-22 00:44 UTC

@Alex Vandiver @Greg Price @Anders Kaseorg FYI; we'll probably want to at least attempt to decide something tomorrow, since this is the main 9.0 regression we've identified resulting from the thumbnailing migration, and I expect the actual implementation here might be a manageable amount of work if we're able to be decisive on what is a good API here.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-07-22 00:55 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-22 21:51 UTC

For zulip-mobile I think we'll skip trying to show the thumbnail in the lightbox while the full image loads.

Unlike zulip-flutter or Zulip web, the lightbox and the message list don't share a cache for fetched images: the message list is in a webview so uses a browser cache, while the lightbox is outside the webview. So to show the thumbnail, we'd have to first go and download the thumbnail from scratch anyway.

When the original image is big enough and the connection is slow enough, that would still be a UX improvement. But it'd come at a cost in using more download capacity and more time, for everyone, as well as adding complexity to the implementation. And the improvement wouldn't be as radical as eagerly showing the thumbnail is in zulip-flutter or Zulip web, because it'd still mean some waiting.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-22 18:58 UTC

Clients kinda do want to know how deep presence history they will have, for documentation, displaying "more than 2 weeks ago" type strings, and the like. A few notes:

- We could make how much history is requested be a parameter the client passes to the server in the `/register` request for how much presence history to fetch, since then strings about how long ago the user must have been last active can then be written in the same codebase.
- Clients might just want to fetch the missing data as needed, which might impact what sort of cutoff makes sense.

It sounds we have two options here - essentialy, request param vs response param?

(2) Having the server dictate how much history it provides, and including an extra field in the presence response data (or maybe `/server_settings` is where this belongs?) telling the client that.

Of these, I feel like (1) should be better since it's not any more complicated and lets clients customize? So a client-side parameter makes sense to me.

## trimming date_joined

*2024-07-27 to 2024-12-16 · 48 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/trimming.20date_joined/with/1904593)*

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-27 21:05 UTC

`realm_users[].date_joined` is a significant part of the `state_data` we send, largely because it has unnecessary microsecond-level precision (unless the viewer is a spectator, to whom we only send the day). Reducing its precision would have this effect on the *total* size of `state_data` here:

| strategy | uncompressed | compressed |
| - | - | - |
| now | 17036373 | 3802079 |
| `+00:00` → `Z` | 16883883 (-0.9%) | 3800957 (-0.0%) |
| second | 16670397 (-2.1%) | 3640763 (-4.2%) |
| minute | 16578903 (-2.7%) | 3575558 (-6.0%) |
| hour | 16487409 (-3.2%) | 3512013 (-7.6%) |
| day | 16365417 (-3.9%) | 3457747 (-9.1%) |
| remove `date_joined` | 15541971 (-8.8%) | 3377724 (-11.2%) |

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-27 21:28 UTC

Neat!

When you say `state_data`, does that correspond to the response from /api/register-queue?

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-27 21:28 UTC

I don't see any valid use case for finer than minute-level precision, so that seems like an easy win.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-27 21:32 UTC

Hour- and minute-level precision can I guess be useful about users that joined very recently. Also for accurately showing even just the date but in the viewer's own time zone.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-27 21:33 UTC

Do we use that information for anything other than showing in the user's profile modal, though?

If not, this would be a good candidate to leave out of the initial data entirely, and let the client fetch lazily on demand.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-27 21:33 UTC

(With I guess a client capability)

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-27 21:38 UTC

As I've mentioned elsewhere before, I think the main metric of concern in the size of the /api/register-queue response (or the equivalent initial data for web) is the compressed size, since the time to just download N bytes of that response is what can really blow up loading times when someone's on a slow connection.

The uncompressed size shows up in I guess the client's memory use. But one megabyte of RAM isn't a material issue on basically any device capable of running a Zulip client, while one megabyte of added download size can be very significant when on a slow and flaky connection.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-27 21:38 UTC

And conveniently, the "compressed" column which I'm therefore focusing on is the one this optimization looks best in.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-27 21:42 UTC

We’ll need to do lazy on-demand fetching of *all* data about other users and their subscriptions if we’re going to make major improvements here. I'm looking for easy minor improvements for now.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-27 23:55 UTC

Thanks for digging into this! Optimizing the compressed size is one of my goals for the 10.0 release cycle.

(replying to Greg Price)
> If not, this would be a good candidate to leave out of the initial data entirely, and let the client fetch lazily on demand.

Yeah, agreed. If it were something on the user card, we might want to have it without a fetch to the server, but the user profiles are rarely accessed enough that it seems fine to have to do a fetch.

It might still feel like a UX regression to have those not load instantly, or to have a distracting loading indicator on the "Date joined" element. If we wanted to avoid it needing to wait for a network call often, options include:
- Making it optional for the server to send it, and only sending it for a subset of users who've been online recently; this might get a 100x factor on chat.zulip.org with it being very rare that users would actually see the situation where it's not already available.
- Fetching it when a user opens the user card preemptively, under the theory that the main way one gets to a user profile is via the user card (Though one can directly navigate to it via URL, for example).

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-28 00:04 UTC

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-28 00:08 UTC

Data about other users and their subscriptions is about 90.5% of the payload.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-28 00:24 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-31 17:52 UTC

I guess back to the simplest optimization of trimming `date_join`, thoughts on how we want to go about trimming `date_joined` precision? I could imagine even trimming in the database itself to minute-level precision, in that we have `RealmAuditLog` if we really need to know the precise moment something happened. 

But probably doing at the API layer in `format_user_row`, which does `date_joined=row["date_joined"].isoformat()`, would be pretty reasonable. I think the better options are:
- Minute-level precision: Removes 54% slight majority of the entropy, won't impact display at all because AFAIK no time zone has sub-minute offsets, and if they did, it'd be vanishingly rare.
- Hour-level precision: Removes 68% of the entropy, and won't impact display except in close to midnight in those rare timezones with multiple-of-15-minute offsets from UTC, which is probably quite rare to come up.
- Day-level precision: Removes 80% of the entropy, may result in day values changing due to timezones, which seems annoying, especially for users who joined very recently.

I guess there's also 15-minute-precision or 5-minute precision, which might be slightly more efficient than minute-level precision without the potential offset downsides.

## trimming subscriber data #34244

*2024-07-29 to 2025-12-30 · 275 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/trimming.20subscriber.20data.20.2334244/with/1905468)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-29 17:59 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> | key | uncompressed | compressed | | - | - | - | | `subscriptions` | 4523593 (26.6%) | 1713341 (45.1%) | | `realm_users` | 10610837 (62.3%) | 1588919 (41.8%) | | `never_subscribed` | 446588 (2.6%) | 133180 (3.5%) | | `realm_user_groups` | 357699 (2.1%) | 130897 (3.4%) | | `realm_bots` | 419470 (2.5 …

So as noted here, about half of the compressed size for loading `/` on chat.zulip.org is the subscribers matrix: Which other users are subscribed to which channels. Let's talk about options for managing that data structure.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-29 18:00 UTC

This is one of the more awkward data sets to try to trim, in that it's large but also definitely used immediately upon mage load: The web app uses that information for typeahead sorting (fine to load lazily or something, but not great to skip entirely) and channel settings, but also to display the main right-sidebar view.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-29 18:05 UTC

- One idea would be to just lazy-load the data, and have the right sidebar have an initial state without an "In this conversation|channel" section that live-updates when we have the data.
- A refinement on that would be to add some sort of client-side caching across sessions, with all the trade-offs that come with that. For mobile, this is kinda the long-lived event queue concept ... but one could imagine doing something fancy with it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-29 18:10 UTC

Another idea that has been percolating in my head a little bit is whether we could get away with sending a subset of subscriber data and still present the right-sidebar UI that we do today. A specific concept would be the following:
- Using some concept of being low priority for the right sidebar, like "long-term idle", the server sends as subscriber data the full matrix for active users or small channels, but only the count of inactive user subscribers, and the right sidebar just shows those inactive subscribers as a "4 more users" sort of UI component. (And presumably the client would fetch the full data set for a given stream in the channel settings UI if one goes to the "subscribers" tab there, or the full set for a given user when accessing their user profile).
- If one of those users becomes active again, the server notifies the client of their subscriptions, including some sort of flag letting it know that these totals should be subtracted from the anonymous counts the client has.

I guess ideally the set of users excluded this way should correspond with which users we might defer sending other metadata for, since the `realm_users` data set is about the same size.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-31 07:04 UTC

If the goal isn't about reducing total bandwidth costs, and is focused on more quickly loading to a functioning, interactive experience, then loading asynchronously seems like a pretty straightforward way forward.

Asynchronously but not lazily: that is, we'd load it eagerly after the app starts up, in the same way as we load message history.

That way, most of the time you'd have the data and wouldn't need to wait for it to load. There'd still need to be some kind of answer for what the right sidebar does when the data hasn't been loaded yet, but it wouldn't be critical to the overall UX.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-31 17:55 UTC

Yeah the two right-sidebar answers are:
- Show a loading indicator during that initial period.
- Display users without any "In this ..." heading, and just shows the a single list without either the "In this channel" or "Others" heading, like we do in views like Inbox/Recent normally.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-31 18:14 UTC

Let's look at how this deferring that fetch would work. I think the implementation plan for the web app would be as follows:
- We might need some API changes to offer a good API for getting the appropriate subscriber data. https://zulip.com/api/get-subscriptions offers `include_subscribers`, but https://zulip.com/api/get-streams does not. Meanwhile https://zulip.com/api/get-subscribers only targets a single channel. The web app expects to have subscriber data to all channels, so none of those is quite the right API.
- We work through how to adjust the dozen modules that call into `peer_data.ts` for the race where the data isn't available yet. Stream settings, wildcard-mention validation, user profiles, the buddy list, and rendering tooltips for hovering the top-navbar are all affected in some way.
- Another challenge would be tweaking the `server_events_dispatch` system to hold onto `peer_add/peer_remove` events until we have the data, so we can apply those deltas on top of what we fetch from the server to get a consistent view. This might be hard to get right without also holding other `subscription` events, which in turn might get messy, so I think the most practical thing to do would be to adjust the existing `finished_initial_fetch` mechanism (where we don't process any events until the first `GET /messages` fetch returns) to also wait for this request to return before doing any live-update.

And then once we've settled those challenges, the actual change would be pretty straightforward:
- The web app would pass `include_subscribers=False` to `fetch_initial_state_date` in `POST /register`.
- The web app would immediately on load call the appropriate API endpoint to get subscriber data, do `peer_data.initialize` and call `finished_initial_subscribers_fetch` when that succeeds.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-31 18:18 UTC

That at least sounds like a very doable list of changes, albeit with significant effort. There are few things that would remain unfortunate about the endpoint of that work.
- We're still fetching the same amount of data.
- You still don't get a fully functional app until that data is fetched. In particular, there's no live-update until it finishes, which could feel buggy in some situations, even if there still is a prominent loading indicator.
- We have to do a bunch of fiddly and hard-to-maintain (just because it's only briefly run code) work for the dozen UI components mentioned above to have them do something reasonable in the case that we don't have the full expected subscriber data.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-31 18:23 UTC

I think the next refinement on that algorithm would be to still send the **number** of subscribers to each channel in the initial payloads, which I'm sure we could work out how to cache such that it doesn't impact the server's work much to send it. 

Almost all of the UI elements noted above only actually need subscriber counts, or only need the data for the channel or user you're currently clicked on (say, the "Subscribers" tab in channel settings, the right sidebar, or the user profile "Channels" tab). So some set of techniques involving those things could greatly reduce our dependence on having the full subscriber matrix.

It could be that adding the subscriber counts to the API first would save a lot of the fiddly work mentioned above, so that would be worth considering.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-31 18:48 UTC

Given all that, I think my proposal here would be the following sequence:
- Add some sort of `subscriber_count` field to `channel` objects in the API. Some care may be required here; we might need to exclude bots from the count, `apply_events` might be nontrivial, etc.
- Add the API for fetching the full subscriber matrix for a client-provided set of channels noted above.
- Add some sort of default-false setting for whether to fetch subscribers in the initial fetch or just after, which we'd enable in the development environment when trying to test parts of this implementation. As part of this, there'd be a `peer_data.has_full_subscriber_matrix()` function or something we can use in checks for the details below.
- Integrate that data set into the `stream_data`/`peer_data` modules, such that we can handle requests for the size of a channel if `!peer_data.has_full_subscriber_matrix`. 
- Audit callers of the `peer_data` module's other query functions other than the buddy list, and make them support fetching the subscriber data directly if `!peer_data.has_full_subscriber_matrix`. So for example, `stream_data.get_streams_for_user`, used by the user profile, would become an async function that asks the server for that user's subscriptions (may need a new API endpoint?). And we'd need something similar for the "Subscribers" tab in channel settings.
- Make the buddy list support falling back to not showing an "In this channel" section if it doesn't have the subscriber matrix yet.
- Figure out what we need to do around `server_events_dispatch`; there might be a simpler plan that just involves `peer_data` events being saved for future application to the returned subscriber matrix payload.
- Make the setting enabled for everyone.

And I think if we do all that, we might be able to avoid some of the messy `finished_initial_fetch` blocking; the app would just transparently work fine during the window when we don't have full subscriber data yet.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-13 20:02 UTC

Now that the web app's right sidebar design has more or less stabilized, I'd like to think a bit more about the plan for this, because the data set is huge (almost half of the `/` payload), and it seems like the changes required to make it less huge are a lot more localized in impact than #**api design>defer loading user data**.

Here's a refinement on that last proposal (#**api design>trimming subscriber data@1907695**):

- Add an `active_human_subscriber_count` field to `stream` objects in the API. Some care may be required here; we might need to exclude bots from the count, `apply_events` might be nontrivial as a result, etc. But this would be the value required to show total subscriber counts in the right sidebar or otherwise on a client that has only partial data about the subscribers.
- Add a client capability `partial_subscriber_matrix`, which would allow the server to send a partial subscriber matrix to clients at its discretion (presumably the initial algorithm would send only the subset of users that are most active, but one could imagine some fancier stuff like sending the full set of users for all small channels).
- In the web app, declare that capability with a `peer_data.has_full_subscriber_matrix(stream_id)` function.
- Integrate that data set into the `stream_data`/`peer_data` modules, such that we can handle requests for the size of a channel if `!peer_data.has_full_subscriber_matrix(stream_id)`. 
- Audit callers of the `peer_data` module's other query functions other than the buddy list, and make them support fetching the subscriber data directly if `!peer_data.has_full_subscriber_matrix(stream_id)`. So for example, `stream_data.get_streams_for_user`, used by the user profile, would become an async function that asks the server for that user's subscriptions (may need a new API endpoint?). And we'd need something similar for the "Subscribers" tab in channel settings, to fetch the full subscribers for a given channel.
- Add an API endpoint for fetching the full subscriber matrix for a client-provided set of channels, if we find single-channel requests with https://zulip.com/api/get-subscribers are not sufficient for the above.
- The right-sidebar buddy list would fall back to either just not showing the "In this channel" section if it doesn't have the full subscriber matrix yet, or showing its partial data (we support that today for large orgs today).
- Figure out what we need to do around `server_events_dispatch`; there might be a simpler plan that just involves `peer_data` events being saved for future application to the returned subscriber matrix payload.

And then if we do ask the server, there's two approaches:
- We can fetch the entire subscriber set for a channel when navigating to the channel before we render the sidebar. The advantage here is that once you jump to the next topic in the channel, you're all good.
- We can do simple API calls of the form "Is user X subscribed to channel Y" (or maybe a bulk one).

I think @Alya Abbott's thoughts on other things we'd like to do if changing the count on CHANNELS sound about as complex as the plan that doesn't require that, so let's go with not changing the definitions. So I think the overall plan is roughly this:
- We complete #**api design>peer_remove events when deactivating a user** so that the `peer_add/peer_remove` sync protocol is sound in the absence of having an originally dense subscriber matrix.
- We complete #**api design>channel human_subscriber_count** so that we can do `get_subscriber_count` without a dense subscriber matrix.
- We specify that the initial sparse subscriber matrix data is guaranteed to include (1) All bot users in the organization, (2) All recently present users in the organizations. I think a smart algorithm would include (3) All users who are subscribed to small channels (say, <100 human subscribers) that you are also subscribed to. Notably, we probably want the matrix to be by-user, not by-channel, which is why I'm thinking we just include those users in the set we fetch. But that would not be specified in the API.
  - This entails the client having code that lets it ask the server for the subscriber data for users that are present but not present in its data set. We may want a new bulk endpoint "get all subscriptions for these X users" for this.
  - We probably want a dedicated topic for this, but possibly we'll just want to change the existing `include_subscribers` boolean parameter to also accept the string "partial" as a way to ask for that.
- When you click into a channel the first time in a session, we fetch the full set of subscribers for that channel in the background, similar to how we fetch the set of topics in that channel in the background. 
- The `peer_data` module perhaps gets fancy, since it'll have to track both channels and users for which it knows it has full data, and be able to use that understanding usefully. Stuff like `is_subscribed(user_id, channel_id)` would check whether `channel_id` is in `full_data_channels`, or `user_id` is in `full_data_users`, or something.
- We implement the the "no number" technique for the participant gap case above.

With the techniques mentioned above, we expect this little race where it's not initially displayed would come up for a fairly narrow set of situations: Your first click into a channel with 100+ subscribers in an organization with 1000+ users, if the topic you land in has a user who participated in that topic but hasn't been active for a while, the CHANNEL and OTHERS counts show up after amoment.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-03-28 21:39 UTC

I think there's one more thorny technical issue to discuss, which is that the definition above of a good "initial sparse subscriber matrix" is a data structure clients need to do somewhat complex work to maintain. In particular, the ways it can change are:
- New user or bot created => ok: we get `peer_add` events with the full data for that user, so can mark ourselves as having complete data for the user.
- User deactivated => ok: We will get `peer_remove` events.
- User joins/leaves channel => ok; we get `peer_add/remove` events. Well, if the user or channel is something we are maintaining, we can apply the event and preserve that we have full data for those users and channels. But if it's not, do we just discard it? I think we might need to store these to correctly manage the race issues described below, and apply them on top of data for either the user or channel if we fetch such data later.
- User becomes online => the client will no longer have accurate
- Races between our fetch and events => Now that we'll be fetching "who are all the subscribers to channel X" separately from `POST /register`, we need to consider the possibility that we'll get data that is out of sync from the events we've already received, because, say, the database was fetched a moment before that user was subscribed. To manage this, we may need to store `peer_add`/`peer_remove` events related to channels/users for which we do not have complete data and combine it appropriately.

The idea is that the final version of #**api design>Extending include_subscriber for parse subscriber data** that we put into the API will have some additional guarantees. Probably something like:
- If the organization has N or fewer users, it'll include a full subscriber matrix.
- If the organization has M or fewer recently online users, it'll include the partial subscriber matrix for all recently online users. (Or maybe this is unconditional).
- Otherwise, it'll include a partial subscriber matrix that is guaranteed to include the subscriber matrix for M recently online users, but not guaranteed to be everyone recently online in the organization. (Maybe -- we might decide not to implement this possibility, as it's not a requirement for our near-term goals)

If we do, say, N=M>600, then the current right sidebar rendering algorithm will not require any changes to display the sidebar using only the partial data.

*2024-07-29 to 2026-08-12 · 158 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/defer.20loading.20user.20data/with/1905486)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-29 18:16 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-29 19:53 UTC

I think we definitely want to fix the loading cost. I see 3 broad approaches, each with their own trade-offs:
- Sending fewer users in the initial fetch, but fetching the rest of the users asynchronously just after, and having some components, like the right sidebar, `await` until we have the rest of the users (So the sidebar would have a 10s loading indicator). This is probably easiest to engineer and maintain, but it also doesn't avoid fetching the full data set -- but it would let you browse recent messages immediately.
- Sending fewer users in the initial fetch and reworking every component that interacts with user objects to fetch data on demand. This would be pretty efficient in terms of network, but come with various UX compromises.
- Having the client cache data and the protocol support just asking for the changes in these fairly stable larger data sets. Given the 5MB limit for browser local storage in most browsers, this has some challenges (we'd have to store compressed blobs, and we'd have to manage bugs and data format changes). But it would likely also be the most end-to-end efficient option in terms of how small payloads could be, with the fewest usability impacts.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-29 19:59 UTC

Just to spell out what option 3 would look like for `realm_user`, if we added a cursor of the form `last_user_update_id` on `UserProfile`, the client could, on `receiving` its `/` payload (which would not contain user data) send its `register` API request asking for `realm_user` with a  `last_user_update_id` based on what it has in its cache, and get back two things: A list of all valid user IDs, and the full user objects just for users whose `last_user_update_id` was greater than that cutoff, and then it would delete any user objects not in the list of valid user IDs from its cache object, and substitute in the updated user objects, store to the cache, and be ready with the full user data set.

(In the web app, we'd probably not want to write to the cache on every live-update event, because compressing and writing 1.5MB of data is expensive. But in the mobile or desktop apps, where we'd potentially have access to unlimited storage quota rather than the 5MB hard limit in the browser, we'd be able to usage a different storage mechanism without that trade-off. But even the web app algorithm would be fine in practice).

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-29 20:05 UTC

Advantages of this approach include:
- It'd be fast and small; especially in the case that you you're loading your browser window less than a day since the last time you did it, this would usually be substantially smaller than sending data for the last 1k users would be.
- The fiddly, potentially hard-to-test logic would be localized to just this subsystem, rather than every feature that interacts with user objects (which is ~every feature), since we'd have the full user data set early in app initialization. 

Disadvantages include:
- Potential issues with the cache or its update algorithm being buggy, leading to misbehaving clients.
- Errors from hitting the local storage limit for browsers with insufficient maximum quota available. Presumably solvable with the desktop app, but kinda annoying.
- Potential server-side bugs with failing to update `last_user_update_id` when updating some data outside the `UserProfile` table that goes into the calculation of `realm_user` objects, like custom profile field values.
- Manual updates to user objects or their dependencies (like custom profile fields) that don't properly update `last_user_update_id` would not live-update properly.
- The `last_user_update_id` field, if it were actually an ID, would be an enumerable cursor with some data leakage impact; limited guest users who don't have access to the full data set could still find out "how many other users in this realm have changed their user metadata" by changing their own settings and seeing how the cursor changes.
- It would not solve the first-load experience issue for logged-out spectators or new browser windows.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-29 20:10 UTC

- You can’t evaluate a cache without thinking about what happens on cache misses—caching never helps first-time visitors and rarely helps infrequent visitors.
- I do not want every website I visit to store several megabytes of useless data. Zulip might have a particularly privileged place in my life but it doesn’t in most.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-29 20:12 UTC

I think Zulip does have the property that most page-loads are by frequent users, so from a "how much end user time do we save?" standpoint, non-first-load performance is very important. But the first-load performance is important from a first impressions standpoint, if nothing else, and that might argue for also doing the `await` on cache misses if we do the cache approach.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-29 20:15 UTC

For the desktop app in particular, you've already got a whole browser, and I think adding several megabytes of cached data on disk to make it load much more quickly would be a good trade-off for almost anyone who downloaded that. 

I agree the web app is a slightly more complicated scenario, but given that local storage is stored on disk and likely only loaded into memory as needed, I would think with modern disk sizes it would be quite rare that it would matter to have a 1.5MB compressed object on disk?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-29 20:19 UTC

I mean, Zulip isn’t privileged enough to me that I want to run an Electron app to use it—I use the web app. And I think it’s fair to evaluate wasteful decisions by websites on the standard of “what if every website did this?”

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-29 20:31 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-29 20:37 UTC

We can always add new techniques in future years. Logic for whether to cache can also be based on logic that considers the user's usage patterns. So a potential fancy approach would be:
- Cold-cache behavior is the `async/await` approach -- relatively simple for the web app to implement, but still consumes a lot of bandwidth on a bad network -- but only after showing you content.
- Whether to store data in the cache at all is controlled by a yes/no/auto setting, where "auto" could be some basic heuristic based on organization size (no need if <1000 users) and the user's usage history.
- We use the `last_user_update_id` cache-update algorithm detailed above, which would be shared by the mobile apps (which, like a desktop app, don't have the same storage trade-offs since you already are paying the disk cost for the app itself).

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-29 20:45 UTC

I think to really analyze that, we need to consider the alternative. Looking at what an implementation for instead rendering components when we have a model where the web app just lives with having incomplete data would look like:
- Components that just need data for a single user, like a user card, can presumably just call a `people.get_user_by_id` type function that does an `async/await` fetch of data for the user in question. We need to be very very careful to not fall into this technique in code paths that try to access hundreds of users in a loop, though, since that'd work in series. But this would cover the great majority of widgets.
- API requests that learn about a fixed list of users, like `GET /messages` responses, would presumably want to do a bulk-fetch of the set of user IDs they need to avoid sending off like 150 single-user HTTP requests in sequence. (Or maybe have some fancier protocol where the server knows to send those without an RTT, but simplest is just for the client to ask the server). There might not be a ton of these; possibly it's just fetching messages and the direct messages "more conversations" endpoint handlers.
- Components that need to match against users would need component-specific custom changes. This includes the right sidebar, the left sidebar DMs section, channel/group settings lists of subscribers, typeahead, "manage users", etc. It's this category that feels like potentially a lot of complexity, with a lot of hard-to-test-for bugs to manage, to me.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-04-11 01:09 UTC

So now that #**api design>trimming subscriber data #34244** is progressing, I wanted to start trying to write down the strategy we've selected for this feature.

- When doing `POST /register`, clients can request `partial_realm_user` data; it could be done as a client capability, or possibly just a valid entry in `fetch_event_types`. 
- When that's requested, the server sends a few things:
    - A `realm_user` style data set that is any subset of the users in the organization. (Probably will be something like recently active users + DM partners of the acting user + all bots). The only guarantee made will be that all bots are included. (We may want to consider declaring that cross-realm bots appear here in this mode to clean up the legacy detail of them having a separate list).
    - A `valid_user_ids` array of all valid user IDs in the organization. This allows the client to know when it is processing a user ID for which it doesn't have `realm_user` data whether it should expect to need to fetch the user.
- Clients with typeahead/filtering of users will use a new API to query "users who match `ti`" and return all organization users who match that prefix (the client may send the set of user IDs that it has locally that already match it to save bandwidth). We may have a temporary period where they just fetch the full user early in the session to defer doing this work.
- Clients supporting this API will turn `valid_user_ids` into a set, and when they are asked for data on an unfetched user for display purposes, will typically have these strategies available.

**Strategy 1**: Create a temporary/fake user object using `people.make_user` and display that, possibly with special display behavior that just shows a loading indicator for their name (2) Add the user to an `unfetched_users` data set, and (3) triggers a fetch of the users in that data set from the server, and (4) live-update all rendering of that fake user once we have their actual data.

**Strategy 2**: Do async code to fetch the actual users before displaying something, basically passing whatever the function we were in when we discovered the gap as a `success` handler for the fetch as a next callback. 

**Strategy 3**: For some code paths, say `GET /messages`, the server may have an option to send user objects referenced in those messages to save a round-trip -- basically a replacement for the existing `display_recipient` feature. Current thinking is we would probably not use this strategy often or possibly even at all.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-04-11 01:10 UTC

My current thinking is that probably we can get away with using Strategy 1 as the default/base plan for most everything, but we may find places that doesn't feel nice as work on this.

Like with #**api design>trimming subscriber data #34244**, I think we'll want to set up the ability to work on changes a la #**api design>Extending include_subscriber for parse subscriber data** without having any impact on the production user experience.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-04-16 17:11 UTC

We need a bit more of an object just because code displaying a user wants various subsets of name/status emoji/avatar/is_bot/etc. We may want a type of `UnknownUser | User` to be returned in most code paths where we're going to be displaying a user.

Here's how I'm thinking `valid_user_ids` list would be helpful. When we try to fetch a user by ID, and we get a response from the server that it's not valid, we'd want to cache that information, just like we would if we got a real user object back. So the client needs some data structure that is tracking that, and needs to keep that up-to-date and deal with potential races between new user creation and those requests. 

- It would allow functions that just need to check if IDs are valid or non-bots to skip `async` behavior -- they can just do their thing (usually, displaying an error that the user ID is invalid). For example, to render the `/#narrow/dm/15` view, knowing if user ID 15 is valid materially impacts whether we show an "invalid view" error or show a message feed. If we add `async` to that logic, we'd also end up needing a check for whether the user is still looking at the view in question after `await`ing the answer for whether the ID is valid. I expect that kind of check to be an annoying and deep well of rare race bugs.
- If we try to fetch a user ID, and hear back that it's valid, we store the user. But if we learn it is not valid, we need somewhere to cache that fact. So we're likely to need a `Set` of valid user IDs in the client.

That said, we probably don't need a separate `valid_user_ids` to do this -- I just had the thought that the membership of system groups can be unioned together to compute that data set.

I'm a little wary of `async function get_by_user_id`, so I would consider here the concept of `unhydrated_user`.

My hypothesis is that the expense of user calls (in both layers) is the hydration of the users, not actually getting a list of valid user_ids.  (I think there's one place where my hypothesis breaks down, but humor me anyway).

If we have the concept of an unhyrdrated user, then the server can always send back at least the ids of all users, but when the server determines that either it doesn't want to compute/send full user info right away for its own expense and/or the server determines that it doesn't want to burden the network or client with full payloads, then the server just sends back an unhydrated user with something like `{user_id: 42, hydrated: false}`. 

And then the client, when it gets unhydrated users, can immediately build a full, or least almost-full object, with stand-in values that make sense.  I suspect you'd be able to pretty easily intercept most relevant server responses and events in a strategic way such that you don't have a ton of code to flesh out the unhydrated user with stand-in values.

(I know I am probably just re-stating some ideas here, but maybe the concept of "hyrdration" resonates at least in terms of naming things.)

Last night I wrote some code in Python to handle this exact type of problem for my flet client, and I think it should be quite easy to port to JS/TS, as I mostly avoided things like decorators, context managers, descriptors, etc.  Here's the code:

https://github.com/showell/zulip-flet/blob/main/api/deferred_user.py

There's a very detailed comment at the top of the file, but here's the executive summary:

* use DeferredUser instead of User in the data types for the structures you render
* use DeferredUserFactory.create_user to make the users
* await DeferredUserFactory.finalize() after you've built your objects (e.g. messages, reactions, etc.)
* use deferred_user.full_object() instead of user (or, as in the example in the docs, use deferred_sender.full_object() instead of sender)

I've tested the code in a message-rendering context, but the DeferredUser code can work in any context.

**Chris Bobbe** · 2026-07-15 23:03 UTC

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2026-07-16 05:29 UTC

This - https://gist.github.com/amanagr/bac19ee24ed9e78f0057a0d4d82ae2c2#solution-overview

1. **Render immediately** with whatever users the server sent (recently active + DM partners + all bots).
2. **Show placeholders** for unknown users — "(loading...)" display name, `/avatar/{user_id}` for avatar.
3. **Fetch missing users in the background** via a throttled, batched queue.
4. **Re-render UI components** when real data arrives via callbacks.
5. **Server-side typeahead API** for searching across all users without needing them loaded locally.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-08-12 14:29 UTC

That said, I think the key design question is whether we have the API endpoint return a set of user IDs or user objects. The former is nice and compact, but requires an extra RTT to get the actual users. ## column-oriented user data

*2024-07-31 to 2025-03-26 · 22 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/column-oriented.20user.20data/with/1908008)*

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-31 21:54 UTC

For reducing the size of the /api/register-queue response as we've been discussing in some other threads here this week, one effective thing we can do is to take the user data (which is the bulk of the initial data for mobile, and about 40% of it for web) and express it in a form that compresses better, by transposing it. Instead of a (very long) list of objects, we'd make it an object of (very long) lists.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-31 21:54 UTC

As I described at https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/243-mobile-team/topic/shrinking.20the.20initial.20load/near/1907268 in #**mobile-team>shrinking the initial load**, there are lots of different fields in each user (17 of them), and many of them have quite boring patterns: they're usually null, or usually false, or usually of the form `userNNN@chat.zulip.org`.  But because they're all intermingled with each other, those patterns aren't as accessible to the compressor as they could be.

If we transpose the data so that each of those fields is grouped together as one long array:
```
$ <register2.json jq '
    .realm_users | (map(keys) | flatten | unique) as $kk
    | map(. as $r | $kk | map($r[.]))
    | transpose
  ' -c >transpose2.json
```

then all the same information is present, but it compresses to 25% smaller (310kB smaller) with `gzip -1`, and similar results (25–29% smaller) for other compression encodings and settings I tried.

For mobile's entire /api/register-queue response, that's about an 18% savings. For web it'll be a smaller percentage savings, perhaps 10%, because the subscriber data bulks up the denominator.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-31 21:56 UTC

From an API perspective, clearly this would need to be a [client capability](https://chat.zulip.org/api/register-queue#parameter-client_capabilities), as it's not backward-compatible for a client that doesn't know about it.

Probably this would be a client capability where we don't regard the old/default way as deprecated — the transposed, column-oriented format is definitely less conventional for JSON, and a simple client that's not worrying about performance is likely to find it more annoying to deal with.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-31 21:59 UTC

When introducing this, I'd be in favor of having the same client capability fix a longstanding wart in this part of the API: instead of having `realm_users` and `realm_non_active_users` and `cross_realm_bots` as three separate lists that have to be combined to get the actual list of all users, when this client capability is set, the user data would be in one object that combines all three.

In addition to fixing an API wart, that'd enhance the compression by further bringing similar data together in the stream.

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-31 22:02 UTC

> If we transpose the data so that each of those fields is grouped together as one long array:

To make this concrete, this means the data would look like
```json
{
  "user_id": [1, 3, 4, …],
  "delivery_email": [null, null, "name@example.com", …],
  "is_bot": [false, false, false, …],
  …
}
```

instead of like
```json
[
  {"user_id": 1, "delivery_email": null, "is_bot": false, …},
  {"user_id": 3, "delivery_email": null, "is_bot": false, …},
  {"user_id": 4, "delivery_email": "name@example.com", "is_bot": false, …},
  …
]
```

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-31 22:04 UTC

For naming, perhaps:
* just `users` for the property in the /api/register-queue response
* for the [client capability](https://chat.zulip.org/api/register-queue#parameter-client_capabilities)… `user_data_columnar`? `user_list_columnar`? `user_data_transposed`?

**Greg Price** · 2024-07-31 22:06 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)
> then all the same information is present, but it compresses to 25% smaller (310kB smaller)

Oh and it should also be smaller in uncompressed form, since it doesn't have to repeat the keys like `"delivery_email"` over and over. I didn't record numbers for that, though, since the compressed size is the figure I [believe is important](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/378-api-design/topic/trimming.20date_joined/near/1904603) for the user's experience.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-31 23:39 UTC

So before we go too far down this path, I do wonder if we would get similar results by using some fancier format than JSON, like protocol buffers, for passing that data structure to clients where we really want to optimize the compressed size.

**Greg Price** · 2024-08-01 00:34 UTC

Potentially some other encoding instead of JSON could help too. Two thoughts on that:
* The better compression by grouping columns together instead of rows is fundamental to how any stream-based compressor (like gzip) works — if we switched to protobufs or anything else, there'd be a similar opportunity for savings to be had by using a column-oriented arrangement in that encoding instead of a row-oriented arrangement in that encoding.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-01 00:39 UTC

Well, except that the whole collection of `is_foo` booleans might be encoded as a single bitword in an optimized compressor like that; I just don't have good intuition for what to expect in that setting.

**Greg Price** · 2024-08-01 00:39 UTC

* JSON is extremely fast to serialize and deserialize, especially in a web client. Partly because it's pretty simple, and partly because a ton of engineering effort has gone into the implementations.

  For the web client, I think it's going to be impossible to find an alternate format that won't involve a slowdown in deserialization, probably enough to be noticeable when on a fast connection (where the download time isn't as big a contributor).

  Even in a client where we can ship native code of our choosing, it may be impossible to beat JSON for deserialization speed, and may be difficult to find an alternative that doesn't involve a slowdown there.

  For example if you're running a service on Node, it turns out JSON is the fastest option, because the JSON implementation in V8 is faster than anything else you could use, even with the ability to ship native code.

**Greg Price** · 2024-08-01 00:41 UTC

The `is_foo` booleans we can just drop (in favor of `role`), as long as we're making incompatible changes. But they also compress very well — they were a very small contributor in Anders's experiment even with the existing row-based arrangement, and in a column-oriented arrangement they'd be well under one bit per user.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-02 19:49 UTC

At the data model layer, I think there's basically only a handful of fields that make sense:
- `id` -- unique identifier so one can delete/edit these by ID.
- `user_id` -- which user this belongs to.
- `date_created` -- I could imagine some future UI wanting to display metadata like this, so seems reasonable to store it.
- `content` -- the actual text of the saved reply. I think `content` rather than `text` is probably a better name just because it's literally text that would be inserted into the `content` field of a message (possibly alongside other content).
- Maybe `order`. Some notion of sort order might be useful, a la custom profile fields. We could probably copy the API we use for that, which is a bit awkward in that dragging a thing from top to bottom often involves a write to every row for that user/realm to change all the numbers, if we don't want to think about this.
- Maybe `rendered_content`, if we want the server to do Markdown rendering on it so that it can be displayed on the client. Not sure this is a feature we'd need/want.

**Greg Price** · 2024-08-13 17:53 UTC
