**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-13 18:02 UTC

So this is a data model change that I'm not sure whether or not makes sense.

The problem statement is that we have a tool, `manage.py delete_user`, which deletes a user's metadata to the extent possible, including clearing the record of their email address, deleting any avatar, custom profile field data, etc. It can optionally leave behind a placeholder user object to hold any non-deleted messages the user sent. There are a few potential use cases for it:
- Fixing a duplicated user (sometimes happens if someone uses the wrong account for SSO).
- Individuals who want their data deleted as per GDPR.
- Removing a spammer/malicious user completely.

There is a desire to expose some version of his capability in the UI. If we were to do that, there is some display logic, like user cards and user profiles, that might want to show these users differently from a normal deactivated user.

## reset users to default

*2024-08-30 to 2025-03-13 · 22 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/reset.20users.20to.20default/with/1934436)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-30 18:25 UTC

For #**design>reset users to default**, let's use this thread to design the API for an organization owner to reset various preference settings for other users. We need to be careful about security in this API design; there's a few security-sensitive settings, basically those in the "privacy" panel, like `email_address_visibility`, that should be unavailable. Probably it won't be hard to do that in the server internals.

The existing related API endpoint is `realm/user_settings_defaults`, which accepts basically every user-setting as possible parameters. I think this makes sense to be a new API endpoint: It only needs a few parameters:
- `setting` (str): Which setting to bulk-reset users value of to the organization-level default.
- `target_users` (group-setting value): Which users to target; presumably this would be a group-setting value, so one would target the entire organization via the "role:everyone" group, but we'd have a standard group input in the UI.
- `skip_if_already_edited` (boolean): Skip modifying this setting for those users in the target set who have at any point previously modified this setting themselves. This name may not be ideal.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-30 18:29 UTC

I think the main design question that might suggest an alternative approach is whether we want a `value` field to allow bulk-setting to a specific value, not just the current organization default. There's no plan to include that in the UI, but one can imagine that being quite handy for API automation doing bulk-onboarding of users in some subset of an organization.

If we want that, I think that would argue for instead just adding optional parameters to the main `realm/user_settings_defaults` endpoint, basically to avoid needing another copy of the ~50 line list of settings and their types/validation code. Or maybe doing that virtually in the implementation: Using a separate URL, but having the same backend function process it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-30 18:29 UTC

Maybe that alternative design is more flexible and thus less likely for us to need to rework it in the future, and not necessarily significantly more work.

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-06 21:58 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> The existing related API endpoint is `realm/user_settings_defaults`

( /api/update-realm-user-settings-defaults , for a link)

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> I think the main design question that might suggest an alternative approach is whether we want a `value` field to allow bulk-setting to a specific value, not just the current organization default. There's no plan to include that in the UI, but one can imagine that being quite handy for API automatio …

That does sound potentially useful.

In particular I think if we include a `target_users` parameter rather than having that always effectively be `role:everyone`, then it no longer especially makes sense for this to be tied to what the realm-wide defaults are. If you're updating the setting for some subset of users, then the value you want for them might well be different from the realm-wide default you want for new users.

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-06 22:07 UTC

> If we want that, I think that would argue for instead just adding optional parameters to the main `realm/user_settings_defaults` endpoint,

I don't follow this part, though. Once we're providing a value and decoupling it from the realm-wide defaults, it seems like it really shouldn't be part of the realm-wide-defaults endpoint.


>  basically to avoid needing another copy of the ~50 line list of settings and their types/validation code. Or maybe doing that virtually in the implementation: Using a separate URL, but having the same backend function process it.

## Update user, queried by real email - new endpoint

*2024-09-05 to 2024-10-23 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/Update.20user.2C.20queried.20by.20real.20email.20-.20new.20endpoint/with/1937253)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2024-09-05 22:09 UTC

In #31332, as part of adding an API functionality to allow administrators with a special new permission to update emails of users in the organization, we ended up deciding to add a new general `Update User` endpoint:
- It's meant to be just a copy of `PATCH /users/{user_id}`, but the user look up is by email: `PATCH /users/{email]`
- Fetches the user by `.delivery_email` **if** the client has the permission to view that user's email. Otherwise returns `No such user`, to prevent admins from guessing emails of users who want to hide theirs.
- After fetching the user, calls `update_user_backend` so the exact same code as `PATCH /users/{user_id}`.

The main issue with this approach as stated above is that `/users/{email}` also has a `GET` method. However, `GET`  fetches the user by the `.email` attribute. So  these two methods have an inconsistent meaning for the `{email}`. I guess the main ideas for what to do would be to either:

- Just give this a new path. Instead of `PATCH /users/{email}` this can be `PATCH /users/update_by_real_email/{email}` or whatever.
- Change `GET /users/{email}` to fetch the user in the same way as this new `PATCH /users/{email}`.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2024-09-05 22:14 UTC

Another fine detail to consider how exactly it should work is the exact user fetch logic:

> Fetches the user by `.delivery_email` **if** the client has the permission to view that user's email. Otherwise returns `No such user`, to prevent admins from guessing emails of users who want to hide theirs.

Alternatively this could be:
- If the `{email}` is an attempted "real" address, then it works like the above.
- If the `{email}` is of the dummy format `user{id}@zulip.example.com`, fetch the user by `id` (or `email`? But that feels inferior since it would fail on target users whose `.email` is their real email due to having `EMAIL_ADDRESS_VISIBILITY_EVERYONE`, for no good reason?)

This could be particularly nice if we go with ``Change `GET /users/{email}` to fetch the user in the same way as this new `PATCH /users/{email}`.``, by keeping the behavior compatible with clients who may be querying that endpoint with  dummy emails.

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-06 03:08 UTC

(replying to Mateusz Mandera)
> The main issue with this approach as stated above is that `/users/{email}` also has a `GET` method. However, `GET` fetches the user by the `.email` attribute. So these two methods have an inconsistent meaning for the `{email}`. I guess the main ideas for what to do would be to either: - Just give th …

We've previously had a request (but I'm currently on mobile, so not pulling up the thread at the moment) for the get-user-by-email endpoint to accept real/delivery emails, when the requesting user has access to see the given user's delivery email. That would be convenient for use cases where the users are managed from some external system that identifies them by email address — which is a common situation in corporate or institutional settings (with or without Zulip).

I think we can do that while still having it always accept Zulip API emails too. There won't be an ambiguity, because a user's Zulip API 
email is always either (a) their delivery email, or (b) a fake email that shouldn't be any user's delivery email.

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-06 03:08 UTC

(We should probably enforce that latter property, if we don't already: not allow a delivery email that has the shape of this realm's fake emails.)

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-06 03:10 UTC

Then if we make that change to /api/get-user-by-email , I think we can have this new update-user-by-email endpoint look up the user in the same way.

Which I think is the same as your last suggestion above.

## Idempotency-Key HTTP header

*2024-09-10 to 2026-10-13 · 53 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/Idempotency-Key.20HTTP.20header/with/1939581)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-10 19:09 UTC

As detailed in #**issues>📂 Duplicate sending bug**, especially [starting here](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/9-issues/topic/.F0.9F.93.82.20Duplicate.20sending.20bug/near/1938315), we had an issue in the web app where some unknown thing retried an HTTP POST request for sending a message 8 minutes after the original message, resulting in a duplicate send.

After some discussion of options, @Chase Schelthoff suggested that we might want to use an `Idempotency-Key` HTTP header, which at least Stripe uses to allow client-side retries of requests (https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency) to generate at-most-once semantics for their HTTP POST requests in the presence of networking or other failures.

The idea would be that clients could pass a random such header on HTTP POST requests, and the server would be able to ignore requests where it has already seen that idempotency key for a given user, maybe with some expiry time like an hour.

(The simple networking failure that would most benefit from this being that an HTTP request reaches the server, but the network connection drops before the client receives the HTTP response, such that the client has no way of knowing its request was successfully processed by the server).

**Zixuan James Li** · 2024-09-15 18:07 UTC

To my understanding, the key is treated analogue to resource ID.

The first time the idempotency key is seen the server puts an exclusive lock on it. Until the original request completes, concurrent requests on the same resource are conflicting; after the original request completes, subsequent requests gets the cached response.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2024-09-15 18:13 UTC

In any case, the request only gets processed the first time the server sees the key, so we never get duplications.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-16 15:28 UTC

If the database server is separate from the lockserver, then this a great example of a [classic distributed computing problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_Generals%27_Problem). Choosing how to resolve it is [the CAP theorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CAP_theorem), which says you can only get two of consistency, availability, or partition tolerance.  That is, if we want partition tolerance (the ability to handle the network suddenly going out between lock server and database server) and consistency (we actually do make requests idempotent) then we are *required* to sacrifice availability (sometimes we will be stuck with the lock held, and unclear if the work was done).

We can solve that problem by putting the lock *within* the database transaction, which makes it not a distributed systems problem -- we can assume PostgreSQL processes can always talk to each other (i.e. accepting the impossibly tiny chance of "partition" between PostgreSQL processes on the same server).  

A simple implementation in PostgreSQL might be:

```sql
START TRANSACTION;

INSERT INTO idempotency(uuid_column_with_unique_key)
 VALUES ('abcdef');

-- do work

UPDATE idempotency
   SET completed = true
 WHERE uuid_column_with_unique_key = 'abcdef';

COMMIT;
```

This enforces that only one request can ever complete the work with the given key, and that checking if the work was done is simple.  The *failure mode* of this implementation is that in the event of two concurrent requests, the second one will block on the `INSERT` until the first succeeds or fails, and then either abort or continue (respectively).

Solving *that* means we can't use the `INSERT` as the lock, but instead need to use a row-level lock:

```sql
INSERT INTO idempotency(uuid_column_with_unique_key)
 VALUES ('abcdef')
 ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

START TRANSACTION;

SELECT completed FROM idempotency
 WHERE uuid_column_with_unique_key = 'abcdef'
 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;  -- immediately aborts if something else has the lock

-- check completed, and abort if it's true

-- do work

UPDATE idempotency
   SET completed = true
 WHERE uuid_column_with_unique_key = 'abcdef';

COMMIT;
```

No row in `idempotency`?  Never seen the request.
A matching *locked* row in `idempotency`?  Something else is doing the work.
A matching unlocked, non-`completed` row in `idempotency`? Something *tried* to do the work and failed.
A matching unlocked, `completed` row?  Something succeeded in doing the work.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2026-10-13 07:07 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> After some discussion of options, @Chase Schelthoff suggested that we might want to use an `Idempotency-Key` HTTP header, which at least Stripe uses to allow client-side retries of requests (https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency) to generate at-most-once semantics for their HTTP POST requests in …

Noting that #40238 implements this idea.  PR and the backend thread has all the details. Noting some important points here:

* POST /messages is the only endpoint which supports `Idempotency-Key` HTTP header right now.
* Header value is a valid UUID - otherwise 400 response code
* If a request with same key is in progress - 409 response code - Retry with the same key
* Clients should retry with different key for response code other than 409 and 5xx.
* Message send failure errors are not cached.
* Successful message sends are cached for 24 hours.

Because deactivated groups can't be used for anything (i.e. they can't be the value of a setting or a subgroup of another group), it doesn't seem very important whether one can use the API to inspect deactivated groups. ## Updates for PreregistrationRealm creation

*2024-09-12 to 2024-09-12 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/Updates.20for.20PreregistrationRealm.20creation/with/1940729)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-12 14:19 UTC

As part of the workflow for a more seamless import process during realm creation, we're going  to want to do the import in a background worker.  This means that we need a channel to provide at very least success/failure messages back to the client from a background worker -- and ideally also progress reports.

The only authentication token we have at this stage is the confirmation key which is associated with the PreregistrationRealm, which is passed around in form parameters.

Since this is a state where we necessarily don't have a UserProfile (since we're still creating the realm), we can't use our existing events system.  In the short term, we probably just want to have the client poll a status endpoint of some sort.  In the longer term, we may want to consider ways of making unauth'd (but somehow still identifiable as tied to a specific PreregistrationUser / PreregistrationRealm object) event queues with our existing Tornado service, since it's possible we could do that in a way which would also support anonymous live-update of realms once they're created.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-12 14:23 UTC

AFAIK, we don't currently have any non-web way of making new realms (there's nothing to support it under `/api/v1`) so this polled realm-creation-status endpoint is necessarily going to only be used by the web UI to start off.  It may *only ever* be used by the web UI, if it gets replaced by some form of our existing event queue.  This means that there's a tension between wanting all of the API endpoints to live under `/api/v1`, and the fact that this realm-creation-status API endpoint will be auth'd in a way that no other API endpoint is.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-12 22:42 UTC

Probably polling is to right answer for v1. We likely do want to make a way for Tornado to support unauthenticated users eventually (it would be nice for the public access feature), but that seems like a big dependency to add.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-12 22:44 UTC

I think it's fine to have a set of temporary/web-only API endpoints under the `/accounts/register/import` namespace for this, and we can always move later; I don't see mobile support for data import as being a near-term desire.

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-12 23:08 UTC

That reasoning all sounds right to me.


## Endpoint for tusd

*2024-09-12 to 2024-09-16 · 15 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/Endpoint.20for.20tusd/with/1940778)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-12 15:14 UTC

We're adding support for large file uploads, which use the `tusd` server to accept chunked uploads.   These will let us accept arbitrarily-large files, as well as resumable uploads. The `tusd` server makes HTTP hook requests to Django, passing along authentication headers, which lets us have the chunked upload endpoints have the same authentication as our usual cookie-session and API-key dual endpoints (e.g. `/user_uploads`).  However, the *responses* are not using our API standards, but rather [the `tus` standard](https://tus.io/protocols/resumable-upload).

We intend to switch to using this endpoint for all file uploads from the browser, and potentially also mobile in the future.  Old-style `POST /user_uploads` will of course continue to be supported.

What URL space should we be claiming for the `tusd` server?  I don't think it belongs under `/api/v1` or `/json` because it doesn't follow *our* API.  We could use `/user_uploads/chunked/` or similar, but we also do intent to use it for non-`user_uploads` information (see #**backend>slack conversion storage**) -- so something more top-level might make sense.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-12 17:12 UTC

We use `/api/v1/external/...` for incoming webhook integrations, so there's some precedent for using that type prefix for an API we didn't design.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-12 17:13 UTC

I think an `/api/v1/tus/` could be defensible.

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-12 20:38 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> We use `/api/v1/external/...` for incoming webhook integrations, so there's some precedent for using that type prefix for an API we didn't design.

I'm not as familiar with those. What do those look like?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-12 20:58 UTC

Generally just an API endpoint of the form `POST {realm_uri}/api/v1/external/{integration_name}`

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-14 02:59 UTC

There is also the question of where we should put the URL for the hooks that tusd calls into.

Specifically, tusd makes POST requests to a configurable HTTP endpoint, passing along whatever authentication information it got when the web client posted to e.g. `/api/v1/tus`.  These POST requests from tusd into Django are used to (a) authenticate the uploads, (b) give Django an opportunity to tell tusd where the upload should end up, and (c) let Django know when the file upload is completed and do whatever needs to be done from there.

`/api/v1/tus/hooks` would be a natural location, though off because it kinda onion-layers which server gets which paths.  It's also kind a violation of the tus spec, which wants everything under the tus server's URL to be available to it (e.g. for a file named `hooks`).

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-14 03:00 UTC

These hook requests will only ever come from localhost (until we gain the feature of being able to split the tusd server onto its own host)

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-16 16:33 UTC

If these are localhost-only, `/api/v1/internal/` is our namespace for that, so maybe `/api/v1/internal/tus-hooks/` could be OK?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-16 16:33 UTC

This is the relevant section of `urls.py`:
```
# Used internally for communication between command-line, Django,                                       
# and Tornado processes                                                                                 
urls += [                                                                                               
    path("api/internal/email_mirror_message", email_mirror_message),                                    
    path("api/internal/notify_tornado", notify),                                                        
    path("api/internal/web_reload_clients", web_reload_clients),                                        
    path("api/v1/events/internal", get_events_internal),                                                
]                                                                                                       
```

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-16 16:42 UTC

I think you mean `/api/internal/` not `/api/v1/internal`?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-16 16:43 UTC

But yeah, that'd make sense.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-16 16:45 UTC

This will require carving out an exemption for the HTTP -> HTTPS redirect, for localhost -- unlike the other clients of that namespace, tusd follows the redirect and rejects the TLS certificate because of hostname mismatch, and there' no override for that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-16 17:08 UTC

Yeah, that seems probably OK.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-16 17:10 UTC

That doesn't seem like it exposes any security gap that we didn't already have -- if you can snoop packets going over `lo`, I'm pretty sure that we are already exposing secrets.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-16 17:24 UTC

Possibly. I think an attacker who can snoop packets on localhost has likely already thoroughly compromised the system.

## Message matches narrow

*2024-09-24 to 2025-03-28 · 31 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/Message.20matches.20narrow/with/1947769)*

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-09-24 14:07 UTC

For completing this TODO in `update_views_filtered_on_message_property`:
```js
// In case of multiple messages, we just rerender the view
// since it is likely to use similar amount of resources to
// fetching the messages and rerendering the view.
if (messages_to_fetch.length > 1 || !filter.can_apply_locally()) {
    // TODO: Might be better to check if `/messages/matches_narrow`
    // rather than doing a full rerender.
    message_view.show(filter.terms(), {
        then_select_id: msg_list.selected_id(),
        then_select_offset: msg_list.selected_row().get_offset_to_window().top,
        trigger: "message property update",
        force_rerender: true,
    });
```

So, after replacing the `message_view.show` call with `/messages/matches_narrow` check, we will likely have to fetch messages that we just checked in the backend. So, to avoid another cycle of work here, would it make sense to add a parameter to `/messages/matches_narrow` API endpoint like `include_full_message_object_if_matched` that would add the mesage objects to the API response if they matched successfully?


Another direction to go that might be more useful in the future is to add an API endpoint to query a list of messages which can also include a `narrow` parameter to filter the requested messages if the match the narrow.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-24 17:40 UTC

Yeah I think making a generic API endpoint that supports taking a list of up to 1K messages and just fetches those if the current user has access to them seems like it'd have more generic utility. I think this is not the only time that we've thought it might be handy to have that.

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-24 18:13 UTC

For this use case, it sounds like the idea would be that the endpoint takes both
* a list of message IDs
* and a narrow

and applies both filters conjunctively, i.e. with an AND.

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-24 18:16 UTC

So it would be like /api/get-messages in having the same parameters `narrow` and also `client_gravatar` and `apply_markdown`.

But then instead of `anchor`, `include_anchor`, `num_before`, and `num_after`, it would have an alternative way of saying what subset of the narrow to include, in message-ID terms: it would take a parameter named like `message_ids` and return only messages with those IDs.

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-24 18:20 UTC

Potentially the way to do this would be as just a new parameter on /api/get-messages. It'd be mutually exclusive with `anchor`, `include_anchor`, `num_before`, `num_after`.

I'm not sure there's a use case for that, though. Potentially a search UI could benefit from something like `grep -C`, but that'd work differently because the point would be to show context that *doesn't* match the narrow.)

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-30 20:01 UTC

## LLM summaries

*2024-09-24 to 2025-01-28 · 32 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/LLM.20summaries/with/1948352)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-24 23:16 UTC

So we've been discussing in #**design>LLM conversation summaries** the idea of having an LLM summaries feature. I'd like to talk about how one could hook it up in the API in a sensible way.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-24 23:24 UTC

In some ways, just doing a summary using the HTML the client already has would be fastest. But from a security, rate-limiting and caching standpoint, we probably want the server to be involved, and at that point whatever the client has isn't really useful. So here's some notes on a direction:
- An endpoint that accepts a conversation (perhaps in `narrow` format parameter, but maybe v1 would be limited to just accepting topics), and returns a summary for that. These could presumably be cached with some invalidation when messages in it are added or edited, if that feels appropriate.
- Server first checks if the feature is enabled, any rate limits, etc.
- Server fetches the relevant conversation from the database, formats it, and sends it to the LLM summarizer API, and returns the summary for the client to display.
- Probably it should allow plain-text in the summaries for security reasons; we don't have a cheap way to validate HTML from an LLM, and probably Markdown-rendering of a response wouldn't be worth it, but it could be considered.
- Presumably the same API endpoint could be extended with some sort of query-type parameter if we wanted to have a "Ask an LLM to help debug what I posted in chat" kind of feature or anything else of that form later.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-24 23:29 UTC

So I'm imagining something that maybe looks a bit like `GET /api/v1/messages/summary` with a `narrow` parameter a la `GET /messages`. A few questions:
- How would we want to limit the total amount of content sent to the LLM if a topic has thousands of messages? Probably some sort of truncation to only the most recent N messages and/or most recent N tokens would be reasonable, but I'm not sure what a good design would be. Probably at an API design layer, the server does what it thinks is best. It might not need to tell the client that it truncated; I'm kinda imagining that some version of telling the LLM that "Can you please summarize the following, which are the last 127 messages of ..." might be better than telling the client that truncation occurred.
- Probably there will be a lot of internal details about exactly what fields get shipped to the model, but those likely don't impact the API here.

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-24 23:34 UTC

Yeah, I think whatever truncation the server does doesn't need to be described in the response. It'll just be part of the general fact that the summaries aren't reliable (and in practice should be small compared to the general unreliability of LLMs).

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-24 23:36 UTC

It might not even be truncation exactly — for example we might have the server send the first 10 messages as well as the last 100 or whatever. Those could be more helpful context than the 10 messages from 110th-most-recent to 101st-most-recent.

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-24 23:42 UTC

For the format of the text — we'll probably want to handle lists, and bold. Current LLMs really like emitting those.

Even if we can do without them for the current design of a summaries UI, they'd be needed for somewhat-longer summaries, so we'll want to think about how we'd handle them.

Then once we have those, some other Markdown features like italics are probably no extra work.

I don't know what LLMs' APIs customarily do for expressing that formatting. Is it HTML? We might be able to write the prompt so it emits Markdown. (And occasionally its Markdown will be wrong but ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ that's LLMs. It won't hurt anything beyond the readability of that one summary.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-25 00:12 UTC

Yeah, I think probably having it emit Markdown and running our Markdown processor on it would at least be reasonably easy to make safe. I don't really want to spend time sanitizing LLM-generated HTML; seems like a security nightmare.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-10-04 14:51 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> * How would we want to limit the total amount of content sent to the LLM if a topic has thousands of messages? Probably some sort of truncation to only the most recent N messages and/or most recent N tokens would be reasonable, but I'm not sure what a good design would be. Probably at an API design …

We can divide the context in N number of chunks and extract key points from them sequentially such they next generated set of key points have the context of the previous one. This can be cached. Then generate a summary based on those key points.

This is something called Rolling summary.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-10-04 16:44 UTC

Yeah, that might be a workable strategy to avoid passing the whole conversation to a model every time someone sends a new message and then asks for an AI summary. I don't know whether usage patterns would particularly match that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-17 00:13 UTC

So I think we're at the point in the #**backend>LLM summaries** effort that we should try to define what we want this API endpoint to look like.  From a UI standpoint, I imagine mostly topic views will be what people care to summarize, but I don't see a reason not to do the specification defined above of `GET /api/v1/messages/summary`, with a `narrow` parameter.

I imagine features like a rolling summary would probably be internal to the server's implementation, not visible to the API, so I think we don't need to think about those too hard today.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-17 00:14 UTC

I think our current expectations are that we'll want the summaries to be plain-text. We can consider just accepting the `apply_markdown` parameter like `GET /messages` does, and running the Markdown processor on the summary if that's true. But I think it's probably fine to not offer that feature for v1, since it adds complexity; we can always add it later with a default of `false`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-17 00:18 UTC

So I propose adding a new `GET /api/v1/messages/summary` API endpoint, that accepts a single parameter, a `narrow` specification identical to `GET /messages`, except maybe with some backwards-compatibility encodings not implemented if that makes our life easier. And then we may in the future add parameters for:
- Message ID range limits, details TBD as the protocole evolves.
- Limiting to unread messages (Which probably doesn't want to be just `is:unread` in the query, since we probably want to ask the AI summarize the unread messages for someone who has read the not-unread messages).
- Markdown-rendering the output via an `apply_markdown` parameter.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-12-17 06:49 UTC

I think it would be pretty common for users to demand that summaries be generated for a range of messages especially if they are being charged on a per token basis. Even if we don't allow that, it is not uncommon for a topic to contain very old messages which are irrelevant to the recent ongoing conversation in that topic. So, we should atleast allow for the API endpoint to accept a message id parameter after which the summaries will be generated.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-17 17:41 UTC

I don't expect users to be charged on a per-token basis; our current modeling is that users will just have a (unreasonably high for normal use) limit for how many queries they can do to prevent abuse. (But that limit will be metered in units that scale with tokens, rather than just a number of requests, to have it align well with costs).

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-17 17:41 UTC

I expect we will add future parameters around a message ID range, but I don't think we should do that preemptively until we know how we're presenting the UI to users.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-22 19:47 UTC

So I'm about to merge #33138, which implements an API endpoint along the lines of what we'd described above (a single `narrow` parameter), but is disabled in production and undocumented; I expect we'll do an API feature level bump when we have played with it enough to be ready to document it and enable it outside development environments and chat.zulip.org.

One thing that I'm realizing we probably will want to add to the design for the benefit of clients is a field in the `register` response indicating whether the server has a topic summarization model available, such that clients can write code to show UI for topic summarization if and only if the server will be able to service such requests for that user.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-22 19:49 UTC

This could, in theory, depend not only on if the server has a model, but also details like whether the realm is on a paid plan or perhaps a realm-level "which users can access AI features" setting.

**Greg Price** · 2025-01-22 23:17 UTC

What's the semantics of saying the response is plain-text?

Is the expectation that a browser-based client, for example, will take the response, HTML-escape it, and stick it all in a single `<p>` element (and let embedded newlines create sort-of paragraphs)? So then any `*` and so on that the model might emit will become just literal asterisks the user sees.

**Greg Price** · 2025-01-22 23:18 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> One thing that I'm realizing we probably will want to add to the design for the benefit of clients is a field in the `register` response indicating whether the server has a topic summarization model available, such that clients can write code to show UI for topic summarization if and only if the ser …

Yeah, this sounds good.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-22 23:37 UTC

That sounds like the expected semantics if we keep it plain-text. I'm kinda guessing we'll either change that or add an `apply_markdown` parameter to the endpoint once we've tried it a bit more.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-22 23:37 UTC

Thoughts on what to call such a parameter?

**Greg Price** · 2025-01-23 00:04 UTC

If we end up with a parameter for that, I'd expect its meaning to be a little more than just whether the server should apply Markdown processing to the result (the meaning `apply_markdown` has in other places like /api/get-messages) — I'd expect that when true, we'd try to get the LLM to emit Markdown, and when false, we'd try to get it to emit plain text that isn't trying to be Markdown.

So perhaps a good name for such a parameter would be `content_type`, with values `text/plain` and `text/html`. (And perhaps also `text/markdown`, which would probably have the server ask the LLM for the same Markdown it'd use for `text/html` but just not convert it to HTML.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-23 00:50 UTC

Yeah, that'd be reasonable. I agree we'd want to have the prompt vary for it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-28 21:15 UTC

For the field in the response for whether topic summarization is supported by the server, a few considerations:
- I think we want a `server_` prefix, as this field should isolate the question whether the server supports topic summarization from considerations about who in the organization can use it. For settings UI implementation, I think that separation is probably important in a future world where we have a realm-level setting to disable topic summarization for the organization, or require a paid plan to use it, or whatever. (One wants to not offer to option to enable topic summarization if the server doesn't support it).
- Something to the effect of `summarization` probably should be in the name of the API field. Clients shouldn't care what models are being used for what, but we're currently imagining something like a `TOPIC_SUMMARIZATION_MODEL_PARAMS` type of setting name for the server, with a view that if we add some other capability, like having an AI compose a reply for you or translate, that might very well use a different model. So presumably some self-hosted will configured a topic summarization model or a translation model, but not both.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-28 21:16 UTC

So a few directions one could go are along the lines of the following:
- `server_has_summary_model`
- `server_has_summarization_model`
- `server_can_summarize_topics`
- `server_summarization_model_enabled`

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-28 21:18 UTC

I don't know if we want `topic` in the name; probably if we add a "please generate a topic name for the message I'm drafting" query, that'll use the same model as summarizing an existing topic, with a different prompt. Or at least support doing that as a fallback option.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-28 21:19 UTC

I feel like `server_has_summarization_model` feels more readable to me than `has_summary_model`, so thoughts on that option?

**Greg Price** · 2025-01-28 21:24 UTC

Yeah, I think "topic" doesn't need to be in the name — if in the future we introduce some other feature that's about summarization but not of a topic at a time, it'll likely be the same model involved and so this server-level flag will be the same.

**Greg Price** · 2025-01-28 21:25 UTC

And I agree, `server_has_summary_model` sounds like it's about a "summary model", which sounds like it's describing the model itself as a summary (or, as "summary" in the adjective sense — whatever either of those would mean here) and not talking about a model that summarizes.

**Greg Price** · 2025-01-28 21:28 UTC

Oh, I kind of like `server_can_summarize_topics`, though.

It straightforwardly says this feature is enabled, or isn't — no further logic needed to work that out. If there's a future feature that also involves the same model underneath, the more relevant thing to the client is whether the server offers that feature, and this way there doesn't need to be a feature-level check or anything like that, just looking at the flag.

**Greg Price** · 2025-01-28 21:28 UTC

It also translates naturally to realm-level or user-level settings with the same name `can_summarize_topics`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-28 21:29 UTC

Ahh, yeah, that's a good point. Or a `realm.can_summarize_topics_group`, if it's a group-valued permissions setting for which users in the organization get to use it. (Not sure that's likely, but it's good the name would feel very natural)

**Greg Price** · 2024-10-04 20:27 UTC

The important case for putting multiple properties in one `update_dict` event (vs. a series of several events) is when they're logically coupled so that a mixed state with some but not all of the updates wouldn't make sense. When that's the case, sending a single event means clients go atomically from one consistent state to another, without going through the mixed states.

**Greg Price** · 2024-10-04 20:29 UTC

More generally I'd encourage sending multiple updates as a single event — when the API already supports doing so, as it does with `realm`/`update_dict` ­— any time the updates feel like a single operation.

That's helpful just in case there turns out to be a subtle way that an in-between state would be broken, even if that way isn't obvious.

We currently have two different endpoints for updating members `POST user_groups/{user_group_id}/members` and updating subgroups `POST user_groups/{user_group_id}/subgroups`.

As discussed in #**design>UI for adding subgroups #31834**, we would use the existing UI for adding members to add subgroups.

So, since the UI is such that we would add members and subgroups together on a single click, @Tim Abbott suggested we could probably pass a `subgroups` parameter to `POST user_groups/{user_group_id}/members` endpoint instead of doing two API requests. Any feedback?

**Greg Price** · 2024-10-11 21:43 UTC

Combining those into one request makes a lot of sense.

We should make sure that the API continues to let the client express the user's intent of adding or removing particular members/subgroups, rather than sending a new complete list of members/subgroups. That's important for the reasons documented here:
https://zulip.com/api/group-setting-values#updating-group-setting-values
which we discussed in some threads in this channel earlier this year.

**Greg Price** · 2024-10-11 21:44 UTC

So currently /api/update-user-group-members and /api/update-user-group-subgroups each take an `add` parameter and a `delete` parameter. If we combine them by adding more parameters to /api/update-user-group-members , then a good solution would be to add two parameters named like `add_subgroups` and `delete_subgroups`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-10-11 21:58 UTC

Yeah that plan sounds good to me.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2024-10-11 22:13 UTC

I'm wondering if we want to make the entire operation atomic. If we failed to add members but could successfully create the subgroups, do we rollback the changes?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-10-12 00:40 UTC

The existing function has an outer transaction, so I expect we'd try to preserve that property.

I think the main question for this audience is what we want the HTML format to be. Here's what is proposed in the PR:
```
<a class="stream-topic-message" data-stream-id="{channel_id}" '
        f'href="/#narrow/stream/{channel_id}-{channel_name}/topic/{topic_name}/near/{message_id}">'
        f"#{channel_name} > {topic_name} @ 💬</a>
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-10-30 23:02 UTC

Just checked, and it looks like the web app does use the `data-stream-id` values to display the current name for channels that have been renamed:
``` js
    $content.find("a.stream-topic").each(function (): void {                                            
        const stream_id_string = $(this).attr("data-stream-id");                                        
        assert(stream_id_string !== undefined);                                                         
        const stream_id = Number.parseInt(stream_id_string, 10);                                        
        if (stream_id && !$(this).find(".highlight").length) {                                          
            // Display the current name for stream if it is not                                         
            // being displayed in search highlight.                                                     
            const stream_name = sub_store.maybe_get_stream_name(stream_id);                             
            if (stream_name !== undefined) {                                                            
                // If the stream has been deleted,                                                      
                // sub_store.maybe_get_stream_name might return                                         
                // undefined.  Otherwise, display the current stream name.                              
                const text = $(this).text();                                                            
                $(this).text("#" + stream_name + text.slice(text.indexOf(" > ")));                      
            }                                                                                           
        }                                                                                               
    });                                                                                                 
```

Generally I've made the parser fairly paranoid about having important semantics it didn't know about go over its head. So when it sees a CSS class it didn't expect, it behaves with the assumption that it's some new feature it doesn't know how to handle, rather than trying to round it off to something it does know about.

Concretely that looks like [this](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-flutter/blob/ffa41be876743ee9b57982c7a315e6f97fe65491/lib/model/content.dart#L856-L858) for the condition recognizing a plain old link:

```

## general chat api changes

*2024-11-06 to 2025-07-06 · 280 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/general.20chat.20api.20changes/with/1976707)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-06 19:50 UTC

In #**design>general chat / default topic**, we're planning to redesign the ugly "(no topic)" thing that Zulip currently uses if a topic is not specified in favor of a "general chat" string, which is intended to be displayed in italics, and represented in the API as the empty string (no topic). Let's use this thread to work out the API design transitions involved in introducing this.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-06 19:57 UTC

I think most simply API clients probably don't require any special handling for this -- they likely will process the empty string like they would any other string. But there's several issues to discuss for Zulip apps:
- Even simple apps like `zulip-archive` might generate a 0-width string for the topic name, which can't be clicked on.
- Every client app would need new logic for displaying the `""` topic as "*general chat*", including most subtly in the compose area.
- We could do extra work in the server to offer a compatibility mode for older clients, principally `zulip-mobile`, to send "general chat" to the client rather than `""`. This may not be a good use of resources, mainly in that it might be a LOT of work to adjust all the relevant code paths in the server (delivering messages, `unread_msgs`, etc.) to check that client capability. And I expect the alternative of just adding display-layer code to display the topic differently in the inbox, topic list, and message feed views would be a lot less work if we decide the timeline suggests we should do this for `zulip-mobile`. So my temptation would be to attempt to implement basic display support for this in `zulip-flutter` early in the project, see how much work that is, and decide based on that how to proceed.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-06 20:09 UTC

Some initial thoughts on how the protocol should work:
- The `(no topic)` topic continues to potentially exist and have no special behavior -- I think we intend no automated migration on that. (Users can do it by hand if they used that topic). Clients should remove the existing logic related to using "(no topic)" with an empty topic input box as of the API feature level introducing this feature.
- Previously, `""` was illegal as a topic on channel messages. Now, it is legal, and clients should display it as *general chat*. (Clients may not need a feature level check for this detail because the empty topic was previously impossible.)
- The `realm_mandatory_topics` setting is redefined to controlling whether you can use the empty string rather than controlling whether you can use "(no topic)".
- We likely need to specify how clients should display mentions of empty topics, which syntactically would most naturally be written as `#**design>**`, but could be displayed with the `*general chat*` part written. Depending on the answers to the next two questions, this might most correctly be client-side behavior.
- A key question is where the string "general chat" should come from. A possibly wise theory would be to make it be provided by the server via the API, in that doing so would permit UX changes in what this is called without a complex protocol migration (The most likely time for changes in the name is during the testing process, if we find "general chat" is not the best name). One version would be that the server sends a `server_empty_topic_display_name` field to clients in the `/register` response containing the string "general chat", translated into the user's configured language. 
- I think we've also seen at least one person request a setting to control the name of the "general chat" topic in their organization, or maybe per-channel. Presumably, if we had such a feature and that were specified, that'd just take precedence over the (internationalized) default. We may find it wise to decide if we're going to offer such a thing, and if so, to build it in to the API design from the beginning.

* [/api/get-message#fetch-a-single-message](https://zulip.com/api/get-message#fetch-a-single-message)
   * Same thing as the previous one for this endpoint too.

Yeah, zulip-mobile ignores `muted_topics` events for current servers, so if the server stops sending them then that will have no effect on zulip-mobile.

```js
    case EVENT_MUTED_TOPICS: {
      if (getZulipFeatureLevel(globalState) >= 134) {
        // TODO(server-6.0): Drop this muted_topics event type entirely.
        // This event type is obsoleted by `user_topic`, so we can ignore it.
        //
        // The server sends both types of events, because we
        // don't set event_types in our /register request:
        //   https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/21251#issuecomment-1133466148
        // But if we interpreted the muted_topics events as usual,
        // we'd throw away all policies other than None or Muted.
        return state;
      }
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-07 07:08 UTC

So #32330 is up with an incomplete prototype of the server support for allowing the `""` topic and handling legacy clients that don't know about "general chat" yet. It seems pretty plausible, but probably it's worth waiting until tests and docs and written before others try to review. Essentially what it does is:
- Adds a new `empty_topic_name` client capability, and rewrites `""` to `"general chat"`
- Makes both `/register` response data and events that reference a topic (message send/deletion, mark unread, `user_topic`, etc.) translate `""` to `"general chat"` before returning it to clients. 
- For incoming send/move message requests, and presumably once it's done, searches too, translating "general chat" to "".

Remaining, as I understand it, are:
- Search / narrowing support around this. One detail that may be messy is keyword searches for "general chat" probably are not going to match the topic, though `topic:""` will, so that might be a thing we ignore for v1? Not sure if it's problematic.
- API code for telling modern clients how to spell "general chat" in their organization.
- Desktop and web app support for displaying the topic as designed.
- Email/mobile push notification formatting support.

So I'd like to make a plan for merging #32330 as a useful checkpoint after the feedback I've posted (some technical, and some docs). As detailed above, this fully implements the `empty_topic_name` client capability for translating the `""` topic to `"general chat"` in the `register`, `events`, and some other API surfaces. I think the intermediate state will be:

- No clients set the `empty_topic_name` client capability, nor should any.
- No changes in behavior for clients that do not set that client capability unless they specifically try to send to the `""` or `"general chat"` topic name.
- Existing clients sending to the "general chat" topic will find it stored in the `""` topic in the server, but that behavior will be essentially invisible to clients that that do not advertise the `"empty_topic_name"` client capability, because the server will rewrite it back to "general chat" when serving data about that topic to those clients.
- The one known place where it is not invisible is search/filtering code, where searching for "general chat" will be busted.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-02-03 21:21 UTC

OK, so there's a bit of a snafu with how this works. We have this bit of logic for parsing channel link URLs:
``` js
   /*
   ...
    We have legacy slugs that are just the name                                                         
    of the stream:                                                                                      
                                                                                                        
        stream-name                                                                                     
                                                                                                        
    And it's plausible that old stream slugs will have                                                  
    be based on stream names that collide with modern                                                   
    slugs:                                                                                              
                                                                                                        
        4-horseman                                                                                      
        411                                                                                             
        2016-election                                                                                   
                                                                                                        
    If there is any ambiguity about whether a stream slug                                               
    is old or modern, we prefer modern, as long as the integer                                          
    prefix matches a real stream id. We return undefined if the                                         
    operand has an unexpected shape, or has the old shape (stream                                       
    name but no ID) and we don't know of a stream by the given name.                                    
    */                                                                                                  
                                                                                                        
    // "New" (2018) format: ${stream_id}-${stream_name} .                                               
    const match = /^(\d+)(?:-.*)?$/.exec(slug);                                                         
    const newFormatStreamId = match ? Number.parseInt(match[1]!, 10) : null;                            
    if (newFormatStreamId !== null && stream_info.get(newFormatStreamId)) {                             
        return newFormatStreamId;                                                                       
    }                                                                                                   
```

     if (newFormatStreamId !== null && stream_info.get(newFormatStreamId)) {
         return newFormatStreamId;
     }
 
     // Old format: just stream name.  This case is relevant indefinitely,
     // so that links in old conversations (including off-platform like GitHub)
     // continue to work.
     const stream = get_sub_by_name(slug);
     if (stream) {
         return stream.stream_id;
     }
 
+    if (!require_accessible_channels && newFormatStreamId !== null) {
+        // If this is a context where parsing inaccessible channels is possible, 
+        // and we've extracted a number, assume it's modern format and the channel ID.
+        return newFormatStreamId;
+    }
+
     // Unexpected shape, or the old shape and we don't know of a stream with
     // the given name.
     return undefined;
 }
```

**Greg Price** · 2025-02-03 21:50 UTC

I recommend a simpler solution, which is the thing we have [in zulip-mobile](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-mobile/blob/7519372c2d78e87c8cd908f4f1bceaa99f8c3d81/src/utils/internalLinks.js#L84C1-L108C1) and zulip-flutter:
```js
  // "New" (2018) format: ${stream_id}-${stream_name} .
  const match = /^([\d]+)(?:-.*)?$/.exec(operand);
  const newFormatStreamId = match ? parseInt(match[1], 10) : null;
  if (newFormatStreamId != null && streamsById.has(newFormatStreamId)) {
    return newFormatStreamId;
  }

  // Old format: just stream name.  This case is relevant indefinitely,
  // so that links in old conversations continue to work.
  const streamName = decodeHashComponent(operand);
  const stream = streamsByName.get(streamName);
  if (stream) {
    return stream.stream_id;
  }

  if (newFormatStreamId != null) {
    // Neither format found a Stream, so it's hidden or doesn't exist. But
    // at least we have a stream ID; give that to the caller. (See jsdoc.)
    return newFormatStreamId;
  }

  // Unexpected shape, or the old shape and we don't know of a stream with
  // the given name.
  return null;
```

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2025-04-09 06:52 UTC

From what I've read so far - and please send me to current docs if this is finalized - the transition is broadly from, pre-10.0:
- no relevant capability
- send: clients adjust `""` to `"(no topic)"` before sending to server (`""` would be rejected)
- get-messages: responses with `"(no topic)"` are just like any other topic (except for rename rules?)
- get-stream-topics: as per get-messages

to post >=10.0:
- a capability which affects requests (other than get-messages?)
- send: clients can send to `""`, which is a new, extra 'no topic' equivalent; clients display as ~`"general chat"` (more generally `realm_empty_topic_display_name` from `register` or similar)
- get-messages: 
  - modern clients pass `allow_empty_topic_name=True`, and can extract the special `""` topic, treating it as the appropriate name (eg. '*general chat*', distinct from 'general chat')
  - old clients aren't aware of that parameter, and just see 'general chat' topics from modern clients and '(no topic)' topics from older clients
- get-stream-topics: as per get-messages, depending if the added parameter is understood, via the capability

**Steve Howell** · 2025-07-01 01:49 UTC

Code **always** evolves from booleans to enums.  It never evolves in the other direction, at least in my experience.  Despite the exponential explosion that would make you think otherwise.  As soon as you have even three or four booleans around the same feature, the annoyance of managing which booleans are mutually exclusive or whatever far outweighs the tedium of 2^n - x enum values.

**Steve Howell** · 2025-07-01 02:06 UTC

Enums are particularly useful for writing test code.  Suppose that you have five conceptual boolean decisions that theoretically lead to 32 possible states, but only 25 of them are logically possible due to inter-dependencies between the boolean decisions.  Once you kind of statically lay out what those 25 states are, it's pretty simple to visually inspect whether test code is thorough, whereas line coverage tools might not force you to be thorough.

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-12 00:55 UTC

Conveniently the impact of this incompatibility is fairly mild, because it appears only in an event (and not one of the super-frequent event types, like `message`).

In general when the mobile app hits an exception in polling the event queue, or within its own code for applying an event, it recovers by creating a new event queue. So the effect visible to the user is
* the loading indicator appears at the top of the screen, and then the data gets refreshed;
* meanwhile there's a "toast" popup at the bottom of the screen, saying an error occurred.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-12 01:40 UTC

Yeah, that seems pretty reasonable. The web app just reports the exception to Sentry and drops the event, which also seems fine as an approach.

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-12 01:50 UTC

In principle that's risky, because it means the state is probably out of sync now and it's hard to predict the consequences of that.

In practice I guess it hasn't become a notable problem in all these years.

This is also perhaps another point where it helps that on mobile, reloading is somewhat less intrusive than on web, because it's just the data being reloaded and not the client-side code (cf #**api design>mobile re-registration after server version update@2297726**). So it's fairly inexpensive for us to just do the safe thing.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-12 02:00 UTC

Yeah, it is important here that we aggressively fix those Sentry errors. We're more concerned with avoiding accidental thundering herds here than rare minor desynchronization of a client.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-12 02:01 UTC

Just to spell it out: If an unparseable event gets sent to everyone in an organization, all of that organization's clients would reload at once if we triggered an immediate reload on such parse failures.

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-12 02:05 UTC

Fair point!

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-12 02:08 UTC

So potentially the ideal behavior here would be (a) report the error in Sentry, and then (b) reload data — but (c) only after a random timeout, similar to what we do when a new version is deployed on the server (#**api design>mobile re-registration after server version update@2296051**).

That way a thundering herd is avoided, but also there's a bound on how long the client continues to have some data wrong due to dropping an event.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-12 22:42 UTC

Yeah, that seems right.

## can_administer_channel_group

*2024-11-27 to 2024-12-05 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/can_administer_channel_group/with/1989572)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-27 23:28 UTC

So I'm not sure we've talked about this recently. Obviously for a long time we've had the plan to use the new groups-based permissions frameworks for permissions on channels. 

The most important of those is `can_administer_channel_group`: the set of people who can administer a given channel (currently, that is hardcoded to organization administrators, with some restrictions around their ability to interact with private channels that they are not subscribed to). #32429 is working towards implementing it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-27 23:32 UTC

I think the main client-side migration that we'll need to manage is that probably there are various places that are hardcoded as checking the administrator role in the organization that will need to also check this setting for permission to do things. I've not finished reading the PR, but presumably all sorts of stuff, like deleting messages, may need to check it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-28 00:12 UTC

#**design>Make channel management permissions configurable #31959@1959772** is the main chat.zulip.org thread for the design of this; @Shubham Padia FYI.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-28 00:12 UTC

If there are any concerns with naming or compatibility, let me know. The PR is fairly far along in terms of the server and web app code, so the most likely place it gets stuck is client compatibility.

I think other clients don't have a ton of administrative features implemented.

**Greg Price** · 2024-12-04 04:50 UTC

In zulip-mobile we offer the UI to edit a channel (its name, description, and 4-way private/public setting) just if the user is an admin.

So with this change, some users might have permission to make those edits but won't get the UI for it on mobile; and if the group is narrower than admins, some users might get the UI but then get errors if they try to use it.

I think that's fine and we don't need to fix it. I expect it's quite rare for people to try to edit those settings on mobile; it's rare to need to edit them at all.

**Greg Price** · 2024-12-04 04:51 UTC

For zulip-flutter I just filed #F1102 as a post-launch issue to offer that channel-settings UI in the first place, and I made a note of this new API feature there.

**Shubham Padia** · 2024-12-04 10:03 UTC

> and if the group is narrower than admins, some users might get the UI but then get errors if they try to use it.

Admins will have permission to administer public channels and (private channels they are subscribed to) whether they are part of `can_administer_channel_group` or not.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-05 00:12 UTC

I think the right way to express it is fairly simple. Users can administer a channel fully if both:
- They have configured administrative privileges for the channel (either by being an organization administrator or being in `can_administer_channel_group`).
- They have access to the channel's message history (either by being a subscriber or having access to public channels).

If they only have the former, they can do basic administration (rename/edit description/etc.) only.

I think the legacy mobile app should only have failures in one direction.

**Greg Price** · 2024-12-05 00:36 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> - […] - They have access to the channel's message history (either by being a subscriber or having access to public channels). If they only have the latter, they can do basic administration (rename/edit description/etc.) only.

Wait, so anyone who can read a channel can rename it or edit its description? That doesn't sound right.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-05 00:39 UTC

No, was a typo, meant "former" -- had swapped the order for clarity and intended to swap that word but failed to do it :). Edited the original so it's a userful reference.

## in-home filter definition

*2024-12-09 to 2024-12-10 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/in-home.20filter.20definition/with/1996228)*

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-12-09 09:13 UTC

We don't have a proper definition of `in:home` narrow right now which is the narrow filter for `Combined feed`. 

One of the questions I am unsure about is if it should include `mentioned`messages from muted channels. See [here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/32579#discussion_r1871152634) and #**issues>✔ Empty combined feed**  for more context.

We exclude muted streams and followed or unmuted topics in the `in:home` filter which makes sense.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-12-09 09:15 UTC

The help page needs to be expanded to reflect what it includes exactly as well - https://zulip.com/help/combined-feed

**Alya Abbott** · 2024-12-09 16:46 UTC

My understanding of what's intended is what the help center says:

> all the unmuted messages you have received

**Alya Abbott** · 2024-12-09 16:47 UTC

So, what's excluded is:

- Messages in muted topics in any channel
- Messages in default topics in muted channels
- Messages sent by muted users

**Alya Abbott** · 2024-12-09 16:49 UTC

Mentions are not relevant to this definition. For example, you might not want @-everyone mentions to constantly keep bringing a topic you muted back to your attention.

If you want to notice @-mentions, you should do it by automatically following the topic:

[Screenshot 2024-12-09 at 08.48.06@2x.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/6c/2uuh8A7dbYm4FnSmM-hp95DR/Screenshot-2024-12-09-at-08.48.062x.png)

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-10 00:34 UTC

Historically, it has been the case that mentions in muted channels/topics were included in the combined feed. I think that historical behavior is no longer desirable and should be removed to the extent it still exists in clients.

I believe we added it circa 2014, long before the introduction of the followed topics mechanism, because it seemed bad for mentions to not be in your combined feed just because you'd muted a channel. With the new followed topics features in place, you can ensure that all mentions are in your combined feed by just using the setting to auto-follow topics; and probably if you re-muted the topic after the mentor, you don't need that mention prioritized for you.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-10 00:36 UTC

So I think it's correct to not consider mentions in that calculation today. We might want to check if any clients have behavior of that form cribbed from the web app implementation, in addition to making sure we've removed it in the web app correctly. 

And I suppose if we're really worried here, we could consider documenting on the "combined feed" page that if you'd like to make sure mentions always appear in your combined feed, even in muted channels/topics, you can enable the setting to follow topics where you are mentioned. But I'm not sure that's worth the effort/clutter in the docs.

## Left sidebar custom and pinned views

*2024-12-13 to 2025-05-23 · 49 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/Left.20sidebar.20custom.20and.20pinned.20views/with/2003174)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-13 18:30 UTC

In #**feedback>user research: views in left sidebar** / #32528, we're establishing a part of the API design for two core features:
- Being able to hide some of the built-in pinned views in the web/desktop app left sidebar, so that they sit in the VIEWS `vdots` menu.
- Being able a add custom views to the VIEWS section of the sidebar, like a search you need to check often. 

The current API that's proposed to support both of those applications is a new `pinned_views` event type synced to clients that request the event type, with `add/remove/update` events keyed by `"op"`, basically following the patterns of other event types. The object has the following fields:
- `view_id: str`: Unique ID for this configuration row, used for deletion/updates, and also to identify which are default views, like `"inbox"` would be for the inbox view.
- `is_pinned: bool`: Whether it should be shown expanded or hidden in the `vdots` menu. 
- `name: str | None`: User-facing display name for the view. Is `None` for built-views, and a string the user entered for any custom views.
- `url_hash: str | None`: What navigation occurs when clicking on the view. Is `None` for built-in views, and a string containing the URL hash for custom ones, e.g. `#narrow/sender/7` for the messages sent by a given user.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-13 18:34 UTC

So concretely, the two features suggested above would be implemented as follows:
- `view_id="reactions"`, `is_pinned=false` with the other fields `null` would be how you hide the "reactions" view in the 3-dots menu rather than having it take up space when you don't plan to use it.
- `view_id=???`, `is_pinned=true`, `name="Messages involving turtles"`, `url_hash="/#narrow/search/turtles"` would be a pinned custom view for messages involving turtles.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-13 18:39 UTC

I see a few things that might need to change here:
- I'm not sure how `view_id` would be generated for the custom views feature. I suppose the system could just generate something from the `name` or URL, or just use the row ID in the database, say `"178"`, which is not currently exposed to the API at all.
- There's currently no mechanism for controlling the order of these. I guess later we can add an integer `order` field and allow dragging, so it's probably not required to design that now, other than note that we'd likely end up needing to instantiate all the default views in the table should anyone actually do the drag, so every row for that user can have an `order` value that one can then sort by.
- `pinned_views` as the table/event type name feels a bit misleading when one of the flags is whether it's pinned or in the menu. I think `views` would be too short. `web_views` somehow reminds me too much of `webviews`, which is an unrelated technical term; I'm also not sure if we'd want to potentially have the mobile apps support this feature in its own way (at least the custom views part would likely be easy if we had a place to list it).

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-13 18:40 UTC

At the same time, a name like `custom_views` feels like it's a bit of a weird promise to me, in that we're also potentially putting the default views in this table; they do get customized in how they're shown, though, so maybe it could be OK?

**Aditya Kasaudhan** · 2024-12-13 19:34 UTC

I have a quick question about the handling of `view_id` in the implementation. For built-in views, it makes sense to pass the predefined `view_id` in the request. However, for custom views, should `view_id` be `None` in the request payload, with the system then generating it on the backend? Additionally, for the initial implementation of custom views, I am considering using the `url_hash` as the `view_id` for uniquenesssince it seems like a stable option. Does that align with requirement?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-13 20:10 UTC

Yeah, OK, there is a theory that `view_id` doesn't not need to exist in this form -- it should either be an integer ID if we feel the need for one, or we should just use the `url_hash` for identification of views, since we would indeed be using the same values for default views.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-13 20:11 UTC

So I think my new proposal is:
- Delete `view_id` from the above.
- Make `url_hash` no longer optional. The web client will just have implicit rows for the default views identified by the `url_hash` being `inbox` or `narrow/has/reaction/sender/me` (Reactions) or whatever. (Is `url_hash` a good name for this encoding?)

**Aditya Kasaudhan** · 2024-12-13 20:35 UTC

That makes sense, but now I'm wondering how we should handle `BUILT_IN_VIEWS`. Do we need to maintain the `url_hash` for views like 'inbox' and 'narrow/has/reaction/sender/me' (Reactions), or should we instantiate all default views in the table, which would also help with controlling the order of these ?

**Aditya Kasaudhan** · 2024-12-13 20:39 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> * Is `url_hash` a good name for this encoding?
Since the `url_hash` now serves as an identifier also in this table, In my opinion, it might be better to choose a more descriptive name.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-13 21:16 UTC

I don't want to make millions of rows just saying that the default views exist if we can avoid it; it'll make changes to that part of the app involve a lot more migration pain.

**Aditya Kasaudhan** · 2024-12-14 08:31 UTC

Is using the URL path to pass the `url_hash` parameter (e.g., `pinned_views/<path:url_hash>`) a good practice for the `PATCH` and `DELETE` endpoints, or would it be better to use a query parameter or a database-generated ID instead?

P.S.: I am using `path` for now since I have seen `<path:` already used at some places.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-16 18:19 UTC

That might be reasonable. We just have to be careful about encoding.

**Aditya Kasaudhan** · 2024-12-17 17:52 UTC

I’ve tried to align changes to match the current API design. Please have a look at #32528 and let me know if there’s anything I can improve further.

**Aditya Kasaudhan** · 2025-02-17 19:28 UTC

I would like to request review of PR  #32528, please let me know if there’s anything I can improve further.

**Greg Price** · 2025-02-17 21:42 UTC

Catching up on this thread now.

Rather than "hash", a good term would be ["fragment"](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-url-fragment). The name `url_hash` sounds like it's potentially a hash of a URL — as in passing the URL through a hash function.

**Greg Price** · 2025-02-17 21:47 UTC

In the new /api/get-pinned-views and the new `pinned_views` field of the register response, does the list include all the built-in views? Or do those only appear when there's non-default data about them, like saying they're hidden?

I think either answer could be reasonable but we should make sure it's clearly specified in the API.

**Greg Price** · 2025-02-17 21:48 UTC

(I agree we should avoid encoding the default state of things in the database — but it'd be easy for the server to materialize the corresponding data when responding to these API requests, even when it's not there in the database)

**Greg Price** · 2025-02-17 21:58 UTC

Rather than PATCH and DELETE, I think it would be better to make those be POST requests too, at appropriate distinct URL paths.

For example, the four endpoints here could be
`GET /pinned_views/list`
`POST /pinned_views/add`
`POST /pinned_views/edit`
`POST /pinned_views/delete`

**Greg Price** · 2025-02-17 21:59 UTC

It'd be possible to make PATCH and DELETE be appropriate here, but that would involve changing the other endpoints to complete the pattern. As @Anders Kaseorg wrote on a previous thread:

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> My take is that `DELETE /foo` is appropriate for an API where `/foo` was a valid URL referring to some object, and after the call `/foo` is no longer a valid URL and the object is gone. It should not be used for an API that doesn’t exactly match that description (e.g. the object is deactivated and m …

**Greg Price** · 2025-02-17 22:02 UTC

And I'd say something similar about PATCH: `PATCH /foo` is appropriate where `/foo` was a valid URL referring to some object, and the body of the PATCH request is describing how that object should be edited. It should not be used for an API that doesn’t exactly match that description (e.g., you're modifying some sub-object that doesn't have its own URL and is only ever fetched as part of a larger object), because in that case it's just a loose analogy.

**Greg Price** · 2025-02-17 22:04 UTC

I like the idea of using the URL fragment (aka `url_hash`) as the unique identifier for the view. It's naturally nice and unique, and it solves the problem of how to refer to the built-in views.

**Greg Price** · 2025-02-17 22:05 UTC

I don't love the name `pinned_views`, because they're not necessarily pinned — after all there's that `is_pinned` boolean, which can be false, and much of the point of the feature is the ability to un-pin views that to date have been always pinned.

I don't immediately have a better suggestion, though.

- `GET /navigation_views/`: Get all navigation views.
- `POST /navigation_views/`: Create a navigation view configuration.
- `DELETE /navigation_views/{view_ud}`: Delete the navigation view configuration.

Saved snippets doesn't have a `PATCH` interface, but that would be naturally:
- `PATCH /navigation_views/{view_id}`: Edit an existing navigation view configuration.

**Greg Price** · 2025-02-19 03:12 UTC

Re PATCH and DELETE vs. POST: ultimately it doesn't matter that much to me, because as far as mobile is concerned, the URLs get encoded once in the bindings and then they're basically an implementation detail; the rest of the code just makes function calls, so like
```dart
await editNavigationView(connection, urlFragment: fragment, isPinned: true);
```
or whatever.

The one really concrete way that either PATCH or DELETE can lead us awry, that I know of, is if we later want more parameters on the endpoint we put at DELETE. As we learned at #**api design>Invalid HTTP DELETE requests**, that's invalid under the RFC and isn't really supported by OpenAPI. But this seems like a case where that's fairly unlikely to happen.

**Greg Price** · 2025-02-19 03:14 UTC

`GET /navigation_views/{view_id}`
which gets that individual view's details, so that `/navigation_views/{view_id}` is clearly the URL path of a resource which the PATCH and DELETE methods are acting on. But the lack of that isn't outright wrong, as long I guess as we could in principle have such an endpoint and it would make sense (which I think is true here).

**Greg Price** · 2025-02-19 03:16 UTC
