**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-10 19:42 UTC

I think from a practical standpoint, I wonder if we want the following specification for now:
- We update the spec as detailed in #**api design>procedurally generated avatars@2274716** so clients handle unknown values in the future.
- We implement new avatar sources with a model where the server sends "U" as its API `avatar_source` to legacy clients, so we're not reliant on clients updating in order to have a uniform experience.
- Each new algorithm can have its own approach for how the server implements handling the `/avatar` URLs. It is probably a valid approach to just compute on the fly, and use caching headers, if it's fast enough, or it could manually upload/cache the file, depending on the details of how fast the generation code is. We'll probably want to just use "on the fly with caching" for some prototyping deployments, so we don't need to run a loop over all users in order to test a new algorithm.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-29 00:37 UTC

OK, so I think the core question is what a good salt is. I see a few options:
- `realm_url`: A public field we have, which unfortunately can change for an existing realm, if the company renames.
- `realm_uuid`: A field we already have for the push notifications API but isn't currently shared with clients.
- `realm_date_created`: The timestamp when the realm was created. 
- `jdenticon_salt`: A new field. Could be any of the above, but the key thing from the API standpoint is it'd be something the server computes with whatever algorithm it likes, that it perhaps promises will be mostly stable over time, but could potentially be different rules among these for different realms over time.

Since we do let folks change subdomains without import/export, I'm a bit reluctant to use `realm_url` as a salt, so I think we should look at whether the `realm_uuid` is a valid that could be sent to clients, and if that doesn't work, we should probably just look at, `jdenticon_salt`, which the server can happy to set in some static fashion, like a hash of the timestamp or prefix of the UUID or something.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-30 01:16 UTC

Yeah, `realm_avatar_salt` is reasonable. We do already have a secret, `AVATAR_SALT`, which I think we'd need to rename: It's a salt used for constructing filenames for avatars that are predictable from the user ID, but only for the server. But that's OK.

`realm_uuid` as salt works.

Benefits I can think of:
* Globally unique. So after export-import, even if user ID changes the avatar will stay the same.
* During import, we don't need to regenerate the Jdenticon avatars, we can export the images like we do for user-uploaded avatars.

Changes required:
* Include UUID for each user in API response (for clients to generate) vs single `realm.uuid`. For a realm with, say 30k users, it'd be "36 * 30k" bytes - nearly 1MB.
* Some code changes in export-import to handle exported Jdenticon images.

**Greg Price** · 2026-02-10 02:52 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-02-10 20:02 UTC

Yeah exactly one of the key performance problems that we need to be careful about here is not sending 1MB of uncompressible entropy to clients for no reason.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-02-10 20:03 UTC

I don't see any downsides for using `realm_uuid` as salt. It's not like there's anything malicious you can do with the ability to know what the auto-generated avatar for a user will be.


## ✔ defer loading user data (digression)

*2025-05-29 to 2025-05-30 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/.E2.9C.94.20defer.20loading.20user.20data.20.28digression.29/with/2183397)*

**Notification Bot** · 2025-05-29 23:03 UTC

[A message](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/defer.20loading.20user.20data.20.28digression.29/near/2183397) was moved here from #**api design>defer loading user data** by @Steve Howell.

**Steve Howell** · 2025-05-29 23:04 UTC

I have a flet client that renders messages, very much like the official Zulip client, and I want full `sender` objects so that I can show the sender's name and avatar.  When I fetch messages, I just get user_ids, so, at least in theory, I have to go back to the server to hydrate the user objects.

**Steve Howell** · 2025-05-29 23:06 UTC

Here's my current approach, which suffers from the O(N) problem:

~~~ py
    async def get_messages_sent_by_user(self, user: User) -> list[Message]:
        all_messages = self.database.message_table.get_rows()
        messages = [m for m in all_messages if m.sender_id == user.id]
        hydrated_messages = [(await HydratedMessage.create(message=m, service=self)) for m in messages]
        return sorted(hydrated_messages, key=lambda m: m.timestamp)
~~~

The bad news is that every call to HydratedMessage can potentially create a round trip.  The good news is that I have already isolated my rendering code from async worries.

**Steve Howell** · 2025-05-29 23:07 UTC

The render itself is completely synchronous:

~~~ py
    def populate(self, service, hydrated_message, *, width):
        sender = hydrated_message.sender

        item = ft.Row(
            controls=[
                ft.Image(src=sender.avatar_url, height=30),
                ft.Column(
                    controls=[
                        ft.Text(sender.name, size=14),
                        ft.Markdown(
                            hydrated_message.content,
                            selectable=True,
                            expand=True,
                            width=width,
                            auto_follow_links=True,
                        ),
                    ]
                ),
            ],
            vertical_alignment=ft.CrossAxisAlignment.START,
            expand=True,
        )

        self.control = ft.Container(
            item,
            border=ft.border.all(1, ft.Colors.GREY_200),
            padding=5,
            expand=True,
        )
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2025-05-29 23:08 UTC

But going back to the bad news, my `HydratedMessage` class is instantiated asynchronously, and if I have N messages, I have up to N round trips:

~~~ py
@dataclass
class HydratedMessage:
    sender: User
    content: str
    timestamp: int

    @staticmethod
    async def create(*, message, service):
        return HydratedMessage(
            sender=await service.get_user(message.sender_id),
            content=message.content,
            timestamp=message.content,
        )
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2025-05-29 23:14 UTC

The way that I intend to solve this tomorrow is to introduce two classes:
* DeferredUserFactory
* DeferredUser

And then `HydratedMessage` will have `deferred_sender` instead of `sender`.  When I go to the render code, I'll replace `sender = hydrated_message.sender` with something like `sender = hydrated_message.deferred_sender.value()`, and the rest of the render code will remain the same (and synchronous).  And then  the `get_messages_sent_by_user` function will remain async overall, but the async portion will move outside of the list comprehension into something like `await deferred_user_factory.finalize()`.

And then the `finalize()` function will iterate through synchronous calls to something like `get_cached_user` and then do an async call to `get_remote_users`.

**Steve Howell** · 2025-05-29 23:33 UTC

When I initially instantiate the `DeferredUser` object, it will only have an id, of course.  The call to the factory's `finalize`method will give it an actual value (in the context of doing bulk operations).  And that's what will force me to call `deferred_sender.value()`, because I want to avoid as much magic as possible.  The `value()` function will fail in an extremely obvious way if the `finalize` method does not get called.

**Steve Howell** · 2025-05-29 23:34 UTC

(as will direct attribute calls)

**Steve Howell** · 2025-05-30 12:15 UTC

Done. See https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/defer.20loading.20user.20data/near/2183824 for more details.

Here is some feedback regarding the creation of users by means of the API. We create organisations for use in conferences. The accounts of all participants are created programmatically, ahead of the event and the users are later invited to log in. We notice two things about the logic that applies to this use case:

## E2EE - error raised by bouncer

*2025-06-19 to 2025-07-10 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/E2EE.20-.20error.20raised.20by.20bouncer/with/2199403)*

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-06-19 15:30 UTC

[Draft ZAP](https://github.com/prakhar1144/zulip-architecture/blob/encrypt-push-notification/zaps/0002-encrypt-push-notifications.md)

**Error Handling:**

These are the possible error situations not discussed in ZAP
* `remote_realm` not found on bouncer. 

In older endpoint, [we don't do anything](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/0d17f34ff54f2cd23d251a8bb251b0119b637164/zilencer/views.py#L452) -- we try to associate the `RemotePushDeviceToken` with the `RemoteRealm`, but if not found, we simply log and move on. `RemotePushDeviceToken` has `server` field which is always set. 

In the ZAP, we plan to only have `remote_realm` / `realm` on `RemotePushDevice`. I think in the case of this error the server should just "Upload realm info and re-try" -- it'd work.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-06-19 15:31 UTC

* In case of validation error related to `push_token`, `token_kind`, etc, the server should follow a similar approach:
```
If the error is due to an invalid bouncer_public_key, don't retry and forget the push_account_id.
Include an additional reason field with the value "invalid bouncer_public_key" in the event sent
to remove the push_account_id from the push_account_ids map (see the  Miscellaneous section).
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-06-19 20:24 UTC

Both of those proposals sound right to me.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-07-07 01:03 UTC

One question that I came to while reading the ZAP: Should an expired `timestamp` happen before or after the check for whether the check for whether the `push_device_id` is already registered.
- If we check timestamp first, we maximally deny information to replay attacks, which seems good.
- If we check timestamp second, then a server might get the expired-timestamp error and delete the `PushDevice` even though things were working, which seems bad.

I think the answer is we should check it first, and the server-side error handling code should not delete the `PushDevice` entry for expired-timestamp errors if its database shows the request already successfully registered. (I think this should be very rare but could come up with restoring stale days-old backups. Those may need their own consideration, but the fact we have a stale duplicate registration request in a queue should not matter).

The ZAP proposes that order, and I've added this as explanation for why we do that for now, pending objections.

> 3. ii. If neither `RemotePushDevice.remote_realm` nor `RemotePushDevice.realm` corresponds to the authenticated server making the request, fail with error.

It says that in the section for sending notifications, but I think the same should apply for registering a device too. That's an error condition that shouldn't happen, and so the bouncer should just give an error.

## options for notifying new channel subscribers

*2025-06-19 to 2025-09-08 · 24 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/options.20for.20notifying.20new.20channel.20subscribers/with/2199784)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-06-19 20:21 UTC

So in #31206, we have a new feature that would allow controlling whether we send an automated DM to new subscribers when users are bulk-added to channels. The server won't do that for bulk operations of more than 100 users regardless of the user preference (i.e. the option isn't offered in that case).

The PR proposes adding a few fields:
- `max_subs_for_notification`: The constant that is 100 above. I think `max_bulk_new_subscription_messages`. might be the most clear name?
- `send_notification_to_new_users`: The boolean for whether the client requests these "you were subscribed" notices. The server ignores this field and just treats it as False if there are too many subscribers, rather than throwing an error.  (See also the next detail). I think `send_new_subscription_messages` would be a better name.
- `notification_bot_dms_sent`: Field in the subscribe response for whether the notices were in fact sent, so the client can know if the server ignored its value. I think `new_subscription_messages_sent` would be most clear.

Thoughts? The PR is otherwise complete, and it's not a very important detail, but the current names definitely don't fit our patterns.

The name makes sense there because that's a table on one device which may be about several different accounts, and because that field is the one that's used in the push-notifications protocol identifies each account as distinct from the other accounts in that table — so it's an ID for the account, and specifically the push ID for the account.

Didn't understand this part!

I think the suggestion is, when the registration to bouncer fails:
1. Save the `error_code` in the database. (`error_code` a new column)
2. Update the status to "failed" from "pending" ("failed" a new valid value apart from "active" and "pending")
3. Send the event (with `error_code` and updated `status`)

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-07-10 21:18 UTC

Question: If the server does not have a configured way to deliver push notifications at all, do we want clients to receive `push_account` metadata in their `register_queue` response? Some context:
- It'd save a very cheap database query to do so.
- This is usually not a transient state, but you could imagine some circumstances where the settings get commented out briefly.
- I think with our protocol, a client that saw an empty `push_account` list will delete its local state. I think that would be kinda bad in that it would make the transient state of "server stopped having notifications configured" result in a much longer-lasting state of "clients deleted their metadata and won't get it back until next startup". 
- It's possible that failure mode wouldn't happen, because the client may check `push_notifications_enabled` type fields before calling into the `push_account` list code. But that seems fragile to rely on / plan around.

Overall my leaning is towards not trying to be clever and save that database query here, and in fact adding a comment referencing this logic so nobody tries to be clever in the future. If the server wants to delete it `PushToken` records, it can do that, but if it's not done so, that may signal intent to later re-enable mobile notifications.

**Greg Price** · 2025-07-10 21:21 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> Overall my leaning is towards not trying to be clever and save that database query here, and in fact adding a comment referencing this logic so nobody tries to be clever in the future.

Yeah, that sounds good to me.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-07-10 21:25 UTC

Proposed comment: 
> We intentionally don't try to save a database query if push_notifications_configured() is False, in order to avoid risk of clients deleting their Account records if the server has its mobile notifications configuration temporarily disabled.

[Get events](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/ce/VPP5_mpEJoFWuHfwqv5pGmut/image.png)

(You could imagine some sort of "retrying" state being relevant or something).
- I think we don't currently set the metadata to say explicitly that the `error_code` field is optional.

## E2EE - APNs payload

*2025-07-03 to 2025-07-25 · 31 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/E2EE.20-.20APNs.20payload/with/2212231)*

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-07-03 11:18 UTC

Currently, this is the JSON payload we send to APNs:
```py
{
 "aps": {
   "alert": {
      "title": get_apns_alert_title(message, user_profile.default_language),
      "subtitle": get_apns_alert_subtitle(message, ...),
      "body": content, # calculated from message.rendered_content
   },
   "sound": "default",
   "badge": get_apns_badge_count(user_profile),
 },
 # Custom data
 "zulip": {
   "stream_id": ...,
   "topic": ...,
   "pm_users": ...,
   .
   .
 }
}
```

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-07-03 11:19 UTC

Now, the data in `alert` dictionary and custom data (`stream_id`, `topic`, etc) needs to be encrypted.

The [recommended approach](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/usernotifications/generating-a-remote-notification#Create-the-JSON-payload) is:
> Don’t include customer information or any sensitive data, like a credit card number, in a notification’s payload. If you must include customer information or sensitive data, encrypt it before adding it to the payload. You can use a notification service app extension to decrypt the data on the user’s device. For more information, see [Modifying content in newly delivered notifications](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/usernotifications/modifying-content-in-newly-delivered-notifications).

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-07-03 11:19 UTC

So, I think we would be to following the [documented approach](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/usernotifications/modifying-content-in-newly-delivered-notifications).

At high-level:
> Modifying a remote notification requires a notification service app extension, which you include inside your iOS app bundle. The app extension receives the contents of your remote notifications before the system displays them to the user, giving you time to update the notification payload

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-07-03 11:20 UTC

The JSON payload will be:
```json
{
   "aps" : {
      "mutable-content" : 1,
      "alert" : {
         "title" : "TBD",
         "subtitle" : "TBD",
         "body"  : "TBD"
     },
   },
   "ENCRYPTED_DATA" : "base-64 encoded encrypted data"
}
```

We will put all those fields which needs to be encrypted in a simple map and encrypt.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-07-03 17:01 UTC

It'll be easier to get to a final version of this sort of thing for Android. But I think probably title/subtitle/body should be fixed strings. Options that seem natural to me include:
- The empty string for all 3, if that works.
- Fixed text that does not depend on any input, if it doesn't.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-07-03 17:13 UTC

It shouldn't be an empty string.

[Docs mention](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/usernotifications/modifying-content-in-newly-delivered-notifications#:~:text=If%20you%20fail%20to%20call%20the%20completion%20handler%20from%20either%20method%2C%20the%20system%20displays%20the%20original%20contents%20of%20the%20notification.):
> Your [`didReceive(_:withContentHandler:)`](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/usernotifications/unnotificationserviceextension/didreceive(_:withcontenthandler:)) method has only about 30 seconds to modify the payload and call the provided completion handler. If your code takes longer than that, the system calls the [`serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire()`](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/usernotifications/unnotificationserviceextension/serviceextensiontimewillexpire()) method, at which point you must return whatever you can to the system immediately. If you fail to call the completion handler from either method, the system displays the original contents of the notification.

So, the provided string will be a fallback if it takes longer than 30s to modify the payload.

I think we should use a generic fixed string and client will update the title / subtitle / body after decrypting the `encrypted_data`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-07-03 17:16 UTC

I expect the client code won't be using the network at all to process it, so taking more than 30 seconds shouldn't come up often. Sounds like it should be an error string. 

I think we can start with something like:
- title: "New notification".
- The other two fields being the empty string. 

Ultimately this will be something for the mobile/design team to refine interactively in testing, so placeholder values like the above are fine for now.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-07-03 17:21 UTC

Yeah, just wanted to get a confirmation on if we're fine with this approach.

This approach is a bit different from how we currently handle push notifications in iOS. 
Addition: "notification service app extension included inside your iOS app bundle"

For FCM, there's no major changes. So didn't flag that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-07-17 23:52 UTC

So there's a few more fields we need to think about that are in the envelope APNs payload:
- Priority. Since that's part of the envelope, we'd need an explicit field in what the server sends the bouncer if we want that to not always be "high". I think the only reasonable thing to do is have a "priority" field alongside `"encrypted_data"` in the mobile push request that the server sends the bouncer.
- APNs has a `time_to_live` field; FCM has something similar, which is basically how long the event can be in the APNs server before being deleted. Do we want this to be in the protocol, or just to hardcode something in the bouncer, like 28 days?
- The `push_type`: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/usernotifications/sending-notification-requests-to-apns#Know-when-to-use-push-types. I think this basically aligns with `priority` for us; `background` will be used with medium-priority for remove notifications, `alert` will be used with high priority for new messages.

https://developer.apple.com/documentation/usernotifications/sending-notification-requests-to-apns#Send-a-POST-request-to-APNs
and we're talking about headers `apns-priority` and `apns-push-type`.

(replying to Tim Abbott)

For `apns-expiration`, I'm inclined to leave it out. The [default behavior is](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/usernotifications/sending-notification-requests-to-apns):
> As a best-effort service, APNs may reorder notifications you send to the same device token. If APNs can’t deliver a notification immediately, it may store the notification for 30 days or less, depending on the date you specify in the `apns-expiration` header. (so 30 days) and I don't feel like a shorter expiration would be an improvement.

**Greg Price** · 2025-07-22 23:59 UTC

I think the only reasonable thing to do is have a "priority" field alongside `"encrypted_data"` in the mobile push request that the server sends th …

**Greg Price** · 2025-07-23 00:02 UTC

As a matter of API design, I think it'd be good for us to avoid making up our own names for each of these. Instead, let's have the server send to the bouncer the exact APNs payload it wants to send, and the exact APNs-specified HTTP headers it wants to include (out of the handful of headers the bouncer lets the server specify).

Then the bouncer validates all that against a precise schema, and then sends it.

**Greg Price** · 2025-07-23 00:04 UTC

That's helpful because it saves us from having to invent names and semantics for each of these different elements, and mentally translate those back and forth when we're reading code, or debugging and reading logs. Instead we just say what's allowed, and the details of what those mean are whatever meaning APNs gives to them.

**Greg Price** · 2025-07-23 00:07 UTC

would instead look like this:
```json
{

    "aps" : {
      "mutable-content" : 1,
      "alert" : {
        "title" : "New notification",
      },
    },
    "encrypted_data" : "base-64 encoded encrypted data",
  },
}
```

**Greg Price** · 2025-07-23 00:14 UTC

I think the HTTP headers we'd want the server to specify for APNs would be:
* `apns-push-type`, allowing only the values `alert` and `background`
* `apns-priority`, allowing only the values 10, 5, and I guess 1 (which is the third value accepted by APNs), why not
* … and one more: `apns-topic`.

  This is the app ID. I want to avoid hard-coding on the server or the bouncer that every app that can receive notifications (or E2EE notifications) has the app ID `org.zulip.Zulip` or whatever — at a minimum, it's useful to have the ability to have debug builds with a different app ID.

## E2EE - Is push_account_id unique for a user?

*2025-07-10 to 2025-07-10 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/E2EE.20-.20Is.20push_account_id.20unique.20for.20a.20user.3F/with/2218600)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-07-10 21:21 UTC

In https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/34836#discussion_r2198028677, we create a unique index on `(user, push_account_id)` on the local Zulip server, with the intent being to allow us to handle duplicate requests from a client correctly.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-07-10 21:23 UTC

I think that's reasonable -- the client is choosing those randomly, so they should ~never collide. But there's a case I wanted to bring up: During mobile device backup-restore onto a new phone, do we need to worry about two devices having the same `push_account_id` for that reason? I think the answer is no, if the mobile app correctly doesn't transfer the `Account` table.

But I guess I was wondering if there's any server-side protection worth trying to do here, keeping in mind that adding some sort of unique ID like the mobile device's hardware IDs has privacy downsides that seem not worth it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-07-10 21:24 UTC

Currently it says:
> The client is responsible for ensuring that these secrets are stored as securely as possible, including excluding them from device backups.

which applies to `push_private_key` and `last_acked_push_token` because those are secrets, and `push_public_key` because it's fairly clear the client has no interest in keeping it around without the corresponding private key, but doesn't as clearly apply to `push_account_id`.

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-02 06:48 UTC

I was thinking today about how the server and client should behave when the server isn't configured for notifications, and came across the error logic quoted above. I see it's right at the top of the view function:
```py
@human_users_only
@typed_endpoint
def register_push_device(
    # …
) -> HttpResponse:
    if not (settings.ZILENCER_ENABLED or uses_notification_bouncer()):
        raise PushServiceNotConfiguredError
```

That means the /api/register-push-device request itself will fail, and neither the push key nor push token will be saved by the server.

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-02 06:50 UTC

We wrote a different behavior into the old push-registration flow:
```py
@human_users_only
@typed_endpoint
def add_android_reg_id(
    request: HttpRequest, user_profile: UserProfile, *, token: str
) -> HttpResponse:
    validate_token(token, PushDeviceToken.FCM)
    add_push_device_token(user_profile, token, PushDeviceToken.FCM)
    return json_success(request)
```

```py
def add_push_device_token(
    user_profile: UserProfile, token_str: str, kind: int, ios_app_id: str | None = None
) -> None:
    logger.info(
        "Registering push device: %d %r %d %r", user_profile.id, token_str, kind, ios_app_id
    )

    # Regardless of whether we're using the push notifications
    # bouncer, we want to store a PushDeviceToken record locally.
    # These can be used to discern whether the user has any mobile
    # devices configured, and is also where we will store encryption
    # keys for mobile push notifications.
    PushDeviceToken.objects.bulk_create(
        [
            PushDeviceToken(
                # …
            ),
        ],
        ignore_conflicts=True,
    )

    if not uses_notification_bouncer():
        return

    # … then sends info to the bouncer …
```

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-02 06:52 UTC

So in the old flow, it always saves the token, even if it's not currently connected to the bouncer (nor shares a database with the bouncer, which is what `settings.ZILENCER_ENABLED` is pointing at above).

And the comment indicates a plan to also always save an encryption key.

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-02 07:04 UTC

We could continue to do the same thing in the new flow: always record the data, and return success (unless something goes wrong within that task).

Then if notifications aren't configured, the step that necessarily fails is trying to talk to the bouncer to send it the token. The protocol has a separate place for us to indicate errors in that step: the `push_registration_error_code` field on the device object. So the failure can be indicated there.

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-02 07:07 UTC

I guess maybe the thing that goes into deciding how we want that to work is: what happens when
* a server doesn't have push notifications configured;
* it has a bunch of users, some of them using the mobile app;
* then the server admins go and set up push notifications?

In the legacy system, I believe the idea is that notifications would start working immediately for the existing mobile users, because the server already has their tokens. Though I guess for that to work, the server would need to go tell the bouncer about all the existing devices? Not sure if we actually have that logic.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-03-02 23:00 UTC

I don't think any such logic existed. I mostly recall our thinking about handling case where you had an interruption of connection to the bouncer (due to firewall, credentials, etc.)...

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-03-02 23:01 UTC

But I think in this new design, where the server is able to hold onto requests for the bouncer in a queue and retry them, I think it was a design goal to be able to do that well?

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-03-02 23:03 UTC

I guess a key thing to distinguish is "No connection to bouncer" vs "Not on a plan where the bouncer will do things". My recollection is the key change 1-2 years ago is to make it very easy to have ToS/connection to the bouncer configured during server setup, and then have whether those tokens do anything depend on the plan, but for it to be commonly the case that client apps are registering tokens with the bouncer whenever the self-hosted server has the push notifications service enabled, so that one can have everything work instantly once the site in on an approved community or paid plan.

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-03 01:22 UTC

Yeah, that sounds right. So I guess the main next question is: in that case "Not on a plan where the bouncer will do things", how does the current code behave in the new E2EE paths? Does the registration make it to the bouncer, so that everything works except the step of actually sending notifications?

@Prakhar Pratyush would you determine the current answer to that? From the scrollback above in July it looks like we weren't thinking about this aspect at the time, so there might be some logic we'll want to adjust here.

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-03 01:25 UTC

And then with that context in mind, I believe the way we'll actually want to use this value in the client:

(replying to Greg Price)
> looking at `realm_push_notifications_enabled` in the /api/register-queue snapshot

is that it tells us whether actually sending notifications is expected to work (contrary to what I said about it above in July, where I thought it would also describe whether *registering* for notifications would work).

Specifically, if the server has a connection to the bouncer, but not a plan where the bouncer will do things, then
* the server will accept /api/register-push-device requests, and successfully pass the tokens to the bouncer, and that success will be reflected in the device records, just the same as when notifications are fully working;
* but actual notifications won't happen, and `realm_push_notifications_enabled` will be false in order to let the client know that's the case (so it can appropriately warn the user).

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2026-03-03 06:13 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)
> "Not on a plan where the bouncer will do things", how does the current code behave in the new E2EE paths? Does the registration make it to the bouncer, so that everything works except the step of actually sending notifications?

Yes, registration makes it to the bouncer. Send notification won't succeed.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2026-03-03 06:19 UTC

We don't have a test for this case, which is important, I'll add one.

## E2EE - token expired

*2025-07-15 to 2025-07-17 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/E2EE.20-.20token.20expired/with/2221513)*

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-07-15 19:04 UTC

ZAP [mentions](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-architecture/blob/main/zaps/0002-encrypt-push-notifications.md#expired-tokens):
> * If APNs or FCM indicates to the push bouncer that the token is invalid or expired, the push bouncer sets `expired_time` to now. In that case — or if the push bouncer gets a notification for an invalid device or a device with `expired_time` already set — it returns an error to the server that the `device_id` is no longer valid, and the server removes it.
  
> * The push bouncer can safely garbage-collect `RemotePushDevice` records whose `expired_time` is sufficiently far in the past, using a longer threshold than `PUSH_REGISTRATION_LIVENESS_TIMEOUT`. (Keeping them around for that a while allows us to avoid angering APNs/FCM with repeat notification attempts to tokens it already rejected.)

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-07-15 19:04 UTC

The discussion in the paper doc regarding "Keeping them around for that a while allows us to avoid angering APNs/FCM" was:

@Greg Price said:
> there could even be an in-flight request to create a new record with that token. Which is why we keep the tombstone record around so that we can recognize those as duplicates, until the device has been gone long enough that any request dating from when it existed would be rejected as stale instead.

> ​​One thing we’re assuming there is that if APNs/FCM tells us that the token is invalid or expired, then there is no longer a client that’s going to be making a new registration request with that token, because the app was uninstalled from that device or is otherwise gone.

> In particular if it didn’t get a successful response from the server when it last tried to register (which may be the case even if the request actually succeeded on the server — the connection may have failed before the response), then it retries. That’s already the current app’s behavior

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-07-15 19:04 UTC

Question is: since there won't be any client to make a registration request with that token (if APNs/FCM has told that the token is invalid), then what's this "in-flight request to create a record" we're talking about ?

The server attempts to send push notification only when registration to bouncer and server is successful.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-07-15 20:23 UTC

I think the critical part for managing APNs/FCM reputation is that the bouncer knows to not send any with a non-null `expired_time`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-07-15 20:25 UTC

Having the bouncer not immediately those records is valuable for allowing the server to garbage-collect its `PushDevice` data structures; I think as noted there, the client will likely figure it out just fine.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-07-15 20:27 UTC

I think ultimately the right protocol here may involve the bouncer not having a cron job to delete expired tokens directly at all; instead, we probably want a cron job on the server, which asks asks the bouncer what `PushDevice` entries associated with it are expired, and then the server deletes those from its local records, and tells the bouncer it can now delete them?

**Greg Price** · 2025-07-17 03:17 UTC

@Prakhar Pratyush [schrieb](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/E2EE.20-.20token.20expired/near/2221515):
> Question is: since there won't be any client to make a registration request with that token (if APNs/FCM has told that the token is invalid), then what's this "in-flight request to create a record" we're talking about ?

Concretely in terms of the current spec: that means a PushDevice record on the server where `encrypted_push_registration` is non-null.

**Greg Price** · 2025-07-17 03:19 UTC

After all, that field basically contains a request which the client has asked to be passed on to the bouncer. The server might in the future (for example, an hour from now) make a fresh attempt to send that request on to the bouncer; that's this substep:
> * On other errors, including 5xx errors and network errors:
>
>   Wait in order to back off, using exponential random backoff according to standard practice. Then, asynchronously, retry the request.

So when the server does that, it's important that the bouncer still has the tombstone RemotePushDevice record. That's what lets it know that it's already seen that token and learned it's expired.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-07-17 03:31 UTC

> when the server does that, it's important that the bouncer still has the tombstone RemotePushDevice record

If the server is still retrying (registration is in-progress), there'd be no attempt to send push notification to the device (because it's not registered yet) and hence there's no way for APNs / FCM to tell whether the token is expired or not to bouncer (and set `expired_time` on `RemotePushDevice`).

If the server is still retrying to register to bouncer, the RemotePushDevice record doesn't exist at all.

**Greg Price** · 2025-07-17 03:41 UTC

Hmm. I'm not sure that's always true, though — consider the type of scenario Tim pointed out in another context, where a server got backed up and then restored.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-07-17 17:23 UTC

I think the combination of likelihood and harm is pretty low though -- sending another request with an expired token and learning (again) that it's expired is negligible impact. So I agree it's not important to add complexity to avoid that outcome.


## remove_payload_gcm

*2025-07-24 to 2025-07-24 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/remove_payload_gcm/with/2228674)*

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-07-24 06:22 UTC

```py
def get_remove_payload_gcm(
    user_profile: UserProfile,
    message_ids: list[int],
) -> tuple[dict[str, Any], dict[str, Any]]:
    """A `remove` payload + options, for Android via FCM."""
    gcm_payload = get_base_payload(user_profile)
    gcm_payload.update(
        event="remove",
        zulip_message_ids=",".join(str(id) for id in message_ids),
        # Older clients (all clients older than 2019-02-13) look only at
        # `zulip_message_id` and ignore `zulip_message_ids`.  Do our best.
        zulip_message_id=message_ids[0],
    )
    gcm_options = {"priority": "normal"}
    return gcm_payload, gcm_options
```

I think we can safely remove `zulip_message_id` at this point; there won't be clients older than that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-07-24 15:12 UTC

Correct, we only need to think about new clients for this new protocol.

**Greg Price** · 2025-07-24 17:01 UTC

Yeah. We can also freely remove that at this point for the old protocol, since the clients that use `zulip_message_ids` have been out for years and we no longer support older client versions that don't.

The commit implementing this: 9869153ae80febf6dca29e4a136a7b4d20ea32f9

Regarding the 4096 byte limit, we have:
````spoiler Send truncated message IDs
```py
    # APNs has a 4KB limit on the maximum size of messages, which
    # translated to several hundred message IDs in one of these
    # notifications. In rare cases, it's possible for someone to mark
    # thousands of push notification eligible messages as read at
    # once. We could handle this situation with a loop, but we choose
    # to truncate instead to avoid extra network traffic, because it's
    # very likely the user has manually cleared the notifications in
    # their mobile device's UI anyway.
    #
    # When truncating, we keep only the newest N messages in this
    # remove event. This is optimal because older messages are the
    # ones most likely to have already been manually cleared at some
    # point in the past.
    #
    # We choose 200 here because a 10-digit message ID plus a comma and
    # space consume 12 bytes, and 12 x 200 = 2400 bytes is still well
    # below the 4KB limit (leaving plenty of space for metadata).
    MAX_APNS_MESSAGE_IDS = 200
    truncated_message_ids = sorted(message_ids)[-MAX_APNS_MESSAGE_IDS:]
    gcm_payload, gcm_options = get_remove_payload_gcm(user_profile, truncated_message_ids)
    apns_payload = get_remove_payload_apns(user_profile, truncated_message_ids)
```
````

**Greg Price** · 2025-10-17 17:45 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> - Should `zulip_message_ids` in the `remove` notification format be a JSON list rather than a string joining numbers with `,`s? I feel like we might have done that for a reason given the 4096 byte limit on notification size.

We did that because FCM payloads are actually string-string maps, not JSON objects.

(For example see `data` at https://firebase.google.com/docs/reference/fcm/rest/v1/projects.messages .)

Now that we're using JSON (because we're serializing it ourselves, so can use whatever format we want), that's not a constraint.

**Greg Price** · 2025-10-17 17:47 UTC

For a single possibly-long list of ints, making it JSON isn't really any longer than the old format — effectively it just adds `[` and `]` around the old format, so two bytes. (Certainly we should be omitting whitespace in the JSON.) So a proper JSON list sounds good.

**Greg Price** · 2025-10-17 17:56 UTC

> I guess a related question is whether the server should be compressing these JSON blobs before encrypting them.

I think there probably isn't a lot to gain from that — these are generally short anyway.

* The `message` type contains just a single message. The way it could get long is if the message is long. But in that case we should cut it off anyway at no more than a few hundred characters — the notification UI won't fit more than that anyway.

* The `remove` type has a list of message IDs. If there are 200 of them (the max we send, comfortably above the max 100 or so notifications that might actually be live on the device), and the message IDs are in the billions so 10 digits long, that's $$ 200 \cdot (10 + 1) = 2200 $$ bytes including the commas. (2202 bytes including the brackets.)

  So that still fits easily in a 4kiB limit, but might benefit from compression. If we wanted to compress it, though, I think the way to start would be with delta-compression on the numeric values: send the first ID, but then the *difference* between the first and second IDs, between the second and third IDs, etc., rather than the subsequent IDs themselves. I expect that'd get a lot further than purely throwing a generic compressor at it.

*2025-08-04 to 2025-08-07 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/E2EE.20test.20push.20notification/with/2236009)*

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-08-06 15:29 UTC

I went through the existing implementation & discussion related to it in #**api design>#23997 Endpoint for test notification**

I think it'd make more sense to have a separate endpoint.

Roughly the proposed design is:
* `POST mobile_push/e2ee/test_notification` with `push_account_id` optional parameter.
* If `push_account_id` is provided, send notification to that particular device of the user. Otherwise, send notification to all registered devices for the user.
* Prepare the `payload_data_to_encrypt` (Note: the current implementation prepares the major parts of payload on bouncer, but for E2EE case we need to do it on server itself)
* Then simply use `send_push_notifications` with minor tweaks to let error from bouncer propagate to client.

I think we can avoid a new endpoint on bouncer (parallel to `remotes/push/test_notification`) by using the `send_push_notifications` codepath (the above approach) we already have.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-08-06 17:20 UTC

Sounds reasonable to me. I agree the bouncer shouldn't require any changes.

## unregister push device

*2025-08-28 to 2026-09-11 · 38 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/unregister.20push.20device/with/2250938)*

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-08-28 14:09 UTC

Looking at zulip-flutter code, we use [/api/remove-apns-token](https://zulip.com/api/remove-apns-token) and [/api/remove-fcm-token](https://zulip.com/api/remove-fcm-token) endpoints to unregister token when a user logs out.

So I think we need an API endpoint to unregister for the E2EE case.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-08-28 14:09 UTC

I'll propose an API design if this makes sense.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-08-28 18:06 UTC

Yes, that sounds correct.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-09-01 11:17 UTC

There's two possible design.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-09-01 11:17 UTC

### Approach 1

`DELETE /mobile_push/register`

1. Client makes a request to the endpoint with `push_account_id` in the request body.
2. Server queries `PushDevice` table to fetch the row based on `(user, push_account_id)`
    a. If no such row exists, return 200 response.
    b. If row exists, set `unregistered` field (a new boolean field on PushDevice model) to `true` & return 200.
    c. If the fetched row has `unregistered` field already set to `true`, return 200 - idempotency.
3. We will extend the GC code (planned in #35368) to query rows with `unregistered = true`, ask bouncer to delete corresponding `RemotePushDevice` rows if registered + delete these rows on server --  in short GC will handle the actual deletion from db.

Note: We'll have to make minor changes to our "send push notification" & "register push device" codepath (with tests) to handle rows with `unregistered` flag set correctly.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-09-01 11:18 UTC

### Approach 2

`DELETE /mobile_push/register`

1. Client makes a request to the endpoint with `push_account_id` in the request body.
1.  Server queries `PushDevice` table to fetch the row based on `(user, push_account_id)`
  1. If no such row exists, return 200 response.
  1. if `row.error_code != null` -- delete the row and return 200. Since `error_code != null`, it means there's no corresponding row registered on bouncer.
  1. If `row.error_code == null`
    1. If `row.bouncer_device_id != null` -- Send a DELETE request to bouncer to delete corresponding row on bouncer, on success response from bouncer delete the `row` on server and return 200.
    1. If `row.bouncer_device_id == null`-- This is for the case where server is trying to register a push device to bouncer asynchronously & received a request from the client in parallel to unregister. There's a race b/w "server => bouncer" request to register & "client => server" request to unregister. 
One of the possible solutions is to set an `unregistered` flag instead of deleting the row from the db (when client requests server to unregister) & return 200. Now, when the server receives a response from the bouncer (of request which was running in parallel) it can do one of the following two:
      1. On error response, just delete the `push_device` row on server.
      1. On success response, send a request to bouncer to delete corresponding row + delete the row on server (if deletion request to bouncer succeeds).

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-09-01 11:23 UTC

Approach 2 was the first design I wrote down, revised it to Approach 1 (which I think is a lot simpler and will serve our purpose).

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-09-02 13:51 UTC

We should not use `DELETE` as the HTTP method unless the URL we are using is expected to 404 after the request completes.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-09-02 14:08 UTC

I think option (1) still has the bones of the same race condition still hidden inside of it, unless we're careful.

1. Server starts device registration, has to retry bouncer request
2. Server gets unregistration request, sets row to `unregistered=False`
3. Cron job runs, deletes local row; bouncer knows nothing of the device, does nothing
4. Retry to the bouncer finally happens, registering the device with the bouncer
5. End result is that the "unregistered" device is registered on the bouncer but not locally, and we send a `push_device` event to the user implying that the registration was successful.

We need to be sure to recheck our assumptions in `handle_register_push_device_to_bouncer`, in short -- if we're a retry, things may have changed since before.  And doing that rechecking will require taking a `select_for_update` lock.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-09-02 14:15 UTC

And the cron jobs will also have to `select_for_update` in a transaction to also remove those races.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2025-09-02 14:45 UTC

(replying to Alex Vandiver)
> 3. Cron job runs, deletes local row; bouncer knows nothing of the device, does nothing

Yeah, I missed to think about this case.

I think we can also handle it in this way:
Cron job checks if registration is in progress (`push_deivice.bouncer_device_id == null` and `push_device.error_code == null`), then skip the GC for the `push_device` row for now.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-09-02 14:53 UTC

Unless you've got row locking in both places, you still have a race -- albeit a smaller one.  If the cron job runs *after* the request to the bouncer has completed, but *before* we're updated the local row, we still end up in inconsistent state.

You need row locking here, believe me. :)

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-09-02 14:54 UTC

Anytime you have concurrency and some sort of "check and change" pattern, you need some way to enforce that the state doesn't change between those two steps.

**Greg Price** · 2025-09-03 19:41 UTC

I think it's not actually necessary to add these.

When the user tells the app to log out of an account, the app will delete its private key for notifications from that account, along with the rest of that account record in the app's local database. So it becomes cryptographically impossible to read any notifications the server subsequently sends to that client, which means sending them is harmless apart from the waste of a few kilobytes.

Then as far as those wasted kilobytes are concerned, I think the solution is to garbage-collect push devices that we haven't heard from in a while. That's what we need in any case for handling the case where the user uninstalled the Zulip app, or wiped/discarded the device, and I expect both of those are much more common than using the "log out" feature on an individual account anyway.

**Greg Price** · 2025-09-03 19:50 UTC

In the existing/legacy notifications design, we've needed those endpoints because otherwise the server keeps sending notifications and they *keep appearing* in the notifications UI, which is a disturbing symptom; see #F1264 and previously #M5763 and #M3469.

(On Android, we can prevent that at the time we get the notification, which we did to fix #F1264; on iOS, that hasn't been possible pending having our own client-side code control showing notifications there too, #F1265.)

But it's fundamentally not a reliable solution anyway: we might not be able to reach the server at the time the user is trying to log out. That's why #F1264 happened in the first place — we were already using these endpoints when we got that report.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-09-04 19:47 UTC

I think it'd be better to have the endpoints, even if we cannot guarantee that they will always be called. The user expectation is that when you log out on a device, one doesn't have any data related to your account continuing to be delivered to that device, even if it's encrypted. After all, there's information in the pattern of when messages arrive. Also, we waste resources having the server deliver mobile notifications that the client will ignore for weeks.

Issues with the server being offline seem solvable. For example, when on your mobile device you tap to remove an account, we can attempt to delete fully on the server (potentially including in the future asking it to shred the client's unique API key), and if that fails, present the user a modal saying we couldn't reach the server, with "retry", "delete anyway", "Cancel".

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> For example, when on your mobile device you tap to remove an account, we can attempt to delete fully on the server (potentially including in the future asking it to shred the client's unique API key), and if that fails, present the user a modal saying we couldn't reach the server, with "retry", "del …

I don't think I've ever seen an app present a modal like that. I expect a user who sees it would find it puzzling and frustrating.

Again, most users who want to log out of Zulip probably won't ever use this "log out" feature in the first place — they'll just uninstall the app. That's the normal thing to do for most mobile apps. (Really the only reason to do anything different is if you have multiple accounts, and want to remain logged into some of them.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-09-08 23:55 UTC

It's not super common to have accounts with multiple servers involved. But I expect if a Discord organization is down when you try to remove it from your account in their mobile app, you do get an error trying to remove it. (Discord sometimes has this sort of partial outage of only some servers). Our context is different because self-hosted servers may stop existing permanently independently of each other.

If we don't like the idea of having visible error handling, we can decide that the removal is best-effort, with or without retries for some period. But it seems wrong from a defense-in-depth security standpoint to me to not attempt to unsubscribe from notifications when removing the account from the device.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-09-08 23:58 UTC

Regarding Uninstalling the app: I imagine that will result in there being fairly immediate feedback the next time APNs or FCM tries to send something to that user, so the push notifications will stop coming.

Removing one account of several on the device will not have that effect; if the user has other active Zulip accounts, I'm not sure what mechanism would prevent that device would not continue receiving and ignoring encrypted mobile notifications for that user for months afterwards, if the user hasn't deactivated their Zulip account.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-09-09 00:00 UTC

The only factor limiting that being forever would be a "last re-registered" check, which we need to be careful about making too short, since a user who only reads Zulip notifications on their lock screen but never actually opens the Zulip app is, I think, not possible for the bouncer component to distinguish from a user who removed that organization from their Zulip client entirely?

**Chris Bobbe** · 2026-06-16 08:20 UTC

*2025-08-29 to 2025-08-29 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/adding.20expires_timestamp.20to.20temporary.20file.20URL.20response/with/2251856)*

**Lauryn Menard** · 2025-08-29 15:13 UTC

In #**api documentation>get-file-temporary-url in left sidebar**, as we're looking at adding the endpoint for getting a public temporary URL for an uploaded file to the API documentation, the question came up as to whether it makes sense to add an `expires_timestamp` to the response.

@Alex Vandiver [ha dicho](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/412-api-documentation/topic/get-file-temporary-url.20in.20left.20sidebar/near/2250771):
> We should possibly mention somewhere in there that "temporary" means 60 seconds, though it can be overridden in `SIGNED_ACCESS_TOKEN_VALIDITY_IN_SECONDS` in server settings (and I don't think the server tells the client the value currently, which might be considered a bug).

**Lauryn Menard** · 2025-08-29 15:15 UTC

Currently, the response only returns the temporary URL:

```yaml
      responses:
        "200":
          description: Success.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                allOf:
                  - $ref: "#/components/schemas/JsonSuccessBase"
                  - additionalProperties: false
                    properties:
                      result: {}
                      msg: {}
                      ignored_parameters_unsupported: {}
                      url:

                          without Zulip's normal API authentication.
                    example:

                        "result": "success",
                        "url": "/user_uploads/temporary/322F32632F39765378464E4C...",
                      }
```

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-08-29 15:27 UTC

I do think this is one of the "settings" that there is ~no reason for anyone to adjust.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-08-29 15:28 UTC

In that it should be viewed more as a constant, than a setting.  Which doesn't mean we shouldn't include it in the response, just that we should think about it as providing additional helpful information, not providing information about server configuration

**Lauryn Menard** · 2025-08-29 15:30 UTC

I'm guessing what we might want to send in the response is a timestamp of when that specific temporary URL would expire vs sending value of the server setting?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-08-29 15:38 UTC

Yup, I agree that it's more useful to put it in the tempoary-file-url response than in `/server-settings`.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-08-29 15:39 UTC

There's the very slight complication that the URL encodes the time it was created, and the expiration (and thus setting) is checked at access time.  So if the setting changed after the URL was generated, it could be valid for longer/shorter than the original response claimed.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-08-29 15:40 UTC

But there's no reaason to change the setting, so I don't think we need to worry about that potential complication.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-08-29 16:55 UTC

Yeah, I think that complication is Fine. Will be a transient error that can be recovered from easily, for a change that probably only happens during server setup. (Like, maybe if your server is on Mars you make it 10 minutes... but also where's your S3 backend hosted anyway?).

The reason I was thinking of putting the actual expiration time in the response, rather than say the 60s, is that will naturally manage any network latencies or the like for you.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-08-29 16:55 UTC

Thoughts on `expires_timestamp` as the variable name?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-08-29 17:07 UTC

`expires_timestamp` seems fine.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-08-29 17:09 UTC

OK. I think we should just make the change and move on; it's not likely to be a very important detail, so doesn't deserve undue attention.


## Old API feature levels

*2025-08-29 to 2025-09-17 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/Old.20API.20feature.20levels/with/2252021)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-08-29 17:02 UTC

I wonder if we should have a policy on garbage-collecting inline documentation on old API feature levels that no clients currently target. (E.g., deleting the **Changes** entries in `zulip.yaml` for feature levels prior to Zulip 7.0 at this point).

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-08-29 17:03 UTC

There's an argument that they're potentially still useful for understanding the history of the API. For example, when working on a client, one might be reading code that handles the format used by 5.0, even if the client no longer targets versions older than 7.0.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-08-29 17:03 UTC

But they will eventually be a significant source of clutter in the API documentation if we literally never delete them.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-08-29 17:07 UTC

I guess my current thinking is that we can leave them as-is until we start to feel the clutter is actually annoying, since it may be nontrivial to do a systematic sweep... but if at some point we've done a sweep of the 3 main client codebases for legacy code dealing with such old feature levels, it'd be reasonable to do a bulk deletion pass.

**Greg Price** · 2025-09-10 03:17 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> The answer is “whatever [`nacl.public.SealedBox`](https://pynacl.readthedocs.io/en/latest/public/#nacl-public-sealedbox) does”. https://libsodium.gitbook.io/doc/public-key_cryptography/sealed_boxes#algorithm-details

This is helpful because it's different from what I'd guessed above! (#**api design>E2EE - cryptography@2256964**)

**Greg Price** · 2025-09-10 03:17 UTC

In particular, libsodium's `crypto_box_seal` uses NaCl's `crypto_box`, but it answers a question which the latter leaves open about how to use it — the question of how to pick the nonce.

Which is something that can have many right answers, but also many wrong answers, and I believe a wrong answer can be fatal to security.

The libsodium "sealed box" answer is that the sender generates an ephemeral keypair, and doesn't use any long-term secret key. Because the sender's key is different each time, it doesn't matter that a nonce might get re-used. (Then it also picks the nonce effectively at random too, which I believe is just for good measure.)

**Greg Price** · 2025-09-10 03:20 UTC

So this choice of cryptographic construction LGTM so far — next step is to actually implement the client side.

Should definitely get documented, though. The key is that to encrypt a message to a recipient, we use a libsodium sealed box. (Which happens to be something built atop NaCl — but is not at all specified by NaCl itself.)

**Greg Price** · 2025-09-10 03:25 UTC

I'd also feel a bit better if there were some evidence of actual cryptographers looking at the construction that libsodium defines as a "sealed box", and validating that it seems secure.

The NaCl docs are full of references to the literature, because the author is a cryptographer. The libsodium docs don't have even a single link, AFAICT, to any analysis of their own innovations. The "sealed box" isn't doing *much* beyond what NaCl itself provides, which is why the fact they don't justify it is only a small worry… but it's also not entirely confidence-inspiring that they don't appear to feel the need to try.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2025-09-10 05:07 UTC

Agreed with all of that. The modern standard that I’m starting to see get recommended for this use case is [HPKE](https://blog.cloudflare.com/hybrid-public-key-encryption/) ([RFC 9180](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9180.html)); maybe we should consider that if we find credible libraries?

- Python: [PyHPKE](https://pyhpke.readthedocs.io/), [PyCryptodome](https://www.pycryptodome.org/src/protocol/hpke), [hpke.py](https://pypi.org/project/hpke/), [Tink](https://developers.google.com/tink/exchange-data#python)
- Rust: [orion](https://docs.rs/orion/0.17.11/orion/hazardous/hpke/), [rust-hpke](https://crates.io/crates/hpke), [hpke-rs](https://crates.io/crates/hpke-rs)
- JavaScript: [@hpke/core](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@hpke/core), [@turnkey/crypto](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@turnkey/crypto), [hpke-js](https://www.npmjs.com/package/hpke-js)

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-09-10 17:19 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2025-09-10 19:59 UTC

Hmm, interesting idea, thanks.

It looks like that Dart implementation only supports the NIST P-256 curve. I don't love that choice, for the reasons DJB was pointing out in the '00s and '10s:
https://safecurves.cr.yp.to/

**Greg Price** · 2025-09-10 20:05 UTC

Here's a more radical thought I had this morning: are we benefiting from using asymmetric crypto at all for the notifications? I think we're not.

In particular, the libsodium "sealed box" is *unauthenticated* by design. The sender doesn't use any secret of its own, after all (except an ephemeral one it just made up for the one message). The sender could have been anyone, as long as they had the receiver's public key.

In the context of the full design, I think we still have authenticity… but only because the device's public key is effectively kept secret.

**Greg Price** · 2025-09-10 20:07 UTC

If we're relying on the public key being kept secret, though, then that's a security risk — it'd be easy to end up with code somewhere that treats the public key as *public*, and can leak it.

That conceptual mismatch also seems like a hint that there might be a cleaner design.

**Greg Price** · 2025-09-10 20:09 UTC

What if we instead used symmetric crypto? The client still generates a secret key; but now it sends that same key to the server. We rely on TLS as usual to keep it confidential on its way there. Then when sending a notification, the server uses that secret key to encrypt (with authenticated encryption).

**Greg Price** · 2025-09-10 20:11 UTC

Alternatively if we used HPKE, its Base mode looks to have similar properties to libsodium "sealed box", so the same reasoning applies.

HPKE also has an Auth mode, which uses a sender secret key to get authentication. But to make use of that, we'd need the client (the recipient) to know a public key for the server (the sender). That's not something that's in the current design.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2025-09-10 20:16 UTC

The current design also has the client asymmetrically encrypt the `PushRegistration` to the bouncer, which I think was to avoid revealing the APNs/FCM token to the server so a malicious server doesn’t eat up our rate limits.

**Greg Price** · 2025-09-10 20:16 UTC

Yeah. That part definitely wants asymmetric crypto (unless we were to decide to not encrypt it at all).

**Greg Price** · 2025-09-10 21:37 UTC

Concretely, I think using symmetric crypto here would look like:
* Editing the details already in [ZAP 2](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-architecture/blob/main/zaps/0002-encrypt-push-notifications.md):
  * Rename `push_public_key` everywhere to `push_key`.
  * Remove `push_private_key`. Where it's used to decrypt, use `push_key` instead.
  * Where the term "asymmetric key pair" appears in reference to those keys, document `push_key` as a symmetric key instead.
* For the specific cryptosystem:
  * Use libsodium's `crypto_secretbox_easy` ([doc](https://libsodium.gitbook.io/doc/secret-key_cryptography/secretbox), [NaCl doc](https://nacl.cr.yp.to/secretbox.html)), which provides authenticated encryption using XSalsa20 and Poly1305.
  * Use random nonces. The nonces are 24 bytes = 192 bits, so the chance of collision is negligible.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-09-11 00:36 UTC

Seems like a good idea to me. It have other benefits (speed, payload sizes) too.

**Greg Price** · 2025-09-20 01:15 UTC

Sent https://github.com/zulip/zulip-architecture/pull/4 to make those changes.

## gravatar sha256 migration

*2025-10-13 to 2025-10-13 · 1 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/gravatar.20sha256.20migration/with/2276747)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-10-13 17:20 UTC

It looks like https://docs.gravatar.com/rest/hash/ now supports sha256. I don't know when it changed, but looks like sometime last year, in that Wordpress, the main Gravatar customer, switched to using it in the last year: https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/60638.

So I think we should be able to update the following things:
- The API's `client_gravatar` specification should specify clients should use `sha256` to generate the URL.
- The Zulip server, when generating gravatar URLs, can use the new algorithm.
- Our clients can switch to using the new URL structure after verifying it works.

It is unclear to me how much this improves actual security; hashing email addresses will always be vulnerable to enumeration attacks. But at the very least it'll let us remove this last dependency on `md5`.

## order of reactions

*2025-10-28 to 2026-03-04 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/order.20of.20reactions/with/2286686)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-10-28 18:14 UTC

Does the reactions API allow clients to know, for a message where multiple users reacted with the same emoji reaction, which user was the first to add that reaction?

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-10-28 18:14 UTC

It came up in discussing the algorithms in #**feedback>favourite emoji list**.

I don't think we have an `order by` that would guarantee that?  PostgreSQL may happen to provide that currently.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-10-28 18:35 UTC

Looks like we actually do:
```python3
class Reaction(AbstractReaction):
    message = models.ForeignKey(Message, on_delete=CASCADE)

    @override
    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.user_profile.email} / {self.message.id} / {self.emoji_name}"

    @staticmethod
    def get_raw_db_rows(needed_ids: list[int]) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
        fields = [
            "message_id",
            "emoji_name",
            "emoji_code",
            "reaction_type",
            "user_profile_id",
        ]
        # The ordering is important here, as it makes it convenient
        # for clients to display reactions in order without
        # client-side sorting code.
        return Reaction.objects.filter(message_id__in=needed_ids).values(*fields).order_by("id")

I don't see any current promise in the OpenAPI spec of that.  But seems like could add one.

The order given by the server is the order the mobile app already shows the "who reacted" list in, except for moving the self-user to the front of the list. So while there's nothing wider that goes wrong if it's out of order… the order is shown to the user, who might naturally notice a pattern that it's in the order that people added the reactions.

## mobile re-registration after server version update

*2025-11-04 to 2025-11-12 · 19 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/mobile.20re-registration.20after.20server.20version.20update/with/2291909)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-04 19:33 UTC

What is the current protocol regarding when the mobile clients will re-do `POST /register` after a server version update?

I think this may be important once we start doing longer event queues. We occasionally do database migrations to, say, fix database corruption, which do not do `send_event` calls for the state changes that they make to correct the database. Currently, the web app is protected against stale corrupted state because it will reload within 30m after a server update. 

And the mobile apps are protected because the 10 minute idle expiration time on event queues, in practice, will never last long enough to make it 24 hours. Since we're planning on changing that, I'd like to check that we have a good protocol here.

**Chris Bobbe** · 2025-11-04 20:57 UTC

Our plan for #F477 ("Have data ready on app startup") and longer-lived event queues is to make a fresh event queue after a random delay spread over a long period, like 1 hour.

**Chris Bobbe** · 2025-11-04 20:58 UTC

This is discussed at the end of the issue description for #F1271 "Handle restart events".

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-04 21:01 UTC

That plan sounds good to me. Some care should be taken to handle the case that multiple `restart` events arrive before an actual reload occurs. I guess preventing the later ones from resetting the time should work fine.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-04 21:02 UTC

I think though, for mobile, there isn't the same thundering herd issue we on web, since the clients are not always-active in the same way.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-04 21:03 UTC

I guess I'm not sure how those semantics would interact in practice with "The phone is probably going to be in someone's pocket with the screen off in an hour."

**Chris Bobbe** · 2025-11-04 21:08 UTC

We could maybe not make it time-based at all, and instead just write in the client-side db a flag that says "re-register next time the app goes from closed/backgrounded to open/foregrounded"?

**Chris Bobbe** · 2025-11-04 21:09 UTC

(Or that plus add "if X time has passed".)

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-04 23:14 UTC

Yeah.

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-08 06:06 UTC

Yeah, I think we'll still want the random time-delay — it'll just mean that we re-register at the next opportunity after that time.

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-08 06:13 UTC

If we implement #F1271 before #F477 (which I think is likely, because #F1271 is fundamentally easy and #F477 is much more complex), that will just look like setting a timer, same as any other backoff. The event queue ID itself isn't in the database and doesn't outlive the app's running process; so the timer doesn't need to either.

After #F477, we'll be saving the event queue ID in the database (along with all the numerous kinds of data that the event queue gives us — that part is why #F477 is a substantial project). So the random timer for when to replace the event queue should be written to the database alongside it, as mentioned above. (As well as setting an actual in-process timer.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-10 05:32 UTC

OK that seems reasonable. I remain uncertain what scale of timer would make sense; I think it's very possible that the on-server-update mobile load will be 1% of what we get for desktop even if we do a very short timer. I would be comfortable with mobile following the `basic_idle_timeout` algorithm here.

``` js
             // We're now planning to execute a reload of the browser, usually                           
            // to get an updated version of the Zulip web app code.  Because in                         
            // most cases all browsers will be receiving this notice at the                             
            // same or similar times, we need to randomize the time that we do                          
            // this in order to avoid a thundering herd overloading the server.                         
            //                                                                                          
            // Additionally, we try to do this reload at a time the user will                           
            // not notice.  So completely idle clients will reload first;                               
            // those will an open compose box will wait until the message has                           
            // been sent (or until it's clear the user isn't likely to send it).                        
            //                                                                                          
            // And then we unconditionally reload sometime after 30 minutes                             
            // even if there is continued activity, because we don't support                            
            // old JavaScript versions against newer servers and eventually                             
            // letting that situation continue will lead to users seeing bugs.                          
            //                                                                                          
            // It's a little odd that how this timeout logic works with                                 
            // compose box resets including the random variance, but that                               
            // makes it simple to reason about: We know that reloads will be                            
            // spread over at least 5 minutes in all cases.                                             
                                                                                                        
            let idle_control: ReturnType<JQuery["idle"]>;                                               
            const random_variance = util.random_int(0, 1000 * 60 * 5);                                  
            const unconditional_timeout = 1000 * 60 * 30 + random_variance;                             
            const composing_idle_timeout = 1000 * 60 * 7 + random_variance;                             
            const basic_idle_timeout = 1000 * 60 * 1 + random_variance;                                 
```

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-12 01:09 UTC

Cool, thanks — so that's a 5-minute random spread, plus one of three different constant delays depending on some conditions of how the user is using the app.

That means the resulting peak traffic is at least what it would be with a 15-minute spread — that's the result if all three conditions are equally common. More likely, one of them dominates, and the peak traffic is close to what it would be with a simple 5-minute spread.

I'll add a note in #F1271. Once we have it implemented, we can always experiment and pick the value.

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-12 01:13 UTC

The mobile app does have somewhat different needs here than web, because only the data is getting reloaded and not the client-side code.
* On the one hand, that means less pressure to reload quickly: there's a smaller surface area for possible incompatibilities. In fact with rare exceptions I think we've managed the API such that there's no incorrect behavior that results from carrying on with the old data, only missing features. (The most recent such exception is described in #F1271 and was a couple of years ago.)
* On the other hand, that means there's less cost to reloading right in front of the user's eyes, so less need to try to find an idle moment. I think the main potentially-annoying effect is that if you've scrolled a ways through a message feed, you'll get reset to the position you started at.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-12 01:35 UTC

The things we save in the web app on one of these reloads are:
- The current view's identity.
- Scroll position in the current view.
- Left sidebar scroll position.
- Compose box state (current draft text).

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-12 01:36 UTC

I think if mobile avoided losing drafts and preserved the scroll position (basically a pair of the `message_id` and the scroll offset from the top of the screen of the top of that message), it'd be pretty much transparent unless you're in the process of long-pressing a menu or something.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-12 01:37 UTC

But at the same time, I feel like mobile workflows tend to be shorter, and you're much more likely to be able to just wait until the user isn't in the middle of something.

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-12 01:47 UTC

We already avoid losing drafts when reloading state, so it's pretty much down to the scroll position in the message feed.

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-12 01:47 UTC

(And only the message feed, not other views like the inbox — the reason the message feed is affected is that we reload its messages from scratch.)
