**Greg Price** · 2026-01-14 21:39 UTC

Thinking about this some more, I think the design we want looks like:
* Each client device for a given user/account has a record on the server, which may get updated over time but not replaced with a new one.

  Tying things to a single record that gets updated over time, rather than creating fresh records, is important to avoid the problem @Prakhar Pratyush pointed out at #**api design>E2EE - key rotation@2296330**  above: when making a change, we don't want an intermediate state where the server sends double notifications (or no notifications).

  * We've long wanted something exactly like this data structure for reasons unrelated to push notifications — in particular it's a prerequisite for 2FA #9521, as explained at #17939.

    In order to make it smooth to use these later for a general list of the user's logged-in devices, as at #17939, I think a good name would be just "devices" without "push".

    These can appear in the API as a field on /api/register-queue and with events to update them. At present these "device" objects will have only the fields relevant to push notifications. In the future they'll gain other fields for #17939.

    These records will have their own IDs (`device_id`), generated on the server like we do for most of our database tables.

  * In the future for #17939 these records will need to be able to exist in a state where no push notifications are set up: we'll need to create them as part of login, and we'll also want to have them for e.g. desktop clients. So we might as well set them up that way from the beginning, which doesn't really add any work whereas changing that later would take some work.

    And then it's probably cleanest if these records are created through their own endpoint, rather than as a side effect of a notifications-specific endpoint. That does mean an extra round trip before push notifications get set up; but it only happens once after logging in, so it's not a significant cost.

**Greg Price** · 2026-01-14 21:39 UTC

* On the server, the device record may have a `push_key` field… and a `push_key_id`. There is no longer a `push_account_id`.

  The `push_key_id` replaces some of the uses of `push_account_id`: in particular, it gets included in the notification payloads. But it's no longer an ID for the account itself in any sense, because it will change over time: every time the client makes up a new `push_key` in order to rotate the key, it will make up a corresponding new `push_key_id`.

  The `push_key_id` appears on the device objects in the API, but naturally the `push_key` itself does not.

  This solves the problem described at #**api design>E2EE - key rotation@2351299** about the client tracking the state of trying to rotate the key: the device object in `devices` will have either the old `push_key_id` or the new one.

* When sending a notification, the server will include `push_key_id` as well as `device_id` and `encrypted_content`. That way the bouncer doesn't need to know `push_key_id` (or `push_account_id`) in its table, so that when the client rotates the key the server can make that update locally without talking to the bouncer.

* On the bouncer, instead of deduplicating a record by its token and `push_account_id`, the record can be deduplicated by its (remote) realm and token.

  This means that a record may be used for several accounts in the same realm, if they use the same token (which means they're on a single actual device, so belong to a single human user). Ideally it'd be conceptually cleanest to avoid that, but I think it's fine in practice, and don't see a way to avoid it without more complexity. OTOH I'd be more wary of sharing a record across different realms and different servers, in order to be careful about potentially leaking information from one server a person uses to a different server.

  Effectively the record on the bouncer is about the push token, just duplicated for different realms for isolation. It's fine that this means we'll create a new record when the token changes; the server is the party responsible for picking a single token per device to send a given notification to.

I believe this covers all the ways `push_account_id` is used in [ZAP 2](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-architecture/blob/main/zaps/0002-encrypt-push-notifications.md).

**Greg Price** · 2026-01-14 21:40 UTC

Then there's tokens, and updating tokens. These updates have the same concern mentioned above at #**api design>E2EE - key rotation@2351299** about how the client tracks the state.

I think a clean way to accomplish the job of a "request ID" parameter here is to use a token ID: a short hash, say 32 bits long, of the token. (We could use the token itself, except that our current design avoids leaking that to the server.)

And then to solve the problem of tracking the state of an update, the server basically needs to make a distinction between the last value it's confirmed with the bouncer, and the value it's currently trying to set on the bouncer. So:

* On the server, the device record may have fields `push_token_id`, `pending_push_token_id`, `pending_encrypted_push_registration`, `pending_bouncer_public_key`, `push_registration_error_code`.

  On the device objects in the API, it includes `push_token_id`, `pending_push_token_id`, `push_registration_error_code`.

* The client checks if the device object's `pending_push_token_id ?? push_token_id` matches the current token it's given by the device platform; if they don't match, then it makes a request to tell the server the new token.

* The client also checks if the device object's `push_token_id` matches the current token. If they don't match, it may warn the user that notifications are not set up. (The loudness of the warning may depend on how recently its own database shows it started telling the server the current token; if it was just a minute ago, the warning might appear only within a settings or troubleshooting screen.) The warning might consult `push_registration_error_code` for details.

* At registration time, the client computes `push_token_id` and sends it to the server in the clear alongside the other parameters. The server passes it on to the bouncer. The bouncer verifies that it matches the hash of the actual `token_id`, after decrypting the latter.

**Greg Price** · 2026-01-14 21:40 UTC

We could go a bit further, eliminating `bouncer_device_id`:

* At notification time, the server includes `push_token_id` rather than a `device_id`.

* Now there's no need for a `bouncer_device_id` on the server's record, and so no need for a `device_id` on the bouncer's record.

Example:
* A push registration was successful (on server + bouncer)
* A request to rotate token
* Another request to rotate token (new token value, for some reason) , while the previous rotate request is in progress.

There's a race between the two requests to bouncer to update token_id. The first request failed due to network error and server retries, the second request succeeds in the meantime, the first request succeeds later; this results in setting the `token_id` of first request to `device.push_token_id` instead of the `token_id` of the second request.

**Pieter K** · 2025-11-14 11:37 UTC

#36489 wants to add supported moderation categories to the API.

In #36489 @Tim Abbott proposed `server_moderation_request_types`for its name, and it'll be a sorted list of objects. In the server, the reason types are declared as follows:
```python
   REPORT_MESSAGE_REASONS = {
        "spam": gettext_lazy("Spam"),
        "harassment": gettext_lazy("Harassment"),
        "inappropriate": gettext_lazy("Inappropriate content"),
        "norms": gettext_lazy("Violates community norms"),
        "other": gettext_lazy("Other reason"),
    }
``` 

Just a thought, but If we have plans to include other form of moderation requests (like "report a user"), perhaps it'd be better if we narrow the name down to something related to message report (e.g., `server_message_report_types`)? server_moderation_request_types : [

            "name": "Other reason"

    ]

And for the order of the reason types, is there a specific way we want to sort them? I think alphabetical but have the "other" option at the bottom is probably common for this kind of UI?
```python   
   REPORT_MESSAGE_REASONS = {
        "harassment": gettext_lazy("Harassment"),
        "inappropriate": gettext_lazy("Inappropriate content"),
        "spam": gettext_lazy("Spam"),

**Chris Bobbe** · 2026-02-19 01:52 UTC

> We should update the docs for `report_type` to say instead it must be one of the supported types from `server_report_message_types`.

(replying to Tim Abbott)

but I think this is fairly called a change in the protocol (at Zulip 12.0, FL 435) :slight_smile:. The change is:

- For old servers, clients should consider `report_type` to have these allowed values: "spam", "harassment", "inappropriate", "norms", "other".
- For new servers, clients should consider the allowed values to be the `key`s in `server_report_message_types`.

If current servers want to guarantee support for the old protocol, that's fine. ## owner_full_content_access

*2025-11-25 to 2025-12-01 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/owner_full_content_access/with/2310829)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-25 00:05 UTC

A complaint about Zulip's models is that there's no easy way to have Zulip as a product offer access that matches the security model that many corporate users do, i.e., the IT organization can access everyone's accounts. This isn't a blocker for their work, since they can just use SSO to access the account and do things as the user. But we'd like to add a way that an organization can be hand-tagged as having that sort of corporate access security model. Here's a proposal for how that would work:

- We add a new `realm` property, say `owner_full_content_access`, which defines whether the organization's owner will have the ability to access private content in the organization in the Zulip UI. (Not editable in the UI). The intended use case is corporate organizations where users have no expectation of privacy from the organization itself. (Say, your login is controlled by the company).
- At first, it'll only be possible to enable via manual management command, so we can build the experience without having to think much about inconsistency for organizations with this enabled.
- In organizations with `owner_full_content_access`, "Standard" data exports you can do via the UI are effectively "full without consent".
- In organizations with `owner_full_content_access`, "Privacy settings" shows the export consent as disabled and checked always, with a tooltip or something explaining the story.
- We plan to adjust onboarding for `owner_full_content_access` organizations to include some disclosure about how private your messages are. (Not a blocker for manual use of the feature, because export-without-consent is already the status quo, documented in /help/, for organizations we'd add this flag to).
- We plan to later add a `realm` setting, say `can_access_all_content_group`, which allows users with the permission to join any channel. If `owner_fill_content_access`, it can be the OWNERS, ADMINS, or NOBODY system group. Otherwise, its only permitted value is NOBODY (aka the status quo). 
- We plan to later allow organizations to select this mode during realm creation, once we've done the above.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-25 00:05 UTC

Thoughts on that overall plan and in particular the field names?

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-25 00:33 UTC

Sounds reasonable.

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-25 00:34 UTC

What should the transition look like for Zulip servers in general? For Zulip Cloud, we'll need to go through and set this flag to true or false appropriately for different realms to reflect Zulip Cloud's policies as applied to those realms.

For other servers… probably "true" will normally be the right answer. I guess we could have a migration set it to true by default, and put something in the upgrade notes to tell server admins to set it to false if they want to promise that realm owners won't have such access.

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-25 00:35 UTC

> - At first, it'll only be possible to enable via manual management command, so we can build the experience without having to think much about inconsistency for organizations with this enabled.

It sounds like there'll be a transition period during which
* this property exists and is being sent to clients,
* but a false value doesn't mean anything, because (at least on Zulip Cloud) the property has only been set for a few realms by hand, not for all the realms where the site's policies mean the effective value should be true.

So during that transition period, the web app should avoid making any UI changes that highlight when the value is false, or draw any inferences from that to tell the user that realm owners don't have this access.

Maybe that's all we need for handling that aspect of a transition. There isn't any surface in the mobile app where I'd expect we would naturally surface that information anyway anytime soon.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-25 00:36 UTC

I was expecting that mostly existing installations will have `owner_full_content_access` stay `False`, and have an upgrade note letting folks know how to change it via management command.

For Cloud, we'd use the same on-request process that we use for without-consent exports by corporations to validate requests to change it to True today.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-25 00:39 UTC

In other words, the scope of the current effort is allowing new organizations to opt into the `owner_full_content_access` behavior. I expect we'll be careful in the documentation to just frame things accurately as statements to the effect of "If `owner_full_content_access` is true, than owners can do XYZ via the Zulip settings panel as follows ...". And the existing documentation, which details how `!owner_full_content_access` works, will have "unless `owner_full_content_access`..." added in a few places.

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-25 00:42 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> I was expecting that mostly existing installations will have `owner_full_content_access` stay `False`, and have an upgrade note letting folks know how to change it via management command.

Hmm, OK.

The risk there is that to the extent we add anything saying that owners *can't* read your messages, that won't necessarily be true. So we'll need to be careful with wording.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-25 00:47 UTC

We already have language on that front, and it is already the case that we document compliance exports etc., as mechanisms that can override that. We can do an audit on that text, but there is no change from status quo in the `False` state anticipated here. https://zulip.com/help/export-your-organization#full-export-without-member-consent

I think if in the future we add a feature that lets you switch your organization outside the rules defined there, it'll probably look like "First delete material for which administrators don't have data-export consent", i.e., matching what they'd end up with if they did an export-with-consent and the re-imported that. But the goals for the moment are to procrastinate defining such a process and just let new organizations, and self-hosted systems where there is no expectation of privacy from IT, into the treatment they want.

**Shubham Padia** · 2025-11-26 08:27 UTC

> For Zulip Cloud, we'll need to go through and set this flag to true or false appropriately for different realms to reflect Zulip Cloud's policies as applied to those realms.

The default will be set to false, but do we have a way to tell for which orgs the backfill should be true? Or we start with false and then notify the admins on ways to change this?

**Shubham Padia** · 2025-11-26 08:37 UTC

#**backend>owner_full_content_access** , #**design>owner_full_content_access**

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-26 17:45 UTC

I expect it will only every be changed from False to True in Zulip Cloud as a result of a support conversation where they present evidence that they can already control the accounts. Typically this is very straightforward, e.g., everyone has a `@example.com` email address. There's no issue to manage here, especially for the API design.

**Shubham Padia** · 2025-11-28 06:32 UTC

> * In organizations with `owner_full_content_access`, "Standard" data exports you can do via the UI are effectively "full without consent".

I looked into this, RealmExport has following 3 types:

```
    EXPORT_PUBLIC = 1
    EXPORT_FULL_WITH_CONSENT = 2
    EXPORT_FULL_WITHOUT_CONSENT = 3
```

Currently, the export endpoint accepts `export_type`, an int which can either be 1 or 2. 

To accomodate the requirement above, we have 3 options.

1. We keep the API unchanged, but on getting EXPORT_FULL_WITH_CONSENT, we do EXPORT_FULL_WITHOUT_CONSENT is owner_full_content_access. Not my choice, the client is saying something else but the backend is doing something else.
2. We change the frontend code to chose between 2 and 3, based on whether owner_full_content_access is true or not. We still have to revalidate it on backend.
3. We accept two strings `PUBLIC` and `STANDARD` as the export type. For public we always map it to EXPORT_PUBLIC and for STANDARD, we map it to 2 or 3 based on the value of EXPORT_FULL_WITHOUT_CONSENT.

I like option 3 the best, since we don't have to check for owner_full_content_access on the frontend in that case and produce an error if the client is passing an option which they don't have the permission for.

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-29 16:56 UTC

If the user wants an export of all the data, I think they'll want to know if they lack permission for that, and get an error rather than a silently incomplete export.

So that would point to option 2. (Or to a variation where the client can use names like "public", "full_with_consent", "full_without_consent" rather than opaque numbers 1, 2, 3.)

**Shubham Padia** · 2025-12-01 03:37 UTC

Yeah, if we're changing the API contract, might as well use verbose names that map back to the values in the backend. I'm thinking we won't need to keep backwards compatibility for this API since only web app might be invoking this for now?

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-12-01 04:48 UTC

Option 2 seems fine. We can certainly change the API to use our modern enum string pattern while we're touching it if you like. 

I do expect there is likely someone using the API directly from a cron job, but probably it's very few people and we can notify them when deploying if that feels useful.

> When pasting URLs into Zulip from services like GitHub where the Zulip installation has a Linkifier configured, it'd be great if we could convert those URLs into the linkifier format so that they look nicer. **Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-26 00:24 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-26 00:25 UTC

Feedback appreciated! I think the feature doesn't look very hard now that we've discovered there exist JS URL template libraries that can do the otherwise complex-seeming actual reversal part for us.

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-26 01:01 UTC

Sounds reasonable to me.

> (Note that we will need to do both Python and JS implementations of this format).

And Dart, right? For pasting into the mobile compose box.

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-26 01:03 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> I think the only piece of this picture that doesn't feel clean to me is the `reverse_template` specification; if there's a better definition than "regex substitutions with escaping" for how those are supposed to work.

Hmm, so the `{…}` format looks aimed at being parallel to the RFC 6570 URL template format. How does one escape a literal `{` there?

… I guess the answer might be that you percent-encode it, i.e. write `%7b`. I don't see any mention in [RFC 6570](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6570.html) of an escaping mechanism. That doesn't seem like something to copy here, then, since these templates aren't producing URLs.

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-26 01:09 UTC

That semantics for `reverse_template` doesn't actually feel particularly unclean to me. It's very crisp to specify, and as long as there's a way to express a literal `{` it doesn't have any odd corners where things can't be expressed.

We should be sure to validate that `reverse_template` values are well-formed:
* Any `{` is followed either by `{`, or by a syntactically valid variable name (per [the RFC's definition](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6570.html#section-2.3)) and then `}`.
* The variable names correspond to variables actually found in the forward template.

That also means that if we ever want to extend the syntax for some reason, we have syntactic space to do so with forms that the initial version rejects as invalid.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-26 05:13 UTC

The theory is the round-tripping test might end up enforcing those variable name checks implicitly. But if it somehow doesn't entail that, yes we would want an explicit check.

And yes, we'd want a Dart implementation for mobile; https://github.com/google/uri.dart seems to have the `match` function one would want.

**Greg Price** · 2025-11-26 06:23 UTC

In #36832, we're adding support for a new search operator, `mentions`, which accepts a user and filters for messages that (directly) mention that user ID. Some notes:
- I'm currently thinking this should diverge from historical narrow operators that take a user and just accept user IDs, and not also "Zulip API emails". **Greg Price** · 2025-12-12 19:51 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> - I'm currently thinking this should diverge from historical narrow operators that take a user and just accept user IDs, and not also "Zulip API emails". It's easy to support both, so it's mainly a question of whether we want to be moving away from accepting "Zulip API emails" in the search API and …

I think there's basically one use case which identifying users by email can have, apart from backward-compatibility: in an institutional environment, it's common for each user to have a canonical username which is used across a variety of systems, and that can be expressed as a canonical email address.

So I'd expect that in many corporate, university, or other institutional environments that are using Zulip, every user in the realm has an email address which is completely predictable given the user's identity as seen in the other systems people there are using.

If you're writing any kind of integration in that environment, it can be extremely convenient to be able to refer to a user when talking to Zulip by using that email address. If you have to use a Zulip user ID instead, then that's either an extra Zulip API request to look up the user ID by email address, or else a database that has to be managed elsewhere to map their canonical username to their Zulip user ID.

**Greg Price** · 2025-12-12 19:52 UTC

So broadly I think it's good for us to continue to *accept* emails to identify users, even in new areas of API.

The thing we should move away from is where the API *requires* the use of emails, and doesn't accept user IDs. There are a few pockets of that remaining in the API, but not many.

## Link to sent messages

*2025-12-16 to 2026-01-16 · 30 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/Link.20to.20sent.20messages/with/2327855)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-12-16 01:32 UTC

So we have this old issue open in #15327 for a useful feature: Having the API endpoint to send a message return a URL that clients can use to point specifically to that message. There's a few questions we need to answer before we can implement it, which is likely not much work:
- What URL style(s) to offer? I think the variant that is most obviously useful is a /channel/topic/near/ link (or the equivalent in a DM conversation). 
- What to call the field in the API response? 

Currently, [the API response](https://zulip.com/api/send-message#response) has an object with two non-metadata fields: `id` and `automatic_new_visibility_policy`, so I imagine we'd just add a `link` or `message_link` field to the response containing the URL. Here's the current example:

```
{
    "automatic_new_visibility_policy": 2,
    "id": 42,
    "msg": "",
    "result": "success"
}
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-02 17:57 UTC

I reviewed this. One problem that we ran into is the `markdown_link` field doesn't have a standard text label to use for DMs; we're currently just having that equal `message_url` for this version.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-02 18:04 UTC

The subtle detail that needs some attention that if you somehow had a bot that had permission to post messages into a channel that it doesn't have permission to read the name of, then the bot will receive in the `markdown_link` response a URL that may encode the name of the channel.

This could slightly change the security model of incoming webhook integrations that only have permission to send messages (E.g., to all public channels in the organization). Options include:
- Having the `markdown_link` logic start with checking if the sender has metadata access to the channel or otherwise can already read the channel name, and skip encoding the channel name in that case (i.e., doing `/{channel_id}/` instead of `/{channel_id}-{channel_name_slug}/` for that part of the URL). 
- Just always using the ID-only format, or always using it for bots.
- Deciding that we're OK with this potential information leak to incoming webhook providers.

**Greg Price** · 2026-01-05 23:20 UTC

Interesting point.

I'd rather avoid poking a hole in our security/privacy model, even a small one. And I think it wouldn't be hard to write the implementation to get this right.

**Greg Price** · 2026-01-05 23:21 UTC

So that'd mean the first of those options, except I believe "in that case" is meant to be the opposite, like "otherwise" — right? I.e., if the sender lacks access to read the channel name, then use the ID-only format; if they have access, then use the format with the name included.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-05 23:37 UTC

Yeah, that's correct.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-05 23:38 UTC

So I think the main thing that will be tricky here is seeing if we can do the logic in a place where we know whether the sending user has access to that channel's name. I don't want to add one or more database queries to the message-send code path for a detail like this. So that's a codebase research question.

**Greg Price** · 2026-01-05 23:48 UTC

If we can't do it without adding a DB query to the message-send path, then I think a reasonable fallback would be to always use the ID-only format.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-05 23:48 UTC

Yeah, that sounds right to me.

```diff
diff --git a/zerver/actions/realm_settings.py b/zerver/actions/realm_settings.py

## permission to bot owner to move messages between channels

*2026-01-07 to 2026-01-08 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/permission.20to.20bot.20owner.20to.20move.20messages.20between.20channels/with/2346131)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2026-01-07 03:28 UTC

We check whether the user has permission to post to a channel based on `can_send_message_message_group` (and `can_create_topic_group` if the topic is new), when moving messages from one channel to another.

For bots, we only allowed moving if the bot had permission to post to the target channel. But when sending messages to a channel, we allow bot to post to a channel even when the bot owner has permission to post to that channel.

Are we fine with having the same behavior for moving as well? That would mean the bot will be allowed to move messages to the target channel if the bot owner has permission to post in that channel based on  `can_send_message_message_group` (and `can_create_topic_group` if the topic is new). #37258 does that but wanted to confirm once here if we are fine with that change.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-08 00:38 UTC

I'm a bit uncomfortable with this one. The security analysis for the rule that bots can post in places that their owner can takes significantly into account the fact that the risk from bots posting messages is very low. Moving messages is a lot more complex of a risk analysis. (I t's also possible we will want to remove that hardcoded bot rule in favor of some other mechanism, so building more things on top of that seems risky).

What other permissions checks would the bot need to pass in order to make use of this adjusted capability?

E.g., incoming webhook bots never have permission to move messages at all.

**Sahil Batra** · 2026-01-08 06:17 UTC

I don't think we have any other special checks for bots for moving messages. Bots can move the messages if they can access the messages, access the target stream, and are part of the relevant setting related groups, i.e. group for settings controlling message moving permissions, `can_send_message_group` for the target stream and `can_create_topic_group` for the target stream if the topic doesn't exist from before. 

And the PR changes the behavior to allow if the bot is not part of the `can_send_message_group` for the target stream but its owner is.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-08 19:20 UTC

Well, I think here's the situation more precisely:
- Incoming webhook bots can't access the API endpoints for moving messages, so this doesn't actually entail any new permissions for them.
- Generic bots are likely to often be in the groups with permission to move messages, though, for organizations that give "all members" that role. In such a case, it's probably not important whether we use the owner's permissions specifically for checking `can_send_message_group`, which is very much a secondary limitation on moving messages; the key security checks are whether you can move the messages FROM where they currently are, and those checks would still require the bot to themself have been given that permission. The very limited check on the acceptability of the destination entailed in `can_send_message_group` is about whether the user can add any messages to that target channel, and we already allow the bot to do that.

I think this is probably fine. But we should be planning to remove the feature of bots getting to use the owner's permissions for sending messages in favor of a more explicit model that will likely take some time to design.

**Greg Price** · 2026-01-08 19:28 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> But we should be planning to remove the feature of bots getting to use the owner's permissions for sending messages in favor of a more explicit model that will likely take some time to design.

:100:

## Deleting users

*2026-01-09 to 2026-10-09 · 29 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/Deleting.20users/with/2348076)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-09 00:59 UTC

Historically, we've not offered any mechanism via the API to delete users; just deactivate them. But there was a management command, which deletes all of a user's metadata, but also had some minor database corruption problems. We offered it as a management command originally just to avoid people manually deleting users via SQL in ways that had major database corruption problems.

Recently, we've completed a set of work to make the `do_delete_user` function hopefully not have any database corruption problems. There's a question, then, under what circumstances should it be offered in the API?

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-09 01:00 UTC

In general I think it's valuable to be really cautious about this sort of thing, because destructive irreversible actions have negative impact of compromised accounts. This particular API endpoint is a bit of a middle ground on that front. Part of not corrupting the database is that it renames the user to "Deleted User" and scrubs metadata, not deleting the user object entirely.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-09 01:02 UTC

Currently, we have a few existing API capabilities that are offered only via manual request via the `change_user_role` management command: `can_create_users`, `can_forge_sender`, and `can_change_user_emails`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-09 01:02 UTC

So I think the simplest story here would be to just add a new capability to that set, `delete_users`, and then add an API endpoint that allows deleting users that requires that capability.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-09 01:03 UTC

(I imagine that the field would just sit on the `UserProfile` object in the server and not actually appear in say the `realm` object in the API, but the endpoint for deletion and security model would be parts of the API.)

**Greg Price** · 2026-01-09 01:29 UTC

Sure, sounds like a good plan.

Separately, I don't seem to be getting these events at all in my testing. The steps are:
* Create an event queue.

  * Expected behavior: a `push_device` event appears, with status `pending`. (Later, ideally, another with `active`.)
  * Actual behavior: no event appears, even after several minutes.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2026-01-14 12:52 UTC

(replying to Prakhar Pratyush)
> But I'd expect the client to receive an event with "failed" status b/c of `InvalidBouncerPublicKeyError`.

We figured out, this was due to `PUSH_REGISTRATION_ENCRYPTION_KEYS` not set on bouncer. So `InvalidBouncerPublicKeyError` was not  raised - resulting in no "failed" status event. Server started to retry as bouncer returned 5xx.
```
    assert settings.PUSH_REGISTRATION_ENCRYPTION_KEYS
    if bouncer_public_key not in settings.PUSH_REGISTRATION_ENCRYPTION_KEYS:
        raise InvalidBouncerPublicKeyError
```

## attachment events for deletion notifications

*2026-01-14 to 2026-02-18 · 53 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/attachment.20events.20for.20deletion.20notifications/with/2352864)*

**Naman Kumar** · 2026-01-14 10:06 UTC

Hi! I'm working on #37425 (notifying all recipients when attachments are deleted) and would like feedback on the API design before finalizing the implementation. The PR is https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/37433

## Current Implementation

When an attachment is deleted, we send an 

attachment event with `op: "remove"` to all users who had access to messages containing that attachment.
[image.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/97/bclCwpgfdOpzUhr9INdOAWnK/image.png)

**Event recipients:**
* All users who can see any message containing this attachment (channel subscribers + DM participants)
* Always includes the attachment owner
**Expected client behavior:**
* Clients should re-render the messages in `message_ids` to update/remove the attachment UI
* Update the upload space counter

## Event Type Definition

[image.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/c7/zjq1OUnQyV5h5ZEy65bzPuPP/image.png)

## Questions for Review

1. **Event format**: Is this format suitable for all clients (web, mobile, Flutter)? 
  
2. **Message IDs**: Should we include `message_ids` in the event? The alternative would be for clients to track which messages contain attachments locally, but that seems more complex.
  
3. **Alternative approaches**:
  
  * **Option A (current)**: Single 
    
    attachment event with `message_ids`
  * **Option B**: Send individual `update_message` events for each affected message instead
  * **Option C**: Include full attachment details in the removal event (though the attachment is already deleted)

## Implementation Details

Recipients are calculated using `event_recipient_ids_for_action_on_messages()` which handles:
* DM messages: all participants
* Channel messages: subscribers with access to that message

This ensures we only notify users who could see the attachment in the first place

The existing event has a kind of odd structure where there's that `attachment` field which is an object containing just one property, `id`. (A more natural structure would have been to have an `attachment_id` field directly.)

**Greg Price** · 2026-01-23 23:33 UTC

I think the original reason for the odd nested structure is that it makes things sort of resemble the other two operations on that event type, `add` and `update`. Each of those has an `attachment` field which is an object with a bunch of details about the attachment. This `attachment` field can be seen as a subset of those fields: just `id`.

**Greg Price** · 2026-01-23 23:37 UTC

Both of those operations already contain details on messages that refer to the attachment. So if the point of these `attachment` objects is to resemble the ones found on those operations, then it'd be good to make the message details on this other operation match the details found on those too.

The structure of those is a bit odd, though: `messages` is an array of objects, each of which has `id` for the message ID… and `date_sent`. What is `date_sent` used for?

The latter used to be much odder, too; we've cleaned it up a couple of times, including recently:
> * `date_sent`: integer Time when the message was sent as a UNIX timestamp. **Changes**: Before Zulip 12.0 (feature level 443), this value was milliseconds since the epoch, not seconds. Changed in Zulip 3.0 (feature level 22). This field was previously strangely called `name` and was a floating point …

**Greg Price** · 2026-02-10 04:02 UTC

For the events with op `update`, we have a few different choices for how to represent the updates. Several different conventions seem to exist already in our API.

I think probably the cleanest option is:
* The event has `device_id`.
* Each other field of a device object can appear also on the event. All are optional.
* When a field is absent, that means it didn't change; otherwise, it changes to the value it has in the event.
* In particular, this means there's a distinction between absent and null (for the nullable fields): absent means no change, while null (which is possible only for the nullable fields) means changing to null.

**Greg Price** · 2026-02-10 04:04 UTC

* Give the event a pair of fields like `property` and `value`, where `property` is the name of the field/property getting updated. This is annoying to write down types for. Moreover it breaks down once you want to update multiple fields at the same time — and we'll already here have several fields updating at once.

*2026-02-02 to 2026-02-17 · 33 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/E2EE.20-.20token.20IDs/with/2369051)*

(replying to Greg Price)
> * At registration time, the client computes `push_token_id` and sends it to the server in the clear alongside the other parameters. The server passes it on to the bouncer. The bouncer verifies that it matches the hash of the actual `token_id`, after decrypting the latter.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2026-02-02 17:49 UTC

@Greg Price,  What's the exact logic we're planning for the client to calculate token ID ?

SHA-256 , then `int` from the first 4 bytes ?

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2026-02-02 17:51 UTC

Also, I was wondering if we should use 64-bit integer to minimize the probability of collision ?

**Greg Price** · 2026-02-02 23:06 UTC

Good question. Yeah, this is exactly what my client-side draft does:
> SHA-256 , then `int` from the first 4 bytes ?

There's one more detail both sides need to agree on, which is the byte order. My implementation uses little-endian:
```dart
static int computeTokenId(String token) {
  final hash = sha256.convert(token.codeUnits).bytes;
  return hash[0] + (hash[1] << 8) + (hash[2] << 16) + (hash[3] << 24);
}
```

**Greg Price** · 2026-02-02 23:09 UTC

(replying to Prakhar Pratyush)
> Also, I was wondering if we should use 64-bit integer to minimize the probability of collision ?

Hmm yeah, thinking more, that's a good idea. They need to be unique within a realm, and the birthday problem means that at 32 bits that becomes likely around 2^16 users in a realm, which is a perfectly reasonable number.

At 64 bits, that becomes likely only around 2^32 users, which is far too many for a single realm. At a reasonable upper bound like a million users, ~2^20, the probability of collision is around $$ 2^{-25} $$, which is negligible.

**Greg Price** · 2026-02-02 23:13 UTC

At 64 bits, though, it becomes inconvenient to encode it as an int. (Because it wouldn't work as a JS number. Neither end of this protocol right now uses JS, but e.g. the web client will be seeing these and potentially in the future consuming them somehow. And in general it seems prudent to avoid putting into our API any numbers that wouldn't behave nicely in JS.)

So we should probably instead take the first 8 bytes of the SHA-256 hash, and encode those as say base64.

**Greg Price** · 2026-02-03 02:13 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)
> So we should probably instead take the first 8 bytes of the SHA-256 hash, and encode those as say base64.

**elle** · 2026-02-10 21:43 UTC

The point is that the KECCAK hash function (which SHAKE256 is based on) is a sponge function, and SHAKE256 is designed for a tunable output.

for example, using `hashlib`:

```python
import hashlib

h = hashlib.shake_256(b"test")
h.hexdigest(8) // == 'b54ff7255705a71e'
```

So, you are not just naively taking a 64-bit truncation of the underlying hash function output.

Regarding the security of SHA-256 vs SHA3-256, well NIST had a whole standardization process around it, and I'm not going to recount all the reasons a new SHA standard was necessary.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-3

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2026-02-10 22:39 UTC

SHAKE256 *is* a naïve truncation of the state, for any digest length up to 1088 bits (136 bytes); its sponge construction only re-hashes the 1600 bit state after 1088 bits are extracted. There’s nothing wrong with a naïve truncation of SHA-256, either; indeed, that’s what SHA-224 is (with different initial values for domain separation). Any attack on a truncation of a cryptographic hash function would be considered an attack on the entire function.

**Greg Price** · 2026-02-11 21:14 UTC

Cool, thanks. Let's stick to SHA-256, then, since implementations for it are more conveniently available.

**elle** · 2026-02-12 15:00 UTC

I mean, there appears to be wide support for sha3 in all of the most popular programming languages. So, I'm not sure what you mean by "more conveniently available".

Regarding the truncation, SHAKE256 was purpose-built for tunable output length, and the libraries implementing provide safe, footgun-free interfaces (to the extent that's possible with cryptography).

Whether SHA-256, SHA3-256, or SHAKE256  is used, I would recommend to use the non-truncated output to avoid collisions. Especially for SHA-256, there is a worldwide network of computers rentable to find collisions (cryptominers).

Cryptography is hard, and all kinds of seemingly harmless modifications to standard usage lead to non-obvious attacks.

**Greg Price** · 2026-02-12 23:56 UTC

Indeed, there's a worldwide network of crypto miners computing SHA-256 hashes. That should increase your estimate of its security, because it means that there are a lot of people who would love to find an attack on SHA-256, and it seems like none of them have — all those miners are still computing the hashes with brute force.

which sounded to me like you were saying you'd seen news of such an attack. I found that surprising, and I was curious to hear more.

**Greg Price** · 2026-02-13 00:03 UTC

Which is a valid concern in general, and definitely when using any kind of crypto primitive it's important to ask oneself the question of whether you're using it in a way that it's designed to support. But I think we've now done that thinking above.

**elle** · 2026-02-13 18:49 UTC

here is a recent paper of using a SAT solver on reduced round SHA-256: https://arxiv.org/html/2406.20072v1

that attack ultimately proved that SHA-256 is still secure against collision attacks. part of what makes it secure is the number of rounds involved, another is the output length. cryptominers (at least against Bitcoin-like chains) are attacking collisions on double-SHA-256, and difficulty is tuned by the number of leading zeroes required for a collision.

by reducing (truncating) the output length, you are reducing the overall search space needed to find a collision. full-length SHA-256 has 2^256 bit security, truncated 32-bit SHA-256 has **at best** 2^32 bit security.  2^64 bit security for this use-case might be alright, but the safest route is to use the full output to avoid introducing unknown attack vectors.

we're also talking about cryptanalysis, so the best attacks are not going to be public.

*2026-02-05 to 2026-02-06 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/date_joined.20field.20usage/with/2371711)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2026-02-05 17:42 UTC

Currently, `date_joined` field for a user is set to the date when the user object was created. In #**design>managing imported users** it was discussed to change the behavior to -
- For users who haven't logged in even once (i.e. not activated their account), the `date_joined` field would be set to the date when the user object would be created. This can happen for users whose `UserProfile` objects are created not through the normal registration flow like when the organization is imported or when an admin creates a user through API or management command.
-  For users who have logged in once (i.e. activated their account), the `date_joined` field would be set to the date they logged in for the first time. So, for users who go through the registration flow themselves, it will be same as the date the `UserProfile` object was created.

As of now, we might check `tos_version` field for user to decide if user is logging in for the first time or not, but this is being discussed in #**design>managing imported users** .

*2026-02-13 to 2026-02-17 · 19 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/image.20preview.20size.20setting/with/2379149)*

So in #**design>image preview sizing / settings**, we're working on adding a setting for controlling the size of images. We should discuss a few things:
- The field is called `realm_image_thumbnail_size`. Is that a good name? I think no `web` prefix is correct in that I'd expect other clients to want to try to adjust how they size images in some client-appropriate way based on these values. 
- The current values accepted by the API are the strings `small`/`medium` / `large`. (Current default is "small"). - We're thinking it should be a realm-level setting at first, since that helps viewers all see the same thing (and that matches what the sender previewed). We can consider making a user-level override later if feedback makes that feed warranted.

I think for admins, the best answer is to just have the default value for the group be naturally converted from the previous behavior. (I.e., either it's "everyone" or "admins" depending on the value of the old setting).

And then if you want it to be the nobody group, you can do that value ... and maybe in that case admins wouldn't be able to change anyone's name? Not sure what's best there -- can you confirm what the current behavior there is in `main`?

(I don't think it's a problem that admins could later change the setting, but I can imagine wanting to turn off admins changing names completely when they're synced from LDAP).

**Greg Price** · 2026-02-25 02:20 UTC

I think the "own" version is helpful — it's a reasonable feature to allow admins to change others' names, in some kinds of organizations, so it's good to be clear that this isn't about that feature.

**Greg Price** · 2026-02-25 02:22 UTC

And I like this plan:

> I think for admins, the best answer is to just have the default value for the group be naturally converted from the previous behavior. (I.e., either it's "everyone" or "admins" depending on the value of the old setting).

In particular that means that from a client perspective there's no special behavior involved in interpreting this setting — the group the setting says is exactly the group that has the permission.

**Aadithya** · 2026-02-25 08:08 UTC

Current behaviour in `main` is that 
1. If `name_changes_disabled` = `false` everyone can change their own name.
2. If `name_changes_disabled` = `true` admins can still change their own name.
3. Admins can change other users’ names regardless of this setting.

Essentially admins can change their own name and other users' name regardless of the setting.


With the new group-based permissions if admins are excluded from `can_change_own_name_group` then we would get this sort of counter-intuitive behavior where admins cannot change their own name but can change other admins names.
I'm not exactly sure what behavior makes more sense here.

**Greg Price** · 2026-02-25 19:59 UTC

I see, thanks.

I think the cleanest semantics is probably:
* There's a group which is allowed to change any user's name. This group is hardcoded to `role:administrators` and we aren't currently planning to change that (though in principle we could certainly make it a setting, if there's a user request for that in the future).
* There's a group which is allowed to change their own name (`can_change_own_name_group`).
* Name changes are permitted just when they're permitted by either of those two permissions.

That would mean that admins are always able to change their own names, as well as others' names, regardless of whether they're in the new setting's group. And if we have a reason to change that situation in the future, we can cleanly do so by turning the "change any user's name" permission into a group.

**Greg Price** · 2026-02-25 20:02 UTC

And then the settings UI should make clear that admins can change anyone's name regardless (at a minimum, have an "(i)" link to the relevant page of the help center); and it should probably avoid offering "nobody" as an option for that setting, just to reduce confusion. The server might as well allow the group to be anything the users choose, though.

**Aadithya** · 2026-02-25 20:49 UTC

What do you think about instead adding a boolean setting like `can_admins_change_any_user_name` to control whether administrators can change any user’s name?

- If `true`, admins can change both their own name and other users’ names regardless of `can_change_own_name_group`.
- If `false`, admins’ ability to change their own name would depend on `can_change_own_name_group`, and changing other users’ names would be disabled.

I can’t really think of a scenario for allowing non-admins (maybe moderators?) to change any users names. Maybe offering it as a boolean setting would give organizations clearer control instead.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-02-26 22:06 UTC

I don't think we want to add new boolean permissions settings. A group setting with restricted possible values of nobody/owners/admins would be a valid option, but I'd rather not incur the cost of adding a setting with this weak of a motive.

So I suggest we stick with the design @Greg Price proposed.

in `main ` this follows `name_changes_disabled` where the field is locked when changes are disabled and editable otherwise.

with the migration to `can_change_own_name_group` should this instead depend on whether the newly created user would have permission to change their own name immediately after account creation, based on their initial role and any preregistration or invite groups they are added to?

**Vijay Hiremath** · 2026-03-10 11:26 UTC

I went through the `communities_view` code and wanted to share some findings that might be helpful for the API design discussion.

The view currently builds each entry with these fields: 
`id`
`name`
`realm_url`
`logo_url` (via `get_realm_icon_url`)
`description`
`org_type_key`.

A couple of things worth noting:

1. `get_realm_icon_url` only deals with the realm icon. It has nothing to do with `realm_logo_url` or `realm_night_logo_url`, so those fields don't need to be part of the response. The field name in the API should probably be `icon_url` rather than `logo_url` to avoid confusion.

2. `org_type_key` is what powers the category filters (`opensource`, `research`, `community`) on the directory page, so it should be included in the response.

3. `date_created` isn't part of the current view at all, so I'm not sure there's a reason to add it.

For the endpoint itself, I think a single `GET /api/v1/communities` is sufficient for the discovery use case. A per-ID endpoint doesn't seem necessary right now.

My Proposed response fields: 
`id`
`name`
`realm_url`
`icon_url`
`description`
`org_type`

## E2EE - clear legacy token registration

*2026-03-10 to 2026-04-05 · 37 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/E2EE.20-.20clear.20legacy.20token.20registration/with/2403887)*

**Chris Bobbe** · 2026-03-10 04:29 UTC

When registering a push device ([`POST /mobile_push/register`](https://zulip.com/api/register-push-device)), the server could use `token_id` and `token_kind` to remove the token's legacy non-E2EE registration, if any. The current plan ([discussion](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/243-mobile-team/topic/E2EE.20notifications.3A.20troubleshooting.20page/near/2403851)) has been for the client to make a separate request for that, but that request might fail, and I think that would cause duplicate notifications.

`token_id` isn't the token itself, but it's enough to identify whether it matches a given token ([doc](https://zulip.com/api/register-push-device#parameter-token_id)):
> Identifier for the FCM/APNs provided token to the device, produced by taking the first 8 bytes of the SHA-256 hash of the token, then encoding those bytes using standard Base64 encoding as defined in RFC 4648.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-03-10 04:46 UTC

Hmm, would this be a step for the server to do, for the bouncer to do, or both?

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-10 05:18 UTC

**Chris Bobbe** · 2026-03-10 05:25 UTC

(The server and the bouncer both have a record of the token, right; I think the server would remove its record and also tell the bouncer to remove its. Whatever `/api/remove-fcm-token` does :slight_smile:)

Right

Actually, the existing design is to delete such tokens on bouncer as well as server - if FCM/APNs returns an error that the token expired while attempting to send notification.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2026-03-12 14:56 UTC

So, I think we've two options:

2. The discussed approach in this thread. When the async `register_push_device_to_bouncer` step succeeds, perform the legacy token deletion step. This can fail too, but more robust than client trying out.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2026-03-12 15:11 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-12 18:19 UTC

(replying to Prakhar Pratyush)
> Even if some of them fails, it'll get cleared out after the `token` rotation step (~1 month)

I believe token rotation by FCM or APNs is rare. I'm not sure it really ever happens in practice; it's just something the FCM docs warn might sometimes happen. (I don't recall whether it's even a theoretical possibility for APNs.)

You might be thinking of the recommended practice described in #F322, based on FCM docs, which says the client should repeat the token to the server about once a month. Then the server, if it doesn't hear again from a client in maybe two months, should conclude the client has gone away and stop sending to it.

With the new protocol, the client is doing its part of that practice. We don't currently have concrete plans to have the server do the other side of it.

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-12 18:23 UTC

(replying to Prakhar Pratyush)
> Actually, the existing design is to delete such tokens on bouncer as well as server - if FCM/APNs returns an error that the token expired while attempting to send notification. So even without making any changes, when `token` rotation happens, these legacy tokens will get cleared out.

It's true that that should cause us to stop sending notifications to a device where the app has been uninstalled.

There's another case, though, where the app hasn't been uninstalled from the device but the user just no longer uses it there. Either they've stopped using that device, or they've stopped using Zulip; or maybe they've just stopped using the Zulip mobile app.

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-12 18:23 UTC

In that case, it's possible that at a certain point Apple or Google's systems will decide to invalidate the token  and so this existing mechanism will cause us to stop sending to it. In particular if the device is completely offline, I expect that eventually they'll do that, perhaps after a few months.

I'm not sure they necessarily ever do that if the user just isn't using the app, though.

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-12 18:26 UTC

In any case, all of that is kind of a side discussion to the concrete thing this thread is about:

When the client successfully registers a token for E2EE notifications, we should clear out any existing legacy registration on that account *for the same token*.

That's a token that is by definition current and belongs to an actively used install of the app — we just got a registration for it. The thing we want to do here is just to avoid sending duplicate plaintext copies of the notifications we're going to be sending encrypted.

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-14 01:47 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-14 01:51 UTC

So if the server finds it's unable to talk to the bouncer, it still needs to record locally the fact that it shouldn't send notifications for the given token.

The simplest way to do that is to just delete its local record of the token. I think that's probably OK even if it's failed to reach the bouncer to tell it to delete the token.

If that's not OK, then we can solve the problem by adding a boolean column on the local token table, named like `is_active`, and setting that to false at the top of this function. That way even if we don't reach the bottom of the function (and so delete the token entirely), we'll have that information recorded.

And then when sending legacy notifications, filter to `is_active=True`.

*2026-03-10 to 2026-04-24 · 20 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/Display.20.2Emov.20files.20if.20browser.20supports.20them/with/2404852)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-03-10 19:49 UTC

#37751 suggests just trying to render `.mov` files in messages, and using JS to hide the `video` element if the browser doesn't actually support them.  We generally don't conditionally hide UI elements based on client properties, so this is probably only reasonable if we verify (via browser testing, especially on non-iOS devices) that the support is sufficiently broad.

But this would also be a change to `INLINE_MIME_TYPES`, which is an API change.

Do we know how supported `video/quicktime` videos are on Android and iOS Flutter?

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-03-10 20:16 UTC

We believe Chromium-based browsers would support this, and possibly Firefox (despite documentation to the contract), so mobile would be the most relevant platform that might not work.

Of course if the mobile client can do detection of whether it can support it, and just show a link (sans broken preview), that would probably be fine.

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-10 21:13 UTC

On mobile we play videos using [`package:video_player`](https://pub.dev/documentation/video_player/latest/). On iOS that uses Apple's `AVPlayer`, which unsurprisingly supports QuickTime:
https://developer.apple.com/documentation/avfoundation/avplayer

On Android it uses an Android feature called ExoPlayer, which doesn't appear to mention QuickTime in its list of supported formats:
https://developer.android.com/media/media3/exoplayer/supported-formats

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-10 21:15 UTC

Here's an ancient (2015) comment by a maintainer in the ExoPlayer issue tracker:
https://github.com/google/ExoPlayer/issues/958#issuecomment-157007319
> Note that we don't officially claim to support QuickTime files, so whilst we'll fix things to correctly play this sample, we're supporting QuickTime on a "best effort" case only. For best compatibility, you should use MP4 instead.

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-10 21:16 UTC

So… it might probably work on Android too? Hard to predict how complete that "best effort" support is in practice.

**Greg Price** · 2026-03-10 21:24 UTC

Here's the one other issue I've found in that tracker about QuickTime format:
https://github.com/google/ExoPlayer/issues/8073

In that one, ExoPlayer rejects the file and they decline to change that behavior, after observing:
> This is because the input file does not have any ftyp box. This box is mandatory in the MP4 format but not in the QuickTime format (but it is strongly recommended).

So hopefully an unusual case, but shows there are definitely limits to how far they'll support QuickTime format.

## realm_emoji update is quadratic

*2026-04-01 to 2026-04-15 · 34 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/realm_emoji.20update.20is.20quadratic/with/2424291)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-04-01 13:24 UTC

The https://zulip.com/api/get-events#realm_emoji-update event is used for both additions and removals of realm emoji -- so sends the whole set of emoji at once.  Which is fine for reasonable numbers of emoji, but takes quadratic space for realms that are rapidly uploading hundreds (...or thousands, for some reason) of emoji.

We need to switch to "add" and "remove" ops.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-04-01 14:27 UTC

Pushed #38787 for the draft at that.

**Greg Price** · 2026-04-01 19:36 UTC

Seems good to fix!

Mobile consumes these events. So to make this change compatibly, we'll need to control it with I guess a `client_capabilities` flag.

**Greg Price** · 2026-04-01 19:36 UTC

(i.e. https://zulip.com/api/register-queue#parameter-client_capabilities )

**Greg Price** · 2026-04-01 19:39 UTC

Do we ever actually remove realm emoji from the list? It kind of looks like we instead just set the `deactivated` field to true.

(Which is helpful for rendering past messages and reactions that used the old emoji.)

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-04-01 20:23 UTC

We don't ever remove, no, only mark as deactivated

**Greg Price** · 2026-04-01 20:25 UTC

The op name `remove` feels like the wrong match for these events; it's really more of an update, as the client is expected to keep the record around and just modify it. When we use the op name `remove` elsewhere, it generally means the client should delete the record because the thing is gone.

**Greg Price** · 2026-04-01 20:26 UTC

I kind of feel like the two ops here should be just one, with a meaning like INSERT ON CONFLICT UPDATE.

**Greg Price** · 2026-04-01 20:27 UTC

My first choice for that name might actually be `update`. Awkward that that's taken by the existing "here's the new whole list" event, though.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-04-01 20:28 UTC

A client capability would mostly address that, though?

I think it may be possible to edit their properties in the future. So maybe just `add` and `update_dict` operations make sense (the latter for editing?).

**Greg Price** · 2026-04-01 20:31 UTC

We're already editing one property, namely `deactivated`. So the idea of having just one op for this event type is that the number of properties on these objects is so small, there's little benefit in trying to send just the one or handful that changed rather than the whole updated object.

**Greg Price** · 2026-04-01 20:37 UTC

We could certainly also do an `update_dict` style of event.

We've had a few different formats we've used for those in different parts of the data model. The example I'd reach for is [`device/update`](https://zulip.com/api/get-events#device-update), since that's one we designed recently and I'm happy with.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-04-03 18:15 UTC

I can swap to a client capability.  I'll note that the motivation for this is that clients requiring the full set of emoji on every addition [led to a Zulip Cloud outage](https://status.zulip.com/incidents/h41gq5xz18cc), so leaving that as an option means that complicit clients can make it easier to DoS the server.

I feel it's also worth asking how long we intend to support historical client capabilities, before swapping their defaults, or removing them.  The earliest capability is from 2.1.0, which is more than 6 years ago -- and I don't think any modern clients support talking to a Zulip 2.1.0 server anymore.

**Greg Price** · 2026-04-03 20:24 UTC

Yeah, to date we haven't felt much urgency to remove any individual client capability, and as a result I believe we've never yet bothered to remove any.

(I think [the doc](https://zulip.com/api/register-queue#parameter-client_capabilities) confirms that: if we had, then there should be a **Changes:** note naming the capability that used to exist and saying when it went away.)

**Greg Price** · 2026-04-03 20:24 UTC

Our policy, though, is that we're happy to break any client versions that are over 12 months old:
https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/overview/release-lifecycle.html#server-and-client-app-compatibility
So for this change, we could set a reminder for ourselves somewhere to come back in a year and remove it.

As soon as we've settled in this thread on a specific plan, I'll file a mobile issue to implement it. Should be simple to do, so if we prioritize it we can easily have it out in the next release (which I expect to be in a couple of weeks).

**Greg Price** · 2026-04-03 20:26 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)
> Yeah, to date we haven't felt much urgency to remove any individual client capability, and as a result I believe we've never yet bothered to remove any.

Oh, I guess the doc does indicate we've effectively removed one of them:
> `user_settings_object`: Has no effect with modern servers. Previously, this was a boolean for whether the client supported the modern [`user_settings` event type](https://zulip.com/api/get-events#user_settings-update) […]

(And because it still has its own sub-entry, the **Changes:** note lives there rather than at the top of `client_capabilities`.)

Looks like that's the only one, though.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-04-03 20:34 UTC

Hm, OK.  I'll circle back when I have a firm `update` model to propose, but I expect it'll be modeled on the `device/update` one where we supply `emoji_id` and non-null values for keys that need to be updated.  Which works because no fields on the object are themselves nullable (well, `filename` is in the database, but that's for internal reasons and clients never see a null there).

**Greg Price** · 2026-04-03 20:37 UTC

Sounds good. Note that the `device/update` scheme works even when some of the fields are nullable — in fact that's true for device objects. The key is that when we're not updating a given field, we don't include it in the event at all.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-04-03 20:38 UTC

Ah, sure -- the difference between the key being not present, and present and null.

**Greg Price** · 2026-04-03 20:42 UTC

Yeah, exactly. That distinction between "absent" and "present with value null" is very easy for a client in JS to model, because it means `event.foo` is undefined vs. null.

It's a little less off-the-shelf for clients in other languages where there's a more sensible single "nullish" concept, because a JSON deserializer is likely to default to mapping both "absent" and "null" to that same concept. But it should still be quite doable, because plenty of other JSON-based APIs will sometimes need the distinction. In the Flutter client we have a little [`JsonNullable`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-flutter/blob/0054c7a710ce0b4292ea68f5a228792372f1022c/lib/api/model/json.dart) class that we use for the few places in the Zulip API where we need that distinction.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-04-11 05:49 UTC

Updated #38787.

We can't use the "update" name for the op, because that's the existing name of the all-emoji event, and OpenAPI doesn't have a way to express that the schema type varies by if the client has a capability.

So it's the "edit" op.  Same semantics of `device/update`, but at current only might send `deactivated` as a property to update.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-04-11 14:48 UTC

Does it match the semantics of `update_dict` operations?

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-04-12 03:56 UTC

(I'm just thinking about if we can avoid having a new `edit` op that is only used for this one thing)

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-04-12 04:16 UTC

PR otherwise basically looks good; I merged some of the prep commits via a separate PR just now.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-04-13 20:18 UTC

It's not quite the semantics of `realm/update_dict` -- that has a `data` key with the updated properties on it as a dict.  I was modeling off of `device/update` which @Greg Price linked to, where the updated properties are on the top-level dict (so co-mingled with `op` and other generic-event properties).  I'll switch the verb to `update_dict` and push the changed properties into a `data` key.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-04-13 20:19 UTC

@Greg Price thoughts on whether that's the right way to go?

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-04-13 20:20 UTC

It would be good to just get this settled so we can integrate the improvement.

**Greg Price** · 2026-04-13 21:19 UTC

I don't mind if the changed properties get pushed into a `data` object. That's certainly cleaner in some ways, though it's a bit more fuss to deserialize it.

I don't like the `update_dict` name, though, and would like to avoid repeating it. The name gives the suggestion that the corresponding `realm/update` shape of event is the normal way for an "update" to work, and that this is a special "dict" style of update, whereas I would much rather have the norm be that this sort of update is the one to use and the `realm/update` shape is the old clunkier way that shouldn't be imitated.

To distinguish from the existing `update`, perhaps `update_one`?

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-04-13 21:40 UTC

Fine with me.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-04-15 18:57 UTC

I don't love how this proliferates more names, but I don't see any way around it.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-04-15 18:58 UTC

I'll push a version with `update_one` as the name, and the properties moved into `dict`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-04-15 22:19 UTC

I made some tweaks to the audit logs story in #38787, and have it marked to merge once CI passes.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-04-15 22:20 UTC

**Agnish Bauri** · 2026-04-14 18:38 UTC

In the review that followed, Lauryn sparked two questions that I believe would need to be discussed before I make any further changes to the PR:

1. The current restriction uses is_bot, which allows all four bot types: `DEFAULT_BOT`, `SERVICE_BOT`, `EMBEDDED_BOT`, and `OUTGOING_WEBHOOK_BOT`. The help center docs describe bot storage as a feature for interactive bots specifically (i.e. `DEFAULT_BOT`). Should we restrict to that type only, or is "any bot account" the right scope?
2. We followed the pattern of `require_realm_admin` and `OrganizationAdministratorRequiredError`, which use error code `UNAUTHORIZED_PRINCIPAL` with HTTP 400 and message "Must be an organization administrator". By analogy we would use `UNAUTHORIZED_PRINCIPAL` + HTTP 400 + "Must be a bot user". The alternative is HTTP 403 (Forbidden), which might be more semantically correct for an authorization check. Which would be preferred here?

## Sending date_created for realm emoji.

*2026-04-18 to 2026-04-20 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/Sending.20date_created.20for.20realm.20emoji.2E/with/2437909)*

**Apoorva Pendse** · 2026-04-18 05:47 UTC

For the recent custom emoji bonus specified in #37134, I've opened #38755.

The point mentioned in the issue:

> Give newly uploaded custom emoji a bonus just for the first week after they're created: * 6 points for emoji you uploaded [number updated] * 2 points for emoji uploaded by others. [number updated]


I use `default=datetime.datetime(2001, 1, 1, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc)` to backfill the dates for existing realm emojis, for the new `date_created` column we'd need to add.

```spoiler migration
```python3
import datetime

import django.utils.timezone
from django.db import migrations, models


class Migration(migrations.Migration):
    dependencies = [
        ("zerver", "0792_fix_animated_emoji_still_images"),
    ]

    operations = [
        # For backfilling existing custom emojis.
        migrations.AddField(
            model_name="realmemoji",
            name="date_created",
            field=models.DateTimeField(
                default=datetime.datetime(2001, 1, 1, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc)
            ),
        ),
        migrations.AlterField(
            model_name="realmemoji",
            name="date_created",
            field=models.DateTimeField(default=django.utils.timezone.now),
        ),
    ]
```
```

@Tim Abbott said on [GH](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/38755#discussion_r3088543923):
> Have we had an API design discussion on this detail? This 2001 date certainly deserves a comment if we're running with that; but I'm not sure if it'd be better to go with null for the default.

Do folks have thoughts on what the default value for existing realm emojis should be?

For realm imports, I set `date_created` to the time of import. Some data sources like rocketchat may have enough data to infer the actual creation date, but I think it’s best to defer that extraction as a follow-up.

I’m using `2001-01-01` so that we don’t grant bonuses to already existing realm emojis, but we can also do something similar to UserGroup:


````spoiler date_created documentation for user group
```
        date_created:
          type: integer
          nullable: true
          description: |
            The UNIX timestamp for when the user group was created, in UTC seconds.

            A `null` value means the user group has no recorded date, which is often
            because the user group is very old, or because it was created via a data
            import tool or [management command][management-commands].

            **Changes**: New in Zulip 10.0 (feature level 292).
            [management-commands]: https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/production/management-commands.html
```
````

## API retry-after value in the past #39213

*2026-05-12 to 2026-08-18 · 33 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/API.20retry-after.20value.20in.20the.20past.20.2339213/with/2456589)*

**Emily Sutherlin** · 2026-05-12 17:51 UTC

Filed in GitHub as #39213:

When sending messages via the API (in bursts), I got a response with a retry-after that by the time I received the response were already in the past, due to zulip server's own latency and network latency. For example:

{"result":"error","msg":"API usage exceeded rate limit; see https://zulip.com/api/http-headers#rate-limiting-response-headers","code":"RATE_LIMIT_HIT","retry-after":0.008374929428100586}

I think in general it would make sense to round the value to a ms level and if the value is below at least 50ms (practically 100ms would make even more sense) accept it without rate limiting, since rate limiting it just creates additional server load (since the request can be retried immediately, since the time to starting processing is always >50ms, practically from tests it seems to be >200ms for zulip given an already established connection)

**Lauryn Menard** · 2026-05-20 13:53 UTC

I wonder if this is a discussion that should be moved to API design. I also don't know what the best practices are around network latency when sending out rate limiting errors.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2026-05-20 13:53 UTC

Would be great for other folks to chime in here.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-05-20 14:10 UTC

I do not think you should change the rate-limiting protocol to allow requests which would have been allowed 100ms in the future, but are out of quota now.  I have not done the modeling, but I expect that would produce unfair and undesirable effects.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-05-20 14:11 UTC

I think the argument that "it would generate *less* load to just answer it now instead of 429'ing and the client coming back in 50ms" is bogus, because we generate 429's rather fast.  And there is *utility* to spreading the load to >50ms later -- that's the whole point of the rate-limit.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-05-20 14:12 UTC

IMHO the only change that we should do here is to tell the client the timestamp that the server generated the rate-limit response.  The server is not responsible for the client showing up 0.8ms too early.

I think this can also be moved to either #**backend** or #**api design**

## PATCH /bots: editing `bot_type` and service config (#31389)

*2026-05-21 to 2026-05-26 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/PATCH.20.2Fbots.3A.20editing.20.60bot_type.60.20and.20service.20config.20.28.2331389.29/with/2465317)*

**thedance** · 2026-05-21 16:48 UTC

PR #37576 extends `PATCH /bots/{bot_id}` so an admin can change an existing bot's type and/or its service configuration. Before posting this PR to integration review @Sahil Batra  suggested getting #api-design feedback on the endpoint shape and a couple of behaviors that were flagged during maintainer review.
 
 1. `bot_type` changes wipe service state. When `bot_type` changes, the old `Service` row and the old `BotConfigData` rows are deleted and recreated from the new request. Rationale: the schemas are incompatible across types (a webhook URL is meaningless for an embedded bot, etc.), and silently carrying over stale data risks unexpected behavior. The request must supply whatever fields the new type requires; missing required fields are rejected.
 
 2. `service_name` is now an input on `PATCH /bots/{bot_user_id}`, which also makes it editable on existing bots without a `bot_type` change. For `EMBEDDED_BOT` this updates `Service.name` (validated against the embedded bot list); for `INCOMING_WEBHOOK_BOT` it updates the `integration_id` key in `BotConfigData`; for `OUTGOING_WEBHOOK_BOT` it updates the label name on the `Service` row. `DEFAULT_BOT` rejects `service_name`/`config_data`/`payload_url` updates.
 
 3. `service_name` + `config_data` interaction (no `bot_type` change):
    - If both `service_name` and `config_data` are sent: existing `BotConfigData` keys are dropped as the old keys belong to the old service's config schema, and the new `config_data` is written.
    - If only `service_name` is sent: the existing `config_data` is validated against the new `service_name` first; if validation passes, the existing config is preserved and only `service_name` changes.
    - If only `config_data` is sent: partial update via `set_bot_config` (existing keys preserved, supplied keys overwritten or added).
 
Does this design sound reasonable? Any feedback on the endpoint shape or the interactions described above would be very welcome.  One specific question Sahil flagged ([review comment](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/37576#issuecomment-4323867131)): should clients instead be required to send the full `config_data` object when updating it, rather than the current partial-update behavior?
Thank you!
